context: God continues creating on the fourth and fifth days, making sea creatures, birds, and land animals. Then God decides to create humans in His image to rule over all living things on earth.
God creates humans in His image, giving them authority over all living creatures and the earth. He blesses them to multiply and provides plants for food, concluding the sixth day of creation.

After leaving Elim, the Israelites reach the wilderness of Sin and complain to Moses and Aaron about hunger, longing for Egypt. God promises to provide daily bread from heaven to test their obedience, with a double portion on the sixth day.

God sees Adam alone and decides to create a suitable companion. After naming animals without finding a match, God forms a woman from Adam's rib and presents her to him, establishing the first human partnership in Eden.

After Adam and Eve disobey God by eating the forbidden fruit, God makes them clothes and expels them from the Garden of Eden to prevent them from accessing the tree of life, placing cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the entrance.

After completing creation, God rested on the seventh day and blessed it. Before plants grew, God formed man from dust and placed him in the garden of Eden, where He caused trees, including the tree of life and knowledge, to grow.

After Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit, they hide from God in the Garden of Eden. God questions them, and they admit their disobedience, blaming each other and the serpent. God then curses the serpent and foretells ongoing conflict between it and humanity.

The serpent, more cunning than other animals, questions Eve about God's command. Eve explains the restriction, but the serpent deceives her. Eve and Adam eat the forbidden fruit, realize their nakedness, and hide from God in the Garden of Eden.

This passage describes God creating the universe, starting with the formless earth and darkness, then creating light, separating day and night, forming the sky (heaven), and gathering waters to reveal dry land called Earth and Seas.

God plants a garden in Eden with various trees, including the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil, watered by a river splitting into four. He places Adam there to care for it and commands him not to eat from the knowledge tree, then decides Adam needs a companion.

God pronounces consequences after Adam and Eve eat the forbidden fruit: conflict between the serpent and humanity, increased pain in childbirth for Eve, hardship in labor for Adam, and God clothes them, marking a shift from innocence to experience.

God names the dry land Earth and the gathered waters Seas, then creates plants on Earth. Next, God makes the sun, moon, and stars to separate day from night and mark time, completing the third and fourth days of creation.
The psalmist invites all nations and peoples to praise God, highlighting His enduring mercy and truth, continuing the theme of thanksgiving and universal worship introduced in the previous psalm.

Adam and Eve have two sons, Cain and Abel, who offer sacrifices to God. God favors Abel's offering, causing Cain to become angry and ultimately kill Abel. God confronts Cain about his brother's murder.

Noah, a righteous man in a corrupt and violent world, is introduced along with his sons. God decides to destroy all life with a flood but commands Noah to build a large ark to survive the coming disaster.

God tells Noah he will send a flood to destroy all life on earth but promises to save Noah, his family, and pairs of every animal species by having them enter the ark Noah is instructed to build. Noah obeys God's commands.

God instructs Noah to bring his family and specific numbers of animals into the ark to survive the coming flood. Noah obeys, entering the ark with his family and animals just before the floodwaters begin after seven days.
As humanity multiplies, "sons of God" marry human women, producing mighty men; God sees widespread wickedness and decides to destroy all life, but Noah, a righteous man, finds favor with God.

This passage lists the early descendants of Adam, starting with Seth, born after Abel's death. It records their ages, offspring, and deaths, showing the long lifespans and the continuation of humanity through Seth's line.
This passage continues the genealogy from Enos to Methuselah, listing their ages, offspring, and deaths. It highlights Enoch's unique relationship with God, as he was taken by God instead of dying.

After seven days, the floodwaters began as God opened the deep and the sky, causing rain for 40 days. Noah, his family, and pairs of all animals entered the ark, which floated as the waters rose and covered the earth.

This passage traces the descendants of Cain, highlighting Lamech's family and his claim of vengeance, then shifts to Adam and Eve having Seth, seen as a replacement for Abel, marking the start of people calling on God's name.

This passage lists the long lifespans and descendants of Methuselah and Lamech, highlighting Lamech naming his son Noah, who will later father Shem, Ham, and Japheth, continuing Adam’s lineage after the curse on the ground.

The floodwaters rose and covered all the earth, including the highest mountains, killing every living creature on land. Only Noah, his family, and the animals in the ark survived as the waters prevailed for 150 days.

God confronts Cain after he kills Abel, pronouncing a curse that makes Cain a restless wanderer. God protects Cain with a mark, and Cain settles in Nod, east of Eden, where he starts a family and builds a city named after his son Enoch.

After the floodwaters dried, God told Noah and his family to leave the ark with all the animals to repopulate the earth. Noah then built an altar and offered sacrifices, leading God to promise never to curse the ground or destroy all life again.

After the flood destroyed all life except Noah's family and animals on the ark, God caused the waters to recede. The ark came to rest on Mount Ararat, and Noah sent out a raven to check if the earth was drying.

Noah sends out a raven and then a dove from the ark to check if floodwaters have receded. The dove returns with an olive leaf, signaling dry land, and later does not return, confirming the earth is dry after many months.

After the flood, God blesses Noah and his sons, commanding them to repopulate the earth and granting them dominion over animals for food, with the prohibition against eating blood and a command for justice regarding human life, emphasizing humanity's divine image.

After Noah became drunk and was uncovered in his tent, Shem and Japheth respectfully covered him without looking. Upon waking, Noah cursed Canaan, Ham's son, and blessed Shem and Japheth. Noah lived 350 years more and then died.

God blesses Noah and his sons, commanding them to multiply and establishes a covenant with them and all living creatures that a flood will never again destroy the earth, symbolized by a rainbow in the clouds as a perpetual sign of this promise.

God confirms his covenant with Noah and all living creatures, promising never to flood the earth again and setting the rainbow as its sign. After leaving the ark, Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth respond differently to his vulnerability.

After the flood, people with one language settled in Shinar and began building a city and tower to make a name for themselves. God saw this and confused their language, scattering them across the earth, stopping the city's construction.

This passage traces the genealogy from Reu to Terah, highlighting Terah's family including Abram, Nahor, and Haran. It notes Haran's death in Ur of the Chaldees and Terah's migration with his family toward Canaan, settling in Haran.

Abram and Sarai arrive in Egypt during a famine; Sarai is taken into Pharaoh's house because of her beauty. God afflicts Pharaoh's household with plagues, leading Pharaoh to confront Abram and send them away with their possessions.

God appears to Abram in Canaan, promising the land to his descendants; Abram builds altars at Bethel and near Hai. Facing famine, Abram travels south to Egypt, fearing for his life, he asks Sarai to say she is his sister to protect him.

This passage concludes the story of Babel where God confuses human language and scatters people worldwide, then begins a genealogy of Shem’s descendants, tracing his lineage through Arphaxad to Serug.

Abram, his wife Sarai, and Lot leave Egypt wealthy and travel back to Canaan, settling near Bethel. Their herdsmen quarrel due to limited resources, so Abram offers Lot the choice to separate peacefully to avoid conflict.

This passage lists the descendants of Eber, focusing on his sons Peleg and Joktan, and Joktan's many sons who settled from Mesha to Sephar. It concludes the genealogy of Shem, showing how nations spread after the flood.

This passage lists the descendants of Noah's sons—Japheth, Ham, and Shem—after the flood, detailing their families and the lands they settled. It highlights Nimrod, a mighty hunter and king who founded cities in Shinar, including Babel and Nineveh.

This passage lists the descendants of Ham and Shem, detailing their families, lands, and nations after the flood, including cities like Nineveh and regions inhabited by Canaanites, showing the spread of peoples from Noah's sons.

God commands Abram to leave Haran and promises to make him a great nation; Abram obeys, taking Sarai and Lot to Canaan, where God appears and promises the land to Abram's descendants, leading Abram to build an altar there.

This passage describes a coalition of four kings, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, waging war against five kings including those of Sodom and Gomorrah, in the region near the Salt Sea, after a rebellion against Chedorlaomer's rule.

Abram and Lot separate due to their growing wealth and land needs; Lot chooses the fertile Jordan plain near Sodom, while Abram stays in Canaan. God then promises Abram the land and countless descendants, prompting Abram to settle near Hebron and worship there.

A coalition of kings, including those of Sodom and Gomorrah, battles invading kings led by Chedorlaomer near the Dead Sea. The invaders defeat them, loot the cities, and capture Lot, Abram's nephew, prompting a report to Abram in Mamre.

An escaped survivor informs Abram in Mamre that his nephew Lot was captured. Abram gathers 318 trained servants, pursues and defeats the captors near Dan and Damascus, rescues Lot, and is blessed by Melchizedek, king and priest of Salem.

God instructs Abram to prepare specific animals for a covenant ceremony, then reveals a prophecy about Abram's descendants' future hardships and eventual return to the land, sealing the promise with a symbolic ritual at sunset.

God appears to Abram in a vision, reassuring him and promising descendants despite his childlessness. Abram questions how he will inherit the land, and God instructs him to prepare specific animals for a covenant ceremony.

God confirms His covenant with Abram through a symbolic ritual involving a smoking furnace and burning lamp, promising Abram's descendants the land stretching from Egypt's river to the Euphrates, inhabited by various named peoples.

After Abram's victory over the kings who captured Lot, Melchizedek blesses God for delivering Abram's enemies. The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, but Abram refuses to keep anything to avoid credit for his wealth, except provisions for his allies.

Sarai, Abram's wife, unable to have children, gives her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abram to bear a child. After Hagar conceives, tension arises, leading Hagar to flee into the wilderness near Shur, where an angel finds her.

God promises Abraham that Sarah will bear a son named Isaac, establishing an everlasting covenant through him, while also blessing Ishmael. Abraham reacts with disbelief and prays for Ishmael's well-being before God departs.

After God finishes speaking to Abraham, Abraham immediately obeys God's command by circumcising himself, his son Ishmael, and all the males in his household, marking the covenant God established with him.

God instructs Abraham to keep the covenant through circumcision of every male in his household, including servants and strangers, as a lasting sign. God also changes Sarai's name to Sarah and promises she will bear a son who will be a mother of nations.

God appears to Abram at age 99, renaming him Abraham and promising to make him father of many nations. God establishes an everlasting covenant with Abraham and his descendants, granting them the land of Canaan and requiring their faithfulness.

Hagar, Sarai's maid who fled from harsh treatment, is found by the angel of the LORD near a wilderness spring between Kadesh and Bered. He tells her to return, promises many descendants, and reveals she will bear Abram's son Ishmael.

God appears to Abraham at Mamre as three men visit him. Abraham warmly welcomes them, quickly preparing food and offering hospitality while they rest under a tree, showing his respect and care before they continue their journey.

Three visitors ask Abraham about Sarah, promising she will bear a son despite her old age; Sarah laughs quietly. God questions Abraham about revealing His plans, noting Abraham's future role as a great nation and blessing to all peoples.

Abraham pleads with God not to destroy Sodom if righteous people are found there, negotiating down from fifty to ten. God agrees to spare the city for the sake of the righteous, showing Abraham’s concern for justice.

God speaks to Abraham about his future descendants and justice, then decides to investigate Sodom and Gomorrah's sins. Abraham pleads with God to spare the cities if fifty righteous people are found there.

Lot pleads with the men of Sodom to protect his angelic guests, offering his daughters instead, but they threaten him. The angels rescue Lot, blind the attackers, and warn him to flee the city before its destruction.

Angels warn Lot that God will destroy Sodom due to its wickedness. Lot urges his sons-in-law to flee, but they dismiss him. At dawn, the angels urge Lot and his family to escape quickly to avoid the city's destruction.

Two angels arrive in Sodom at evening; Lot, sitting at the city gate, invites them to stay at his house. After they agree, men of Sodom surround the house, demanding Lot hand over the visitors. Lot pleads with them not to act wickedly.

God destroys Sodom and Gomorrah, sparing only Lot and his family; Lot's wife looks back and turns to salt. Lot flees to Zoar, then to a mountain cave with his daughters, who plan to preserve their family line by seducing him.

After rescuing Lot and his family from Sodom, the angels instruct them to flee without looking back; Lot pleads to escape to nearby Zoar, which is spared, while God destroys Sodom and Gomorrah with fire and brimstone.

Abimelech offers Abraham land to live on and compensates Sarah with silver, acknowledging her protection. Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech's household, who had been unable to have children due to Sarah's presence.

After fleeing Sodom, Lot's daughters, fearing no men remain to marry, get their father drunk and conceive children by him, leading to the origins of the Moabites and Ammonites. This follows the destruction of Sodom and Lot's refuge in a cave.

Abimelech informs his servants about Sarah and Abraham, confronts Abraham about his deception, and Abraham explains his fear for his life. Abimelech then compensates Abraham with livestock and servants and returns Sarah, allowing them to live freely in Gerar.

God fulfills His promise to Sarah and Abraham by giving them a son, Isaac, in their old age. Isaac is circumcised, weaned, and a feast is held, but Sarah sees Hagar’s son Ishmael mocking and asks Abraham to send them away.

Abraham struggles with sending Hagar and her son Ishmael away, but God reassures him and promises to make Ishmael a great nation. Hagar wanders in the wilderness of Beersheba, where God hears Ishmael's cries and comforts her through an angel.

Abraham moves to Gerar in the south, claiming Sarah is his sister. King Abimelech takes her, but God warns him in a dream not to harm her, revealing Abraham's deception and commanding Abimelech to return Sarah to avoid death.

Abraham and Abimelech make a covenant over a well Abraham dug, marking the place Beersheba. After the agreement, Abimelech and his captain return to Philistine land, while Abraham stays there, planting a grove and calling on God.

After making a covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba, God tests Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice his son Isaac in Moriah. Abraham prepares for the journey with Isaac and servants, and Isaac questions the missing lamb for the offering.

Abraham and Isaac reach the mountain God named in Moriah. Isaac questions the missing lamb for sacrifice, Abraham trusts God will provide. Abraham prepares to sacrifice Isaac, but an angel stops him, providing a ram caught nearby instead.

After Abraham's test of faith, God promises to bless him and multiply his descendants; Abraham returns to Beersheba. Then, the genealogy of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, is given, including Bethuel, father of Rebekah.

Abraham, now old and blessed, instructs his eldest servant to swear not to find a wife for Isaac among the Canaanites but from Abraham's own country and family, emphasizing the importance of keeping Isaac away from Canaan.

Abraham's servant swears not to bring Isaac back to Canaan and sets out with camels to Nahor in Mesopotamia. At a well, he prays for guidance to find the right wife for Isaac by a sign involving water.

Abraham negotiates with Ephron the Hittite and the sons of Heth in Hebron to buy the cave of Machpelah as a burial site for Sarah, agreeing to pay four hundred shekels of silver for the field and cave.

God encourages Hagar to care for her son Ishmael, promising he will become a great nation; Ishmael grows up in the wilderness of Paran. Meanwhile, Abimelech and his captain Phichol make a peace covenant with Abraham over a disputed well in the Philistine land.

Sarah has died at age 127 in Hebron, Canaan. Abraham mourns her and negotiates with the Hethites, asking for a burial site. The Hethites offer him choice burial places, and Abraham requests Ephron's cave of Machpelah for purchase.

Abraham pays Ephron 400 shekels of silver to buy the field and cave of Machpelah near Mamre from the Hittites. This land becomes Abraham's burial site where he buries his wife Sarah in Hebron, Canaan.

Abraham’s servant prays for a sign to identify Isaac’s future wife at a well in Nahor’s city. Rebekah, a young woman from Abraham’s family, arrives and offers water to him and his camels, fulfilling the servant’s prayer immediately.
At the well in Nahor's city, Rebekah's brother Laban meets Abraham's servant, who explains his mission to find a wife for Isaac and describes Abraham's blessings and wealth.

Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at the well in Nahor's city, gives her gifts, and asks about lodging. She invites him home, and he praises God for guiding him. Rebekah tells her family, and her brother Laban comes to meet the servant.

Abraham’s servant recounts his mission to find a wife for Isaac, emphasizing Abraham’s instructions to avoid Canaanite women and seek a bride from his own family. He prays for a sign at the well to identify the chosen woman.

Abraham's servant asks Laban and Bethuel for Rebekah's hand for Isaac; they agree, acknowledging God's will. After gifts and hospitality, they consult Rebekah, who consents to leave with the servant to marry Isaac.

Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at the well in Nahor's city, recognizing her as the chosen wife for Isaac. He gives her gifts, worships God, and asks her family for permission to take her to Abraham's son. Laban and Bethuel acknowledge God's will.

Rebekah leaves her family with Abraham’s servant to marry Isaac in the southern land. Isaac sees her arriving, and after the servant explains, Isaac takes Rebekah as his wife, finding comfort after his mother Sarah’s death.

Isaac faces a famine and moves to Gerar, where God instructs him to stay and promises blessings like those given to Abraham. Isaac fears for Rebekah's safety, so he claims she is his sister, but Abimelech discovers the truth.

Isaac marries Rebekah from Padanaram and prays for her to conceive. She bears twins, Esau and Jacob, who grow up with different traits and parental favoritism, setting the stage for future family dynamics.

Abimelech tells Isaac to leave because Isaac has become too powerful in Gerar. Isaac digs wells his father Abraham had dug, faces disputes over water rights, then settles peacefully at Beersheba where God reassures and blesses him.

Isaac lives in Gerar during a famine and lies about Rebekah being his sister to protect himself. Abimelech discovers the truth, warns his people not to harm Isaac or Rebekah, and Isaac prospers, causing envy among the Philistines who then ask him to leave.

Isaac favors his son Esau, while Rebekah favors Jacob. When Esau returns hungry from hunting, he trades his birthright to Jacob for some stew, showing disregard for his inheritance. This sets up future family conflicts.

After Isaac marries Rebekah, Abraham marries Keturah and has more children. He gives his estate to Isaac, sends other sons east, then dies at 175. Isaac and Ishmael bury him in Machpelah; afterward, God blesses Isaac near Lahairoi.

God reassures Isaac at night in Gerar, promising blessings like those given to Abraham. Isaac builds an altar and digs a well. Abimelech and his officials visit to make a peace treaty, recognizing God's favor on Isaac, and they share a meal before swearing the covenant.

Isaac makes a peace treaty with Abimelech and his officials, then his servants find water from a newly dug well, naming it Shebah, which leads to the city Beersheba. Meanwhile, Esau marries two Hittite women, upsetting his parents.

Rebekah instructs Jacob to deceive their blind father Isaac by pretending to be Esau, using goat skins and Esau's clothes, so Jacob can receive Isaac's blessing meant for Esau. Jacob hesitates but obeys his mother.

Isaac, now old and nearly blind, asks his eldest son Esau to hunt and prepare venison for a blessing before he dies. Rebekah overhears and instructs her younger son Jacob to deceive Isaac by bringing goat meat instead.

Jacob, guided by his mother Rebekah, deceives his blind father Isaac by pretending to be Esau to receive his blessing, using goat skins to mimic Esau's hairy hands. Isaac is suspicious but ultimately blesses Jacob.

Esau returns from hunting to Isaac, who realizes he has already blessed Jacob by mistake. Esau laments losing his blessing and pleads with Isaac, who explains Jacob now rules over him, leaving Esau distressed and weeping.

Esau pleads for a blessing from his father Isaac after Jacob deceitfully receives it. Isaac predicts Esau will live by the sword and serve Jacob. Esau hates Jacob and plans to kill him, prompting Rebekah to warn Jacob.

After Abraham's death, God blesses Isaac who settles near the well Lahairoi. The passage lists Ishmael's twelve sons and their territories, notes Ishmael's lifespan and death, then returns to Isaac's lineage and marriage to Rebekah from Padanaram.

Isaac blesses Jacob, thinking he is Esau, and prophesies prosperity and dominance over others. Right after, Esau returns from hunting with food, seeking his father's blessing, but Isaac questions his identity.

Rebekah warns Jacob that Esau plans to kill him for stealing his blessing, urging Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran for safety. She expresses distress to Isaac over Esau’s Hittite wives and fears for Jacob’s marriage.

Isaac blesses Jacob and instructs him not to marry a Canaanite woman, but to go to Padanaram to marry from his mother's family, promising blessings like those given to Abraham. Jacob then departs to Laban’s house.

Jacob, on his journey to Padanaram, dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven with angels ascending and descending, where God reaffirms the covenant promises to him and his descendants; upon waking, Jacob recognizes the sacredness of the place and sets up a stone pillar.

Jacob, after dreaming of a ladder to heaven, sets up a stone pillar at the place he names Bethel and makes a vow to God, promising to worship Him and give a tenth if God protects and provides for him on his journey to Haran.

Isaac sends Jacob to Padanaram to marry from his mother's family, obeying his parents' command. Esau, seeing this, marries Ishmael's daughter. Jacob travels from Beersheba to Haran, rests, and dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven.

Jacob arrives in the land of the people of the east and meets shepherds from Haran at a well. He inquires about Laban, his mother's brother, and learns that Rachel, Laban's daughter, is coming with the sheep.

Jacob meets Rachel, Laban's daughter, at a well in the land of the people of the east. He reveals his identity as Rebekah's son, and Laban welcomes him warmly, offering to pay him for his work. Rachel is introduced as Laban's beautiful younger daughter.

Jacob agrees to work seven years to marry Rachel, whom he loves, but Laban deceives him by giving Leah, his older daughter, instead. Laban insists Jacob must marry Leah first, then serve another seven years for Rachel.

Leah names her son Asher and receives mandrakes from her son Reuben. Rachel trades a night with Jacob for the mandrakes. Leah conceives two more sons, Issachar and Zebulun, and later a daughter, Dinah, continuing the family growth.

Jacob reminds Laban that his wealth has greatly increased since Jacob began working for him, and proposes a wage deal: Jacob will keep only the speckled, spotted, and brown animals as his pay, while Laban removes those from the flock.

Laban agrees to give Rachel to Jacob after he completes a week with Leah, then Jacob serves seven more years. Leah, unloved but fertile, bears four sons, naming them as signs of her hope for Jacob's love, while Rachel remains barren.

Rachel, unable to have children, asks Jacob for offspring; he becomes angry but Rachel offers her maid Bilhah to bear children for her. Bilhah bears two sons, Dan and Naphtali. Leah, now barren, gives her maid Zilpah to Jacob, who also bears two sons, Gad and Asher.

Laban separates his spotted and speckled goats and sheep from Jacob’s flock and distances himself. Jacob uses marked rods at watering troughs to influence the breeding of stronger animals, increasing his own livestock and wealth.

Leah has a daughter named Dinah, then God enables Rachel to bear a son, Joseph. After Joseph's birth, Jacob asks Laban to let him return home with his family, noting his faithful service and the blessings God has given them both.

Jacob learns Laban’s sons accuse him of stealing their inheritance, and he notices Laban’s changed attitude. God tells Jacob to return home. Jacob explains to Rachel and Leah how God protected him despite Laban’s repeated wage changes.

Jacob recounts a dream where God's angel reveals Laban's deceit, urging him to leave Padanaram and return to his family. Rachel and Leah express their estrangement from Laban and support Jacob's decision to obey God's command.

Rachel and Leah agree to follow Jacob as he decides to leave Laban's household with his family and possessions to return to Canaan. Laban pursues Jacob but is warned by God in a dream to be cautious in his dealings with him.

Laban catches up to Jacob in Gilead, confronting him for leaving secretly with his daughters and possessions. He accuses Jacob of stealing his household gods, unaware Rachel has taken them, and demands a search before resolving their dispute.

Laban accuses Jacob of stealing his household gods and searches their tents, unaware Rachel hid them. Jacob confronts Laban, defending his integrity after 20 years of service, and challenges him to prove any wrongdoing before their relatives.

Jacob prepares a large gift of animals to send ahead to his brother Esau, hoping to appease him. He instructs his servants on what to say and then crosses the Jabbok river with his family, anticipating their reunion.

Jacob travels and encounters angels, naming the place Mahanaim. He sends messengers to his brother Esau in Edom, informing him of his wealth and seeking favor. Hearing Esau approaches with 400 men, Jacob fears and divides his people and livestock for safety.

Jacob recounts his 20 years of hard work and unfair treatment by Laban, who responds by claiming ownership of his daughters, grandchildren, and livestock, then proposes making a covenant to settle their dispute peacefully.

Jacob sends his family across the Jabbok river and wrestles alone with a mysterious man until dawn. After the struggle, Jacob is renamed Israel and blesses the man, marking a pivotal moment before meeting his brother Esau.

Jacob, fearing his brother Esau's approach with 400 men, divides his people and livestock into two groups for safety, prays to God for protection, and prepares a large gift of animals to appease Esau, staying overnight before sending the gift ahead.

Jacob and Laban make a covenant on Mount Gilead, setting up a stone pillar and heap as witnesses to their agreement. They promise not to harm each other or cross the boundary, then share a meal before Laban departs back home.

Jacob sees Esau approaching with 400 men and arranges his family strategically. He humbly bows to Esau, who warmly embraces him. Esau asks about Jacob's large group, and Jacob explains they are gifts to gain favor. Esau declines the gifts.

After reconciling with Esau, Esau returns to Seir while Jacob settles in Succoth, builds a house, and then moves to Shechem in Canaan, where he buys land and sets up an altar, marking his presence in the land.

Jacob offers gifts to Esau to show goodwill after their reunion; Esau initially refuses but accepts. They discuss travel plans, with Jacob requesting to go slowly due to his family's needs, and Esau declines to send men with him, then departs for Seir.

Hamor and Shechem propose intermarriage and peaceful coexistence with Jacob's family in Shechem, offering land and trade. Jacob's sons deceitfully agree only if all Shechem's males are circumcised, a condition that pleases Hamor and Shechem.

Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, attack Shechem's city in revenge for Dinah's defilement, killing the men and capturing wealth and people. Jacob fears retaliation from local tribes, but they defend their actions as protecting their sister's honor.

God instructs Jacob to return to Bethel and build an altar; Jacob commands his household to remove foreign gods and purify themselves. They travel safely to Bethel, where Jacob builds an altar, recalling God's past appearance to him. Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, dies and is buried nearby.

This passage lists Esau's wives and children, noting his move from Canaan to Mount Seir due to wealth and land pressures, establishing the Edomites. It introduces Esau's descendants and their clans, connecting to the family history after Isaac's death.

Hamor and his son Shechem agree to the sons of Jacob's demand for circumcision to intermarry, and all the men of Shechem comply. On the third day, when they are weakened, Simeon and Levi attack and kill all the males in the city.

After Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died near Bethel, God appeared to Jacob, renamed him Israel, and blessed him with promises of descendants and land. Jacob marked the site with a stone pillar before traveling toward Ephrath, where Rachel went into difficult labor.

Dinah, Jacob's daughter, is taken and defiled by Shechem, son of Hamor, prince of the Hivites in Canaan. Shechem loves Dinah and asks to marry her. Jacob's sons are angry, and Hamor negotiates marriage and intermarriage with Jacob's family.

This passage lists the sons of Esau's three wives—Adah, Bashemath, and Aholibamah—and identifies their descendants as chiefs or dukes in Edom, showing the establishment of Esau's family leadership in the land of Edom.

This passage lists the dukes descended from Hori in Seir and details the succession of kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings, naming each king, their city, and notable events or family connections.
This passage lists Hadar as king of Edom after Baalhanan, naming his city Pau and wife Mehetabel, then details the dukes descended from Esau, showing the organization of Edom's clans and territories.

Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin near Bethlehem; Jacob marks her grave. Jacob settles near Edar; Reuben sins with Bilhah. The twelve sons of Jacob are listed. Jacob returns to Hebron, where his father Isaac dies and is buried by Jacob and Esau.
This passage lists the descendants and chiefs of Esau (Edom) and the Horite clans living in Seir, detailing family lines and leadership among the people inhabiting the land of Edom.

Jacob lives in Canaan, where his father was a stranger. Joseph, favored by Jacob and wearing a special coat, reports his brothers' misdeeds, causing their hatred. Joseph shares dreams suggesting he will rule over them, increasing their resentment.

Reuben finds Joseph missing from the pit and mourns. Joseph's brothers deceive their father Jacob with a bloodied coat, making him believe Joseph was killed by a wild animal. Meanwhile, Joseph is sold to Potiphar in Egypt.

Reuben stops his brothers from killing Joseph, suggesting they throw him in a dry pit instead. While they eat, Judah proposes selling Joseph to passing Ishmaelite traders, who take Joseph to Egypt. Reuben returns to find Joseph gone and mourns.

Joseph, sent by his father Jacob to find his brothers feeding flocks, is stopped by a man who directs him to Dothan. His brothers, seeing him approach, plot to kill him, but Reuben intervenes to save Joseph by suggesting they throw him into a pit instead.

Joseph shares two dreams with his brothers and father, suggesting he will rule over them, which increases their hatred and envy. Jacob sends Joseph from Hebron to Shechem to check on his brothers and flocks, where a man finds Joseph wandering.

Judah separates from his brothers and marries a Canaanite woman, Shuah, fathering three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. He arranges a marriage for Er with Tamar, but God kills Er and Onan for their wickedness.

After being sold by his brothers, Joseph arrives in Egypt and is bought by Potiphar, Pharaoh’s captain. Joseph prospers under God’s favor, becomes overseer of Potiphar’s household, and gains his trust, while Potiphar’s wife begins to desire Joseph.

Judah meets a veiled woman by the road near Timnath, not knowing she is his daughter-in-law Tamar. They agree on a pledge for payment, he sleeps with her, then sends a servant to retrieve his items, but she is gone and cannot be found.

Judah's sons Er and Onan die, so Judah tells Tamar to wait for his youngest son Shelah to marry her. After Judah's wife dies, Tamar disguises herself and waits by the road to Timnath, where Judah encounters her, not recognizing her as his daughter-in-law.
Potiphar’s wife tries to seduce Joseph in Egypt, but he flees, leaving his garment behind. She falsely accuses him of assault, leading Potiphar to imprison Joseph despite his innocence.

Judah agrees Tamar can keep his pledge after failing to find her. Later, accused of prostitution and pregnancy, Tamar reveals Judah’s tokens, proving his paternity. Judah admits her righteousness, and Tamar gives birth to twins, Pharez and Zarah.

After Joseph was falsely accused by Potiphar’s wife, Potiphar imprisoned him in Egypt. Despite this, God favored Joseph, granting him kindness from the prison keeper who put Joseph in charge of all prisoners and their affairs.
In Egypt, Potiphar's wife repeatedly tries to seduce Joseph, who refuses, citing loyalty to his master and God. One day, she grabs his garment as he flees, but he escapes without sinning.

After Joseph gained favor in prison, Pharaoh’s chief butler and baker were imprisoned for offending Pharaoh. While confined together, they each had troubling dreams, and Joseph offered to interpret them, asking for their stories.

Pharaoh, troubled by his dreams, calls Egypt's magicians who cannot interpret them. The chief butler recalls Joseph's accurate interpretations while imprisoned, leading Pharaoh to summon Joseph from the dungeon to explain the dreams.

Joseph, imprisoned in Egypt, speaks with Pharaoh’s chief butler and baker who have been jailed; he offers to interpret their dreams, revealing the butler’s dream predicts his release and restoration to service in three days.

Two years after Joseph interpreted dreams in prison, Pharaoh dreams twice by the Nile about seven healthy cows eaten by seven unhealthy ones, and seven good ears of corn devoured by seven thin ears; none of Egypt's magicians can interpret these dreams.

Pharaoh summons Joseph from prison to interpret his troubling dream about seven healthy cows eaten by seven unhealthy ones, a dream no Egyptian magicians could explain, marking a turning point in Joseph's rise to power in Egypt.

Joseph explains to Pharaoh that God revealed seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine in Egypt, urging Pharaoh to appoint a wise man to store food during the good years to prepare for the coming famine.

Pharaoh describes his dream of seven healthy cows and ears of corn followed by seven thin ones that consume the good ones. Joseph explains the dream predicts seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine in Egypt.

Joseph, imprisoned in Egypt, interprets dreams for Pharaoh’s chief butler and baker, predicting the butler’s restoration and the baker’s execution. Despite this, the butler forgets Joseph after his release.

Pharaoh approves Joseph's plan to store food for the coming famine and appoints him as second-in-command over Egypt, giving him authority and honors, recognizing Joseph's wisdom and God's guidance in interpreting the dreams.

Pharaoh appoints Joseph as ruler over Egypt, gives him a new name, and marries him to Asenath. Joseph, now 30, oversees the land during seven years of plenty, storing vast food supplies, and has two sons before the famine begins.

Joseph names his two sons in Egypt, reflecting God's blessings during hardship. The seven years of plenty end, and the predicted famine begins, but Egypt has food stored. People from Egypt and other lands come to Joseph to buy grain during the famine.

Jacob sends his sons, except Benjamin, to Egypt to buy grain during the famine. Joseph, now Egypt's governor, recognizes his brothers but hides his identity and accuses them of spying, recalling his earlier dreams about them.

Joseph tests his brothers by demanding they bring Benjamin to Egypt to prove their honesty, while secretly understanding their guilt over Joseph's past. He imprisons Simeon but returns their money and fills their sacks with grain before they leave.

Joseph's brothers return to their father Jacob in Canaan, reporting Joseph's demand to bring Benjamin to Egypt. They find their money returned in their sacks, causing fear, and Jacob worries about losing Benjamin after already losing Joseph and Simeon.

Joseph’s brothers insist they came to Egypt only to buy food, not as spies. Joseph accuses them again, demands their youngest brother come to prove their honesty, imprisons one brother, then releases the rest with grain to take home.

Judah assures his father Israel he will personally guarantee Benjamin's safe return to convince him to send Benjamin to Egypt. Israel agrees, instructs them to bring gifts and double money, and they set out to meet Joseph again.

Joseph’s brothers discover their money returned in their sacks, causing fear. They report to their father Jacob in Canaan about the harsh treatment by Egypt’s ruler, who demands they bring their youngest brother Benjamin to prove their honesty.

Jacob’s sons return to Egypt with Benjamin and gifts to buy food during the famine. Joseph, now a ruler, invites them to dine with him, but they fear punishment over the money found in their sacks on their first trip.

Joseph recognizes his full brother Benjamin among his brothers who came to Egypt to buy food. Overcome with emotion, Joseph weeps privately, then hosts a separate meal for Egyptians and Hebrews, honoring Benjamin with a larger portion.

Joseph’s brothers explain they brought extra money to buy food, unaware who returned the first money. Joseph reassures them, reveals Simeon, welcomes them, and notices Benjamin, showing his deep emotion toward his youngest brother.

Joseph instructs his steward to secretly place his silver cup in Benjamin's sack after filling the brothers' sacks with food and money. After they leave the city, Joseph sends the steward to accuse them of theft, testing their honesty.

Joseph accuses his brothers of stealing his silver cup, threatening death or servitude for the culprit. They deny guilt, and the cup is found with Benjamin. Judah pleads for mercy, and Joseph spares the others, keeping Benjamin as a servant.
During a severe famine, Jacob's sons report Joseph's demand to bring Benjamin to Egypt to buy food. Judah persuades their father Jacob to send Benjamin with them to ensure their safe return.
Joseph reveals his identity to his brothers in Egypt after years of separation, explaining that God sent him ahead to save lives during the famine and that he now holds a high position under Pharaoh.

Joseph declares the man with the cup will be his servant, but lets the others go home. Judah pleads, explaining their father’s love for Benjamin and his refusal to send him away, recounting Joseph’s demand that Benjamin come to Egypt.

Joseph reveals to his brothers that God made him ruler in Egypt and urges them to bring their father Jacob to live near him in Goshen during the famine. He emotionally embraces Benjamin and his brothers, confirming his identity.

Joseph sends gifts to his father Jacob in Canaan and sends his brothers back with provisions. They report Joseph is alive and a ruler in Egypt, which initially shocks Jacob but then revives his hope to see Joseph before he dies.

Joseph embraces and weeps with his brothers, who then speak with him. Pharaoh learns of their arrival, welcomes them, and commands Joseph to invite his family to Egypt with provisions and wagons for their journey.
Jacob's family arrives in Egypt, and this passage lists the sons and grandsons of Leah, Zilpah, and Rachel, detailing the extended family that traveled with Jacob from Canaan to Egypt.

Judah explains to Joseph how their father Jacob insisted that Benjamin must accompany them to Egypt, fearing for his life since he lost his other son, and offers to stay as Joseph’s servant instead to protect Benjamin and spare their father grief.

Jacob (also called Israel) prepares to move his entire family from Canaan to Egypt after God reassures him in a vision. His sons carry him and their families, along with their possessions, as they begin their journey to Egypt.

Jacob's family, including his sons and grandsons from Rachel, Bilhah, Dan, and Naphtali, are listed as they journey to Egypt. Judah leads the way to Goshen, where Joseph is, marking the family's arrival in Egypt.

Pharaoh asks Jacob his age during their meeting in Egypt. Joseph settles his family in the fertile land of Rameses and provides for them amid a severe famine affecting both Egypt and Canaan. Joseph collects money for grain sales.

Joseph informs Pharaoh that his family from Canaan has arrived in Goshen, presents five brothers, who explain they are shepherds seeking pasture due to famine. Pharaoh welcomes them to settle in Goshen and honors Jacob, who blesses Pharaoh.

Judah leads Jacob's family to Goshen in Egypt, where Joseph warmly reunites with his father. Joseph plans to tell Pharaoh about his family, advising them to present themselves as shepherds to secure their settlement in Goshen.

During the severe famine in Egypt and Canaan, Joseph collects all the money for grain, then accepts livestock in exchange when money runs out. The people offer their land and themselves as servants to Pharaoh to survive the ongoing famine.

During the severe famine in Egypt, the people offer to sell their land and become servants to Pharaoh in exchange for food. Joseph buys all the land for Pharaoh, except the priests' land, and sets a system where Egyptians give a fifth of their crops to Pharaoh.

Joseph establishes a law requiring Egyptians to give Pharaoh a fifth of their crops, securing Pharaoh's control during famine. Israel lives in Goshen, grows prosperous, and before dying, asks Joseph to bury him in Canaan, not Egypt.

Jacob (Israel), now old and nearly blind, meets Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh for the first time in Egypt. He embraces them and intentionally crosses his hands to bless the younger Ephraim over the firstborn Manasseh.

Jacob insists that Ephraim, the younger son, will be greater than Manasseh, blessing both before his death and affirming Joseph's special inheritance in the land of Canaan, promising God's presence with Joseph's family.

Jacob, also called Israel, blesses Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, intentionally placing his right hand on the younger Ephraim’s head, signaling a special blessing despite Joseph’s protest, affirming Ephraim’s future prominence.

Joseph brings his sons Manasseh and Ephraim to visit his father Jacob, who is sick in Egypt. Jacob recalls God's promise to bless his descendants in Canaan and adopts Joseph's sons as his own, asking who they are.

Jacob gathers his twelve sons to pronounce prophetic blessings and warnings about their futures. He begins by addressing Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, highlighting their strengths and flaws, setting the tone for each tribe's destiny.

Jacob pronounces blessings and prophecies over his sons, describing Judah's leadership and strength, Zebulun's coastal dwelling, Issachar's labor, Dan's judgment and cunning, Gad's struggles and victories, and Asher's abundance, outlining their future roles among Israel's tribes.
Jacob finishes blessing each of his twelve sons, instructs them to bury him with his ancestors in the cave of Machpelah in Canaan, and then dies, concluding his final words to his sons.

Jacob continues blessing his twelve sons, describing the future traits and fortunes of each tribe, including Asher, Naphtali, Joseph, and Benjamin, summarizing the blessings he gives to all his sons before his death.

After Jacob's death, Joseph mourns deeply and arranges for his embalming. He asks Pharaoh's permission to bury Jacob in Canaan, which Pharaoh grants, and Joseph leads a large Egyptian and family procession to honor his father's burial.

Joseph leads a large company, including his brothers and Pharaoh’s servants, from Egypt to Canaan to bury their father Jacob at Machpelah. They mourn deeply at Atad, beyond Jordan, witnessed by local Canaanites, then return to Egypt.

After burying their father Jacob in Canaan, Joseph and his brothers return to Egypt. Fearing Joseph's revenge for past wrongs, they ask for forgiveness, but Joseph reassures them, showing kindness and promising to care for them.

Joseph lives out his days in Egypt with his family, witnessing his grandchildren grow. Before dying, he assures his brothers that God will bring their descendants back to Canaan, and he makes them promise to carry his bones there.

This passage lists Jacob's twelve sons who moved to Egypt, noting their descendants grew numerous. After Joseph and his generation died, a new Egyptian king feared the Israelites' growing population and enslaved them, forcing them to build cities.

A Levite couple hides their newborn son to protect him from Pharaoh's order to kill Hebrew boys. When they can no longer hide him, they place him in a basket by the Nile, where Pharaoh's daughter finds and adopts him, hiring his mother as nurse.

The Israelites in Egypt are oppressed with harsh labor, yet they keep growing in number. Pharaoh orders Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill newborn boys, but they disobey, fearing God. Pharaoh then commands all Egyptians to drown Hebrew boys.

Moses, tending Jethro's flock near Mount Horeb, encounters a burning bush that is not consumed. God calls to him from the bush, revealing Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and commands Moses to remove his shoes on holy ground.

After Moses kills an Egyptian, Pharaoh seeks to kill him, so Moses flees to Midian, helps Reuel's daughters at a well, marries Zipporah, and has a son. Meanwhile, Israelite suffering in Egypt grows, and God hears their cries and remembers His covenant.

God speaks to Moses from the burning bush on Mount Horeb, revealing Himself as the God of Abraham and promising to rescue the Israelites from Egyptian slavery. God commissions Moses to confront Pharaoh, but Moses doubts his ability.
Pharaoh’s daughter adopts Moses and hires his mother to nurse him. As an adult, Moses kills an Egyptian oppressing a Hebrew, then flees to Midian after Pharaoh seeks to kill him for this act.

Moses questions his ability to confront Pharaoh and free Israel, and God assures him of divine presence and authority, revealing His name "I AM" and linking to the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

God instructs Moses to tell the elders of Israel that the LORD, their ancestors' God, has appeared to him and will deliver them from Egypt to a fertile land. Moses is to request Pharaoh for a three-day journey to worship God, though God predicts Pharaoh will refuse.

Moses doubts the Israelites will believe him as God's messenger. God shows Moses two signs—a rod turning into a serpent and a hand becoming leprous then healed—to prove His presence and convince the people.

God is speaking to Moses, giving him signs to perform if the Israelites or Egyptians don't believe him, and addressing Moses' concerns about his speaking ability by promising to help and sending Aaron to assist him.

God, displeased with Moses' hesitation, appoints Aaron, Moses' brother, as his spokesperson. Moses seeks permission from Jethro to return to Egypt, then sets out with his family and God's rod to confront Pharaoh.

Moses shares God's message and signs with his brother Aaron. Together, they meet the Israelite elders, and Aaron performs the signs, leading the people to believe and worship, acknowledging God's care for their suffering in Egypt.

God tells Moses that Pharaoh will refuse to free the Israelites at first, but after God sends plagues on Egypt, Pharaoh will let them go. The Israelites will gain favor and take valuable goods from the Egyptians as they leave.

Moses leaves Midian with his family, carrying God's rod, to confront Pharaoh in Egypt. God warns Moses of Pharaoh's hardened heart and threatens Egypt's firstborn. Zipporah circumcises their son to save Moses. Aaron meets Moses at Mount Sinai.

Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh in Egypt, demanding freedom for the Israelites to worship in the wilderness. Pharaoh refuses, questioning the LORD's authority, and punishes the Israelites by increasing their labor demands.

The Israelite officers complain to Pharaoh about the harsh brick-making demands without straw, but Pharaoh accuses them of laziness and increases their workload. The officers blame Moses and Aaron, who then pray to God, distressed by the worsening situation.

Pharaoh orders the Israelites' brick quota unchanged but stops supplying straw, forcing them to gather it themselves. Taskmasters pressure the workers, and Israelite officers are beaten for unmet quotas, leading them to plead with Pharaoh for relief.

God lists the family heads of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, including Moses and Aaron's lineage, to establish their heritage and authority as he prepares Moses to confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out of Egypt.

God reassures Moses in Egypt that He will force Pharaoh to release the Israelites, reminding him of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and promising to free the Israelites from Egyptian slavery and claim them as His people.
This passage lists the family members of Levi, including Aaron and Moses, who God commands to lead Israel out of Egypt. Moses expresses doubt about his ability to speak to Pharaoh effectively.

God reassures Moses that He will free the Israelites from Egyptian bondage and bring them to the promised land. Moses tells this to the Israelites, who are too distressed to listen. God then commands Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh again.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to perform a miracle before Pharaoh by turning Aaron's rod into a serpent, which outmatches the Egyptian magicians' similar acts, but Pharaoh's heart remains hardened against freeing the Israelites.

God instructs Moses to demand Pharaoh release the Israelites, warning that Pharaoh has refused so far. Moses and Aaron perform the first plague by turning the Nile's water into blood, demonstrating God's power before Pharaoh and his officials.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh in Egypt, declaring Moses as a god-like figure and Aaron as his prophet. God warns Pharaoh's heart will be hardened, leading to signs and wonders to free the Israelites. Moses and Aaron obey.

Moses and Aaron perform God's miracle by turning the Nile into blood before Pharaoh and his court, causing fish to die and water to stink. Despite Egyptian magicians copying this, Pharaoh's heart remains hardened, and the crisis lasts seven days.

God warns Pharaoh through Moses that a severe hailstorm will strike Egypt, sparing only those who heed the warning by bringing their livestock indoors, demonstrating God's power as Pharaoh continues to resist freeing the Israelites.

God instructs Moses to warn Pharaoh that if he refuses to free the Israelites, a deadly disease will strike Egyptian livestock but spare Israel's animals. The next day, all Egyptian cattle die, yet Pharaoh's heart remains hardened.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to use furnace ashes to cause painful boils on Egyptians and their animals, demonstrating His power. Despite this, Pharaoh's heart remains hardened, and God commands Moses to demand Israel's release again.

Pharaoh admits his fault and asks Moses to pray for the hail to stop, promising to release the Israelites. Moses prays, the storm ends, but Pharaoh hardens his heart again and refuses to free the people, fulfilling God's warning.

Moses warns Pharaoh of a severe hailstorm sent by God to punish Egypt, sparing only Goshen where the Israelites live. After the devastating hail, Pharaoh admits his wrongdoing and asks Moses to pray for relief, promising to release the Israelites.

After Pharaoh briefly relents from the plague of frogs, God commands Moses and Aaron to bring a new plague of lice upon Egypt. Despite the magicians' failed attempts to replicate it, Pharaoh's heart remains hardened as God prepares another demand for Israel's release.

God tells Moses to confront Pharaoh again, explaining that He has hardened Pharaoh's heart to display His power through signs. Moses warns Pharaoh of an impending locust plague if he refuses to free the Israelites from Egypt.

Pharaoh asks Moses and Aaron to pray to God to remove the frogs plaguing Egypt, promising to release the Israelites to worship. God ends the plague, but Pharaoh hardens his heart and refuses to free the people.

Moses warns Pharaoh of a devastating locust plague that will fill Egyptian homes, prompting Pharaoh’s officials to urge release of the Israelites. Pharaoh reluctantly allows only the men to go, and Moses and Aaron leave his presence.

God instructs Moses to warn Pharaoh that if he refuses to free the Israelites, swarms of flies will invade Egypt except Goshen, where the Israelites live. The flies come, causing Pharaoh to ask Moses and Aaron to sacrifice to God in Egypt.

Pharaoh tells Moses and Aaron they may sacrifice to God in Egypt, but Moses insists they must go three days into the wilderness. Pharaoh agrees but limits their travel. Moses prays to remove the flies, which God does, yet Pharaoh still refuses to free the Israelites.

Pharaoh admits his sin and asks Moses to pray for relief from the locust plague. God sends a strong west wind to remove the locusts, but then hardens Pharaoh’s heart. Moses brings darkness over Egypt, yet Israel has light, and Pharaoh allows the Israelites to go with some restrictions.

God tells Moses about the final plague that will force Pharaoh to release the Israelites. Moses instructs the people to borrow valuables from Egyptians, as God grants favor to Israel and warns of the coming death of all Egyptian firstborns.

God instructs Moses to demand Pharaoh release the Israelites or face a plague of frogs. Aaron causes frogs to cover Egypt, including Pharaoh's palace. Even Pharaoh's magicians replicate the plague, leading Pharaoh to ask Moses and Aaron to pray for relief.

Pharaoh reluctantly expels only the men of Israel, rejecting their full request. God then sends a devastating locust plague across Egypt, consuming all remaining crops, prompting Pharaoh to urgently admit his sin to Moses and Aaron.

Pharaoh reluctantly agrees to let the Israelites go but refuses to let their livestock or sacrifices leave Egypt. Moses insists all must go for worship, but God hardens Pharaoh’s heart, who then angrily orders Moses away, threatening death if they meet again.

God instructs Moses and Aaron in Egypt to establish a new calendar starting this month and commands the Israelites to prepare a spotless lamb for each household, to be sacrificed and eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs on the evening of the 14th day.

God instructs Moses and Aaron in Egypt to have the Israelites remove all leaven and eat unleavened bread for seven days as part of the Passover. Moses then tells the elders to prepare the lamb and mark their doorposts with its blood for protection.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites to observe the Passover as a lasting memorial of their deliverance from Egypt. After the final plague kills all Egyptian firstborns, Pharaoh urgently summons Moses and Aaron to let the Israelites leave.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to establish the Feast of Unleavened Bread as a lasting memorial for Israel, commemorating their deliverance from Egypt, with strict rules about eating unleavened bread for seven days and holding holy assemblies on the first and seventh days.

God tells Moses that no harm will come to the Israelites during the coming plague, showing God's protection over them. Despite Moses and Aaron performing miracles, Pharaoh's anger grows, and God hardens his heart to increase His signs in Egypt.

Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron at night, urging the Israelites to leave Egypt quickly after the final plague. The Israelites prepare to depart, borrowing valuables from Egyptians and traveling from Rameses to Succoth with a large group and livestock.

God instructs Moses to consecrate all firstborn to Him and commands the Israelites to remember their Exodus day by eating unleavened bread for seven days each year as a lasting memorial of their deliverance from Egypt.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to tell the Israelites in Egypt how to prepare and eat the Passover meal, marking their protection from the coming plague on Egypt's firstborn and establishing a lasting memorial feast.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on the Passover rules, emphasizing that only circumcised Israelites and foreigners who join them may partake, and that the Israelites obey these commands as they begin their exodus from Egypt.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites to teach their children about the Exodus as a lasting sign and memorial, and commands them to dedicate all firstborn males of people and animals to the Lord, with specific rules for redeeming firstborn donkeys.

As the Israelites leave Egypt after 430 years, a mixed group including others and many animals depart with them, eating unleavened bread due to haste. God instructs Moses and Aaron on Passover rules, limiting participation to circumcised Israelites and servants.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites to redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb and to redeem their firstborn sons, explaining this practice as a reminder of God's powerful deliverance from Egypt after the death of the firstborn there.

God instructs the Israelites to remember their deliverance from Egypt with signs on their bodies. After Pharaoh lets them go, God leads them on a longer route through the wilderness, guiding them by a cloud by day and fire by night as they journey from Succoth to Etham.
Moses encourages the fearful Israelites at the Red Sea to trust God's deliverance. God instructs Moses to part the sea, promising to harden Pharaoh's heart so Egypt will witness His power and honor.

God instructs Moses to have the Israelites camp near the sea at Pihahiroth, anticipating Pharaoh will pursue them. Pharaoh prepares his army with 600 chariots to chase after the fleeing Israelites, whom God leads confidently.

Pharaoh pursues the Israelites with his army after they leave Egypt, trapping them by the sea near Pihahiroth. The Israelites fear death in the wilderness and question Moses, who urges them to trust God's deliverance.

As Pharaoh’s army chased the Israelites into the sea, God caused the waters to return, drowning the Egyptians while the Israelites crossed safely on dry ground, leading them to fear and believe in God and Moses.

God tells Moses He will gain honor over Pharaoh and his army. The angel and cloud move behind Israel, creating darkness for Egyptians but light for Israelites. Moses parts the sea with God's power, allowing Israel to cross while Egyptians pursue.
After crossing the Red Sea on dry ground and witnessing the destruction of Pharaoh's army, Moses and the Israelites sing a song praising God's powerful deliverance and victory over their enemies.

Moses and Aaron address the complaining Israelites in the wilderness of Sin, explaining God's plan to provide double food on the sixth day and revealing His glory in a cloud as He hears their complaints.

After crossing the Red Sea, Moses led the Israelites into the wilderness of Shur, where they faced thirst and bitter water at Marah. God showed Moses a tree to sweeten the water and gave laws, then they camped at Elim with abundant water and palm trees.

Moses and the Israelites praise God for defeating Pharaoh's army at the Red Sea. Miriam leads the women in song and dance. Then they begin their journey through the wilderness of Shur, traveling three days without finding water.

Aaron addresses the Israelites who see God's glory in a cloud; God tells Moses He heard their complaints and will provide quail and manna. Quail arrive at night, manna appears by morning, and Moses instructs them to gather it daily by household.

Moses and the Israelites sing a victory song praising God for defeating Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea. The song foretells fear among neighboring nations—Palestina, Edom, Moab, and Canaan—as Israel, God's chosen people, passes safely through.

The Israelites gathered manna daily as instructed by Moses, but some kept leftovers that spoiled overnight, angering Moses. On the sixth day, they gathered double for the Sabbath, and the extra manna stayed fresh until morning, following God's command.

Moses instructs the Israelites to keep manna overnight on the Sabbath, but none appears on the seventh day. God commands rest on the Sabbath, providing double manna the day before. The people name the bread manna, and Moses preserves some as a reminder.

Moses instructs Aaron to preserve an omer of manna as a lasting reminder of God's provision during Israel's 40 years in the wilderness, from their departure from Egypt until reaching Canaan's borders. Aaron places it before the Testimony as commanded.

Joshua leads the Israelites to defeat the Amalekites in battle at Rephidim. God instructs Moses to record this victory as a lasting memorial, and Moses builds an altar named Jehovahnissi, signifying God's ongoing conflict with Amalek.
The Israelites camp at Rephidim but find no water, causing them to complain to Moses. Moses prays to God, who instructs him to strike a rock at Horeb to provide water for the people and elders.

God instructs Moses at Horeb to strike a rock to provide water for the thirsty Israelites, who had been complaining. Soon after, Amalek attacks at Rephidim; Joshua leads Israel’s fight while Moses, Aaron, and Hur support him from a hilltop.

Moses recounts to his father-in-law Jethro all God's acts delivering Israel from Egypt. Jethro praises God, offers sacrifices, and observes Moses judging the people alone all day, questioning his exhausting approach.

Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, observes Moses judging all disputes alone from morning to evening and advises him to delegate responsibilities, teaching the people God's laws and bringing difficult cases to God through Moses.

Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law and priest of Midian, hears of God’s deliverance of Israel from Egypt and brings Moses’ wife Zipporah and their sons to meet him at Mount Sinai, where Moses shares the story of their journey and God’s help.

Jethro advises Moses to delegate judging duties by appointing capable leaders over groups of various sizes to ease his burden. Moses follows this counsel, organizing Israel’s leadership before Jethro returns home.

After leaving Egypt, the Israelites camp at Mount Sinai. God speaks to Moses, instructing him to tell the people about His covenant and their special status if they obey. Moses shares this with the elders, who agree to follow God's commands.

The Israelites agree to obey God's commands, and God instructs Moses to prepare the people for His dramatic appearance on Mount Sinai in three days, warning them to keep a strict boundary around the mountain for their safety.

God speaks directly to the Israelites at Mount Sinai, beginning to give them the Ten Commandments, starting with instructions about worshiping only Him, avoiding idols, respecting His name, and keeping the Sabbath holy.

Moses instructs the Israelites to prepare for God's arrival on Mount Sinai. On the third day, thunder, lightning, and smoke signal God's descent, causing the people to tremble. God calls Moses up the mountain and warns him to keep the people and priests from approaching too closely.

God instructs Moses to have the priests sanctify themselves before approaching Him on Mount Sinai, then tells Moses only he and Aaron may ascend the mountain, while the people and priests must keep their distance to avoid God's wrath. Moses obeys and speaks to the people.

God speaks to the Israelites at Mount Sinai, giving them the Sabbath command and other moral laws. The people witness thunder, lightning, and smoke on the mountain, causing them to stand back in awe and fear.

The Israelites witness thunder, lightning, trumpet sounds, and smoke on Mount Sinai, causing them to fear and ask Moses to speak for them. God instructs Moses to relay laws about worship and altar construction to the people.

God instructs Moses to present laws about Hebrew servants, detailing their service terms, family rights, and conditions for permanent servitude, as well as rules for selling daughters as maidservants, continuing the covenant guidelines given to Israel.

God gives Moses laws about personal injury and property damage, including rules for compensation and punishment when someone is hurt or killed, or when an ox causes death, emphasizing fairness and justice among the Israelites.

God continues giving Moses laws for the Israelites, covering treatment of a servant's betrothed wife, consequences for murder, manslaughter, and assault, and rules for justice and compensation in disputes among the people.

God gives Moses laws about responsibility and compensation for harm caused by oxen, including when an ox kills or injures people or other animals, emphasizing owner accountability in Israelite society.

God gives Moses laws for Israel about theft and property damage, detailing restitution for stolen or harmed livestock, fields, and goods, and consequences for thieves caught breaking in or causing fires.
God gives Moses laws for the Israelites about justice, kindness to the poor, respect for leaders, and proper offerings, emphasizing mercy and holiness as they prepare to live in the Promised Land.

God gives Moses laws about property and theft, including rules for when a neighbor's goods are stolen or lost, and how disputes should be judged fairly among the Israelites during their time in the wilderness.

God gives Moses laws for property damage, borrowing, marriage, and social justice, emphasizing care for strangers, widows, and orphans, with warnings of divine punishment for oppression and idolatry among the Israelites.

God instructs the Israelites through Moses on fair justice: avoid false witness, do not follow crowds in wrongdoing, help even enemies with their lost animals, reject bribes, and treat strangers kindly, recalling their own time as foreigners in Egypt.

God instructs the Israelites through Moses to observe three annual feasts commemorating their deliverance and harvests, to bring offerings properly, and warns them to obey the Angel He sends ahead to guide and protect them into the promised land.

God instructs the Israelites not to oppress foreigners, reminding them of their own past in Egypt. He commands agricultural rest every seventh year, weekly Sabbath rest, avoidance of other gods, and observance of three annual feasts.

God speaks to the Israelites, warning them to obey His angel who will lead them into Canaan to defeat its inhabitants. God promises blessings, protection, and victory over their enemies if they remain faithful and avoid idolatry.

Moses seals God's covenant with Israel by sprinkling blood on the people, then ascends Mount Sinai with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and elders. They witness God's glory as Moses prepares to receive stone tablets with laws for the people.

God invites Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders to worship from a distance while Moses approaches Him alone. Moses relays God's laws to Israel, who agree to obey, then seals the covenant with sacrifices and blood sprinkled on altar and people.

God promises the Israelites that He will send hornets to drive out the Hivites, Canaanites, and Hittites gradually, setting their borders from the Red Sea to the Philistine sea, warning them not to make covenants with these peoples or their gods.

God instructs Moses on Mount Sinai to tell the Israelites to bring offerings willingly for building a sanctuary, detailing materials and the ark's design, so God can dwell among them as shown in the divine pattern.

God instructs Moses on making the tabernacle's outer coverings from rams' skins dyed red and badgers' skins, and details the construction of wooden boards with silver sockets for the south, north, and west sides of the tabernacle.

God instructs Moses on Mount Sinai to make eleven goats' hair curtains as a protective covering for the tabernacle, detailing their size, how to join them with brass clasps, and additional coverings of red-dyed ram skins and badger skins for weatherproofing.

God instructs Moses on building the tabernacle's wooden frame with gold-covered boards and bars, including special corner boards joined by rings, following the design shown on Mount Sinai. This continues detailed construction directions.

God instructs Moses to make the tabernacle's inner covering from ten fine linen curtains with cherub designs, joined in two sets of five with gold clasps, and to add eleven goats' hair curtains as an outer covering, continuing detailed construction directions.

Moses receives instructions from God for the annual Day of Atonement, when the priest makes sacrifices and purifies the sanctuary and people of Israel. This solemn day is a yearly statute for cleansing sins and resting from work.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron, his sons, and all Israel that all animal sacrifices must be brought to the tabernacle for proper offering by priests, forbidding unauthorized slaughter and sacrifice to false gods.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites and foreigners living among them not to eat blood, as it represents life. Hunters must drain and cover blood, and those who eat animals that died naturally or were torn must purify themselves to avoid guilt.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites not to follow the immoral customs of Egypt or Canaan but to obey His laws, including prohibitions against sexual relations with close relatives, emphasizing their identity as His people.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites not to engage in sexual relations with close relatives, listing specific family members whose "nakedness" must not be uncovered, emphasizing the prohibition of incestuous relationships.

God warns the Israelites through Moses that the land is defiled by the previous inhabitants' sins, and if they follow those abominations, they too will be cut off and the land will reject them. They must obey God's laws to avoid this fate.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites not to engage in various forbidden sexual practices, idolatry, or bestiality, warning that such sins defile the land and lead to divine punishment, contrasting Israel’s conduct with that of the nations they will displace.

God commands Moses to tell Aaron, his sons, and all Israel that sacrifices must be brought to the tabernacle and blood must not be eaten, emphasizing blood's role in atonement and warning of severe consequences for disobedience.

God speaks to Moses, instructing the Israelites to be holy like Him, honor parents, keep the Sabbath, avoid idols, properly offer peace sacrifices, and leave parts of their harvest for the poor and strangers as acts of obedience.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites in the wilderness to care for the poor and strangers by leaving some harvest behind, to act honestly and justly in all dealings, and to love and respect their neighbors without hatred or revenge.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel to love their neighbors and avoid grudges, follow laws on purity in agriculture and clothing, address certain sexual offenses with offerings, and observe a waiting period before eating fruit from newly planted trees in the promised land.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel to treat the fourth-year fruit as holy and eat the fifth-year fruit for sustenance, forbids certain practices like eating blood and consulting wizards, commands respect for the elderly, and calls for kindness to strangers living among them.

God commands Moses to warn the Israelites and resident foreigners that anyone offering children to Molech must be put to death, emphasizing holiness and obedience to God's laws to avoid defilement and judgment.

God speaks to Moses, commanding the Israelites to obey His laws, detailing severe punishments for offenses like cursing parents, adultery, incest, homosexuality, and bestiality, emphasizing holiness and separation from other nations.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites to treat foreigners living among them as native-born, love them, and act justly in all measures and judgments, reminding them of their own history as strangers in Egypt.

God instructs Moses to warn Israel against sexual sins including bestiality and incest, prescribing death or exclusion from the community to maintain holiness as they prepare to enter the promised land.

God instructs Moses to warn Israel against forbidden sexual relations and occult practices, emphasizing obedience to His laws to avoid being rejected from the promised land flowing with milk and honey, highlighting Israel's call to holiness and separation from other nations.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron and his sons to avoid eating holy offerings if they are ceremonially unclean, detailing specific conditions that cause uncleanness and emphasizing the need for purity to honor God's sanctity.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron's priestly sons about rules for ritual purity, limiting mourning defilement to close relatives and forbidding certain mourning practices, emphasizing their holiness as they offer sacrifices to the LORD.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron and the priests that the high priest must remain holy, avoid defilement, marry a virgin from his people, and that any priest with physical blemishes must not offer sacrifices.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron and his sons about rules for eating holy offerings, emphasizing purity, who may eat them, and penalties for unintentional misuse, to prevent defiling sacred things in Israel.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron that any priest descended from him with physical defects must not perform sacred offerings but may eat the holy food; this maintains the sanctity of the sanctuary and is communicated to all Israel.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron, his sons, and all Israelites about proper handling of holy offerings, emphasizing that sacrifices must be without blemish to be accepted and that unintentional eating of holy things requires restitution.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites specific rules for offerings: animals must be at least eight days old, mothers and offspring not killed on the same day, and thanksgiving sacrifices eaten the same day. God reminds them to obey and honor His name.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron, his sons, and Israel that peace and freewill offerings must be without blemish to be accepted, detailing unacceptable defects and rules for animal offerings, emphasizing purity and proper timing after birth.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about the seven-day offering and the special sheaf wave offering at harvest time in the promised land, including specific sacrifices and a rule about when they may eat new grain.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites in the promised land to observe a harvest ritual involving offerings and counting fifty days from the Sabbath after the wave sheaf, including specific sacrifices and a prohibition on eating certain grains until the offering is made.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about His appointed feasts, including the weekly Sabbath and annual festivals like Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, emphasizing rest and holy gatherings with specific offerings.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about the Feast of Tabernacles, a seven-day festival in the seventh month with holy gatherings and offerings, including sabbaths on the first and eighth days, celebrating the harvest and honoring the LORD.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about the Day of Atonement on the tenth day of the seventh month, a solemn day of rest and self-affliction with offerings, followed by the seven-day Feast of Tabernacles starting on the fifteenth day.

God instructs Moses about the sacred bread for Aaron and his sons, then a conflict arises in the Israelite camp where a man blasphemes God. Moses is told to have the blasphemer stoned outside the camp, emphasizing the seriousness of honoring God's name.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel to bring pure olive oil for lamps to burn continually in the tabernacle, and Aaron to arrange twelve cakes of fine flour with frankincense on the table weekly as a holy offering for Aaron and his sons.

God instructs Moses to enforce strict justice among the Israelites, including death for blasphemy and murder, equal restitution for harm done, and equal laws for natives and strangers; Moses then commands the community to execute the blasphemer.
