God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites to celebrate the seven-day Feast of Tabernacles in the seventh month, dwelling in booths to remember their time in Egypt, emphasizing its lasting importance for all generations. Moses conveys these laws to the people.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about offerings and holy gatherings during harvest and the seventh month, including a sin offering, peace offerings, and a day of rest with trumpet blasts, emphasizing care for the poor and no work on these sacred days.

God instructs Moses on Mount Sinai to tell Israel to count seven cycles of seven years, then celebrate the 50th year as a Jubilee with trumpet blasts, declaring freedom and land restoration, marking a sacred year of rest and return to possessions.

God instructs Moses on the land's rest cycle and redemption laws in Canaan, emphasizing that the land belongs to God and can be redeemed by relatives or the original owner, with special rules for houses in walled cities.

God instructs Moses on Mount Sinai to tell Israel about the Jubilee year when land returns to original owners and fair pricing applies to sales, promising blessings for obedience and provision during the land's sabbath rest every seventh year.

God instructs Moses on Mount Sinai to tell the Israelites that once they enter the promised land, they must let the land rest every seventh year, allowing crops to grow naturally and providing food for all, including servants and animals, counting seven cycles of seven years.

God instructs Moses at Mount Sinai on laws about redeeming houses in walled cities, villages, and Levitical cities, emphasizing property rights and support for poor relatives or strangers living among the Israelites in the land of Canaan.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites in Canaan to help poor fellow Israelites and foreigners without charging interest, treating them as hired workers until the Jubilee year when they and their families return to their ancestral land.

God instructs the Israelites through Moses on Mount Sinai about treating servants: foreign slaves may be owned permanently, but Israelite servants must be treated fairly and can be redeemed by relatives or themselves if sold to foreigners.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about redeeming a relative sold into servitude, with payment adjusted by years until the Jubilee, ensuring fair treatment and eventual freedom in the Jubilee year, emphasizing Israel as God's servants.

God speaks to the Israelites, commanding them not to make idols and to keep His commandments. He promises blessings like fruitful land, peace, and victory over enemies if they obey, linking obedience to prosperity and His covenant.

God speaks to the Israelites, promising blessings like fruitfulness and His presence if they obey His laws, but warning of severe punishments including disease and defeat by enemies if they break the covenant made after their exodus from Egypt.

God warns the Israelites through Moses that if they disobey His commandments, He will bring severe punishments including defeat by enemies, famine, plagues, and wild beasts, escalating consequences if they continue to rebel.
God warns the Israelites through Moses that if they continue to disobey His covenant, He will punish them severely with war, famine, and destruction, leading to desolation of their cities and land.

God warns the Israelites through Moses that if they disobey, their land will become desolate, they will be scattered among foreign nations, and suffer defeat and despair, continuing the consequences for breaking the covenant given at Mount Sinai.

God warns the Israelites that those who survive exile will suffer for their sins but if they repent sincerely, He will remember His covenant with their ancestors and not utterly reject them despite their punishment and the land's desolation.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel how to value people of different ages and genders when they make special vows, setting specific silver shekel amounts, with priests adjusting values for those who are poor.

God reassures the Israelites through Moses that despite their exile among enemies, He will not abandon or destroy them, but will remember His covenant made with their ancestors at Mount Sinai. This concludes God's laws and promises to Israel.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel how to value vows made to the Lord, including people, animals, and houses; priests assess worth if the vow-maker is poor or if the offering is unclean, with a fifth added if redeemed.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel how to value and redeem houses and fields dedicated to the Lord, including adding a fifth part to the value, with special rules for fields sold or redeemed before or after the year of Jubilee.
God instructs Moses at Sinai to count all Israelite men aged twenty and older who can fight, assigning a leader from each tribe to assist; the passage lists these tribal leaders by name.
Moses, Aaron, and tribal leaders count the men aged 20+ able to fight from Reuben, Simeon, Gad, and Judah tribes in the Sinai wilderness, continuing the census God commanded after Israel left Egypt.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about valuing fields dedicated to the LORD, including rules for redemption and the Jubilee year when land returns to original owners; also, firstborn clean animals belong to God and unclean animals can be redeemed with added value.

Moses and Aaron continue the census of Israelite men able to fight, reporting the numbers from the tribes of Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Ephraim during their encampment at Sinai after leaving Egypt.
Moses and Aaron, following God's command at Sinai, count the men aged 20+ able to fight from the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, and Dan during Israel's wilderness journey after leaving Egypt.

Moses and Aaron, following God's command at Sinai, gathered Israel's leaders and counted all men aged 20+ able to fight, starting with Reuben, Israel's eldest son, numbering 46,500 warriors from that tribe.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about redeeming unclean animals and the rules for devoted things, which are sacred and cannot be redeemed or sold. The passage also details tithes from land and livestock as holy offerings to the LORD.

Moses and Aaron, with tribal leaders, counted 603,550 Israelite men able to fight, excluding Levites. God instructed Moses to assign Levites to care for and carry the tabernacle, setting them apart from the fighting tribes.

Moses and Aaron, with tribal leaders, count the fighting men aged 20+ from the tribes of Dan, Asher, and Naphtali during Israel's wilderness stay after Egypt, continuing the census of Israel's military-ready men by family groups.

God instructs Moses that the Levites are responsible for dismantling, transporting, and setting up the tabernacle, camping around it to protect it, while the rest of Israel camps by their tribes; Israel obeys these commands in the Sinai wilderness.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on how the Israelites are to camp around the tabernacle, starting with the camp of Judah on the east side, led by Nahshon, followed by Issachar and Zebulun, detailing their leaders and troop numbers.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on how the Israelite tribes are to camp around the tabernacle. Here, the tribes of Judah, Reuben, Simeon, and Gad are assigned their positions and leaders, with their army sizes listed and marching order set.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on how the Israelite tribes should camp and march around the tabernacle. The camp of Reuben sets forth second, followed by the Levites with the tabernacle in the center, then the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin on the west side.

God speaks to Moses at Mount Sinai, listing Aaron's sons and recounting Nadab and Abihu's death. God commands Moses to bring the Levites to serve Aaron and care for the tabernacle and Israel's worship.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on the arrangement of the Israelite camps around the tabernacle, detailing the tribes of Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, Dan, Asher, and Naphtali, their leaders, numbers, and marching order.

Moses lists the Merari family of Levites, led by Zuriel, assigned to camp north of the tabernacle and care for its structural elements. Moses, Aaron, and his sons camp east, guarding the sanctuary and Israel's charge.

God instructs Moses to organize the Levite families by their duties and camp positions around the tabernacle. The Kohathites, led by Elizaphan, care for sacred objects, while Eleazar oversees all Levite duties; the Merarites are also named.

God instructs Moses to dedicate the Levites to Aaron and his sons for priestly service, replacing the firstborn of Israel. Moses counts the Levite families—Gershon, Kohath, and Merari—following God's command at Mount Sinai.

Moses reports the total number of Israelite men counted by tribe, excluding Levites, who camped separately around the tabernacle. The tribes, including Dan's large camp, followed God's instructions in their orderly arrangement and movement.

God instructs Moses to count all firstborn Israelite males and to set the Levites apart as a substitute for these firstborn. For the extra firstborn beyond the Levites, a redemption payment is to be collected and given to Aaron and his sons.
God instructs Moses to collect redemption money from the extra firstborn Israelites beyond the Levites, and Moses gives this money to Aaron and his sons, following God's command at Mount Sinai.

Moses lists the families of the Levite tribe, focusing on Gershon's descendants and their duties. The Gershonites, led by Eliasaph, are assigned to care for the tabernacle's coverings and hangings, camping west of the tabernacle.

Moses and Aaron oversee the Levites who camp east of the tabernacle, guarding the sanctuary. God commands Moses to count all Israel's firstborn males, assigning Levites to replace them, and Moses complies with the census.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to count the Kohathite Levites aged 30-50 who serve in the tabernacle, detailing their sacred duties including how Aaron and his sons must carefully cover holy objects like the ark and table before the camp moves.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on how the sons of Kohath must carefully cover and protect the sacred objects of the tabernacle—like the candlestick and altar—using specific cloths and badgers' skins before the camp moves.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on how Aaron and his sons must carefully cover the altar and its vessels with skins before the Kohathites carry them, warning them not to touch holy items; Eleazar oversees the sacred oils and offerings in the tabernacle.

Moses and Aaron count the Kohathite and Gershonite Levites aged 30 to 50 who are eligible to serve in the tabernacle, following God's instructions for organizing the Levites' duties in the Israelite camp.

God instructs Moses to count the Gershonite Levites aged 30 to 50 who serve in the tabernacle, responsible for carrying its curtains and coverings. Aaron’s family, especially Ithamar, oversees their duties and burdens.

God instructs Moses to count the Gershonite and Merarite Levite families aged 30 to 50 for their specific duties in carrying and caring for the tabernacle's structural components, all supervised by Ithamar, Aaron's son.

Moses, Aaron, and Israel's leaders count the Kohathite Levites aged 30 to 50, who serve in the tabernacle, confirming 2,750 eligible men as part of the detailed organization of Levitical duties under priest Ithamar.

Moses and Aaron count the Levite families—the Gershonites and Merarites—aged 30 to 50, who serve in the tabernacle. They total 8,580, fulfilling God's command to organize their ministry and duties in the camp.

God instructs Moses to have the Israelites remove anyone with contagious diseases or ritual impurity from the camp to keep it holy. Then God commands laws for confessing sins and making restitution, with offerings given to the priests.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel that offerings given to priests belong to them, then introduces a ritual for a husband suspecting his wife of adultery without proof, involving a barley offering brought to the priest as a sign of jealousy.

God instructs Moses and Aaron about Eleazar's duties overseeing sacred oils and tabernacle care, commands careful handling of the Kohathites to prevent death, and orders a census of the Gershonite Levites aged 30 to 50 for tabernacle service.

Moses receives instructions from God for a ritual where a husband brings his wife to the priest if he suspects her of infidelity; the priest prepares a barley offering and bitter water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor to test her faithfulness.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel how a priest tests a wife suspected of adultery by making her drink bitter water that brings a curse if she is guilty; this ritual involves an oath, a written curse, and an offering at the tabernacle.

God instructs Moses to have the priest perform a ritual for a jealous husband suspecting his wife of adultery, involving an offering and bitter water; if guilty, the woman suffers a curse, if innocent, she is cleared, and the husband is free of guilt.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about the Nazarite vow, a special dedication involving abstaining from wine, not cutting hair, and avoiding contact with dead bodies, marking a person as holy during their period of separation to the Lord.

God instructs Moses on the Nazarite vow, detailing how a Nazarite must remain holy and avoid death's impurity; if defiled by a sudden death nearby, the Nazarite must perform purification rituals and offerings to restore their consecration.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron and his sons how to bless the Israelites, following the laws about Nazarite vows, emphasizing God's protection, grace, and peace upon His people. This concludes the Nazarite regulations and introduces the priestly blessing.

God instructs Moses on how a Nazarite completes their vow by bringing specific animal and grain offerings to the tabernacle, where the priest presents them to the LORD, marking the end of the Nazarite's consecrated period.

God instructs Moses on the final rituals for a Nazarite vow, including offerings and shaving the Nazarite's head at the tabernacle, symbolizing completion of their consecration and allowing them to drink wine again.

Moses distributes wagons and oxen to the Levite families for tabernacle service, except the Kohathites who carry items. The tribal princes begin offering sacrifices to dedicate the altar, starting with Nahshon of Judah.

After Moses set up and consecrated the tabernacle, tribal leaders Nahshon of Judah and Nethaneel of Issachar each offered detailed sacrifices to dedicate the altar, continuing the ceremony begun by the princes of Israel.

After Moses finished setting up and consecrating the tabernacle and its furnishings, the tribal leaders of Israel brought offerings of wagons and oxen. God instructed Moses to give these to the Levites to support their service in the tabernacle.

After Moses set up and anointed the tabernacle, Israel's tribal leaders offered sacrifices to dedicate the altar; Nethaneel of Issachar and Eliab of Zebulun each presented detailed offerings including silver vessels, animals, and grain.

The princes of Israel continue their daily offerings to dedicate the altar after its anointing; Eliab of Zebulun offers on the third day, followed by Elizur of Reuben on the fourth, each presenting silver vessels, flour, incense, and various animal sacrifices.

The princes of Simeon and Gad, Shelumiel and Eliasaph, each present their elaborate offerings of silver, gold, and various animals to dedicate the altar after its anointing at the newly set-up tabernacle.

Moses records the offerings made by tribal leaders to dedicate the altar after the tabernacle was set up. Elizur of Zebulun and Shelumiel of Simeon each present detailed sacrifices and offerings on the fourth and fifth days.

Princes Eliasaph of Gad and Elishama of Ephraim each present their detailed offerings of silver, gold, animals, and grain for the dedication of the altar after Moses set up and anointed the tabernacle.

God instructs Moses to tell Aaron how to light the seven lamps on the golden candlestick in the tabernacle. Then God commands Moses to purify the Levites with water, shaving, washing, and offerings to prepare them for service.

God instructs Moses to ceremonially purify the Levites with offerings and the laying on of hands by the Israelites, dedicating them to serve in the tabernacle under Aaron and his sons. This follows the instructions about the lampstand and purification rituals.

Princes Pagiel of Asher and Ahira of Naphtali each present their offerings to dedicate the altar after its anointing, continuing the sequence of sacrifices from the leaders of Israel’s twelve tribes at the tabernacle.

Moses records the offerings made by tribal leaders for the altar's dedication at the tabernacle in the wilderness, here detailing Ahiezer of Dan and Pagiel of Asher's sacrifices on the eleventh and twelfth days.

God instructs Moses that the Levites are dedicated to Him instead of the firstborn of Israel, given to Aaron's family to serve in the tabernacle and make atonement, and the Israelites obey these commands to purify and set apart the Levites.

Moses, Aaron, and Israel purified the Levites and set them apart for service at the tabernacle as God commanded. Levites began service at age 25 and retired at 50, then assisted without performing active duties.

Ahira, prince of Naphtali, completes the altar dedication offerings with oxen, rams, goats, and lambs. After all twelve tribal leaders present their gifts, Moses enters the tabernacle and hears God's voice from the mercy seat on the ark.

God instructs Moses in Sinai to have the Israelites observe Passover in its proper time. The people obey, but some men defiled by contact with a corpse cannot participate and ask Moses and Aaron for guidance.

The princes of Israel continue offering their sacrifices to dedicate the altar after its anointing; here Elishama of Ephraim and Gamaliel of Manasseh present their offerings as part of this twelve-day ceremony at the tabernacle.

Moses listens to men defiled by a dead body who missed Passover, then God instructs Moses to allow those unclean or traveling to observe Passover a month later, with the same rules applying to both Israelites and resident foreigners.
God instructs Moses that the Israelites' travel in the wilderness depends on the cloud over the tabernacle; they camp while it stays and journey when it moves, following God's command through Moses.

God instructs Moses that both native Israelites and resident foreigners must observe the Passover the same way. The cloud and fire over the tabernacle guide Israel’s movements in the wilderness, signaling when to camp or journey.

Princes Gamaliel of Manasseh and Abidan of Benjamin each present their offerings of silver, gold, animals, and flour to dedicate the altar after its anointing, continuing the daily sacrifices by tribal leaders at the tabernacle.

God instructs Moses to make two silver trumpets to signal the assembly and the camps of Israel during their travels and battles, with priests blowing them as a lasting ordinance for communication and divine remembrance.

The princes of Israel continue offering sacrifices to dedicate the altar after its anointing; Abidan of Benjamin and Ahiezer of Dan present their offerings, including silver vessels, flour, incense, and various animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings.

God instructs Moses on trumpet signals for war and festivals, then the Israelites begin their journey from Sinai to Paran, led by tribal leaders including Nahshon of Judah and Nethaneel of Issachar, following God's command through Moses.

Moses invites his father-in-law Hobab to join Israel's journey to the promised land. As they travel from Mount Sinai, the ark leads them, guided by God's cloud, with Moses praying for God's protection and presence among the people.

Moses organizes the Israelite tribes for their journey from Sinai, naming leaders for each tribe and assigning the Gershonites, Merarites, and Kohathites to carry the tabernacle and sanctuary as the camp sets out.

Moses organizes the Israelite tribes for their journey, naming leaders for Benjamin, Dan, Asher, and Naphtali. He invites his father-in-law Hobab to join them for guidance in the wilderness, promising blessings in return, but Hobab initially declines.

After the Israelites complained during their journey, God's anger caused a fire in the camp, which Moses prayed to stop. The people then longed for meat, recalling the food they ate in Egypt, while they continued to gather and eat manna provided by God.

Moses questions how to provide meat for 600,000 Israelites for a month, doubting resources. God challenges Moses' doubt, then shares His spirit with seventy elders, who begin prophesying, showing God's power and support for Moses.

As manna falls with the dew, the Israelites complain loudly for meat, angering God and frustrating Moses, who feels overwhelmed by leading the people and pleads with God for relief from his heavy burden.

God transfers some of Moses' spirit to seventy elders, enabling them to prophesy; Eldad and Medad also prophesy in the camp, causing a discussion with Joshua. Then, God sends quails to the Israelites near the camp as food.

Moses expresses his distress to God over leading Israel alone, and God instructs him to gather seventy elders to share leadership. God promises to provide meat for the people for a month, despite their complaints about leaving Egypt.

Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses for marrying an Ethiopian woman and question his unique role as God's prophet. God responds directly to all three at the tabernacle, affirming Moses' special status and expressing anger at their challenge.

God sends a wind bringing quails around the Israelite camp to satisfy their craving for meat, but His anger leads to a deadly plague. The place is named Kibrothhattaavah, and the people then move on to Hazeroth.

After Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses, God's anger causes Miriam to become leprous. Aaron pleads for mercy, and Moses prays for her healing. Miriam is isolated for seven days before the Israelites continue their journey from Hazeroth to Paran.

The spies report to Moses and the Israelites about the various peoples living in Canaan, including the Amalekites and giants. Caleb urges immediate conquest, but the others fear the inhabitants' strength and spread discouraging news.

The twelve spies sent by Moses explore Canaan, gathering fruit as evidence of its fertility. After 40 days, they report back at Kadesh in Paran, describing the land's abundance but also its strong, walled cities and formidable inhabitants.

Moses names Oshea as Jehoshua and sends leaders from each tribe to scout Canaan, instructing them to assess the land, its people, cities, and produce. They explore from Zin to Rehob, visit Hebron, and gather fruit at the brook Eshcol.

God instructs Moses to send one leader from each tribe of Israel to scout the land of Canaan, which God promised to the Israelites. Moses selects these twelve men, all heads of their tribes, and renames Oshea as Jehoshua.

After the spies' fearful report, the Israelites cry out in despair, blaming Moses and Aaron and wanting to return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb urge the people to trust God and enter the good land they explored.

Caleb and Joshua encourage Israel not to fear the land's inhabitants, trusting God's promise. The people react angrily, and God's glory appears. God threatens punishment, but Moses pleads for mercy, citing God's reputation among Egypt and Canaan.

Moses pleads with God not to destroy the Israelites despite their rebellion, reminding Him of His mercy and the nations' perception of His power. God agrees to forgive but declares His glory will fill the earth.

Moses warns the Israelites not to attack the Amalekites and Canaanites without God's presence, but they disobey and are defeated near Hormah, showing the consequences of their rebellion after the negative report about the land.

God declares that those Israelites who repeatedly disobeyed and doubted Him will not enter the Promised Land, except Caleb, but their bodies will die in the wilderness; He commands Moses and Aaron to tell the people their punishment.

God declares judgment on the rebellious Israelites who doubted His promise, causing them to die in the wilderness except for Joshua and Caleb. Moses warns the people not to attack the land, but they insist on going despite the risk.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about specific offerings involving flour, oil, and wine for burnt sacrifices, emphasizing that both native-born Israelites and resident foreigners must follow the same laws and rituals when making these offerings.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about specific offerings to make when they enter the promised land, detailing the amounts of flour, oil, and wine to accompany burnt offerings of lambs, rams, or bulls.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel how to make offerings for unintentional sins, including communal and individual sacrifices, so that both Israelites and foreigners living among them can receive forgiveness through the priest's atonement.

God instructs Moses on how to handle unintentional sins with atonement, but presumption against God's commands leads to severe punishment. A man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is caught, detained, and sentenced to death by stoning as commanded by God.

God commands Moses that a man who broke the Sabbath by gathering sticks is to be stoned by the Israelite community outside the camp. Then God instructs Moses to tell Israel to wear blue fringes on their garments as a reminder to obey His commandments.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel that both natives and foreigners must follow the same laws, including offering the first dough as a gift when they enter the promised land, and if they sin unknowingly, the whole community must offer specific sacrifices for atonement.
Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and On lead 250 Israelite leaders to challenge Moses and Aaron's authority, claiming all are holy. Moses responds by proposing a test with censers to show whom God has chosen.

Moses challenges Korah and the Levites who rebel against his leadership, reminding them of their special role serving at the tabernacle, while Dathan and Abiram refuse to meet Moses, accusing him of selfishly ruling over Israel.

Korah leads a rebellion against Moses and Aaron at the tabernacle. God's glory appears, warning Moses and Aaron to separate from the crowd. Moses tells the people to move away from Korah, Dathan, and Abiram's tents to avoid punishment.

Moses warns the Israelites that if Korah, Dathan, and Abiram die naturally, he is not sent by God, but if the earth swallows them alive, they have defied God. Then the ground splits and swallows them and their families alive.

After Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and their followers rebelled against Moses and Aaron, the earth swallowed them alive, and fire consumed 250 men offering incense. God instructs Moses to make their censers a memorial to warn against unauthorized priestly duties.

God declares that all Israelites aged twenty and above who rebelled will die in the wilderness and not enter Canaan, except Caleb and Joshua; their children will wander for 40 years as punishment for their distrust during the land survey.

Moses instructs Aaron to use incense to stop a deadly plague among the Israelites, which began after Korah's rebellion. Aaron intercedes, standing between the living and dead, halting the plague that killed over 14,700 people.

God instructs Moses to collect a rod from each tribal leader, including Aaron's from Levi, to place in the tabernacle as a sign. The next day, Aaron's rod miraculously blooms, confirming his chosen status and ending Israel's complaints.

The next day, Moses finds Aaron's rod blossomed in the tabernacle, confirming God's choice of Aaron's priesthood. God instructs Moses to keep the rod as a sign to stop Israel's complaints, but the people fear death near the tabernacle.

After Korah's rebellion is punished, Moses instructs Aaron to use censers as a memorial to prevent unauthorized incense offerings. The people then accuse Moses and Aaron of killing God's people, prompting a divine warning and Moses sending Aaron to make atonement to stop a plague.

God instructs Aaron that he and his sons will bear responsibility for the sanctuary's sins, while the Levites, Aaron's relatives, will assist in tabernacle duties but must avoid the sanctuary's sacred vessels to prevent death.

God tells Aaron that the Levites are given to him as a gift to serve in the tabernacle, and Aaron and his sons are appointed as priests to handle offerings and sacred duties, with strict rules about holiness and access.

God instructs Aaron about redeeming certain firstborn animals and the offerings from Israel, granting Aaron and his family a perpetual priestly share. God also assigns the Levites a tenth of Israel as their inheritance for their tabernacle service.

God is instructing Aaron about the sacred portions of offerings and firstfruits that belong to him and his family as priests, detailing what they may eat and how to redeem firstborn humans and unclean animals in Israel.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on the ritual of the red heifer for purification. The one who burns it and the one who gathers its ashes must wash and be unclean until evening. Touching a dead body causes seven days of uncleanness unless purified.

God tells Moses that the Levites receive a tenth of Israel's tithes as their inheritance for serving at the tabernacle, forbidding Israelites from approaching it. The Levites must offer a tenth of their tithes back to the LORD as a sacred offering.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on purification laws: anyone touching a dead body without proper cleansing defiles the tabernacle and is cut off from Israel. Those in a tent with a dead person and uncovered vessels become unclean for seven days.

God instructs Moses and Aaron to tell Israel to bring a flawless red heifer for Eleazar the priest to sacrifice outside the camp; its blood is sprinkled, and the heifer is burned with cedar, hyssop, and scarlet, while the priest and burner become temporarily unclean.

God instructs Moses and Aaron on purification rituals for those who touch dead bodies or graves, detailing the use of ashes from the red heifer mixed with water, sprinkled by a clean person, to restore cleanliness over seven days among the Israelites.
The Israelites arrive at Kadesh in the desert of Zin, where Miriam dies. Facing no water, the people complain bitterly to Moses and Aaron, who then seek God's guidance at the tabernacle.

God instructs Moses to tell the Levites to offer a tenth of their tithes as a special offering to Aaron the priest, which they and their families may eat as their reward for serving in the tabernacle, ensuring they do not defile holy things.

Moses and Aaron meet with God at the tabernacle after the Israelites complain of no water in Kadesh. God commands Moses to speak to a rock to provide water, but Moses strikes it twice instead, leading to God's judgment against them.

Korah, Dathan, and Abiram accuse Moses of leading them to death without promised land, refusing to come up. Moses defends himself, challenges Korah's group to offer incense before the LORD, and the LORD's glory appears to all at the tabernacle.

God tells Moses and Aaron they won't lead Israel into Canaan because they disobeyed at Meribah. Moses then sends a peaceful request to Edom's king for passage through his land, but Edom refuses and threatens war.

The Israelites request passage through Edom's land near Kadesh but are denied and threatened with force. They then travel to Mount Hor, where God commands Moses to transfer Aaron's priestly garments to his son Eleazar before Aaron dies, marking the end of his leadership.

God instructs Moses to remove Aaron's priestly garments and give them to his son Eleazar on Mount Hor, where Aaron dies. Moses and Eleazar descend, and the entire Israelite community mourns Aaron's death for thirty days.
Israelite forces, led by Moses, confront Og, king of Bashan, at Edrei after defeating Sihon. God assures Moses of victory, and Israel kills Og and his people, taking possession of his territory.

Israelites, led by Moses, request passage through Amorite king Sihon's land near Moab, promising not to harm crops or water. Sihon refuses and attacks, but Israel defeats him, taking control of his territory including Heshbon and surrounding cities.

This passage describes Israel's conquest of Amorite lands under Moses' leadership, focusing on King Sihon's city Heshbon and the defeat of Moab and Amorite territories, leading to Israel's settlement there and the upcoming battle with King Og of Bashan.

After Aaron's death on Mount Hor, Israel faces conflict with King Arad in the south; Israel vows to destroy his cities if victorious. They defeat Arad, but then complain about hardships, leading God to send fiery serpents until they repent and Moses prays for them.
After Israel camped near Moab by Jericho, King Balak of Moab feared their growing power and sent messengers to Balaam, a diviner in Pethor, asking him to curse Israel to help defeat them.

Balaam initially refuses Balak's request to curse Israel, but after Balak sends more prestigious messengers and promises rewards, Balaam seeks God's guidance. God permits him to go but commands him to only speak God's words.

Balak, king of Moab, fears Israel's power and sends elders to hire Balaam to curse them. Balaam consults God, who forbids cursing Israel because they are blessed, so Balaam tells the Moabite princes he cannot go with them.

After Israelites were bitten by fiery serpents sent by God for their complaints, they confessed to Moses, who prayed; God instructed him to make a brass serpent on a pole to heal the bitten. Then Israel continued camping near Moab's border.

Balaam sets out with Moabite princes despite God's warning, but God sends an angel to block his path. Balaam's donkey sees the angel and tries to avoid it, leading Balaam to strike the donkey multiple times.

Balaam's donkey miraculously speaks after Balaam beats her for veering off the path; then Balaam sees the angel blocking his way, who explains the donkey saved his life by avoiding the angel's sword. Balaam admits his sin and offers to turn back.

The Israelites camp near the Arnon River, marking Moab's border, recalling past battles. They reach Beer, where God provides water, leading to a song of praise. They then journey through Moabite territory toward Pisgah, overlooking Jeshimon.

After Balaam's encounter with the angel, he agrees to go with Balak's princes but must only speak God's words. Balak meets Balaam near Arnon, offers sacrifices, and takes him to a high place to view the Israelites camped below.

Balaam instructs King Balak of Moab to build seven altars and prepare sacrifices. After offering them, Balaam meets God, who gives him a message to bless Israel instead of cursing them, despite Balak's request.

Balaam, summoned by Balak to curse Israel, blesses them instead after God speaks through him. Balak, frustrated, takes Balaam to a new vantage point at Pisgah to try again, where God again gives Balaam a message to deliver.

Balaam prophesies Israel's strength like a lion, refusing to curse them as God commands. Balak, frustrated, takes Balaam to another high place, Peor, where Balaam again requests altars and sacrifices to seek God's message.

God speaks to Balaam again, instructing him to tell Balak that he must bless Israel, not curse them. Balaam proclaims God's unwavering promise to protect and empower Israel, describing their strength and divine favor despite Balak's hopes.

Balaam, seeing God’s favor on Israel, stops using magic and instead prophesies over Israel’s tribes in the wilderness. He praises their strength and future kingdom, recalling their deliverance from Egypt and their power over enemies.

Balaam, preparing to leave, tells Balak he will reveal Israel's future actions. He prophesies Israel's rising power over Moab, Edom, Amalek, and the Kenites, highlighting their eventual defeat or captivity.

Balaam pronounces prophecies about the Kenites, Asshur, and Eber, foretelling their downfall and captivity. After delivering these oracles, Balaam and Balak part ways, concluding Balaam’s series of blessings and judgments on Israel’s neighbors.

While Israel camped at Shittim, many Israelites engaged in idolatry and immorality with Moabite women, provoking God's anger. Moses ordered punishment, and Phinehas stopped a plague by killing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman publicly.

Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, kills an Israelite leader Zimri and Midianite woman Cozbi to stop a deadly plague caused by Israel's idolatry with Moabite gods, earning God's covenant of peace and an everlasting priesthood for his zeal.

This passage identifies Cozbi, a Midianite leader's daughter killed during Israel's sin at Peor, and records God's command to Moses to attack the Midianites for leading Israel into idolatry and causing a deadly plague.

Balaam, under God's influence, blesses Israel with powerful imagery of strength and protection, angering Balak who wanted curses instead. Balaam reminds Balak he must obey God's commands, not his own desires, and offers to reveal Israel's future.
Moses and Eleazar continue the census of Israelite tribes in Moab near Jericho, listing families of Gad, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, along with their population numbers after the recent plague.

After a deadly plague, God instructs Moses and Eleazar to count all Israelite men over twenty able to fight. Moses and Eleazar begin this census in Moab near Jericho, starting with the tribe of Reuben and its family groups.

Moses and Eleazar recount the families of the tribe of Reuben, including Dathan and Abiram who rebelled with Korah and were swallowed by the earth, then list the families of Simeon and Gad during the census in Moab near Jericho.

Moses and Eleazar count the families of Zebulun and Joseph's sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, listing their clans and numbers in the plains of Moab near Jericho after the plague. Zelophehad's daughters are noted for inheritance purposes.

Moses and Eleazar continue the census of Israelite tribes in Moab, listing the families and numbers of Manasseh, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Dan, as part of organizing the people for land inheritance after the plague.
Moses and Eleazar count the Israelite tribes of Dan, Asher, and Naphtali by their families in the plains of Moab near Jericho, continuing the census after the plague to prepare for land inheritance.

Moses receives God's command to divide the land of Canaan among the 600,730 Israelites counted by tribe, with larger portions for larger tribes. The Levite families are also listed, noting Kohath as the father of Amram.

God affirms the daughters of Zelophehad's claim to their father's inheritance and sets inheritance laws for Israel. Then God tells Moses to view the Promised Land from Mount Abarim before he dies, like Aaron before him.

Moses and Eleazar count the Levite families near Jericho, listing Aaron and Moses' lineage. None of the Sinai generation remain alive except Caleb and Joshua, as God had decreed they would die in the wilderness.

The daughters of Zelophehad, from the tribe of Manasseh, approach Moses and the leaders at the tabernacle to claim their deceased father's inheritance since he had no sons. God affirms their right to inherit among their father's family.

God tells Moses he will soon die because of his past disobedience at Meribah, then Moses asks God to appoint a leader for Israel. God commands Moses to commission Joshua publicly as the new leader before Eleazar and the people.

God instructs Moses to publicly appoint Joshua as leader before Eleazar the priest and all Israel, symbolizing the transfer of authority so the people will obey Joshua; Moses follows these commands, laying hands on Joshua to officially commission him.

God instructs Moses on daily and special offerings for Israel, including sin offerings and burnt offerings during festivals like the Feast of Firstfruits, emphasizing holy convocations and no work on these sacred days.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites to regularly offer two spotless lambs daily as burnt offerings, one in the morning and one in the evening, with accompanying flour, oil, and wine, as a continual sacrifice made at Mount Sinai.

God instructs Moses on monthly burnt offerings with specific drink offerings, plus a sin offering goat. He also commands the Passover and seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread with detailed sacrifices and holy rest days for Israel.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about additional offerings and a holy assembly on the tenth day of the seventh month, including specific burnt offerings and a sin offering, to be made alongside regular monthly and daily sacrifices.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites about the holy convocation on the first day of the seventh month, a day of trumpet blowing and specific burnt offerings, including bullocks, rams, lambs, and a goat for atonement, alongside regular sacrifices.

God instructs Moses on the specific burnt offerings Israel must present daily, weekly on the Sabbath, and monthly, detailing the animals, flour, oil, and wine to be offered as sacrifices pleasing to the LORD.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites the specific burnt offerings and sin offerings to present on the second and third days of the Feast in the seventh month, detailing the number of animals and accompanying meat and drink offerings.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites detailed offerings for the Feast in the seventh month, specifying daily burnt offerings of bulls, rams, lambs, and goats for sin, along with accompanying meat and drink offerings.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about sin offerings and the seven-day feast in the seventh month, including specific burnt offerings of bullocks, rams, lambs, and goats, along with their accompanying meat and drink offerings.

Moses addresses Israel's tribal leaders, relaying God's commands about vows: men must keep their promises to God, and young women’s vows are valid unless their father or husband objects when they hear them.

Moses instructs the Israelites on the sacrifices for the sixth and seventh days of the seventh month's festival, detailing offerings of bullocks, rams, lambs, and goats alongside meat and drink offerings, continuing the prescribed worship rituals.

Moses instructs Israel's tribal leaders on vows, explaining that a husband can confirm or nullify his wife's vows made in his presence, while vows by widows or divorced women remain binding. This clarifies family authority over vows.

God commands Moses to lead Israel in war against the Midianites for their past offenses. Moses organizes 12,000 soldiers, one thousand from each tribe, led by Phinehas, to attack Midian, killing all the men and capturing women, children, and livestock.

Moses instructs the Israelites on the offerings for the eighth day of the seventh month festival, emphasizing a solemn assembly with no work and specific burnt and sin offerings, continuing the detailed sacrificial rituals commanded by the LORD.

Moses orders the Israelite soldiers to kill Midianite males and women who had relations with men, sparing only virgin girls. They must stay outside the camp for seven days and purify themselves, their captives, and belongings according to priest Eleazar's instructions.

Moses explains God's laws about vows made by women, stating a husband can confirm or nullify his wife's vows; if he remains silent, the vows stand, but if he later cancels them, he is responsible for the consequences.

After defeating Midian, the Israelites captured women, children, and livestock, burned their cities, and brought the spoils to Moses and Eleazar at Moab. Moses angrily confronts the army leaders for sparing women who led Israel into sin.

After the battle against Midian, God instructs Moses and Eleazar to purify the soldiers, count the spoils, divide them between warriors and the whole community, and give a portion as an offering to the Lord and to the Levites. Moses obeys.

Moses and Eleazar follow God's command to divide the spoils from the Midianite battle, counting thousands of animals and captives, and giving a portion as a tribute to the Lord through Eleazar the priest.

Moses gives the LORD’s portion of the war spoils to Eleazar the priest and distributes the rest among the Israelites and Levites. The army officers report no losses and offer gold jewelry as a gift to the LORD.

The military leaders of Israel present a gold offering from their personal spoils to Moses and Eleazar as atonement, which is then brought into the tabernacle as a memorial for the people, concluding the campaign against Midian.

Moses reminds the tribes of Gad and Reuben how their ancestors discouraged Israel from entering Canaan after spying the land, causing God's anger and 40 years of wandering; he warns them not to repeat this sin or risk God's judgment again.

The tribes of Reuben and Gad, seeing the fertile land of Gilead suitable for their large cattle herds, request Moses and Eleazar to settle there instead of crossing the Jordan. Moses recalls their ancestors' failure to trust God's promise.

Moses warns Gad and Reuben that refusing to join Israel's battle is sin, but they promise to fight armed alongside Israel before settling in Gilead. Moses then instructs leaders to grant them land if they fulfill this vow.

This passage lists the Israelites' journey stops as they travel through the wilderness toward the Promised Land, moving from Libnah to Mount Hor near Edom's border, continuing their forty-year desert wanderings under Moses' leadership.

Moses records the Israelites' journey from Egypt, detailing their crossing of the Red Sea and travels through various wilderness locations, including Marah, Elim, and Sinai, as they move toward the Promised Land.

The Israelites camped at Mount Hor near Edom, where Aaron died as commanded by God. After his death, they continued their journey through various locations in Moab, camping near the Jordan River close to Jericho.

Moses records the Israelites' journey from Egypt, led by him and Aaron, starting from Rameses after the Passover. They travel through Succoth, Etham, and cross the sea near Pihahiroth, camping at Marah in the wilderness of Etham.

Moses warns the tribes of Gad and Reuben that turning away from God will bring disaster. They promise to build homes east of the Jordan but will fight armed alongside Israel until the land is conquered, seeking Moses' approval.

The tribes of Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh agree to fight alongside Israel before settling east of the Jordan. Moses grants them lands taken from Amorite kings Sihon and Og, and they build cities and secure territories in Gilead.

God instructs Moses to tell the Israelites the precise boundaries of the land of Canaan they will inherit, detailing the southern, western, and northern borders as they prepare to enter and settle the land.

God instructs Moses to define the northern and eastern borders of Canaan, detailing landmarks from Ziphron to the Salt Sea. Moses then tells Israel that nine tribes and half a tribe have received their land east of the Jordan near Jericho.

God tells Moses the leaders from each Israelite tribe, including Eleazar and Joshua, who will oversee dividing the land of Canaan as inheritance, noting that Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh already received land east of the Jordan near Jericho.

God instructs Moses to enforce strict justice for murderers and protect cities of refuge until the high priest dies, emphasizing that shedding innocent blood defiles the land where God dwells with Israel.

God instructs Moses to set laws distinguishing intentional murder from accidental killing, establishing cities of refuge where unintentional killers can seek protection until the high priest's death, ensuring fair judgment among Israel.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel to allocate 48 cities to the Levites in Canaan, including six designated as cities of refuge where those who accidentally kill can seek protection until judged. This follows the division of tribal inheritances.

God instructs Moses on the plains of Moab near Jericho to command Israel to allocate cities and surrounding lands to the Levites, including six designated cities of refuge for those who accidentally kill someone.

God instructs Moses to designate six cities—three east and three west of the Jordan—as refuges for those who kill unintentionally, while defining murder and the role of the avenger of blood in punishing intentional killers among Israel and foreigners.

God instructs Moses to tell Israel about cities of refuge for accidental killers, who must stay there until the high priest dies; if they leave early, they can be killed without guilt. Murderers require two witnesses and cannot be ransomed.

Moses relays God's command to the Israelites, affirming the tribe of Joseph's concern that Zelophehad's daughters marry within their father's tribe to keep land inheritance within each tribe, preserving tribal boundaries in Israel.

Leaders from the Gilead family of Manasseh approach Moses and Israel's leaders to discuss concerns about Zelophehad's daughters inheriting land, fearing their marriage outside the tribe could shift tribal land boundaries; Moses agrees with their point.

Near the Jordan River by Jericho, God instructs Moses to tell Israel to conquer Canaan, remove its inhabitants and idols, and divide the land by lot among tribes, warning that failure to drive out the people will bring trouble.

Moses confirms God's command that the daughters of Zelophehad marry within their father's tribe to keep the inheritance in Manasseh. This law was given to the Israelites near Jericho in Moab, ensuring tribal land boundaries remain intact.

Moses addresses the Israelites near the Red Sea in Moab, recalling God's command from Horeb to leave Mount Sinai and journey toward the lands of the Amorites, Canaanites, and beyond, after defeating kings Sihon and Og.

Moses reminds the Israelites that God commanded them to journey to the land promised to their ancestors and possess it. He explains he cannot lead them alone due to their great number and appoints wise leaders to help govern, which the people agree to.

Moses recounts how the Israelites complained and doubted God's promise to give them Canaan after spies reported giants and fortified cities, leading God to declare that none of that generation would enter the promised land.

Moses recounts how the Israelites agreed to appoint leaders over groups for governance and justice, with Moses as final judge. They then left Horeb, traveled through the wilderness, and reached Kadeshbarnea near the Amorite territory God promised them.

Moses recounts God's judgment that the current generation, except Caleb and Joshua, will not enter Canaan due to their rebellion. The people admit their sin and prepare to fight as commanded, despite God's earlier warning.

Moses recounts how the Israelites admitted their sin and prepared to fight as God commanded, but God forbade it. They disobeyed, fought the Amorites, were defeated, mourned before God, and stayed in Kadesh for many days.

Moses recounts leading Israel around Mount Seir near Edom, instructing them to avoid conflict with Esau's descendants and buy provisions peacefully, as God has blessed their 40 years in the wilderness and guided their journey past Edom toward Moab.

Moses reminds the Israelites at Kadeshbarnea that God has given them the land of the Amorites and urges them to take it. They send twelve spies to scout the land, who report it is good, but the people rebel and complain, doubting God's promise.

Moses recounts Israel's journey past Esau's descendants in Seir and Moab's territory, where God commands them not to fight or take land. They cross the brook Zered after 38 years, during which the previous generation died as God had promised.

Moses recounts that 38 years passed from Kadeshbarnea to crossing the brook Zered, during which the adult warriors died as God had promised. Now God commands him to pass through Ar near Moab without attacking the Ammonites, whose land is reserved for Lot's descendants.
Moses recounts God's command to cross the Arnon River and possess Sihon’s land. Peaceful passage was requested, but Sihon refused, as God hardened his heart to allow Israel to defeat him in battle.

Moses instructs the Israelites not to fight the Ammonites, whose land God has given to them, and recounts the history of giants in the region. He then commands them to cross the Arnon River and prepare to battle Sihon, king of Heshbon.

Moses recounts how Sihon, king of Heshbon, refused Israel passage, leading to battle at Jahaz where Israel, by God's help, defeated Sihon and took his cities, except lands belonging to the Ammonites, which God forbade them to enter.

Moses asks God to let him enter the Promised Land, but God refuses and tells him to view it from Mount Pisgah instead. Moses is instructed to encourage Joshua, who will lead the people into the land beyond the Jordan River.

Moses recounts how the Israelites took livestock and spoils from defeated Amorite kings, gaining land from the Arnon River to Mount Hermon, including Bashan. He then allocated this territory to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.

Moses instructs the Reubenites and Gadites to lead armed before the other Israelites while their families stay in the land given to them until all tribes possess their territories. He encourages Joshua and prays to see the Promised Land beyond Jordan.

Moses recounts how the land of Bashan and Gilead, conquered from King Og, was divided among the tribes of Manasseh, Reuben, and Gad, with instructions for these tribes to lead armed before the rest of Israel into the promised land.

Moses addresses Israel, urging them to obey God's laws exactly to live and inherit the promised land. He reminds them of God's judgment on Baalpeor worshippers and highlights their unique relationship with God among nations.

Moses reminds Israel of God's close presence and unique laws given at Mount Horeb, urging them to remember and teach these commandments to future generations after witnessing God's powerful revelation in fire and voice.

Moses recounts how the Israelites, led by God, defeated Og king of Bashan and his people at Edrei, capturing all his fortified cities in the region of Argob and taking the spoils while destroying the inhabitants.

Moses reminds Israel at Horeb (Mount Sinai) that God gave them the Ten Commandments on stone tablets and instructed him to teach laws for their future land. He warns them not to make or worship idols or celestial bodies.

Moses warns Israel that if they disobey God and worship idols after settling in the promised land, they will be destroyed and scattered among nations, but if they sincerely seek God, they will find Him again.

Moses encourages Israel to seek God wholeheartedly, promising His mercy and faithfulness to their ancestors' covenant. He recalls God's unique acts of deliverance and wonders witnessed by the people during their time in Egypt.

Moses warns Israel not to worship the sun, moon, or stars, reminding them God freed them from Egypt and chose them as His people. He reveals God’s anger that Moses won't enter Canaan, urging them to keep God’s covenant and avoid idolatry.

Moses reminds Israel of God's powerful acts in Egypt and the wilderness, showing His unique authority and love by delivering them and giving them their land, urging them to recognize that the LORD alone is God over heaven and earth.

Moses addresses all Israel, reminding them of God's covenant made at Mount Horeb, where God spoke directly to them through fire. He recalls God's commandments, emphasizing exclusive worship and obedience as they prepare to enter the Promised Land.

The Israelites express fear of dying from hearing God's voice again during the Sinai encounter. God instructs Moses to listen and relay further commandments to the people, who are told to return to their tents while Moses remains to receive detailed laws.

Moses reminds Israel that the LORD is the only God and urges them to obey His laws for their well-being. He then designates three cities east of the Jordan as refuge for accidental killers, concluding his legal instructions after leading them from Egypt.

Moses addresses the Israelites, reminding them of God's commandments given at Mount Horeb, including honoring the Sabbath, respecting parents, and prohibitions against killing, adultery, and stealing, as part of the covenant before entering the Promised Land.

Moses recounts God's commandments, including prohibitions against stealing and coveting, given to the Israelites at Mount Horeb amid fire and darkness. The people, led by tribal heads and elders, express fear of dying from hearing God's voice again.

Moses reviews the laws he taught Israel after their Exodus, recalling their conquest of Amorite kings Sihon and Og east of the Jordan River, and the territory they took from Aroer by the Arnon River to Mount Hermon near Pisgah.

Moses continues instructing the Israelites before they enter Canaan, emphasizing the importance of obeying God's laws, loving God fully, and teaching these commandments to their children daily as a lasting covenant.

Moses is told by God to stay close as God will give him detailed laws to teach Israel, emphasizing strict obedience to God's commands for their well-being and long life in the promised land east of the Jordan River.

Moses instructs the Israelites to remember God's commandments by writing them on their homes and gates, warning them not to forget God after entering the promised land. He urges them to fear God, avoid other gods, and obey His laws faithfully.

Moses instructs the Israelites as they prepare to enter Canaan, warning them to destroy the seven nations there and avoid intermarriage to prevent idolatry, emphasizing their special status as God's chosen holy people.

Moses urges the Israelites to faithfully obey God's laws to live well and possess the promised land. He instructs them to teach their children about God's deliverance from Egypt and the importance of keeping His commandments for their protection and righteousness.

Moses reminds the Israelites that God chose them as a special people not for their numbers but because of His love and promises to their ancestors. He urges them to obey God's commandments, highlighting God's faithfulness and justice.

Moses urges the Israelites to obey God's commandments as they prepare to enter Canaan, describing the land's abundant resources and promising blessings if they remain faithful and thankful to God for the provision.

Moses instructs the Israelites to obey God's laws to receive His blessings in the promised land, including prosperity and health. He warns them to destroy enemy nations and not fear their numbers, trusting God's power to deliver them.

Moses encourages the Israelites not to fear the stronger nations in Canaan, reminding them of God's past deliverance from Egypt and promising God's ongoing support to gradually defeat these peoples and their kings.

Moses continues instructing the Israelites before entering Canaan, emphasizing total destruction of enemy kings and idols to avoid idolatry and curses, reinforcing God's command to keep the land holy and free from pagan influences.

Moses warns the Israelites to remember and thank God for the prosperous land He gives them, cautioning them not to forget Him or credit their own efforts when their wealth and success grow after entering Canaan.

Moses warns the Israelites not to credit their own strength for their wealth but to remember God, who grants them power to prosper and uphold His covenant; forgetting God and worshiping other gods will lead to their destruction like other nations.

Moses reminds the Israelites to obey God's commandments to live and inherit the promised land, recalling their 40 years in the wilderness where God tested and provided for them, teaching reliance on His word and urging reverence and obedience.

Moses reminds Israel that they are not receiving the land because of their goodness but because God promised it to their ancestors; he recalls their repeated rebellion and God's anger during their journey from Egypt to Horeb.

Moses tells Israel they will cross the Jordan River to conquer powerful nations, including the Anakim. He emphasizes God leads them and drives out these nations due to their wickedness, not Israel's righteousness, fulfilling God's promise to their ancestors.

Moses recalls how at Mount Horeb he stayed 40 days without food or water to receive God's stone tablets of the covenant, but God warned him to hurry down because the Israelites had already turned to idolatry by making a molten image.

Moses recounts God telling him to descend Mount Sinai quickly because the Israelites made a golden calf, breaking the covenant. God threatens to destroy them, but Moses intercedes, breaking the stone tablets in anger over their sin.

Moses recounts God instructing him to carve new stone tablets like the first, inscribe the Ten Commandments, and place them in a wooden ark. The Israelites then travel from Beeroth to Mosera, where Aaron dies and Eleazar becomes priest.

Moses recounts praying and fasting for 40 days to intercede for Israel's sins, including the golden calf incident and their repeated rebellion at places like Taberah and Kadeshbarnea, pleading for God's mercy despite their disobedience.

Moses reminds Israel that God owns the heavens and earth and chose them above all people. He urges them to be obedient, just, and loving to strangers, recalling their own time as foreigners in Egypt, and to serve God faithfully for His mighty deeds.

Moses recounts Israel's journey from Gudgodah to Jotbath, the Levites' special role as priests without land inheritance, his 40-day stay on the mountain, God's mercy, and calls Israel to obey and love God as they prepare to enter the promised land.

Moses reminds the Israelites that they have witnessed God's mighty deeds and urges them to obey His commandments to be strong and inherit the promised land, a fertile, rain-dependent land cared for by God, unlike Egypt where they were enslaved.

Moses recounts Israel's ongoing rebellion and describes his 40-day prayers to God, pleading for mercy to spare the people and uphold His promise to their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob despite their stubbornness and sin.

Moses urges the Israelites to love and obey God, reminding the adults present of God's powerful acts in Egypt, the Red Sea, wilderness, and the judgment on Dathan and Abiram, emphasizing their firsthand experience of God's mighty deeds.

Moses instructs the Israelites to keep God's commandments always in mind, teach them to their children, and display them visibly, promising long life and victory over nations as they enter and possess the promised land stretching from wilderness to the Euphrates.

Moses tells the Israelites they will possess vast lands from the wilderness to the Euphrates and sea, with God's protection. He sets before them blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience, instructing them to declare these on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal as they enter Canaan.

Moses tells the Israelites that God watches over the land they will possess and promises blessings like timely rain if they love and obey Him, warning them against idolatry which would bring drought and ruin. They must keep His words close to heart.

Moses instructs the Israelites on laws for worship in the promised land, emphasizing destroying pagan worship sites and bringing offerings only to the one place God will choose for His name to dwell. This follows their preparation to enter Canaan.

Moses instructs the Israelites that once they enter and settle safely in the Promised Land across the Jordan, they will bring offerings to the specific place God chooses, celebrating with their families and including the Levites who have no land inheritance.

Moses instructs the Israelites on proper worship after entering Canaan, emphasizing communal rejoicing with family and servants, centralized offerings at God's chosen place, and dietary rules including eating meat but not blood.

Moses instructs the Israelites on proper worship in the promised land, emphasizing not eating blood, eating offerings at the chosen place, caring for Levites, and allowing meat consumption even if the central sanctuary is far away.

Moses instructs the Israelites on proper worship in the land God gives them, warning against imitating the destroyed nations' idolatry and emphasizing strict obedience to God's commands for their well-being and future.

Moses instructs the Israelites that if the central sanctuary is too distant, they may slaughter and eat animals locally but must not consume blood, which represents life. Sacred offerings must still be brought to the chosen place for sacrifice.

Moses instructs the Israelites to execute any prophet or close relative who secretly urges them to worship other gods, emphasizing loyalty to God who delivered them from Egypt and the need to remove evil from their community.

Moses instructs the Israelites to execute anyone, even close relations, who tries to lead them to worship other gods, and if a whole city turns to idolatry, they must investigate and destroy it completely to prevent corruption among God's people.

Moses warns the Israelites that even if a prophet or dreamer performs signs urging them to worship other gods, they must not listen. This tests their loyalty to God, who delivered them from Egypt, and such false prophets must be put to death to remove evil.

Moses instructs the Israelites to completely destroy any city that turns to idolatry, burning it and its spoils to prevent rebuilding, so God may show mercy and bless them if they obey His commandments.

Moses instructs the Israelites, God's chosen people, on purity laws, forbidding mourning customs and detailing clean and unclean animals for food, emphasizing holiness and obedience to God's commands as they prepare to enter the Promised Land.

Moses instructs the Israelites on dietary laws, listing clean and unclean animals, fish, and birds they may or may not eat, emphasizing their holiness and separation from other nations by following God's commands in the land of Canaan.

Moses instructs the Israelites to bring their tithes to the designated place of worship chosen by God, or convert them to money if too far, to celebrate and honor God with their household and support the Levites who have no land inheritance.

Moses instructs the Israelites in the land God is giving them to cancel debts every seven years, releasing fellow Israelites from loans, but not foreigners. This law promotes social justice and blessings if they obey God's commands.

Moses instructs the Israelites on caring for the poor and releasing Hebrew servants after six years, providing generously for them upon freedom, and allowing lifelong servitude if they choose to stay, recalling their own past slavery in Egypt.

Moses instructs the Israelites to support the Levites, who have no land inheritance, by setting aside tithes every three years to share with them, along with strangers, orphans, and widows living in their towns, ensuring their provision and God's blessing.

Moses instructs the Israelites to celebrate Passover in the month of Abib, commemorating their night escape from Egypt. They must sacrifice and eat the Passover lamb at the designated place chosen by God, avoiding leavened bread for seven days.

Moses instructs the Israelites in the land God gave them to generously lend to their poor fellow Israelites without grudging, warning against withholding help due to the upcoming year of debt release, promising God's blessing for their kindness.

Moses instructs the Israelites to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles joyfully with family, servants, Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows in the place God chooses, remembering their past slavery in Egypt and God's blessings on their harvest.

Moses instructs the Israelites on how to handle servants who choose to stay beyond six years, marking them permanently with an ear pierced at the door. He also commands sanctifying firstborn male animals to God, with rules for their use and consumption.

Moses instructs the Israelites to sacrifice the Passover lamb at the place God will choose, eat unleavened bread for six days, hold a solemn assembly on the seventh, and celebrate the Feast of Weeks with offerings and communal rejoicing.

Moses instructs the Israelites to celebrate a seven-day feast of tabernacles at the place God chooses, appear before God thrice yearly with offerings, appoint fair judges, and avoid idolatry to live justly and inherit the promised land.

Moses instructs the Israelites not to eat animals that died naturally but to give or sell them to foreigners, forbids cooking a young goat in its mother's milk, and commands yearly tithing to be eaten before God at a designated place to foster reverence.

Moses instructs the Israelites on acceptable sacrifices and the punishment for idol worship within their towns, emphasizing the need for multiple witnesses before executing judgment to maintain justice and purity in the community.

Moses instructs the Israelites on executing witnesses in capital cases and resolving difficult legal disputes by consulting priests, Levites, and judges at a designated place chosen by God, emphasizing strict obedience to their rulings.

Moses instructs the Israelites on obeying the priests' and judges' legal decisions without deviation, warns against disobedience, and gives rules for choosing a king from among their own people once they settle in the land God gives them.

Moses instructs the Israelites not to adopt the pagan practices of the nations they will conquer, forbidding witchcraft and divination, emphasizing that such acts are detestable to God and cause those nations to be driven out.

Moses instructs Israel that the Levites, chosen to serve as priests, receive no land inheritance but live on offerings and firstfruits given by the people, ensuring their support as they minister in the place God will choose.

Moses instructs the Israelites on the conduct of their future king, emphasizing limits on horses, wives, and wealth to prevent pride and unfaithfulness. The king must keep a personal copy of the law to guide his rule in Israel.

Moses tells the Israelites that unlike other nations, they must not practice divination. God will raise a prophet like Moses for them to obey, warning that false prophets who speak without God's command will be punished, and their words can be tested by their fulfillment.

Moses instructs the Israelites in the laws God gave them about respecting property boundaries, requiring multiple witnesses for accusations, punishing false witnesses, and enforcing fair justice with equal retribution to maintain order in the promised land.

Moses instructs Israel's officers to allow men with unfinished personal commitments or fear to return home before battle, then appoints army captains; he also commands offering peace to a city before attacking, with terms if peace is accepted.

Moses instructs the Israelites to set aside three cities of refuge for accidental killers and add three more if their territory expands, emphasizing justice by punishing intentional murderers and protecting property boundaries in the land God gives them.

Moses instructs the Israelites that after God gives them the land by removing its current inhabitants, they must set aside three cities as safe havens for those who kill someone unintentionally, protecting them from revenge until a fair trial.

Moses instructs the Israelites before battle, assuring them God is with them. Priests encourage courage, and officers allow men with unfinished personal affairs—new homes, vineyards, or betrothals—to return home to avoid dying before enjoying these blessings.

Moses instructs the Israelites on warfare: if a city offers peace, its people become servants; if it resists, they must besiege it, kill the men, and take the women, children, livestock, and spoil as plunder, applying this to distant cities.

Moses instructs the Israelites on warfare rules: destroy all inhabitants of certain Canaanite cities given as inheritance to prevent idolatry, but preserve fruit trees during long sieges for food, cutting only non-edible trees for siege works.

Moses instructs Israel on treating captive women respectfully after war and on inheritance rights, emphasizing fairness when a firstborn son comes from a less favored wife, ensuring he receives his rightful double portion.

Moses instructs Israel's elders and judges on handling an unsolved murder found in the Promised Land, involving a ritual with a heifer in a valley near the nearest city to declare innocence and seek God's mercy.

The elders of a city near an unknown slain man declare their innocence and ask God to forgive Israel for innocent blood. Then, instructions are given for taking a captive woman as a wife during war, including rituals and a mourning period.

Moses instructs Israel on inheritance rights favoring the firstborn son, even if from a less loved wife, and prescribes stoning for a rebellious son, emphasizing community justice and purity laws about burial after execution in the promised land.

God gives Moses various laws for the Israelites, including rules about clothing, protecting bird nests, building safety, agricultural practices, and wearing fringes on garments, emphasizing holiness and care in daily life.

Moses instructs the Israelites on caring for lost or injured animals belonging to others, emphasizing responsibility and kindness. He also commands distinct clothing for men and women, reflecting cultural and religious norms.

Moses continues instructing Israel on laws about sexual conduct and marriage, detailing punishments for adultery, rape, and premarital relations, emphasizing justice and protection of women within the community.

Moses instructs Israel's elders on handling accusations against a bride's virginity, prescribing penalties for false claims and sexual sins to maintain community purity and justice in Israelite towns.

Moses instructs the Israelites on who may join their community, excluding certain groups and individuals due to physical condition or ancestry, and explains historical reasons for these rules, emphasizing purity and conduct during warfare.

Moses instructs the Israelites on maintaining purity and holiness in their camp during military campaigns, including rules for those ceremonially unclean and escaped servants, emphasizing God's presence among them and justice within the community.

God instructs the Israelites to make fringes on their clothing as a reminder of His laws. If a husband falsely accuses his wife of not being a virgin, her parents present proof to the city elders, who then punish the husband and ensure the marriage remains.

Moses instructs the Israelites on keeping vows made to God and permits them to eat freely from a neighbor’s vineyard or field by hand, but forbids taking produce away, emphasizing respect for others’ property during their journey to possess the land.

Moses instructs the Israelites on divorce laws, remarriage restrictions, and a husband's duty to support his new wife for a year. He also forbids pledging essential tools like millstones, emphasizing fairness and respect in community life.

Moses instructs the Israelites on fair treatment in lending and pledges, forbidding taking essential tools as collateral and condemning kidnapping. He reminds them to follow Levitical laws on leprosy and recalls God's punishment of Miriam after Egypt.

Moses instructs the Israelites on fair treatment of the poor and hired workers, timely payment of wages, just legal judgments, and remembering their own past slavery in Egypt as a reason to act with compassion and justice.

Moses instructs the Israelites on fair legal judgments, limiting punishment to 40 lashes, and introduces the levirate marriage law where a brother must marry his deceased brother’s widow to preserve his family line in Israel.

Moses instructs the Israelites to leave parts of their harvest for the vulnerable—strangers, orphans, and widows—reminding them of their own past slavery in Egypt and God's redemption, emphasizing compassion and justice in their land.

Moses instructs the Israelites on how to treat escaped servants, forbidding oppression and certain immoral practices, and commands fair lending among brethren. He emphasizes the importance of fulfilling vows made to God during their journey to the Promised Land.

Moses instructs Israel on levirate marriage: if a man dies childless, his brother must marry the widow to preserve the family name; refusal leads to public shame. Also, laws forbid dishonest weights and harsh punishment for a woman harming another during a fight.

Moses instructs the Israelites on honest trade practices, forbidding dishonest weights and measures, and commands them to remember Amalek's attack during their Exodus journey, promising to erase Amalek's memory once they settle in the Promised Land.

Moses instructs the Israelites on rejoicing with their families and sharing tithes with Levites, strangers, orphans, and widows, affirming obedience to God's commands and purity in offering these gifts after entering the promised land.

Moses instructs the Israelites on presenting their firstfruits to the priest at the chosen place, recounting their history from a humble ancestor to a great nation freed from Egyptian bondage and settled in the promised land flowing with milk and honey.

The speaker declares obedience to God's commands regarding offerings and asks for God's blessing on Israel and their promised land. This follows instructions for presenting firstfruits and emphasizes Israel's covenant with God upon entering Canaan.

Moses and Israel's elders instruct the people to obey God's commandments and, upon crossing the Jordan River into Canaan, to set up plastered stones on Mount Ebal with the law written on them, build an altar of uncut stones, and offer sacrifices to God.

Moses instructs the Israelites that upon entering and settling in the promised land, they must bring the first fruits to the priest at the designated place of worship as a sign of gratitude and fulfillment of God's promise to their ancestors.

Moses and the Levite priests instruct Israel to write God's law on stones at Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, where tribes will pronounce blessings and curses as a covenant reminder when entering Canaan after crossing the Jordan River.

Moses continues addressing the Israelites, promising blessings like abundant rain, prosperity, and leadership if they obey God's commandments, but warning of curses in city, field, and possessions if they disobey and worship other gods.

Moses continues speaking to the Israelites, promising blessings on their possessions, land, and offspring if they obey God's commandments, highlighting God's faithfulness to their ancestors and the prosperity they will experience in the promised land.
