Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, they will be defeated by enemies, scattered among nations, suffer diseases, madness, and loss of property, and face personal and communal devastation in the land God gave them.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, they will face severe curses including disease, defeat by enemies, and exile from the land God promised them. This follows blessings promised for obedience.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, they will become a disgrace among nations, suffer crop failures, lose their children to captivity, and be dominated by foreigners, reversing their fortunes in the land God gave them.

Moses tells the Israelites that if they obey God's commandments, God will bless them abundantly in their cities, fields, families, and possessions, and will defeat their enemies in the land He is giving them.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, they will suffer severe losses: their livestock taken, children exiled, land consumed by strangers, and they will be afflicted with incurable diseases and exile to foreign nations, becoming a disgrace among all peoples.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, their enemies will besiege their cities in the land God gave them, causing such desperation that even family bonds will break under extreme distress and famine.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, a distant, fierce nation will conquer them, besiege their cities, destroy their land's produce, and oppress them severely throughout the land God gave them.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's law, severe famine and siege will cause desperate acts, including family betrayal and cannibalism, followed by prolonged plagues and diseases like those experienced in Egypt.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God, they will be scattered among foreign nations, forced to serve other gods, live in fear and unrest, and ultimately be taken back to Egypt in captivity, sold as slaves to their enemies.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, He will bring upon them severe diseases and plagues, drastically reduce their population, destroy their land, and scatter them among foreign nations where they will serve unknown gods.

Moses addresses all Israel in Moab, recalling God's miracles in Egypt and their 40 years in the wilderness, including battles won against Sihon and Og. He urges them to keep the covenant for their prosperity.

Moses urges all Israelites in Moab, including leaders and families, to uphold the covenant with God, promising that by doing so, God will establish them as His chosen people, fulfilling promises made to their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Moses addresses all Israel in Moab, reminding them that God's covenant extends beyond their generation, warning against turning to foreign gods despite witnessing their abominations, and cautioning those who ignore curses while falsely trusting in their own peace.

Moses warns Israel that anyone who ignores these curses and falsely believes they are safe will face God's anger and be cut off from Israel, leading future generations and foreigners to witness the land's devastation like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.

Moses warns the Israelites in Moab that if they abandon God's covenant, their land will become desolate like Sodom and Gomorrah, and they will be exiled. He emphasizes that God's hidden plans are His alone, but His revealed laws are for their obedience.

Moses speaks to the Israelites, promising that if they repent and obey God after being scattered among nations, God will gather them back to their ancestral land, bless them, and soften their hearts to love Him fully, while punishing their enemies.

Moses tells the Israelites that if they return to God and obey His commandments, God will bless them abundantly and defeat their enemies. The law is accessible and near, not distant or hidden, so they can follow it faithfully.

Moses and the Levites pronounce a series of curses on Mount Ebal, addressing various sins against neighbors, justice, and family, with the people responding "Amen" to affirm their commitment to obey God's law upon entering the Promised Land.

Moses urges the Israelites to choose life by loving and obeying God, promising blessings in the Promised Land, but warns that turning to other gods will bring death and exile, emphasizing the choice between life and death before them.

Moses encourages Joshua before all Israel to be strong and lead them into the promised land, assuring God's presence. Moses then gives the law to the Levite priests and elders, commanding its public reading every seven years during the Feast of Tabernacles.

Moses addresses all Israel, announcing his age and that God has forbidden him to enter Canaan. He assures them God will lead and defeat their enemies, appoints Joshua as leader, and encourages courage and trust in God's presence.

God appears to Moses in the tabernacle and warns him that after Moses dies, the Israelites will abandon God for foreign gods, leading to punishment. God instructs Moses to write a song as a witness against Israel’s future unfaithfulness.

Moses instructs Israel to gather everyone every seven years at the chosen place to hear the law, ensuring all, including children and foreigners, learn to fear God. God then tells Moses to call Joshua to the tabernacle as Moses' death nears.

Moses instructs Israel to write and teach a song as a future witness against them when they turn from God after entering the promised land. He then charges Joshua to lead Israel courageously into that land, assuring God's presence.

Moses charges Joshua to lead Israel into Canaan and finishes writing the law, instructing the Levites to place it by the ark as a witness. He warns Israel's leaders of future rebellion after his death and recites a song as a testimony.

Moses recounts how God chose and cared for Israel (Jacob) in the wilderness, providing abundantly, but Israel (Jeshurun) became complacent and turned to worshiping foreign gods, provoking God's anger.

Moses continues his song to Israel, warning of God's judgment and vengeance against those who forsake Him, emphasizing God's unique power to give life and execute justice, and declaring His eternal sovereignty over all.

Moses addresses heaven and earth, proclaiming God's perfect justice and faithfulness, while warning Israel for their corruption. He recalls God's care for Israel, chosen as His special inheritance among all nations.

Moses warns Israel that they will abandon God for false gods, provoking His anger. God will hide His face and bring severe punishments, including famine, wild beasts, and destruction, as consequences for their unfaithfulness.

Moses warns Israel of severe punishments for their future disobedience, describing destruction and suffering caused by enemies and divine judgment, contrasting Israel's true God with false gods and corrupt nations symbolized by Sodom and Gomorrah.

Moses warns Israel that God will judge and avenge His enemies but show mercy to His people. Moses and Joshua (Hoshea) finish reciting the song, urging Israel to obey God's law for their survival and prosperity in the promised land.

Moses warns the Israelites that if they disobey God's commandments, they will become subservient to their enemies, suffering hardship and oppression until destruction, as a consequence of not serving God joyfully despite His blessings.

Moses blesses Israel before his death, recalling God's presence from Sinai, Seir, and Paran. He affirms the law given to Jacob's descendants and prays for the tribes of Reuben and Judah's strength and protection.

Moses blesses the tribes of Israel before his death, highlighting God's protection over Benjamin, abundant blessings on Joseph's land, and joy for Zebulun and Issachar, continuing his final words to the gathered tribes in the wilderness.

Moses tells Israel to obey God's law for life and blessing. God then commands Moses to climb Mount Nebo in Moab, view Canaan, but die there due to his earlier disobedience at Meribah, like Aaron before him.

Moses blesses the tribes of Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher, highlighting their strengths and roles in Israel. He praises God's unmatched protection and support for the people of Jeshurun (Israel).
Moses climbs Mount Nebo near Jericho, where God shows him the Promised Land before his death in Moab at age 120; the Israelites mourn him for 30 days, marking the end of his leadership.
Moses blesses Israel, praising God as their unique protector who will defeat their enemies and provide abundant blessings, ensuring Israel's safety and triumph over foes before Moses' death.

Moses blesses the tribes of Judah, Levi, and Benjamin, asking God to protect and empower them. He recalls Levi's testing at Massah and Meribah and highlights their role in teaching God's law to Israel.

After Moses' death in Moab, the Israelites mourned for thirty days. Joshua, empowered by Moses' blessing, led them faithfully, while Moses is remembered as Israel's unparalleled prophet who performed great signs and wonders.

After Moses' death, God speaks to Joshua, Moses' assistant, commanding him to lead the Israelites across the Jordan River into the promised land, assuring him of God's presence and urging courage and obedience to the law given to Moses.

Joshua reminds the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh to support the other Israelites in conquering Canaan while their families stay in their current lands east of the Jordan. They pledge obedience to Joshua as they did to Moses.

Joshua, now leading Israel after Moses, sends two spies from Shittim to secretly scout Jericho. They stay at Rahab's house, who hides them from the king's men sent to capture them, allowing the spies to escape safely.

Rahab asks the Israelite spies to protect her family in exchange for hiding them; they agree and instruct her to mark her window with a scarlet thread as a sign for their protection when they conquer Jericho.

Rahab speaks to the two Israelite spies she hid, acknowledging God's power shown in past victories and asking for protection for her family in return for her help, as the king's men have left searching for the spies.

After hiding from Jericho’s king’s men for three days, the two spies safely return to Joshua at Shittim and report that the people of the land are terrified, confirming God’s promise of victory over the land.

God encourages Joshua to be strong and follow Moses' law closely for success, assuring His presence. Joshua then orders the people to prepare to cross the Jordan River in three days to claim the promised land and reminds certain tribes of their inheritance.

Joshua's spies instruct Rahab to mark her window with a scarlet thread as a sign for protection when Israel invades Jericho, warning her of the consequences if she betrays them; Rahab agrees and hides them until their pursuers give up.

Joshua leads the Israelites to cross the flooded Jordan River near Jericho. As priests carrying the Ark step into the water, the river miraculously stops flowing, allowing the people to cross on dry ground safely.

God speaks to Joshua, promising to honor him like Moses and instructing him to command the priests carrying the ark to stop at the Jordan River. Joshua tells Israel this will prove God's presence as they prepare to cross into Canaan. Twelve men are chosen, one from each tribe.

After all the Israelites crossed the Jordan River on dry ground, God instructed Joshua to have twelve men, one from each tribe, take twelve stones from the riverbed as a lasting memorial of this miraculous event.

Joshua instructs twelve men, one from each tribe, to take stones from the Jordan River where the priests stood with the ark, creating a lasting memorial of God's miracle as the Israelites cross on dry ground.

Joshua leads the Israelites from Shittim to the Jordan River, instructing them to follow the ark of the covenant carried by priests, keeping a distance. He tells them to prepare, as God will perform wonders, and God promises to honor Joshua as He did Moses.

After Israel crossed the Jordan, the Amorite and Canaanite kings lost courage. God then instructed Joshua to circumcise the new generation born in the wilderness, since the original men who left Egypt had died there uncircumcised.

After crossing the Jordan River on dry ground, Joshua and the Israelites camp at Gilgal near Jericho. Joshua sets up twelve stones as a memorial to remind future generations of God's power in parting the waters for their passage.

After crossing the Jordan, the Israelites camp at Gilgal, celebrate Passover, and eat the land's first harvest, ending their manna provision. Near Jericho, Joshua meets a divine warrior who declares the ground holy and instructs him to remove his sandals.

After all Israelites crossed the Jordan River on dry ground, the ark and priests followed. The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh crossed armed, fulfilling Moses' command. Joshua was honored, and the river returned to normal as they camped at Gilgal near Jericho.

Joshua commands the Israelites to march around Jericho with priests blowing trumpets before the ark of the covenant, while armed men lead and follow; the people are instructed to remain silent until told to shout.

Joshua orders the Israelites, newly arrived in Canaan, to circumcise the younger generation born in the wilderness, renewing their covenant. After healing, they camp at Gilgal, celebrate Passover, and mark a new beginning after 40 years wandering.

After Jericho's walls fell, Joshua's spies rescued Rahab and her family, sparing them from the city's destruction. Joshua then cursed anyone who would rebuild Jericho, and his reputation spread throughout the land.

Joshua receives God's instructions to conquer Jericho, a city tightly sealed against Israel. He commands the armed men and priests to march around the city with the ark and trumpets for six days, preparing for a divine intervention on the seventh day.

Joshua leads the Israelites in circling Jericho with priests blowing trumpets before the ark for six days; on the seventh day, they circle seven times, then Joshua commands a shout, declaring the city given by God and instructing them to avoid taking accursed items.

Joshua instructs the Israelites to avoid taking anything accursed from Jericho, dedicating silver and gold to the Lord. After the city's walls fall, they destroy all inhabitants except Rahab and her family, whom the spies rescue as promised.

After Jericho's fall, Israel sins by taking forbidden items, angering God. Joshua scouts Ai near Bethel, sends 3,000 men who are defeated. Joshua mourns before the LORD's ark with elders, showing Israel's distress and need for God's guidance.

Joshua and Israel's elders mourn before the ark after Israel's defeat at Ai, questioning God's purpose in leading them. God reveals Israel's sin of taking forbidden spoils, causing their defeat, and commands them to remove the accursed to regain His favor.
God tells Joshua that Israel's defeat at Ai is due to sin in the camp; they must find and remove the guilty party by tribal and family inspection, or they cannot succeed against their enemies.

Joshua follows God's command to identify who disobeyed by taking forbidden spoils from Jericho; he narrows down to Achan of Judah, who confesses to hiding stolen items in his tent, causing Israel's defeat at Ai.

Achan confesses to stealing forbidden spoils from Jericho, hidden in his tent. Joshua and Israel seize Achan, his family, and possessions, then execute him at the valley of Achor, ending God's anger against Israel after their defeat at Ai.

God encourages Joshua not to fear and commands him to lead Israel’s army to attack Ai, promising victory. Joshua plans a military ambush, using a feigned retreat to lure Ai’s forces out before capturing the city.

Joshua and the Israelites capture the king of Ai alive after defeating the city's inhabitants in battle. They destroy Ai completely, burn it, and hang the king's body publicly as a lasting warning, fulfilling God's command.

God instructs Joshua to ambush Ai after previous defeat; Joshua positions troops west and north of Ai, prepares for battle, and stays overnight in the valley between Bethel and Ai with elders and warriors.

God instructs Joshua to signal the hidden Israelite troops by stretching out his spear toward Ai. The ambush captures and burns the city, trapping the men of Ai, whom Joshua and Israel then defeat, capturing their king alive.

After capturing Ai, Joshua executes its king and honors Moses' command by building an altar on Mount Ebal, offering sacrifices, and publicly reading the law to all Israelites, including leaders and foreigners, divided between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.

Joshua positions his forces around Ai, with an ambush set west of the city. The king of Ai leads his men out to battle, unaware of the ambush, while Joshua pretends to flee, drawing the enemy away from the city as God commands him to signal the attack.

Joshua gathers all the people of Israel, including leaders and priests, at Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim to publicly read and affirm the law of Moses, fulfilling Moses' command to bless the people with blessings and curses.

After Israel's victory at Ai, the kings near the Jordan and Mediterranean unite against Joshua. The Gibeonites, fearing conquest, disguise themselves as distant travelers and approach Joshua's camp at Gilgal to request a peace treaty.

The Gibeonites, pretending to be from a distant land, approach Joshua and Israel claiming to seek a treaty, showing worn-out provisions as proof. Joshua and his leaders accept their offer without consulting God first.

Joshua and the Israelite leaders make a peace treaty with the Gibeonites without consulting God, later discovering they are nearby neighbors. Despite complaints, the leaders honor their oath, sparing the Gibeonites but assigning them menial tasks.

After Joshua's victories over Jericho and Ai, Adonizedec, king of Jerusalem, learns that Gibeon has allied with Israel. Fearing Gibeon's strength, he calls other Amorite kings to join him in attacking Gibeon.

Joshua confronts the Gibeonites for deceiving Israel about their location. Though cursed to serve as woodcutters and water carriers, they are spared from death and assigned to support the Israelite community and the LORD’s altar.
Joshua leads Israel in conquering the cities of Lachish, Eglon, and Hebron, defeating their kings and destroying all inhabitants, continuing the campaign after victories at Libnah and Makkedah.

The five Amorite kings, including Jerusalem's, unite to attack Gibeon for allying with Israel. Gibeon asks Joshua for help, so he leads Israel's army from Gilgal. God assures Joshua of victory, and Israel defeats the Amorites at Gibeon and pursues them to nearby towns.

During a battle at Gibeon, God helped Joshua and the Israelites defeat the Amorite kings by sending hailstones and causing the sun and moon to stand still, allowing Israel to fully defeat their enemies before returning to Gilgal.

Joshua orders the five Amorite kings captured in a cave to be brought out, commands his warriors to show dominance by placing their feet on the kings' necks, then executes and hangs them before returning their bodies to the cave sealed with stones.

After defeating the Amorite armies, Joshua and Israel returned to Gilgal while five enemy kings hid in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua sealed the cave, pursued remaining foes, then captured and brought out the kings.

Joshua orders the five captured kings to be imprisoned again, then leads Israel to conquer Makkedah, Libnah, and Lachish, destroying each city and its king completely, continuing the military campaign in Canaan with God's help.

Joshua and the Israelites conquer Hebron, Debir, and surrounding cities, killing all inhabitants as commanded by God. They defeat all kings from Kadeshbarnea to Gibeon, securing the land before returning to their camp at Gilgal.

After Joshua's victories, Jabin king of Hazor gathers many allied kings and armies from surrounding regions to fight Israel at the waters of Merom. God reassures Joshua of victory, promising to deliver their enemies into Israel's hands.

Joshua follows God's command to destroy the Canaanite cities, burning only Hazor, and takes all their land from Mount Halak to Baalgad. He fights many kings over a long time, with only Gibeon's Hivites making peace with Israel.

Joshua reports that all cities except Gibeon fought Israel; he destroyed the Anakim giants from various mountain regions, fulfilling God's command to Moses by conquering the land and dividing it among the Israelite tribes, ending the war.

Joshua leads the Israelite army in a surprise attack by the waters of Merom, defeating their enemies and destroying Hazor, the leading city, by fire as commanded by God through Moses, while sparing other strong cities.

Moses and the Israelites defeated kings east of the Jordan, giving land to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Joshua then conquered kings west of the Jordan, distributing their lands among Israelite tribes across various regions.

Joshua lists the remaining 15 kings defeated by Israel west of the Jordan, completing a total of 31 kings conquered as part of the land promised to the tribes of Israel. This follows the earlier summary of lands taken east of the Jordan.

This passage lists kings defeated by Moses and the Israelites east of the Jordan River, including Sihon of the Amorites and Og of Bashan, whose lands were given to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.

Joshua, now old, is instructed by God to divide the remaining land among the tribes. This passage details the territory of the tribe of Reuben, noting the defeat of King Og's kingdom and that the Levites receive no land inheritance.

Joshua, now old, is instructed by God to divide the remaining land east of the Jordan among the tribes. This passage details the territory given to Reuben and Gad, including cities and lands formerly ruled by Sihon, and mentions the defeat of Balaam.

Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and tribal leaders distribute Canaan's land by lot to nine tribes and half a tribe, excluding Levites who receive cities. Caleb of Judah reminds Joshua of God's promise made 40 years earlier at Kadeshbarnea.

Joshua, now old, receives God's command to continue dividing the remaining Canaanite lands, including Philistine and northern territories, among the Israelites by lot, as God promises to drive out the current inhabitants before them.

Moses assigns land east of the Jordan River to the tribes of Gad, half of Manasseh, and others, detailing their borders and cities. The Levites receive no land, as their inheritance is the LORD himself. This follows God's command to divide the land.

Caleb asks Joshua to give him the mountain region of Hebron, once inhabited by the Anakim giants, trusting God will help him conquer it. Joshua grants Caleb this land, which remains peaceful because of Caleb's faithfulness.

Caleb, now 85, reminds Joshua at Gilgal that Moses sent him 45 years ago from Kadeshbarnea to scout Canaan. He stayed faithful while others doubted, and Moses promised him the land he walked on. Caleb asks for the mountain with Anakim giants to conquer.

God instructs Joshua to distribute the remaining land, including hill country from Lebanon to Misrephothmaim, among nine tribes and half of Manasseh, recalling Moses' prior conquests over kings like Sihon and Og east of the Jordan River.

This passage describes the detailed boundaries of the tribe of Judah’s territory, including Jerusalem (then inhabited by Jebusites), extending from the Valley of Hinnom to the Mediterranean Sea, outlining the land allotted to Judah’s families.

Joshua describes the borders of Judah's land, focusing on the west coast by the sea. Caleb receives Hebron, conquers Anak's sons, and offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captures Debir, which Othniel takes, leading to Achsah requesting water springs.

Joshua lists the cities and villages that make up the territory inherited by the tribe of Judah, detailing their locations from the southern border near Edom through valleys and hills, showing the extent of Judah's land allotment.

This passage lists numerous cities and their villages within the territory of the tribe of Judah, detailing the extent of their inheritance from the coastal plains near Ashdod and Gaza to the mountainous regions including Hebron and Debir.

Joshua and the priest Eleazar assign land to the tribe of Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn, including Gilead and Bashan. Zelophehad's daughters claim their inheritance before the leaders, following God's command to Moses.

Joshua describes the detailed borders of the tribe of Judah, outlining its southern boundary near the River of Egypt and the Dead Sea, extending northward past key locations including Jerusalem, marking the extent of their allotted land.

Joshua describes the land borders of the tribe of Manasseh, noting shared cities with Ephraim and territories extending to the sea and neighboring tribes. Despite their inheritance, Manasseh could not fully drive out the Canaanite inhabitants.

The passage describes the land boundaries assigned to the tribes of Joseph, specifically Ephraim and Manasseh, including cities like Bethel and Gezer. It notes that the Ephraimites did not fully drive out the Canaanites in Gezer, who remained and paid tribute.

This passage lists cities and villages in Judah's territory, noting that despite their conquests, the tribe of Judah could not remove the Jebusites from Jerusalem, who continued to live there alongside them.

The daughters of Zelophehad from the tribe of Manasseh petition Eleazar, Joshua, and leaders for their inheritance, which God commanded Moses to grant. Manasseh's land includes ten portions plus Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan, with borders near Shechem and Entappuah.

The tribe of Manasseh struggles to drive out Canaanites from their cities, who remain as subjects. The Joseph tribes question Joshua about their small inheritance, and he challenges them to expand into the forested lands despite strong Canaanite enemies.

Joshua describes the southern boundary of Judah's territory, stretching from the Salt Sea near Edom through various landmarks to the River of Egypt, defining the southernmost border of the tribe's land allotment.

Joshua describes the detailed western and southern borders of Benjamin's territory, outlining landmarks from Kirjathjearim through valleys and mountains down to the Jordan River and the Salt Sea, as part of dividing the land among Israel's tribes.

Joshua explains that the Levites receive no land because their inheritance is the priesthood, and some tribes already have land east of Jordan. Joshua then sends men to survey the land, and he casts lots at Shiloh to assign the territory, starting with Benjamin's borders.

The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, descendants of Joseph, express concern about limited land and strong Canaanite enemies with iron chariots. Joshua encourages them to clear the forested mountains and promises more territory despite the challenges.

Joshua gathers the Israelites at Shiloh, where the tabernacle is set up, to address the seven tribes who haven't yet received land. He instructs them to send men to survey and divide the remaining land into seven parts for allocation.

Joshua describes the northern and western borders of Benjamin’s territory, detailing landmarks from the Jordan River near Jericho, through mountains and towns like Bethel and Kirjathjearim, connecting Benjamin’s land to Judah’s territory.

The leaders of Israel cast lots to assign land to the tribe of Simeon, who received cities within Judah's territory because Judah's land was too large. This continues the division of Canaan among the tribes after their conquest.

Joshua continues the division of Canaan among Israel's tribes by lot, now assigning the territory with 22 cities to the tribe of Asher, followed by the beginning of the allotment for the tribe of Naphtali, detailing their borders and cities.

The leaders of Israel are assigning land by lot to the tribe of Naphtali, detailing its borders and cities in northern Canaan, continuing the division of the Promised Land among the tribes as part of Joshua's leadership.

Joshua describes the detailed borders and cities assigned to the tribe of Benjamin, outlining their inheritance east to the Jordan River and including key towns like Jericho and Jerusalem, completing the land division among Israel's tribes at Shiloh.

The tribes of Simeon, Zebulun, and Issachar receive their land inheritances, with Simeon's portion within Judah's territory due to Judah's large allotment. The boundaries and cities for Zebulun and Issachar are then detailed.

Joshua continues the division of Canaan among Israel's tribes by lot, now assigning the territory to Issachar, listing its cities and borders near Jezreel and Jordan, then beginning the allocation for the tribe of Asher.

The tribe of Dan receives their land allotment but finds it too small, so they conquer Leshem and rename it Dan. After all tribes receive their territories, Joshua is given Timnathserah in Mount Ephraim, where he settles.

Joshua receives Timnathserah in Mount Ephraim as his inheritance, fulfilling God's word. Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and tribal leaders complete the land division by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, ending the allotment of Canaan to Israel.

God instructs Joshua to tell Israel to designate cities of refuge for those who kill unintentionally, protecting them from revenge until judgment. Six cities are appointed across Israel, including Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron.

The leaders of the Levite families receive their allotted cities from various Israelite tribes by lot, following God's command through Moses. The Aaronic priests get Hebron in Judah, while Caleb is granted the surrounding fields and villages.

The leaders allocate cities and surrounding lands to the Levites in Canaan, with Caleb receiving fields near Hebron. Aaron's descendants get 13 cities including Hebron, while Kohath's families receive cities in Ephraim, including Shechem as a refuge city.

The leaders of the Levite families approach Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and Israelite tribal leaders at Shiloh to request cities to live in, as commanded by Moses; the Israelites allocate cities by lot from various tribes to the Levite clans.

This passage concludes the allocation of 48 cities with suburbs to the Levites across Israel's tribal lands. It affirms God's fulfillment of His promise to give Israel the land and grant them peace by defeating their enemies.

The Levite families of Kohath and Gershon receive their allotted cities from the tribes of Manasseh, Dan, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali, including cities of refuge like Golan and Kedesh, continuing the distribution of Levitical cities in Canaan.

The Levite families of Gershon and Merari receive their allotted cities from the tribes of Naphtali, Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad, including cities of refuge like Kedesh and Ramoth, totaling 48 cities given to the Levites across Israel.

Joshua speaks to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, praising their faithfulness and instructing them to return to their land east of the Jordan River now that their fellow Israelites have rest in Canaan.

Joshua blesses and sends the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh back to their lands east of the Jordan, urging them to share spoils with their brethren. They build a large altar near the Jordan River upon arrival.

The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh build a large altar near the Jordan River, alarming the rest of Israel. The Israelites gather at Shiloh and send Phinehas and leaders to confront them in Gilead.

Joshua, following God's instructions, designates six cities across Israel—including Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan—as refuge for those who accidentally kill someone, protecting them until a fair trial before the community.

Leaders from all Israel, led by priest Phinehas, confront the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh in Gilead, accusing them of rebellion for building an altar, fearing it breaks their covenant with God and endangers all Israel.

Leaders of Israel confront the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh at Gilead, warning that building an altar beside the LORD’s altar may cause God's anger on all Israel, recalling Achan’s sin that brought punishment on the whole nation.

The leaders of Israel accuse the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh of rebellion for building an altar. These tribes respond, denying disobedience and explaining the altar is a witness to their shared faith despite the Jordan River border.

The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh explain to Israel that they built an altar by the Jordan River as a witness to their shared faith, not for sacrifices, to prevent future disputes about their part in serving the LORD.

The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh explain their altar was not for sacrifices but as a witness of unity with Israel. Phinehas and Israel's leaders accept this, confirming no rebellion, and report back to the rest of Israel in Canaan.

Joshua, now old, urges the Israelites to be brave and obey God's law fully, warning them not to adopt the customs or gods of the remaining nations in the land God promised them, reminding them of God's past victories and ongoing support.

Phinehas and the leaders return from Gilead to report to Israel that the altar built by Reuben and Gad was not for rebellion. Israel is pleased, blesses God, and decides not to fight them. The altar is named Ed as a witness of unity.

Joshua gathers Israel's leaders at Shechem to recount their history, reminding them how God called Abraham from beyond the Euphrates, gave land to his descendants, and delivered them from Egypt through Moses and Aaron.
Joshua, now old, addresses all Israel’s leaders after a long period of peace, reminding them of God’s victories and the remaining lands assigned by lot for their inheritance west of the Jordan River.

Joshua, nearing the end of his life, warns Israel to remain faithful to God and avoid intermarriage with remaining Canaanite nations, cautioning that disobedience will lead to their downfall and loss of the land God gave them.

Joshua recounts God's past deliverances to the Israelites, including their escape from Egypt, crossing the Red Sea, victories over the Amorites and other peoples, and the conquest of Jericho, reminding them of God's faithfulness.

Joshua addresses the tribes of Israel at Shechem, recounting their conquest of Jericho and surrounding peoples, urging them to serve the LORD sincerely and choose whom they will serve, declaring his own family's commitment.

Joshua challenges the Israelites at Shechem to choose whom they will serve, declaring his family's loyalty to the LORD. The people affirm their commitment, acknowledging God's past deliverance, while Joshua warns of the consequences of forsaking Him.

Joshua leads the Israelites in Shechem to renew their commitment to serve the LORD, making a covenant and setting a stone as a witness; then Joshua dies at age 110, marking the end of his leadership after guiding Israel into the Promised Land.

After Joshua's death and burial in Ephraim, a new generation arose in Israel that did not know God or His works. They turned to idol worship, angering God, who allowed their enemies to oppress and distress them as punishment.

After each judge died, the Israelites turned away from God, worshipping other gods and disobeying Him. God allowed remaining nations to stay in the land to test if Israel would remain faithful, unlike their ancestors after Joshua's death.

After Joshua's final covenant with Israel, he dies at 110 and is buried in Timnathserah, Ephraim. Israel serves the LORD during Joshua's and the elders' lifetimes. Joseph's bones are buried in Shechem, and Eleazar, Aaron's son, dies and is buried in Ephraim.

After Joshua's death, the Israelites ask God who should lead the fight against the Canaanites. God chooses Judah, who, with Simeon, defeats Adonibezek and captures Jerusalem, continuing Israel's conquest of the land.

After Judah captured Jerusalem by force, they fought Canaanites in surrounding regions including Hebron and Debir. Caleb promised his daughter Achsah to whoever conquered Debir, and Othniel succeeded, marrying her and securing water springs for their land.

An angel speaks to Israel at Bochim, reminding them of God's covenant and their disobedience in making alliances with local peoples. The people weep and sacrifice there. After Joshua's death, Israel serves God under his elders before a new generation arises.

The tribes of Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan failed to fully drive out the Canaanites from their territories, leading to coexistence or subjugation, while the Amorites controlled certain areas but paid tribute to Joseph's descendants.

This passage explains that God left certain Canaanite nations to test Israel's faithfulness after Joshua's death. Israel intermarried with these peoples, worshipped their gods, and as a result, God allowed King Chushanrishathaim of Mesopotamia to oppress them for eight years.

The tribe of Joseph attacks Bethel (formerly Luz), capturing it with help from a local guide spared with his family. Meanwhile, Manasseh and Ephraim fail to fully drive out Canaanite inhabitants from several towns, who remain as tributaries.

After Israel turned away from God, they were oppressed by Chushanrishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years until God raised Othniel, Caleb’s brother, to deliver them; later, Israel again sinned and was oppressed by Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years.

After Ehud's death, Israel falls into evil again and is oppressed by King Jabin of Canaan and his commander Sisera. Deborah, a prophetess and judge, calls Barak to lead 10,000 men against Sisera near Mount Tabor. Barak insists Deborah accompany him.

Barak agrees to fight Sisera only if Deborah, the prophetess and judge, accompanies him. Deborah joins Barak as he gathers 10,000 men from Zebulun and Naphtali to confront Sisera’s 900 iron chariots near Mount Tabor.

Deborah urges Barak to attack Sisera, leading to a decisive battle near Mount Tabor where Sisera's army is defeated. Sisera flees to Jael's tent, where she welcomes him and offers milk to drink, hiding him under a cloak.

Ehud, a left-handed Israelite judge, secretly kills Eglon, the Moabite king, in his private chamber. After locking the door, Ehud escapes to Seirath and rallies the Israelites on Mount Ephraim to fight Moab.

Sisera, fleeing from Barak's army, seeks refuge in Jael's tent. Jael kills Sisera while he sleeps, enabling Israel to defeat King Jabin of Canaan and secure peace. This follows Deborah and Barak's battle preparations and victory.

Israel served King Eglon of Moab for 18 years due to their disobedience. When they cried out, God raised Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, who brought a secret message and a concealed dagger to Eglon, meeting him alone in a private chamber.

This passage describes Israel's repeated cycle of sin and deliverance after Joshua's death: God allows enemies to oppress them, raises judges to save them, but the people quickly return to idol worship and disobedience, worsening their corruption each time.

Ehud blows a trumpet on Mount Ephraim, leading Israel to defeat the Moabites at the Jordan River, securing 80 years of peace. After him, Shamgar delivers Israel by killing 600 Philistines with an ox goad.

Deborah and Barak sing a victory song praising God for Israel's deliverance from Canaanite oppression, recalling past struggles and urging leaders and judges across Israel to recognize God's power and the people's willing sacrifice.

Deborah calls on Israel's leaders and people, praising their courage and urging Barak to lead. She highlights support from tribes like Ephraim, Benjamin, Zebulun, Issachar, and questions Reuben's hesitation during the battle against Canaanite oppression.

Caleb gives springs to Achsah. Kenites join Judah in southern wilderness. Judah and Simeon conquer cities but can't drive out valley Canaanites. Caleb gets Hebron; Benjamin fails to expel Jebusites from Jerusalem. Joseph attacks Bethel with God's help.

Deborah praises the tribes of Israel for their roles in the battle against Sisera, highlighting Zebulun and Naphtali's bravery and condemning Meroz for not helping. She also blesses Jael for her decisive act against Sisera.

Deborah’s song praises Jael for killing Sisera with a hammer after offering him milk, while Sisera’s mother anxiously awaits his return. The victory brings peace to Israel for forty years after defeating their enemies.

After Israel's victory under Deborah, they again disobey God, leading to seven years of oppression by the Midianites and their allies, who devastate the land, forcing Israelites into hiding and causing great poverty. Israel cries out to God for help.

Gideon builds an altar to God called Jehovahshalom in Ophrah, then follows God's command to destroy his father's Baal altar and grove at night, offering a sacrifice. The next morning, the townspeople discover Gideon is responsible.

The angel of the LORD stays with Gideon at Ophrah, instructing him to prepare a meal. After a miraculous fire consumes the offering, Gideon realizes he has seen a divine messenger and builds an altar called Jehovahshalom.

Gideon gathers troops from Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali to fight Midian. He asks God for a sign using a wool fleece to confirm his calling, and God answers with a miraculous dew pattern overnight.

After Gideon destroys Baal's altar at night, the townspeople want him punished, but his father Joash defends him. Meanwhile, enemies gather in Jezreel, and Gideon, empowered by God's Spirit, rallies troops from Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali.

The Israelites suffer under Midianite oppression and cry out to God. A prophet reminds them of God's past deliverance, then an angel appears to Gideon in Ophrah, calling him a mighty warrior and signaling God's presence with him.

The angel of the LORD appears to Gideon in Ophrah, calling him a mighty warrior despite his doubts about Israel's suffering under Midianite oppression. Gideon asks for reassurance, and the angel agrees to wait for a gift Gideon will prepare.

God tells Gideon to reduce his army by testing how the men drink water at a spring; only 300 who lap water with their hands are kept, while the rest return home, preparing for battle against the Midianites in the valley below.

Gideon keeps only 300 men and sends the rest home before the battle with the Midianites. That night, God tells Gideon to attack, and Gideon spies on the enemy camp, overhearing a dream that predicts Midian's defeat.

Gideon (also called Jerubbaal) and his army camp near the well of Harod, facing the Midianites. God tells Gideon the army is too large and instructs him to reduce the troops by sending away the fearful and testing them at the water.

Gideon arrives at the Midianite camp and overhears a soldier's dream predicting Gideon's victory. Encouraged, Gideon organizes his 300 men into three groups, equipping them with trumpets, pitchers, and lamps, and instructs them on their attack plan.

Gideon kills the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna after his son Jether hesitates. The Israelites ask Gideon to be their ruler, but he declines, requesting gold earrings from the defeated Midianites as tribute.

Gideon instructs his 300 men to blow trumpets, break pitchers, and shout as a surprise attack on the Midianite camp at night. Confused, the enemy flees, and Israelite tribes from Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh join the pursuit.

After Gideon's victory over Midian, the men of Ephraim confront him for not calling them to fight, but he praises their earlier success. Gideon then asks Succoth for food for his weary men, but they refuse, prompting his warning of punishment.

After Gideon's surprise attack on the Midianite camp, Israelite tribes from Naphtali, Asher, Manasseh, and Ephraim join the pursuit, capturing and killing Midianite leaders Oreb and Zeeb, and bringing their heads to Gideon beyond the Jordan River.

After capturing a young man from Succoth who identified the city’s leaders, Gideon confronts Succoth for refusing to aid his weary troops, punishes them, destroys Penuel’s tower, and speaks to the captured Midianite kings about his slain brothers before ordering his son to kill them.

After defeating Midian, Gideon used the gold earrings taken from the enemy to make an ephod in Ophrah, which became a snare for Israel. He lived peacefully for 40 years, had many sons, but after his death, Israel turned to idol worship and forgot his deeds.

Abimelech, son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), persuades his mother's relatives in Shechem to support him as sole ruler instead of his 70 brothers. He kills his brothers at Ophrah, except youngest Jotham, and is made king by Shechem's leaders.

After Abimelech is made king by the men of Shechem and the house of Millo, Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, stands on Mount Gerizim and tells a parable of trees seeking a king, highlighting the rejection of worthy leaders in favor of a bramble.

Jotham warns Shechem about Abimelech's rule, then flees for safety. After three years, God causes conflict between Abimelech and Shechem; Shechem rebels, led by Gaal, who challenges Abimelech's authority while celebrating in the fields.

Jotham, youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), speaks from Mount Gerizim, using a parable of trees to criticize Shechem’s choice of Abimelech as king after he killed his brothers, warning of mutual destruction if their loyalty is false.

In Shechem, Gaal and his followers openly rebel against Abimelech, questioning his authority. Zebul, loyal to Abimelech, secretly warns him, prompting Abimelech to prepare a surprise night attack on the city.

Abimelech defeats Gaal in battle near Shechem, then attacks the city, killing many and destroying it. The survivors hide in the tower of Shechem, the house of the god Berith, as Abimelech prepares to confront them.

Gideon threatens Succoth and Penuel for refusing aid, then attacks Midian’s remaining forces at Karkor, capturing kings Zebah and Zalmunna. He returns early, captures a Succoth youth, and learns about the city’s leaders.

Abimelech and his men secretly camp near Shechem at night, preparing to attack. Gaal, a leader in Shechem, sees Abimelech's forces approaching and challenges them, leading to a battle between Gaal's and Abimelech's troops.

Abimelech attacks the men hiding in the tower of Shechem by setting it on fire, killing about a thousand people. Then he besieges Thebez, but a woman fatally injures him by dropping a millstone on his head during the assault.

Abimelech is fatally wounded by a millstone thrown by a woman during his siege of Thebez; he asks his armor-bearer to kill him to avoid shame. His death ends his violent rule, fulfilling Jotham's curse on Abimelech and the men of Shechem.

After years of oppression by the Ammonites and Philistines in Gilead and beyond Jordan, the Israelites confess their sin of idolatry to God, who reminds them of past deliverances but refuses help until they repent and seek Him alone.

The Israelites admit their sin and ask God for deliverance, removing foreign gods and returning to Him. Meanwhile, the Ammonites camp in Gilead, and Israel gathers at Mizpeh, seeking a leader to fight Ammon.

After Abimelech's death, Tola from Issachar led Israel for 23 years from Shamir, followed by Jair from Gilead who ruled 22 years. Then Israel turned to idol worship, angering God, who allowed the Philistines and Ammonites to oppress them in Gilead for 18 years.

Jephthah, a skilled warrior rejected by his half-brothers in Gilead, lives in Tob with outcasts. When the Ammonites attack Israel, Gilead's elders ask Jephthah to lead them in battle despite past rejection.

The elders of Gilead ask Jephthah, a skilled outcast, to lead them against the Ammonites. He agrees if God grants victory. Jephthah then challenges the Ammonite king's claim over disputed lands taken by Israel after the Exodus.

Jephthah recounts Israel’s journey near Edom and Moab, their request to pass through Amorite land, and the battle where Israel, with God's help, defeated King Sihon and took Amorite territory between Arnon and Jabbok rivers.

Jephthah, chosen leader of Gilead, sends messengers to the Ammonite king who claims Israel took his land. Jephthah responds, explaining Israel never invaded Moab or Ammon but was denied passage through Edom and Moab during their wilderness journey.
Jephthah’s daughter mourns her virginity for two months before Jephthah fulfills his vow to the LORD. This tragic event leads to an annual Israelite custom of lamenting her fate.

The Spirit of the LORD empowered Jephthah as he led Israel to battle against the Ammonites, securing a major victory. Returning home to Mizpeh, Jephthah was met by his only daughter, setting the stage for a tragic fulfillment of his vow.

Jephthah responds to the Ammonite king's claim over land, arguing Israel's rightful possession given past conflicts and divine judgment. The Ammonite king ignores Jephthah's message, and the Spirit of the LORD empowers Jephthah as he prepares to confront Ammon.

Jephthah and the men of Gilead fought the Ephraimites over a dispute about military support, using a pronunciation test to identify fleeing Ephraimites. After Jephthah's six-year judgeship, Ibzan from Bethlehem and then Elon from Zebulun led Israel.

Jephthah returns home to Mizpeh after defeating the Ammonites, and his only daughter greets him joyfully. He mourns because of a vow he made to God, and she asks for two months to mourn her virginity with her friends.

After Jephthah's victory over the Ammonites, the Ephraimites confront him for not involving them in the battle, threatening his home. Jephthah defends his actions, leading to a violent conflict between Gilead and Ephraim in northern Israel.

Manoah speaks with the angel of the LORD, who reiterates instructions for his barren wife to avoid wine and unclean food. Manoah offers a sacrifice, witnessing the angel ascend in the flame, revealing his divine nature.

This passage summarizes the leadership of Elon from Zebulun and Abdon from Ephraim, who each judged Israel for a decade and eight years respectively, noting their deaths and burial places, continuing the record of Israel's judges after Jephthah.

After Israel falls under Philistine control for 40 years, an angel appears to Manoah's barren wife in Zorah, promising she will bear a son who will be a Nazarite and begin to free Israel from the Philistines.

Manoah and his wife receive a second visit from the angel of the LORD, who reiterates the instructions for their unborn son to be a Nazarite, emphasizing strict observance to prepare the child destined to deliver Israel from the Philistines.

Manoah and his wife witness the angel of the LORD ascending in fire from their offering, realizing his divine nature. Despite fear, they trust God's plan, and their son Samson is born and blessed, beginning his Spirit-led role in Dan's territory.

Samson visits Timnath, sees a Philistine woman, and asks his parents to arrange marriage despite their objections. Unaware it’s God’s plan against the Philistines, they go to Timnath where Samson kills a lion by the Spirit’s power.

After killing a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone at Lehi, Samson names the place Ramathlehi, prays for water, and God provides it from the jawbone. Samson then leads Israel for twenty years during Philistine oppression.

Samson is bound by Delilah with new ropes and then with his hair woven into a web, but he breaks free both times. After her persistent urging, he finally reveals that his strength lies in his uncut hair as a Nazarite.

After Samson's wife and her father were burned by the Philistines in retaliation, Samson attacked them fiercely and hid in the rock Etam. The Philistines camped in Judah, and Judah's men confronted Samson, planning to hand him over to the Philistines.

Samson returns to his wife during harvest, but her father refuses him and gives her to Samson's companion. In anger, Samson catches foxes, sets their tails on fire, and burns the Philistines' crops. The Philistines retaliate by burning Samson's wife and her father.

Samson is with Delilah in the valley of Sorek; she tries to learn the secret of his strength for the Philistine lords. He lies twice, bound with green withs and new ropes, but breaks free both times despite men waiting to capture him.

Samson visits Gaza, where the Philistines plan to kill him, but he escapes by carrying off the city gate. Later, he falls in love with Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and the Philistine leaders offer her money to discover the secret of his strength.

Samson poses a riddle to thirty Philistine men at his wedding feast in Timnath, but they cannot solve it. Under pressure, his wife persuades him to reveal the answer, which she then shares with the men, leading to their discovery of the riddle's meaning.

The men of Judah capture Samson to hand him over to the Philistines, but empowered by God's Spirit, he breaks free and kills a thousand Philistine soldiers with a donkey's jawbone at Lehi, naming the place Ramathlehi.

Samson reveals to Delilah that his strength lies in his uncut hair as a Nazarite vow. Delilah betrays him by having his hair shaved while he sleeps, causing him to lose strength; the Philistines capture, blind, and imprison him in Gaza.

Samson reveals the answer to his riddle to the Philistine men in Timnath, then kills thirty of them in Ashkelon, giving their clothes to those who solved it. His anger grows as his wife is given to his friend.

After Samson's hair began to grow back, the Philistine leaders gathered at a temple to celebrate capturing him. They brought Samson out of prison to entertain the crowd, placing him between the temple's supporting pillars in Gaza.

A Levite from Bethlehem in Judah travels to Mount Ephraim and meets Micah, who hires him as a priest, providing payment and lodging. Micah feels assured of God's favor by having a Levite serve in his household shrine.

After Samson's death, the narrative shifts to Micah from Mount Ephraim, who returns stolen silver to his mother and uses some to make idols and set up a private shrine, appointing his son as priest. A Levite from Bethlehem Judah arrives, highlighting Israel's lawlessness without a king.

Samson, blinded and imprisoned by the Philistines in Gaza, prays to God for strength one last time. He pulls down the temple pillars, killing many Philistines and himself. His family then buries him near his hometown, ending his 20-year leadership.

The Danites, lacking a king and land, send five warriors from Zorah and Eshtaol to scout for territory. They stay at Micah's house in Ephraim, meet his Levite priest, and ask him to seek God's guidance on their journey.

The Levite priest blesses the Danite spies who scout Laish, a peaceful city without leadership. Encouraged, the Danites prepare 600 armed men from Zorah and Eshtaol to seize the land, camping first at Kirjathjearim in Judah.

Micah confronts the Danites for stealing his idols and priest, but they warn him to stay silent. Overpowered, Micah returns home while the Danites attack and burn Laish, then rename it Dan and settle there.

The Danites renamed Laish as Dan after their ancestor and established Micah’s graven image there. Jonathan, a Levite descendant, and his sons served as priests for Dan until the land’s captivity, while the house of God remained in Shiloh.

The Danite spies and 600 armed men camp near Kirjathjearim, then visit Micah's house in Ephraim, where they find religious idols and the Levite priest. The spies seize the idols as the priest questions their actions.

The Danite warriors seize Micah’s idols and priest, convincing him to join them as their tribe’s priest. As they leave, Micah’s neighbors confront them, and Micah laments the loss of his gods and priest.

A Levite from Mount Ephraim reconciles with his concubine who had left him for her father’s house in Bethlehem Judah. He stays three days with her father, who warmly hosts them and urges him to stay longer before departing.

Samson visits the Philistine woman he desires in Timnath, finds honey in a lion's carcass, and hosts a feast where he challenges thirty men with a riddle based on this event, offering garments as a wager during the seven-day celebration.

A Levite visits his concubine's father in Bethlehemjudah, where he is urged to stay longer for hospitality. Despite repeated invitations, he departs near evening, reaching Jebus (Jerusalem) as night falls, and his servant suggests lodging there.

A Levite traveling from Bethlehem to Mount Ephraim is welcomed by an old man in Gibeah, who offers hospitality despite the city's dangerous reputation. As they eat, wicked men surround the house demanding to harm the Levite.

A Levite and his servant travel near Jebus (Jerusalem) at sunset, choosing to avoid the Jebusite city and head to Gibeah in Benjamin. There, no one offers lodging until an old Ephraimite man invites them into his home.

In Gibeah, an old man shelters a Levite traveler, but wicked men of the city demand to harm the guest. The host offers his daughter and the Levite’s concubine instead, who is then abused all night and left at the house door at dawn.

After the concubine was abused in Gibeah, she collapses at her husband's house; he then cuts her body into twelve parts and sends them throughout Israel, shocking the people and prompting urgent discussion.

The tribes of Israel gather at Mizpeh to address the horrific crime committed in Gibeah, Benjamin's town. The Levite husband recounts the assault and murder of his concubine, urging the assembly to decide how to respond to this evil.

The tribe of Benjamin fights Israel near Gibeah, initially gaining ground. Israel pretends to retreat, drawing Benjamin out, then ambushes them with hidden troops. God causes Israel to prevail, killing many Benjamites in this fierce battle.

The tribe of Benjamin defeats many Israelites in two battles near Gibeah. The Israelites mourn, seek God's guidance at the sanctuary, and prepare for further conflict, showing their deep distress and desire for divine help.
The Israelites unite to decide how to respond to the crime in Gibeah, Benjamin's city. They demand the guilty be handed over, but Benjamin refuses and prepares for battle against the rest of Israel.

The tribe of Benjamin gathers in Gibeah to fight Israel's other tribes after refusing to hand over criminals. Israel consults God, who commands Judah to lead the attack. Benjamin defeats Israel, killing 22,000 men on the first day of battle.

The Israelites, led by Phinehas, seek God's guidance at the tabernacle before their third battle against Benjamin at Gibeah. God commands them to fight, and the battle begins with Benjamin attacking Israelite forces on the roads near Gibeah.

During the battle at Gibeah, the Israelites pretended to retreat, luring the Benjamites away from the city. Hidden Israelite forces then attacked and burned Gibeah, causing the Benjamites to panic and flee, leading to their defeat.

The Israelites pursued the fleeing Benjamite warriors after a fierce battle near Gibeah, killing 25,000 men and forcing the survivors to hide at the rock of Rimmon for four months, then destroyed Benjamin's cities and livestock.

The Israelites give Benjamin the 400 virgin women from Jabeshgilead as wives, but still lack enough. To preserve Benjamin, elders plan for them to capture wives during a festival in Shiloh, despite their oath not to give daughters to Benjamin.

The Israelites realize the tribe of Jabeshgilead did not join the assembly at Mizpeh, so they send 12,000 warriors to attack Jabeshgilead, sparing only 400 virgin women to give as wives to the remaining Benjaminites at rock Rimmon.

The Israelites instruct the Benjaminites to abduct wives from Shiloh's annual festival to solve their marriage crisis after war. Benjamin rebuilds their cities, and the tribes return home, highlighting the lawlessness of the period without a king.

Naomi's relative Boaz, a wealthy man from Bethlehem, appears as Ruth begins gleaning in his fields. Ruth asks Naomi's permission to gather leftover grain, and Boaz notices her, asking his servant about her identity.

Boaz blesses Ruth for her loyalty to Naomi and invites her to eat with his workers. He instructs his men to protect her and allow her to gather extra grain, which she does until evening, then shares her harvest with Naomi in Bethlehem.

Ruth asks to glean in the fields and stays all day. Boaz, a relative of Naomi's late husband, instructs her to stay close to his workers for protection and praises her loyalty to Naomi and faith in God.

Ruth chooses to stay with her mother-in-law Naomi, rejecting Orpah's departure back to Moab. They return together to Bethlehem, where Naomi expresses her bitterness over her losses during the famine and deaths.
Naomi decides to return from Moab to Judah with her daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth. She urges them to stay in Moab, but while Orpah leaves, Ruth insists on staying with Naomi despite her warnings.

During a famine in the time of the judges, Elimelech and his family from Bethlehem moved to Moab. After Elimelech and his sons died, Naomi decided to return to Judah with her daughters-in-law, having heard the famine had ended.

After defeating Benjamin, the Israelites swear at Mizpeh not to give their daughters as wives to Benjamin. They mourn before God, realize one tribe is nearly lost, and discover Jabeshgilead did not join the assembly at Mizpeh.

Naomi advises Ruth to approach Boaz at the threshing floor at night, following a specific plan to seek his protection as a relative. Ruth obeys, quietly lying at Boaz’s feet as he rests after the harvest work.

Ruth returns to Bethlehem with the barley she gleaned and tells Naomi about Boaz, a relative who showed her kindness. Naomi encourages Ruth to continue gleaning in Boaz’s fields for safety and provision during the harvest.

Ruth approaches Boaz at the threshing floor at Naomi's urging, revealing her identity and requesting his protection as a close relative. Boaz praises her loyalty, promises to help if a nearer kinsman refuses, and keeps their meeting secret until morning.

Boaz announces to the city elders that he has married Ruth to preserve Mahlon's family line. The people bless the union, Ruth bears a son, and Naomi cares for the child, securing her family's future in Bethlehem.
Boaz meets the nearer kinsman at the city gate with ten elders present to discuss redeeming Elimelech’s land. The kinsman agrees to buy it but declines to marry Ruth, passing the right to Boaz.
Naomi cares for her grandson Obed, born to Ruth and Boaz, and the neighbors name him. The passage then traces Obed's genealogy, linking him to King David through the line of Pharez.

Elkanah comforts his wife Hannah, who is deeply distressed over her barrenness during a sacrifice in Shiloh. Hannah prays silently to the LORD, making a vow, while Eli the priest mistakes her quiet prayer for drunkenness.

Boaz negotiates with a closer relative at the city gate to redeem Naomi's land and marry Ruth, following Israelite custom of removing a shoe as a sign of transfer. Boaz announces the purchase publicly to the elders and people.

Hannah explains to Eli the priest that she is deeply sorrowful but sober, not drunk as he suspected. Eli blesses her, and she leaves comforted. Later, Hannah conceives Samuel, whom she promises to dedicate to the LORD after weaning.

Elkanah from Ramathaimzophim has two wives, Hannah and Peninnah; Peninnah has children, but Hannah does not. Each year they go to Shiloh to worship, where Peninnah provokes Hannah over her barrenness, causing her great distress.

Hannah delays bringing her son Samuel to the temple in Shiloh until he is weaned, then presents him to Eli the priest with offerings, dedicating Samuel to serve the LORD as she had vowed during her prayer for a child.

Ruth stays at Boaz's feet overnight as instructed, and he gives her six measures of barley before she returns to Naomi in the city. Naomi encourages Ruth to wait patiently for Boaz to resolve the matter of their marriage.

Hannah praises God in a prayer of thanksgiving at Shiloh, celebrating His power and justice after God answered her prayer for a child, contrasting God's strength with human pride and highlighting His control over life and social status.

Hannah praises God's power and justice, then Elkanah returns home to Ramah. Meanwhile, Eli's corrupt sons exploit sacrifices at Shiloh, taking meat by force, contrasting with young Samuel's faithful service before the LORD.

A prophet confronts Eli at Shiloh, reminding him of God's choice of his family as priests since Egypt, but condemns Eli's sons' corruption and announces God's judgment to end Eli's lineage of priests.

This passage describes corrupt priests in Shiloh demanding raw meat by force from worshippers, causing people to despise offerings to God. Meanwhile, young Samuel faithfully serves the LORD, and Hannah conceives more children after Eli blesses her.

Hannah conceives more children after Samuel, who grows up serving God. Eli, now old, confronts his corrupt sons abusing their priestly roles, but they ignore him. A prophet rebukes Eli, recalling God's covenant with his family from Egypt.

Eli instructs Samuel how to respond when God calls him again. God then reveals to Samuel a judgment against Eli's family for his sons' sins. Samuel is afraid to tell Eli but eventually responds when Eli calls him.

Samuel, a young boy serving under the priest Eli in the temple at Shiloh, hears God calling him during the night but mistakes the voice for Eli's. After the third call, Eli realizes God is speaking to Samuel and instructs him how to respond.

Eli asks Samuel to share the message God gave him, and Samuel tells him everything without hiding anything. Samuel grows up with God's presence, becoming a recognized prophet throughout Israel, with God revealing Himself to Samuel in Shiloh.

A man of God warns Eli in Shiloh that his family will face judgment: his sons Hophni and Phinehas will die, his house will lose power, and a faithful priest will replace them to serve God's anointed forever.

After Samuel's prophetic word spread, Israel battles the Philistines near Ebenezer and suffers heavy losses. The elders decide to bring the ark from Shiloh, where Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas are, hoping it will save them.

As the Israelites bring the ark of the covenant from Shiloh to their camp near Ebenezer, the Philistines fear its arrival but still defeat Israel in battle, killing 30,000 and capturing the ark along with Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas.

After Israel's defeat by the Philistines, a Benjaminite soldier arrives at Shiloh to report to the elderly priest Eli that the ark of God was captured and Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were killed in battle.

A messenger reports to Eli in Shiloh that Israel fled from the Philistines, his sons Hophni and Phinehas died, and the ark was captured. Eli dies from shock, and Phinehas’ wife gives birth but dies, naming her son Ichabod, meaning the glory has departed.

The Philistines, troubled by plagues and destruction after capturing Israel's ark, move it from Ashdod to Gath, then to Ekron, seeking relief from God's judgment that afflicts their cities and people.

After seven months with the Philistines, their leaders consult priests and diviners about how to return the ark of God to Israel, learning they must send it with a trespass offering of golden mice and emerods to stop the plagues afflicting them.

Philistine priests advise their leaders to send the ark of Israel back on a new cart pulled by two unyoked cows, along with golden offerings, to see if the plagues stop and to confirm if God is truly punishing them.

The Philistines sent the ark of the LORD back to Bethshemesh on a cart pulled by two cows, accompanied by golden offerings. The people of Bethshemesh rejoiced, offered sacrifices, and the Philistine leaders returned to Ekron.

At Mizpeh, Samuel leads Israel in fasting and confession of sin. The Philistines attack, but Samuel prays and offers a sacrifice; God thunders against the Philistines, allowing Israel to defeat and chase them to Bethcar.

After the ark was returned by the Philistines, the people of Kirjathjearim placed it in Abinadab's house, where his son Eleazar guarded it. Samuel urged Israel to abandon idols and serve God, leading to a national gathering and repentance at Mizpeh.

After the Philistine lords saw the ark returned to Bethshemesh with golden offerings, many Bethshemites were struck down for looking inside the ark, prompting the survivors to send for the people of Kirjathjearim to take the ark.

Samuel warns the Israelites about the consequences of having a king, explaining how the king will take their sons, daughters, land, and resources for his own use, showing the heavy cost of monarchy after the elders request a king.

After the Philistines captured the ark of God at Ebenezer, they brought it to Ashdod and placed it in Dagon's temple. The next two mornings, the statue of Dagon was found fallen and damaged before the ark, and the people of Ashdod suffered severe afflictions.

As Samuel grows old, he appoints his sons as judges in Israel, but they act corruptly. The elders of Israel come to Samuel at Ramah, asking for a king to rule them like other nations, which displeases Samuel, who then seeks God's guidance.

After God helped Israel defeat the Philistines near Bethcar, Samuel set up a stone called Ebenezer to mark the victory. The Philistines were subdued, Israel regained lost cities, and Samuel judged Israel from Ramah, traveling to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpeh.

Samuel warns Israel about the burdens a king will impose, but the people insist on having a king to be like other nations. Samuel consults God, who tells him to obey the people, and Samuel sends them back to their cities.

Saul, a tall and handsome young man from Benjamin, sets out with a servant to find his father Kish's lost donkeys. They travel through several regions and decide to visit a respected man of God in Zuph for guidance.
Saul and his servant, searching for lost donkeys, decide to visit a respected prophet (seer) in a nearby city for guidance. They ask local girls if the seer is present as they approach the city.
Saul, from the smallest tribe of Benjamin, doubts his importance, but Samuel honors him at a feast and prepares to reveal God's message, marking the start of Saul's anointing as Israel's leader.

Saul and his servant ask local women in the city about the seer Samuel, who has arrived for a sacrifice. God has already told Samuel to expect Saul, whom he will anoint as Israel's leader to save them from the Philistines.

Samuel tells Saul of signs to confirm his anointing as king, including meeting prophets and receiving the Spirit of the Lord, which transforms him. Saul obeys, and the signs occur as Samuel had foretold near the Philistine garrison.

Samuel anoints Saul with oil, signaling his selection by God as leader over Israel. Samuel then gives Saul specific instructions about encounters he will have on his journey, including meeting two men near Rachel’s tomb and three men traveling to Bethel.

God tells Samuel he will send a man from Benjamin to lead Israel and save them from the Philistines. Samuel meets Saul, the chosen man, invites him to eat, and reassures him about his lost donkeys, while Saul questions his own worthiness.

Saul tells his uncle that Samuel revealed the lost donkeys but not the kingdom. Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpeh, reminds them God saved them, and announces their rejection of God by demanding a king. Saul is chosen but initially hides.

Saul meets a group of prophets on a hill, and the Spirit of God comes upon him, causing him to prophesy, surprising those who knew him. Afterward, Saul explains to his uncle their visit to Samuel and the search for the lost donkeys.

The Israelites seek Saul, who is hiding, and God reveals his location. Samuel presents Saul as chosen king, the people acclaim him, and Samuel explains the kingdom's laws. Saul returns to Gibeah with supporters, though some doubt his ability to lead.

Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabeshgilead, threatening to blind their right eyes. The elders ask for seven days to seek help. Messengers reach Saul in Gibeah, who becomes angry as the Spirit of God comes upon him.

Saul leads Israelite troops to a decisive victory over the Ammonites, silencing his critics. Samuel then gathers the people at Gilgal to officially confirm Saul as king, where they celebrate with sacrifices and rejoicing.

Samuel addresses the Israelites after Saul's coronation, affirming his integrity as their leader and reminding them of God's past deliverance through Moses and Aaron, setting the stage for a review of Israel's history and covenant with God.

Saul, newly anointed king, is filled with God's Spirit upon hearing that Jabeshgilead is besieged by Nahash the Ammonite. He rallies Israel's army, sends a warning by oxen pieces, and leads a surprise attack, defeating the Ammonites.

Samuel addresses Israel, recounting their history of God's deliverance and their repeated unfaithfulness, leading to oppression and rescue by judges, culminating in their demand for a human king instead of God as their ruler.

As the Philistines threaten Israel near Michmash, the distressed Israelites hide, and Saul waits in Gilgal for Samuel's arrival to offer sacrifices. When Samuel is late, Saul prematurely offers a burnt offering himself.

Samuel prays to God, who sends thunder and rain during harvest, causing the people to fear God and Samuel. The people ask for Samuel’s prayers, acknowledging their sin in demanding a king, and Samuel urges them to remain faithful to God to avoid destruction.

Samuel addresses the Israelites, reminding them they asked for a human king instead of God as their ruler. He warns them to obey God to prosper, then calls on God to send thunder and rain during harvest, showing their wrongdoing in demanding a king.

Saul, now king for two years, gathers 3,000 men; Jonathan attacks the Philistines at Geba, prompting a large Philistine army to camp at Michmash. Israelite soldiers become fearful and hide in caves and high places.

Jonathan, Saul's son, secretly plans to attack the Philistine garrison near Michmash with his armor-bearer, while Saul and 600 men stay at Gibeah. Jonathan expresses faith that God can save Israel despite their small numbers.

Jonathan, Saul's son, speaks to his armor-bearer about attacking the Philistine garrison near Michmash, setting a sign to confirm God's help. They reveal themselves, and the Philistines invite them up, unaware of the coming attack.

Saul, Jonathan, and their men camp at Gibeah while the Philistines camp at Michmash, dividing their forces to attack. Israel lacks blacksmiths due to Philistine control, so only Saul and Jonathan have swords and spears as battle begins.

Jonathan and his armor-bearer secretly attack the Philistine garrison, killing about twenty men and causing panic. Saul's watchmen see the chaos, and Saul orders a count, noticing Jonathan and his armor-bearer are missing, then calls for the ark of God.

Saul orders the ark of God brought near during battle against the Philistines. Confusion causes the enemy to fight among themselves, and Israel pursues them. Saul then commands a fast until evening to ensure victory.

After Jonathan's attack on the Philistines, the Israelite soldiers, faint from battle, ate meat with blood, violating God's law. Saul ordered them to slaughter animals properly and built his first altar to the LORD to atone for this sin.

Saul leads Israel to defeat the Amalekites, rescuing them from their oppressors. The passage lists Saul's family members and key military leaders, noting ongoing conflict with the Philistines and Saul's practice of recruiting strong warriors.

The prophet Samuel tells King Saul that God commands him to destroy the Amalekites completely for their past attack on Israel. Saul gathers his army, warns the friendly Kenites to leave, and attacks the Amalekites, killing all but capturing their king Agag alive.

During the battle against the Philistines near Michmash, King Saul forbids his troops from eating until evening, causing distress and weakness. Unaware of the oath, Jonathan eats honey and feels renewed, questioning the oath's impact on their victory.

Saul casts lots to find who broke his oath; Jonathan is chosen and admits tasting honey. Saul condemns him, but the people protect Jonathan for his victory. Saul then resumes fighting Israel’s enemies, including Moab, Ammon, Edom, Zobah, Philistines, and Amalekites.

King Saul builds his first altar to God and plans a night attack on the Philistines. He seeks God's guidance but receives no answer. Saul then uses a lot to identify a sin committed that day, resulting in Jonathan being singled out.

Samuel confronts King Saul about the spared livestock from the Amalekites, questioning his obedience to God's command to destroy everything. Saul insists he obeyed, claiming to have killed King Agag and destroyed the Amalekites.

Saul attacks the Amalekites but spares King Agag and the best livestock, disobeying God's command. God regrets making Saul king, and Samuel confronts Saul about the disobedience upon meeting him at Carmel and Gilgal.

Saul defends his actions to Samuel, claiming obedience but admitting the people kept spoils to sacrifice. Samuel rebukes Saul for disobedience, equating rebellion with sin, and declares God has rejected Saul as king. Saul pleads for forgiveness, but Samuel refuses to return with him.

Samuel confronts Saul about his disobedience and announces God's rejection of Saul as king, symbolized by tearing his mantle. Samuel executes King Agag, then departs, never seeing Saul again, though he mourns for him.

God tells Samuel to stop mourning Saul, whom He has rejected as king, and to go secretly to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from Jesse's sons. Samuel arrives in Bethlehem and prepares for a sacrifice with Jesse and his sons.

Samuel is in Bethlehem to anoint a new king as God has rejected Saul. He examines Jesse's sons one by one, but God rejects them all until David, the youngest shepherd, is brought and chosen by God to be anointed.

Saul's servants recommend David, a skilled harp player and warrior from Bethlehem, to soothe Saul's troubling spirit. David is sent by his father Jesse to serve Saul, becoming his armor-bearer and calming him with music.

Samuel anoints David, youngest son of Jesse from Bethlehem, as chosen by God, while God's Spirit leaves Saul, who is then troubled by an evil spirit. Saul's servants suggest finding a skilled harp player to soothe him, and they recommend David.

The Philistine army camps at Shochoh near Azekah, facing Saul's Israelite forces at the valley of Elah. Goliath, a giant warrior from Gath, appears fully armored, challenging Israel from a mountain opposite their camp.
