Goliath, a heavily armed Philistine giant, challenges Israel's army to single combat, causing fear among Saul's men. Meanwhile, David, the youngest son of Jesse from Bethlehem, is introduced as his three older brothers join Saul's battle camp.

David arrives at the Israelite camp during the battle with the Philistines and hears Goliath's challenge. The soldiers fear Goliath, but David asks what reward will be given to the man who defeats him, showing his boldness.

David, the youngest son of Jesse from Bethlehem, is sent by his father to deliver food to his brothers at the Israelite camp in the valley of Elah, where Saul's army is preparing to fight the Philistines, who have challenged Israel for forty days.

Saul explains to Samuel that he offered a burnt offering at Gilgal because the Philistines threatened attack and Samuel delayed coming. Samuel rebukes Saul for disobedience, announces his kingdom will not endure, then departs to Gibeah, where Saul and 600 men stay while Philistines camp at Michmash.

David asks what reward will be given to the man who kills Goliath, and the people agree. His brother Eliab angrily accuses him of pride. David insists he has a reason, and his words reach King Saul, who doubts David’s ability to fight the seasoned Philistine warrior.
David rejects King Saul’s armor because he is unaccustomed to it and instead arms himself with a sling and stones to face Goliath, who mocks him; David declares he fights in the name of Israel’s God.

David assures King Saul he can defeat Goliath, recounting how he protected his sheep from a lion and a bear. Saul offers his armor, but David rejects it, preferring his own familiar weapons before facing the Philistine giant.

After David defeated Goliath, Jonathan, Saul's son, formed a deep friendship with David, giving him his robe and weapons as a sign of their bond. David gained favor with Saul and the people, but the women praised David's victories more than Saul's.

David kills the Philistine Goliath with a sling and sword, causing the Philistine army to flee. David brings Goliath's head to Jerusalem. King Saul asks Abner about David's identity, and David reveals he is Jesse's son from Bethlehem.

After David's victory over Goliath, women praise David's greater success, which angers King Saul and sparks jealousy. Saul's fear grows as David gains favor with the people and God, leading Saul to keep David close but watch him suspiciously.

David confronts Goliath, declaring his trust in God rather than weapons, then kills the giant Philistine with a sling and stone, demonstrating faith and courage before the armies of Israel and Philistia at the Valley of Elah.

King Saul secretly instructs his servants to propose marriage to David, demanding a dangerous bride price of 100 Philistine foreskins, hoping David will be killed. David succeeds, marries Saul’s daughter Michal, but Saul grows increasingly fearful and hostile.

Saul orders Jonathan and his servants to kill David, but Jonathan, who loves David, warns him and pleads with Saul to spare David, reminding him of David's loyalty and bravery. Saul agrees, and Jonathan brings David back to Saul's presence.

David is gaining favor with all Israel and Judah, and King Saul offers his daughter Merab to David as a wife, hoping David will fight the Philistines and be harmed. Merab marries another, but Michal, Saul’s other daughter, loves David, pleasing Saul who plans to use her to trap David.

Jonathan warns David of Saul’s plot to kill him but brings him back to Saul’s presence. David fights the Philistines successfully, but Saul’s jealousy leads him to try killing David with a javelin. Michal helps David escape by deceiving Saul.

King Saul searches for Samuel and David in Ramah but is overcome by the Spirit of God and begins prophesying like them, even stripping off his clothes, showing a surprising spiritual episode amid his pursuit.

David, fleeing King Saul's attempts on his life, confides in Jonathan in Ramah, seeking protection and planning to hide during the new moon festival, while Jonathan promises to support him and watch for Saul's intentions.

David explains to Jonathan his plan to hide in Bethlehem during the family sacrifice to test Saul's intentions, expressing fear for his life. Jonathan reassures David and invites him to discuss their situation privately in a field outside the city.

Saul sends messengers to capture David, but Michal deceives him by placing a dummy in David's bed. David flees to Samuel at Naioth, Ramah. Saul's messengers encounter prophets there and begin prophesying, preventing them from capturing David.

Jonathan meets David in a field to discuss Saul's intentions. He promises to find out Saul's plans and send a signal to David, making a covenant of loyalty and kindness between their families before the new moon festival.

Jonathan tells David a secret signal involving arrows to warn him if Saul plans harm. David hides in the field during the new moon feast, where Saul notices David's empty seat beside him at the king's table in Ramah.

King Saul sits at the meal with Jonathan and Abner, noticing David's absence but says nothing at first. The next day, Saul questions Jonathan about David's absence, and upon hearing David is at a family sacrifice in Bethlehem, Saul becomes angry, accusing Jonathan of siding with David.

Saul angrily confronts his son Jonathan for supporting David and orders David's death. Jonathan defends David, realizes Saul's deadly intent, and mourns. The next morning, Jonathan meets David in the field with a secret signal planned.

Jonathan signals David with arrows to warn him of Saul's intentions, using a secret code known only to them. After the signal, they share an emotional farewell, reaffirming their covenant and friendship before parting ways.

David, fearing King Achish of Gath after fleeing from Saul, pretends to be insane by acting erratically at the city gate, causing Achish to question why he was brought there. This shows David's desperate attempt to protect himself.

David visits Ahimelech the priest at Nob alone, claiming secret orders from King Saul. He requests bread, and Ahimelech gives him consecrated shewbread, as no ordinary bread is available, trusting David's explanation about his men’s purity.

After faking madness before Achish, David escapes to the cave of Adullam where his family and troubled men join him, forming a group of about 400. He then seeks refuge for his parents with the Moabite king and moves to Judah on prophet Gad's advice.

David visits Ahimelech the priest at Nob, requesting bread and weapons while fleeing Saul. Ahimelech gives him consecrated bread and Goliath’s sword. David then flees to King Achish of Gath, where he fears the king after hearing his reputation.

King Saul orders the death of Ahimelech and the priests at Nob, accusing them of aiding David. Doeg the Edomite carries out the massacre, but Abiathar escapes and joins David, who promises to protect him.

Doeg the Edomite reports to King Saul that Ahimelech the priest helped David by giving him food, Goliath's sword, and seeking God's guidance. Saul accuses Ahimelech of conspiring with David and orders his death.

David learns the Philistines are attacking Keilah and asks God for guidance. God tells him to defend the town, so David fights and saves Keilah. Meanwhile, Saul hears David is trapped there and prepares to besiege the city.

Saul orders his men to scout David's hiding places in Ziph, then pursues him to the wilderness of Maon. David narrowly escapes as Saul's forces surround him, but Saul abandons the chase to fight the invading Philistines, while David retreats to Engedi.

After Saul returns from fighting the Philistines, he leads 3,000 men to find David in the wilderness of Engedi. Saul unknowingly enters a cave where David and his men hide; David cuts Saul's robe but spares his life, refusing to harm God's anointed king.

Saul gathers troops to besiege David in Keilah, but David consults God through Abiathar and learns Saul will come and the townspeople will betray him. David escapes with 600 men and hides in the wilderness of Ziph while Saul pursues him daily.

David is hiding from King Saul in the wilderness of Ziph when Jonathan, Saul’s son, visits to encourage him and make a covenant. Meanwhile, the Ziphites inform Saul of David’s location, offering to help capture him.

David stops his men from attacking King Saul in a cave at Engedi, then reveals himself and pleads his innocence, showing Saul the torn skirt as proof he spared his life, appealing to Saul to trust God's judgment between them.

David speaks to Saul in the cave at Engedi, refusing to harm him despite having the chance, and appeals to God's judgment. Saul recognizes David's righteousness, acknowledges his future as king, and makes David swear to protect his descendants.

David sends messengers to Nabal in Carmel, requesting provisions for his men who protected Nabal's shepherds. Nabal rudely refuses, insulting David, prompting David to prepare for armed retaliation with 400 men.

Abigail, Nabal’s wise wife, secretly meets David and his men after Nabal insulted David’s servants. She humbly pleads with David to forgive Nabal and avoid bloodshed, showing her quick action to prevent conflict.

After Samuel's death and burial at Ramah, David moves to the wilderness of Paran. Hearing that Nabal is shearing sheep in Carmel, David sends messengers to greet Nabal and remind him of their peaceful relations with his shepherds.

Abigail speaks to David, urging him to ignore her foolish husband Nabal's insult and praising David's restraint from violence, while blessing David and his men and warning of enemies pursuing him, affirming God's protection over David's life and mission.
David prepares to attack Nabal after his servants report Nabal's insult, but Abigail quickly gathers provisions to intervene, acting without Nabal's knowledge to prevent bloodshed.

Abigail warns David of danger from an enemy seeking his life and urges him to avoid needless bloodshed. David praises her for preventing him from killing Nabal and his household, showing his restraint and trust in God's plan.

After Nabal's death, David praises God for justice and sends for Abigail to marry her; she accepts and joins David, who also marries Ahinoam, while Saul gives David's former wife Michal to another man, Phalti.

David praises Abigail for preventing him from killing Nabal, accepts her gift, and sends her home in peace. Meanwhile, Nabal, unaware of the danger, feasts and gets drunk; after learning Abigail's actions, he falls ill and dies ten days later.

David and Abishai secretly approach King Saul's camp at night while Saul and his men sleep. Abishai urges David to kill Saul, but David refuses, sparing Saul as the LORD's anointed and taking only Saul's spear and water jug.

David speaks to Saul during a nighttime encounter in the wilderness of Ziph, questioning why Saul pursues him and refusing to harm Saul, despite having the chance, emphasizing respect for God's anointed king.

David secretly takes Saul's spear and water jug while Saul and his men sleep, then confronts Abner and Saul from a distance, questioning why Saul pursues him and asserting his innocence. This follows David sparing Saul's life in the wilderness of Ziph.

The Ziphites inform King Saul that David is hiding near the hill of Hachilah. Saul leads 3,000 men to find David in the wilderness of Ziph. David spies on Saul's camp at night with Abishai, finding Saul asleep surrounded by his men.

David refuses to harm King Saul despite having the chance, emphasizing respect for God's anointed. Saul acknowledges his wrongdoing, blesses David, and both part ways peacefully in the wilderness of Ziph.

David, fearing Saul's pursuit, escapes to Gath in Philistine territory with his 600 men and families. King Achish grants David the town of Ziklag, where David lives for over a year, while Saul stops searching for him.

The Philistines prepare for battle against Israel, and Achish trusts David to fight with him. Samuel has died, Saul mourns and banishes witches, but now, facing the Philistine army, Saul seeks a medium at Endor for guidance as God does not answer him.

David lived among the Philistines for over a year, raiding nearby groups and killing all survivors to prevent news from reaching Gath. Achish, king of Gath, trusted David, believing Israel had rejected him, so he accepted David as his servant.
King Saul, desperate for guidance as God no longer answers him, secretly visits a medium in Endor to summon the spirit of the prophet Samuel, despite having banned such practices earlier in Israel.

The Philistine armies gather at Aphek while Israelites camp near Jezreel. Philistine leaders question David's presence with Achish, fearing he might betray them since he is known as Saul's mighty warrior.

King Saul visits a medium at Endor to summon the prophet Samuel's spirit, seeking guidance as the Philistines prepare to fight Israel. Samuel rebukes Saul, reminding him God has rejected him and given the kingdom to David for disobedience.

David and his men return to Ziklag to find it burned and their families taken captive by the Amalekites. Grieving and threatened by his own men, David seeks guidance from God through Abiathar the priest and the ephod.

Samuel's spirit warns Saul that because he disobeyed God, his kingdom will be taken by David, and Israel will fall to the Philistines; Saul is terrified and weak, but a woman at Endor cares for him by preparing food before he leaves.

David consults Abiathar the priest using the ephod to seek God's guidance about pursuing the Amalekite raiders who burned Ziklag. After receiving a positive answer, David leads 400 men in pursuit, finding an exhausted Egyptian servant who provides information about the enemy.

The Philistine leaders reject David's participation in their battle against Israel, fearing his loyalty to King Saul. Achish, their king, reluctantly orders David and his men to leave while the Philistine army camps at Jezreel preparing for war.

The prophet Gad advises David to leave the cave and go to Judah, so David moves to the forest of Hareth. Meanwhile, Saul, in Ramah, accuses his servants of conspiring with David, and Doeg reports David's visit to Ahimelech at Nob.

David and his men have just defeated the Amalekites and recovered all their families and possessions. Some men who stayed behind refuse to share the spoil, but David insists on equal distribution among all.

David insists that all his men, including those who stayed behind at the brook Besor, share equally in the recovered spoil from the Amalekites. He then sends gifts from the spoil to the elders and friends in various towns of Judah, including Hebron.

David questions an Egyptian servant of the Amalekites who reveals their raid on Ziklag. The servant leads David to the raiders, who are feasting, and David attacks them, defeating all but 400 who escape on camels, recovering all captives and spoil.

The Philistines attacked Israel at Mount Gilboa, killing Saul, his sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Melchishua, and many soldiers. Saul, wounded, took his own life to avoid capture, leading to Israelite retreat and Philistine occupation of nearby cities.

After Saul and his sons died in battle on Mount Gilboa, Israelite survivors fled, allowing the Philistines to occupy their cities. The Philistines desecrated Saul's body, but the brave men of Jabeshgilead recovered and honored the bodies with burial and mourning.

Abner supports Saul’s son Ishbosheth as king over Israel, while Judah follows David in Hebron. Abner and Joab, leaders of opposing forces, meet at Gibeon and arrange a contest between their young warriors.

After Saul's death, David asks God where to go and is directed to Hebron, where he moves with his family and followers. The men of Judah anoint him king, and David blesses the people of Jabeshgilead for burying Saul.

After Saul's death, David returns to Ziklag and meets a distressed man from Saul's camp who reports that Saul and his son Jonathan have died in battle on Mount Gilboa, setting the stage for David's response.

An Amalekite man tells David he killed Saul at Saul's request and brought his crown and bracelet. David mourns Saul and Jonathan, then orders the Amalekite's execution for killing God's anointed king.

David condemns the Amalekite who claimed to have killed Saul, then mourns deeply for Saul and Jonathan, praising their strength and lamenting their deaths on Mount Gilboa, urging Judah to remember their legacy.

David mourns the deaths of Saul and Jonathan, praising their strength and lamenting their loss. He calls on the women of Israel to grieve, expressing deep personal sorrow for Jonathan, his close friend and ally.

Abner, commander for Saul's son Ishbosheth, and Joab, David's commander, arrange a duel between twelve warriors each near Gibeon. After a fierce fight, Asahel, Joab's brother, chases Abner but refuses to stop when warned.

After fierce fighting near Gibeon, Abner calls for a ceasefire with Joab to stop the bloodshed between their men. Joab agrees, and Abner retreats to Mahanaim while Joab returns to Hebron, mourning Asahel's death.

During the ongoing war between Saul's and David's houses, David grows stronger and has six sons in Hebron. Abner, supporting Saul's house, is confronted by Ishbosheth over taking Saul's concubine Rizpah, leading to Abner's anger.

Abner confronts Ishbosheth over a dispute about Saul's concubine, then seeks to ally with David to unite Israel. David agrees but demands Michal, his wife, be returned from Ishbosheth before meeting Abner.

David demands the return of his wife Michal from Ishbosheth, who complies. Abner then negotiates with Israel's elders and Benjamin, promoting David as king, and visits David in Hebron with twenty men, where David hosts a feast for them.

Abner visits King David in Hebron with twenty men, promising to unite Israel under David's rule. David hosts a feast and sends Abner away peacefully, but Joab suspects Abner's intentions and secretly recalls him without David's knowledge.

During a battle near Gibeon, Abner kills Asahel, who refuses to stop pursuing him; Joab and Abishai chase Abner until sunset. Benjamin's troops regroup on a hill, and Abner calls for peace, urging Joab to stop the fighting among kinsmen.

Joab secretly kills Abner in Hebron to avenge his brother Asahel's death. David mourns publicly, distancing himself from the murder and honoring Abner with a funeral, showing his sorrow and political tension within his ranks.

Rechab and Baanah, captains under Saul’s son Ishbosheth, kill Ishbosheth in his house and bring his head to David in Hebron, claiming to avenge the king. David condemns their act and orders their execution, burying Ishbosheth with Abner.

King David mourns Abner's violent death, publicly showing grief to prove his innocence. The people understand David did not order the killing, and he acknowledges his own weakness against Joab and his brothers.

David captured Jerusalem from the Jebusites, making it his stronghold called the city of David. He expanded the city, gained support from Hiram of Tyre, and established his kingdom, taking more wives and fathering children there.

After Abner's death in Hebron, Ishbosheth, Saul's son and rival king, is vulnerable; his captains Rechab and Baanah, from Benjamin, secretly kill him while he rests at noon, setting the stage for David's rise.

The tribes of Israel and their elders come to Hebron to affirm David as their king, recognizing his leadership since Saul's reign. David begins his rule at age 30, reigning first over Judah, then all Israel, and captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites.

King David seeks God's guidance on how to fight the Philistines, who have gathered in the valley of Rephaim. God instructs him to attack from behind near the mulberry trees, leading to a decisive victory from Geba to Gazer.

After David's sons are named, the Philistines attack upon hearing David is king. David consults God twice, receiving guidance to defeat them first at Baalperazim, then by ambushing near the mulberry trees in the valley of Rephaim.

David leads Israel in joyfully bringing the ark of the LORD into Jerusalem, offering sacrifices and blessings. Michal, Saul's daughter, watches disapprovingly as David dances before the LORD, highlighting tension between them.

After Uzzah's death for touching the ark, David feared bringing it to Jerusalem and left it at Obededom's house, where God blessed the household. Hearing this, David joyfully brought the ark to the city with sacrifices, dancing, and celebration.

After bringing the ark to Jerusalem with celebration, David blesses his household. Michal, Saul’s daughter, criticizes his behavior, but David defends his joyful worship before the LORD, leading to Michal remaining childless.

After David's victory and rest from enemies, he tells prophet Nathan he lives in a cedar house while God's ark is in a tent. Nathan initially encourages David, but God then questions the need for a temple, recalling His presence in tents since Egypt.

David leads 30,000 chosen men from Baale of Judah to bring the ark of God from Abinadab's house in Gibeah. During the procession, Uzzah touches the ark to steady it and is struck dead by God, causing David to name the place Perezuzzah.

God, through the prophet Nathan, promises King David that his descendants will establish an everlasting kingdom. David responds humbly in prayer, acknowledging God's greatness and the future of his house.
King David prays to God, praising Him and asking for His blessing on David’s house, trusting God’s promise to establish his dynasty forever, following the prophet Nathan’s message from the Lord.

King David prays to the LORD, praising God's unique greatness and faithfulness in redeeming Israel, and asks God to fulfill His promise to establish David's house and kingdom forever. This follows God's covenant message delivered through Nathan.

God speaks to Nathan, instructing him to tell King David that He chose David from a shepherd to lead Israel, defeated his enemies, and will establish David’s descendants and kingdom forever, promising stability and protection for Israel.

King David leads military campaigns against the Philistines, Moabites, Zobah, and Syrians, capturing cities and resources, and establishing garrisons. His victories expand Israel’s territory and influence, with God’s protection noted throughout.

David conquers cities of Hadadezer and takes much brass; Toi king of Hamath sends his son Joram with gifts to David for defeating Hadadezer. David dedicates spoils to the LORD, gains fame, places garrisons in Edom, and rules all Israel with justice.

After his military victories, King David governs all Israel, administering justice. Key officials include Joab as army commander, Jehoshaphat as recorder, priests Zadok and Ahimelech, scribe Seraiah, Benaiah over royal guards, and David’s sons as leaders.

King David promises to Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, to restore Saul's land and provide for him at the royal table. David assigns Ziba and his household to farm the land, and Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem, cared for despite his disability.

King David asks if anyone from Saul’s family remains to show kindness for Jonathan’s sake. Ziba, Saul’s servant, tells David about Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son, who David summons from Lodebar and promises to restore his inheritance and care for him.

Joab and Abishai coordinate their forces to fight the Syrians and Ammonites; Joab defeats the Ammonites, then David leads Israel across the Jordan to battle the Syrians at Helam after their initial defeat.

After the Ammonite king died, his son Hanun took over. David sent messengers to show kindness, but Hanun, misled by his princes, humiliated them by shaving half their beards and cutting their clothes, causing shame before David.

David comforts Hanun, king of Ammon, after his father's death, but Hanun humiliates David's servants. David's army, led by Joab and Abishai, prepares for battle against Ammonites and their Syrian allies near the city gate.

David leads Israel across the Jordan to fight the Syrians at Helam. Israel defeats them decisively, killing many soldiers and their commander Shobach. The allied kings of Hadarezer then make peace and stop aiding Ammon.

King David stays in Jerusalem while Joab leads Israel's army against the Ammonites at Rabbah. From his rooftop, David sees Bathsheba, wife of Uriah, and summons her. Bathsheba becomes pregnant, and David calls Uriah back from battle.
David questions Uriah about the ongoing war with the Ammonites and urges him to go home, but Uriah refuses to leave his comrades in the field, staying in Jerusalem instead during the siege of Rabbah.

David keeps Uriah in Jerusalem, gets him drunk, but Uriah avoids going home. David then sends Uriah with a letter to Joab, ordering Uriah to be placed in deadly battle. Uriah dies fighting near the city under Joab's command.

Joab reports to King David about the battle at Rabbah where Uriah the Hittite was killed. Joab instructs the messenger to explain Uriah’s death carefully to avoid David’s anger, referencing a past siege incident.

The prophet Nathan confronts King David with a parable about a rich man who unjustly takes a poor man's only lamb, provoking David's anger and judgment, setting the stage for Nathan to reveal David's own wrongdoing.

The prophet Nathan confronts King David with a parable revealing David's guilt in Uriah's death and Bathsheba's marriage, pronouncing God's judgment that violence and disgrace will come upon David's household openly.

The prophet Nathan confronts King David about his secret sin, announcing God's judgment that David's child will die. David confesses, prays, and fasts, but the child becomes very ill and dies after seven days, with David's servants hesitant to inform him.
David receives news of Uriah’s death in battle at Rabbah, urges Joab to continue fighting strongly, and later marries Uriah’s widow Bathsheba, who bears him a son; this act displeases the LORD.

After David's child with Bathsheba became very sick, the child died on the seventh day. David mourned but then worshipped God and resumed eating, explaining that fasting couldn't change the child's death, though he hoped for God's mercy while the child lived.

After the death of his first child with Bathsheba, David comforts her and they have another son, Solomon, whom God loves. Meanwhile, Joab captures Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, and David leads the final assault, taking spoils and punishing the people before returning to Jerusalem.

After David's victory at Rabbah, the focus shifts to his family in Jerusalem, where Amnon, David's son, becomes infatuated with his half-sister Tamar. With advice from his cousin Jonadab, Amnon schemes to get Tamar to care for him.
King David sends Tamar to care for his sick son Amnon, who then forces himself on her despite her protests, marking a tragic family conflict that follows David's recent military victory at Rabbah.
Amnon, son of King David, forcibly violates his sister Tamar despite her pleas, then rejects her. Tamar mourns in Absalom’s house, while King David becomes very angry upon hearing the news.
King David is angry after learning Amnon assaulted Tamar. Absalom, who hates Amnon, hosts a sheepshearing feast at Baalhazor and invites all the king’s sons, planning to kill Amnon when he is drunk.

Jonadab reassures King David that only Amnon is dead, not all his sons. Absalom flees to Geshur for three years after killing Amnon, while David mourns and longs to see Absalom again, feeling some relief over Amnon's death.
Absalom orders his servants to kill Amnon during a feast after Amnon assaults Tamar. David hears a false report that all his sons are dead, mourns deeply, but Jonadab clarifies only Amnon was killed.

Joab notices King David misses Absalom and sends a wise woman from Tekoah to plead a fictitious case, illustrating the danger of family strife and the need for mercy, to persuade David to reconcile with Absalom.
A wise woman sent by Joab speaks to King David, urging him to forgive and bring back his banished son Absalom, using a parable to appeal to the king’s sense of justice and compassion for his people.

The wise woman, speaking to King David as instructed by Joab, praises the king's wisdom and reveals Joab's involvement in her plea. David agrees to Joab's plan to bring Absalom back from exile in Geshur.

King David agrees to Joab's plan to bring Absalom back from exile in Geshur, but Absalom is not allowed to see the king. Absalom lives in Jerusalem for two years, noted for his beauty and family, yet remains estranged from David.

A wise woman from Tekoah, sent by Joab, tells King David a story about a family feud to persuade him to forgive Absalom, who has been banished after killing Amnon. David promises protection for her son, showing his willingness to hear her plea.

Absalom asks King David to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow made during his exile in Geshur. While there, Absalom secretly gathers support and allies, including Ahithophel, to start a rebellion against David.

Absalom lives in Jerusalem for two years without seeing King David. After Joab ignores his requests to intercede, Absalom burns Joab's nearby barley field. Joab then persuades David to reconcile with Absalom, who humbly returns to the king.

Absalom, David's son, begins gaining popularity by acting as a judge and greeting people warmly at Jerusalem's gate, winning their support. After many years, he asks King David's permission to go to Hebron to fulfill a vow to the LORD.

A messenger informs King David that Israel's loyalty is with Absalom, prompting David to flee Jerusalem with his household and loyal soldiers, while questioning Ittai the Gittite about accompanying him despite being a foreigner and exile.

King David urges Ittai, a foreigner who recently joined him, to stay behind as David flees Jerusalem due to Absalom's rebellion, but Ittai pledges loyalty and follows. The people weep as they leave the city, with priests carrying the ark of the covenant.

As David flees Jerusalem due to Absalom's rebellion, Zadok and the Levites carry the ark of the covenant out but are instructed to return it to the city. David ascends Mount Olivet weeping, showing his sorrow and uncertainty.

As David flees Jerusalem due to Absalom's rebellion, he mourns on Mount Olivet. He learns Ahithophel has joined Absalom, prays against his counsel, and sends Hushai back to Jerusalem to spy and counter Ahithophel's advice.

David, fleeing from Absalom, meets Ziba, servant of Mephibosheth, who brings provisions and claims Mephibosheth stays in Jerusalem hoping to regain his family’s kingdom. Then Shimei, a Saulite, curses David as he passes Bahurim.

As David flees to Bahurim during Absalom's rebellion, Shimei, a Saulite, curses and throws stones at him, blaming David for Saul's bloodshed. Abishai offers to kill Shimei, but David forbids it, accepting the curse as divinely permitted.

Absalom confronts Hushai about not supporting David, but Hushai pledges loyalty to Israel's chosen king. Absalom then asks Ahithophel for advice, who suggests publicly taking David’s concubines to assert power, which Absalom does in Jerusalem.

King David refuses Abishai's offer to kill Shimei, who curses David as he flees from Absalom's rebellion. Meanwhile, Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel, and David's friend Hushai meets Absalom, pretending loyalty.

Ahithophel advises Absalom to attack King David immediately with 12,000 men, but Absalom seeks Hushai's opinion. Hushai counsels against this, warning that David and his warriors are fierce and prepared for battle.

Hushai advises Absalom against Ahithophel's plan to attack David immediately, suggesting a larger, direct battle instead. Absalom and Israel prefer Hushai's counsel. Hushai then secretly warns priests to inform David to flee from danger.

Jonathan and Ahimaaz, David's messengers, avoid detection by Absalom's men by hiding in a well at Bahurim. After Absalom's servants fail to find them, they safely inform David to flee, prompting David and his followers to cross the Jordan River by morning.
Absalom and Israel camp in Gilead while David reaches Mahanaim. Local allies Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai bring food and supplies to support David and his weary followers in the wilderness.

David and his followers cross the Jordan River safely at dawn, escaping Absalom's rebellion. Ahithophel, whose advice was ignored, returns home and commits suicide. Absalom then crosses Jordan, appoints Amasa as army leader, and camps in Gilead.

King David organizes his troops into three groups under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai before battle against Absalom's forces. The soldiers insist David stay behind for their morale, and David orders his commanders to treat Absalom gently.
After Absalom's death, his body is buried under a pile of stones in a pit, and Ahimaaz and Cushi seek to bring news to King David, with Joab directing who should deliver the message first.

Hushai advises Absalom against Ahithophel’s plan to attack David immediately, warning that David’s experienced warriors will rally if surprised. He suggests Absalom gather all Israel for a full battle, personally leading his forces.

King David instructs his commanders Joab, Abishai, and Ittai to treat Absalom gently during battle against Israel in the wood of Ephraim. Absalom gets caught in a tree, and a man reports this to Joab, who questions why he didn't kill Absalom then.

Ahimaaz insists on running to bring news to King David at Mahanaim after the battle with Absalom's forces. The watchman spots two runners, and Ahimaaz arrives first, reporting that the LORD has delivered David's enemies into his hands.
Ahimaaz and Cushi bring King David news after the battle in the wood of Ephraim. David learns Absalom, his son, is dead and mourns deeply, showing his grief despite the victory over his enemies.

Joab confronts a man who saw Absalom caught in a tree but didn't kill him, citing the king's orders to protect Absalom. Joab then kills Absalom himself, signals the troops to stop, and Absalom's body is buried in a pit as Israel's forces retreat.

After Absalom's death, King David mourns deeply, causing the people to grieve and sneak back into Jerusalem in shame. Joab confronts David, criticizing him for grieving his rebellious son over the loyal soldiers who saved his life.

After Absalom's death, the people question why David hasn't returned to Jerusalem. David urges the leaders of Judah, including Amasa, to bring him back, and they unite to welcome him across the Jordan River, with Shimei coming to meet him.

As King David returns across the Jordan River, Shimei, a Benjamite who previously cursed David, comes with men of Judah to meet him and asks for forgiveness, while Abishai suggests punishing Shimei for his past offense.

Mephibosheth explains his servant's false report to King David and accepts the land division with Ziba. Barzillai, an elderly supporter from Rogelim who aided David at Mahanaim, offers to accompany him over the Jordan River to Jerusalem.

King David refuses to punish Shimei for cursing him, asserting his authority as king. Mephibosheth, Saul’s son, meets David in Jerusalem, explaining he was misled and unable to join the king due to his lameness.

King David crosses the Jordan River with Barzillai's blessing, accompanied by Judah and half of Israel's people. Tensions arise as Israel's men confront Judah's men over who should lead in bringing the king back.

After the wise woman negotiates peace, Sheba is executed and Joab ends the siege, returning to King David in Jerusalem. The passage lists David's key military and administrative officials, showing his restored authority.

A wise woman from Abel speaks to Joab, urging peace and offering to end the siege by handing over Sheba, the rebel leader. The city kills Sheba, sends his head to Joab, who then lifts the siege and returns to King David in Jerusalem.

King David orders Abishai and his forces, including Joab's men, to chase Sheba, a rebel threatening his reign. At Gibeon, Joab kills Amasa, who was leading the troops, then continues the pursuit with Abishai.
After Joab kills Amasa, his men rally to him and continue pursuing Sheba, who flees through Israel to Abel. Joab's forces besiege the city, where a wise woman calls out to negotiate with Joab.

Joab rebukes King David for mourning Absalom and neglecting his loyal soldiers who saved him. Joab urges David to encourage his people, who are divided and questioning why the king fled over Absalom's death.

After Absalom's rebellion, Sheba, a Benjamite, incites Israel to abandon David, causing a split between Israel and Judah. David orders Amasa to gather Judah's men and sends Abishai to pursue Sheba before he fortifies cities.

During David's reign, a three-year famine prompts him to consult God, who reveals it is punishment for Saul's past violence against the Gibeonites, a non-Israelite group. David negotiates with them to atone for Saul's actions.

Barzillai, an elderly supporter who helped David during his exile in Mahanaim, declines to accompany David to Jerusalem due to his old age, but offers his servant Chimham instead; David blesses Barzillai as he crosses the Jordan River back to Israel.

David and his men fight several battles against giant Philistines, including Ishbibenob and others from Gath. Abishai and David’s servants kill these giants, protecting David and Israel in ongoing conflicts.
David praises God in a song of deliverance after being saved from all his enemies, including Saul. He describes God's powerful intervention with vivid imagery of divine wrath and protection.

The Gibeonites demand seven sons of Saul for execution to atone for Saul's past violence against them. King David spares Mephibosheth but hands over seven others, who are killed. Rizpah mourns and guards their bodies until David is informed.

David introduces his mighty warriors, recounting their heroic feats in battles against the Philistines, highlighting their bravery and God's role in granting victory during times when Israel's forces had fled.

David praises God for his faithfulness and justice, affirming his own righteousness and trust in the LORD, who strengthens and guides him in battle, protecting and empowering him as his deliverer and shield.

David, Israel's king and psalmist, speaks his final prophetic words about just leadership under God's guidance, the enduring covenant God made with him, and the fate of wicked men, contrasting faithful rule with destructive enemies.

David praises God’s powerful deliverance, describing God’s majestic presence and mighty acts in rescuing him from overwhelming enemies, affirming his faithfulness and obedience to God’s laws as the reason for this divine protection.

David praises God for giving him strength and skill in battle, enabling him to defeat his enemies completely and establish his rule over foreign peoples who submit to him. This continues his song of thanksgiving for God's deliverance.
David concludes his song of praise to God, celebrating God's protection and deliverance from enemies, affirming God's justice and mercy toward him and his descendants as king over Israel.

This passage describes three of David's elite warriors risking their lives to bring him water from Bethlehem during a Philistine siege. David honors their bravery by pouring out the water as an offering to God instead of drinking it.

After hearing of Rizpah's mourning, King David retrieved Saul and Jonathan's bones from Jabeshgilead and buried them properly in Benjamin, leading to God's favor. Soon after, David fought the Philistines again, growing weak in battle against a giant warrior.

David describes his mighty warriors, highlighting Abishai, Joab’s brother, known for killing 300 men, and Benaiah, famed for heroic feats including slaying Moabite warriors, a lion, and an Egyptian; David appoints Benaiah as his guard captain.
David lists his elite warriors, naming thirty-seven mighty men including Asahel, Joab's brother, and Uriah the Hittite, highlighting their roles and valor as part of his military leadership.

God's anger leads Him to prompt King David to order Joab to count the fighting men in Israel and Judah, despite Joab's objections; Joab and his commanders then survey the land from Dan to Beersheba, including territories east of the Jordan River.

Joab and the army captain finish counting Israel's fighting men across the land, reporting to King David. David feels guilty for ordering the census, and God sends prophet Gad to offer David a choice of three punishments.

After David's census angered God, the prophet Gad offers David a choice of three punishments. David chooses to trust God's mercy, leading to a deadly pestilence that God halts near Jerusalem at Araunah's threshing floor.

As a deadly plague strikes Jerusalem, God stops the angel of destruction near Araunah's threshing floor. David confesses his sin, and prophet Gad instructs him to build an altar there. David approaches Araunah to buy the land for the altar.

Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, visits the aging King David to remind him of his promise that Solomon would succeed him. She warns that Adonijah is acting as king without David's knowledge, and Nathan the prophet arrives to support her plea.

Adonijah gathers his supporters to declare himself king, excluding key allies of David and Solomon. Nathan the prophet warns Bathsheba about Adonijah's actions and advises her to remind David of his promise that Solomon would succeed him.

King David meets Araunah the Jebusite to buy his threshing floor for building an altar to stop the plague. Araunah offers it freely, but David insists on paying, then offers sacrifices, leading to the plague's end.

While Bathsheba speaks to the aging King David about Adonijah's self-proclaimed kingship, the prophet Nathan arrives and questions David about Adonijah's actions, highlighting the political tension over the throne succession in Jerusalem.

King David is old and cold, so his servants find Abishag, a young woman, to care for him. Meanwhile, Adonijah, David's son, begins to claim the throne with support from Joab and Abiathar, but key leaders like Nathan and Zadok oppose him.

King David confirms to Bathsheba that Solomon will succeed him as king, fulfilling his oath. He summons Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah to anoint Solomon at Gihon and proclaim him king over Israel and Judah.

King David officially appoints Solomon as his successor over Israel and Judah. Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah anoint Solomon at Gihon, and the people celebrate loudly, which surprises Adonijah and Joab, who had just finished a feast.

After Solomon's anointing, David's servants bless Solomon, and David expresses gratitude for witnessing Solomon's succession. Adonijah, fearing Solomon, seeks sanctuary at the altar, asking for mercy; Solomon spares him if he proves loyal, then sends him home.
As King David nears death, he advises his son Solomon to be strong, follow God's laws, and deal wisely with Joab, who killed two commanders, urging Solomon to ensure Joab does not die peacefully.
Adonijah, Solomon's brother, asks their mother Bathsheba to request Abishag the Shunammite as his wife from King Solomon. Bathsheba approaches Solomon, who honors her and listens to her petition.

Adonijah and his guests hear a trumpet blast signaling Solomon's anointing as king at Gihon by Zadok and Nathan. Jonathan confirms Solomon's coronation, and David's servants bless Solomon, while David acknowledges the event from his bed.

As King David nears death, he advises Solomon to deal wisely with Joab and Shimei, rewarding Barzillai's sons for loyalty. After David's death and burial in Jerusalem, Solomon's reign is established, and Adonijah approaches Bathsheba peacefully.

Bathsheba asks Solomon to give Abishag to Adonijah as a wife, but Solomon sees this as a threat to his rule and orders Adonijah's execution. Solomon spares Abiathar the priest but removes him from office.

King Solomon removes Abiathar from the priesthood, sending him to Anathoth, fulfilling prophecy about Eli's house. Joab, loyal to Adonijah, flees to the tabernacle and clings to the altar; Solomon orders Benaiah to confront him.

King Solomon confronts Shimei for breaking his oath by leaving Jerusalem, reminding him of his past crimes against David. Solomon orders Benaiah to execute Shimei, securing Solomon’s reign over Israel.

King Solomon replaces Benaiah over the army and Zadok as priest, then confines Shimei to Jerusalem under threat of death if he leaves. After three years, Shimei's servants flee to Gath, and he retrieves them, disobeying Solomon's order.

King Solomon orders Benaiah to kill Joab, who fled to the tabernacle for refuge after supporting Adonijah. Joab is executed for past murders, and Benaiah replaces him as commander, while Zadok replaces Abiathar as priest.

King Solomon prays to God for wisdom to govern Israel, acknowledging his youth and the vastness of his people. Pleased by this request, God grants him unparalleled wisdom, along with wealth and honor beyond his asking.

Solomon forms an alliance by marrying Pharaoh’s daughter and continues building projects in Jerusalem. He worships at high places since the temple isn’t finished. At Gibeon, God appears to Solomon in a dream, inviting him to ask for a gift.

King Solomon begins his reign over all Israel, appointing key officials including priests, scribes, military leaders, and twelve officers who manage provisions for the royal household throughout the year.

King Solomon appoints twelve officers across Israel to supply food for his household, each serving a month yearly; the passage lists these officials and their regional jurisdictions, showing Solomon's organized governance after his wise judgment.

King Solomon maintained a vast military and royal household, with officers managing provisions. God granted him extraordinary wisdom, making him renowned worldwide for his proverbs, songs, and knowledge of nature, attracting visitors from many nations.

God appears to Solomon in a dream, granting him wisdom, riches, and honor. Solomon wakes, offers sacrifices in Jerusalem, and soon after two women come to him with a dispute over their children, beginning a famous judgment case.

Two women, both claiming to be the mother of a living child, present their dispute to King Solomon. Solomon proposes to divide the child, revealing the true mother by her plea to save the child, demonstrating his God-given wisdom to all Israel.

This passage lists officials in Benjamin and Gilead under King Solomon, describing Israel and Judah's prosperity and peace. Solomon's extensive kingdom stretches from the Euphrates River to Egypt's border, with abundant provisions and military strength.

Solomon and Hiram of Tyre establish a peaceful alliance, exchanging wheat and oil annually. Solomon mobilizes tens of thousands of workers and officers to quarry stones and prepare timber for building the temple in Jerusalem.

Solomon asks Hiram, king of Tyre, for cedar and fir timber from Lebanon to build the temple, offering payment. Hiram agrees, sending timber by sea, and they establish a trade agreement exchanging wood for wheat and oil annually.

King Hiram of Tyre, a friend of David, sends envoys to Solomon, who explains that now at peace, he plans to build the LORD's temple and requests cedar timber from Lebanon, offering payment and cooperation with Hiram's skilled workers.

Solomon describes the temple's construction details: three chambers of increasing width, stone prepared offsite to keep the site quiet, cedar woodwork, winding stairs, and surrounding chambers supported by cedar beams, completing the building structure.

In Solomon's fourth year as king, he began building the LORD's temple in Jerusalem, detailing its size and structure, including chambers around the walls to support beams without embedding them directly into the stone walls.

Solomon builds chambers around the temple and receives a message from God promising His presence if Solomon obeys. Solomon completes the temple interior with cedar wood carvings, focusing on the most holy place, continuing the detailed construction begun earlier.

King Solomon is describing the interior of the temple he built in Jerusalem, highlighting the cedar wood carvings, gold overlay, and large olive wood cherubim statues placed in the inner sanctuary where the Ark of the Covenant would reside.

King Solomon is completing the inner sanctuary of the temple in Jerusalem, placing large gold-covered cherubim statues and decorating the walls, floors, and doors with intricate carvings and gold, emphasizing the temple's grandeur and sacredness.

Solomon completes the temple doors with detailed carvings and gold, builds the inner court, and finishes the entire temple after seven years of construction, from the foundation laid in his fourth year to completion in his eleventh year.

King Solomon’s craftsman Hiram from Tyre cast two large bronze pillars with ornate tops decorated with pomegranates and lilies, which were installed at the temple’s entrance and named Jachin and Boaz.

After completing the temple, King Solomon spent thirteen years building his own palace complex in Jerusalem, including the grand "house of the forest of Lebanon" and a special porch for his throne, as well as a residence for Pharaoh’s daughter.

Solomon builds a grand house with costly stones and cedar, including a home for Pharaoh’s daughter. He summons Hiram from Tyre, a skilled brass worker, who crafts two large brass pillars for Solomon’s temple project.

King Solomon completes the temple's furnishings, including many gold vessels and implements, and stores treasures dedicated by his father David in the temple, marking the end of the temple construction and preparation.

King Solomon, with the help of Hiram from Tyre, installs two large bronze pillars named Jachin and Boaz at the temple porch, then crafts a large bronze basin called the molten sea, supported by twelve oxen statues, and ten bronze bases for temple vessels.

King Solomon commissions Hiram from Tyre to craft ten large brass bases with detailed decorations and wheels, part of the temple furnishings, continuing the description of the temple's elaborate construction and artistry.

King Solomon’s craftsman Hiram made ten identical bronze bases with detailed engravings and wheels like chariot wheels, each supporting a large laver for washing, arranged five on each side of the temple with the large basin called the sea placed on the southeast side.

King Solomon commissions Hiram of Tyre to complete the bronze furnishings for the temple in Jerusalem, including bases, lavers, and the large "sea" basin, all cast in the Jordan plain near Succoth and Zarthan, marking the completion of temple works.

King Solomon gathers Israel's leaders in Jerusalem during a feast to bring the ark of the covenant from Zion into the newly built temple's most holy place, where priests place it under the cherubim's wings as part of a grand religious ceremony.

As the priests place the ark with the stone tablets in the temple's most holy place in Jerusalem, a cloud fills the temple, symbolizing God's glory. Solomon then declares the temple a permanent dwelling for the LORD, fulfilling his father's vision.

King Solomon addresses the assembly in Jerusalem, blessing Israel and recounting God's promise to David that Solomon would build the temple, fulfilling the divine plan begun with David for God's dwelling place.

King Solomon speaks to the assembly in Jerusalem, acknowledging God's faithfulness in fulfilling His promise to David by allowing Solomon to build the temple and placing the ark there, and he prays for continued blessing on David's descendants.

King Solomon prays before the assembled Israelites in Jerusalem, asking God to keep His promise to David about his descendants' rule and to hear prayers made toward the newly built temple, acknowledging God's greatness beyond the physical house.

King Solomon prays before the assembled Israelites in Jerusalem, asking God to forgive their sins and respond to their prayers during hardships like drought, famine, or enemy attacks, emphasizing God's knowledge of each person's heart.
King Solomon prays in the newly built temple in Jerusalem, asking God to hear Israel's prayers, judge justly, forgive their sins, and restore them if they repent after being defeated by enemies.

King Solomon prays in Jerusalem, asking God to hear and judge all people by their hearts, including foreigners who pray toward the temple, and to support Israel in battle when they pray toward the city and temple he built.

King Solomon prays in Jerusalem, asking God to hear the prayers of Israelites even if they are exiled for sinning, and to forgive and show compassion when they repent and pray toward the temple he built.

After finishing his prayer at the temple dedication in Jerusalem, King Solomon stands and blesses all Israel, praising God's faithfulness to His promises and asking for continued guidance and presence with the people.

King Solomon prays at the temple in Jerusalem, asking God to forgive Israel's sins and show compassion to them even in captivity, recalling God's covenant with their ancestors through Moses after the Exodus from Egypt. Solomon finishes his prayer.

King Solomon concludes his prayer, urging Israel to remain faithful to God. He and all Israel offer massive sacrifices, dedicate the temple in Jerusalem, and celebrate a 14-day festival, rejoicing in God's blessings on David and Israel.

After Solomon completed the temple and his palace, God appeared to him again at Gibeon, affirming His presence in the temple and promising to establish Solomon's throne if he remains faithful like his father David.

God warns Solomon that Israel will suffer if they worship other gods; after 20 years of building the temple and palace with help from Hiram of Tyre, Solomon gives Hiram 20 cities in Galilee, which Hiram dislikes, and levies taxes to fund major construction projects.

King Solomon imposed a labor tax to build the temple, his palace, city walls, and various cities including Gezer, given to his wife by Pharaoh. He also conscripted remaining non-Israelite peoples for forced labor across his kingdom.

Solomon imposed forced labor on remaining non-Israelite peoples but appointed Israelites as leaders and warriors. He completed his palace and temple, built a navy at Eziongeber with help from Hiram of Tyre, and obtained gold from Ophir through sea trade.

The queen of Sheba praises Solomon's wisdom and God's favor on him, gifts him lavishly, and Solomon receives rare almug wood from Hiram's navy to build the temple and palace. She departs after receiving all she requested.

After the queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon in Jerusalem, he fulfilled all her requests and received vast amounts of gold annually. Solomon crafted lavish gold shields, a grand ivory throne with lion decorations, and stored them in the forest of Lebanon.

The queen of Sheba visits King Solomon in Jerusalem, bringing gifts and testing his wisdom with difficult questions. Impressed by his answers, his palace, and his lifestyle, she acknowledges that his reputation for wisdom and prosperity is well deserved.

God speaks to Solomon after the temple's completion, promising to establish Solomon's throne forever if he remains faithful, but warning that turning to other gods will bring judgment and disgrace upon Israel and the temple.

King Solomon increased Jerusalem’s wealth, making silver common and importing abundant cedar wood. He also imported horses and linen from Egypt, trading with neighboring kingdoms like the Hittites and Syrians to support his chariot forces.

King Solomon's wealth and splendor are described, including his golden throne with twelve lions, golden vessels, and a powerful navy trading with Tharshish. His fame for wisdom and riches attracts gifts and visitors from around the world to Jerusalem.

Solomon allowed his foreign wives to worship their gods, angering the LORD who had warned him not to follow other gods. As punishment, God declared He would divide Solomon’s kingdom after his reign, raising Hadad the Edomite as an adversary.

King Solomon, despite God's warnings, married many foreign women from Moab, Ammon, Edom, Zidonians, and Hittites, whose gods led him astray. In his old age, he built high places for their idols near Jerusalem, turning away from God.

Hadad, an Edomite exile in Egypt, asks Pharaoh to return home after David and Joab die. Meanwhile, Rezon becomes king in Damascus, opposing Israel. Jeroboam, Solomon’s servant, rebels due to Solomon’s building projects in Jerusalem.

God raises Hadad, an Edomite royal who fled to Egypt as a child during David's conquest of Edom, as an adversary to Solomon; Hadad gains favor with Pharaoh, marries into the royal family, and later seeks to return to Edom after David and Joab die.

God, speaking through the prophet Ahijah to Jeroboam, explains that because Solomon's descendants have turned from God, the kingdom will be divided: Jeroboam will rule ten tribes, while one tribe remains under Solomon's son for David's sake in Jerusalem.

Jeroboam, a strong and hardworking official under King Solomon, opposes him due to Solomon's building projects in Jerusalem. The prophet Ahijah meets Jeroboam, symbolically tearing his garment to announce God's plan to give Jeroboam ten tribes of Israel.

The prophet Ahijah tells Jeroboam God will make him king over ten tribes of Israel if he obeys, while Solomon tries to kill him. Jeroboam flees to Egypt. Solomon reigns 40 years, then dies; his son Rehoboam succeeds him in Jerusalem.

Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice and harshly refuses to lighten the people's burdens, fulfilling God's prophecy through Ahijah. Israel rebels, rejecting David's line, and kills Rehoboam's tax collector, forcing him to flee to Jerusalem.

King Rehoboam seeks advice on how to respond to Israel's request to lighten Solomon's harsh rule. He rejects the elders' counsel to be kind and instead follows the young men's advice to increase the burden, setting the stage for conflict.

After Rehoboam gathers an army from Judah and Benjamin to fight Israel, God commands through Shemaiah that they must not fight their brethren, so they return home. Jeroboam then builds Shechem and Penuel, fearing people will return loyalty to Rehoboam if they worship in Jerusalem.

Jeroboam fears losing loyalty to Rehoboam if Israelites worship in Jerusalem, so he sets up golden calves in Bethel and Dan, establishes non-Levite priests, and creates a new festival to secure his rule over Israel.

Rehoboam arrives in Shechem where all Israel gathers to crown him king. Jeroboam, recently in Egypt, is called back. The people ask Rehoboam to lighten Solomon's harsh rule, and he seeks advice from Solomon's old counselors on how to respond.

After Rehoboam rejects the people's request, Israel kills his tax collector Adoram and rebels, making Jeroboam king over all tribes except Judah and Benjamin, who remain loyal to Rehoboam in Jerusalem and prepare for war.

A prophet from Judah confronts King Jeroboam at Bethel, condemning his altar and predicting judgment. He performs a sign as the altar splits and ashes spill, while Jeroboam's hand withers when he tries to seize the prophet.

An old prophet in Bethel hears from his sons about the man of God from Judah who condemned Jeroboam's altar. The prophet pursues him, invites him to eat, and lies about a divine message to persuade him to return, despite the man's initial refusal.

After the man of God disobeyed God's command, a lion killed him on the road near Bethel. The old prophet who had deceived him found his body, mourned, and buried him, confirming the deadly consequence of disobedience.
An old prophet in Bethel deceives the man of God from Judah by falsely claiming an angel told him to bring the man back to eat, leading to the man's disobedience and death by a lion on the road.

The old prophet in Bethel buries the dead man of God and instructs his sons to be buried with him, affirming the prophecy against Jeroboam's altar. Jeroboam continues his wrongful practices, leading to judgment on his house.

Jeroboam's son Abijah is sick, so Jeroboam sends his wife disguised to the prophet Ahijah in Shiloh to inquire about the child's fate. Ahijah, though blind, is informed by God of her arrival and recognizes her despite her disguise.

The prophet Ahijah delivers God's judgment to Jeroboam's wife in Shiloh, declaring the death of their sick son and foretells the downfall of Jeroboam's house and Israel due to Jeroboam's sins and idolatry.

Ahijah the prophet, though blind, recognizes Jeroboam's disguised wife in Shiloh and delivers God's judgment against Jeroboam for his idolatry and evil deeds, declaring severe punishment on his house and kingdom.

Jeroboam’s wife returns to Tirzah after visiting prophet Ahijah, and their sick child dies as foretold. Jeroboam reigns 22 years, succeeded by Nadab, while Rehoboam begins ruling Judah, where the people continue sinful practices.

King Rehoboam of Judah led the people into sin by building idols and high places, provoking God’s anger. In his fifth year, Shishak of Egypt invaded Jerusalem, looting the temple and palace treasures. Rehoboam reigned 17 years, succeeded by his son Abijam.

Abijam becomes king of Judah during Jeroboam's reign over Israel, continuing his father's sinful ways. Despite ongoing wars, God preserves David's line, and after Abijam's death, his son Asa succeeds him as king in Jerusalem.

Asa becomes king of Judah during Jeroboam's reign in Israel, ruling 41 years. He reforms religious practices by removing idols and his mother’s idol, yet leaves some high places. War continues with Baasha of Israel, who fortifies Ramah against Judah.

King Baasha of Israel blocks Judah's access by fortifying Ramah; King Asa of Judah responds by bribing Benhadad of Syria to attack Israel's northern cities, forcing Baasha to stop building Ramah and retreat to Tirzah.

The prophet Jehu delivers God's judgment against King Baasha of Israel for leading the people into sin like Jeroboam, declaring Baasha's dynasty will be destroyed. Baasha dies and his son Elah succeeds him in Tirzah.

The altar splits and Jeroboam’s hand withers, then is healed after the man of God prays. The man refuses the king’s offer, obeying God’s command to avoid food and not return the same way. An old prophet in Bethel hears of these events from his sons.

King Baasha of Israel stopped building Ramah after Asa of Judah allied with Syria to attack Israel’s cities. Asa then dismantled Ramah’s fortifications to build other cities. Baasha later killed Nadab, Jeroboam’s son, during a siege at Gibbethon.

The prophet Jehu delivers God's judgment against King Baasha and his family for their evil deeds. After Baasha's death, his son Elah reigns briefly before his servant Zimri kills him, seizes the throne, and kills all Baasha's relatives in Tirzah.

Baasha, from Issachar, killed Nadab during a siege at Gibbethon and became king of Israel in Tirzah. He destroyed Jeroboam's family as prophesied, continued conflict with Asa of Judah, and ruled 24 years, following Jeroboam's sinful ways.

Zimri kills King Elah of Israel and destroys Baasha's family as prophesied by Jehu. Zimri reigns only seven days in Tirzah before Israel's army, supporting Omri, besieges the city. Facing defeat, Zimri burns the palace and dies.

After Zimri's brief reign and suicide by burning the palace in Tirzah, Israel split between supporters of Tibni and Omri; Omri prevailed, ruled twelve years, founded Samaria, but continued evil practices like his predecessors.

Omri became king of Israel, ruling from Samaria, and did more evil than his predecessors by following Jeroboam's sinful ways. His son Ahab succeeded him, married Jezebel, and promoted Baal worship, intensifying Israel's idolatry.
King Ahab of Israel built an altar and a grove for Baal in Samaria, provoking God more than previous kings. Meanwhile, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho, sacrificing his sons as foretold by Joshua.

Elijah stays with a widow in Zarephath, where God miraculously provides food during a famine. When her son dies, Elijah prays, and God restores the boy's life, confirming Elijah's role as a true prophet.

Elijah from Gilead proclaims a drought to King Ahab of Israel, then hides by the brook Cherith where God commands ravens to feed him. When the brook dries, God directs Elijah to Zarephath to be sustained by a widow.

God instructs Elijah to go to Zarephath in Sidon, where a widow will provide for him. Elijah meets her gathering sticks; despite her scarcity, she obeys Elijah’s word, and her meal and oil miraculously last during the drought.

Obadiah, Ahab's servant who secretly protects prophets, fears telling Ahab Elijah is alive because Ahab might kill him. Elijah insists on revealing himself, leading Obadiah to inform Ahab, who confronts Elijah about causing trouble in Israel.

King Ahab confronts Elijah, blaming him for Israel's troubles, but Elijah accuses Ahab's family of idolatry. Elijah calls for a gathering on Mount Carmel with all Israelites and Baal's prophets to challenge their faith.

Elijah challenges the people of Israel and the 450 prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel to prove whose god is real by calling down fire on a prepared sacrifice, highlighting the ongoing conflict between worship of Yahweh and Baal.

Elijah mocks Baal's prophets as they desperately call on their god without response. He then gathers the people, rebuilds the LORD's altar with twelve stones for Israel's tribes, and prepares a soaked sacrifice to demonstrate God's power.

After God sends fire from heaven to prove His power on Mount Carmel, Elijah orders the execution of Baal's prophets. Then Elijah predicts rain after a drought, and a storm begins as he runs ahead of King Ahab to Jezreel.

After Elijah's victory over Baal's prophets, Queen Jezebel threatens his life. Elijah flees to Beersheba, then into the wilderness, where an angel provides food, enabling him to travel 40 days to Mount Horeb, the mountain of God.

Elijah prepares a drenched altar on Mount Carmel to prove God's power, then prays for God to reveal Himself. Fire consumes the sacrifice and water, convincing the gathered Israelites that the LORD is the true God.

After reviving a widow's son, Elijah receives God's command to confront King Ahab during a severe famine in Samaria. Obadiah, Ahab's servant who secretly protects prophets, fears for his life when Elijah reveals himself.

Elijah, hiding in a cave on Mount Horeb, speaks to God about Israel's unfaithfulness and his fear for his life. God instructs him to anoint new leaders and reassures him that 7,000 faithful remain in Israel.

God reassures Elijah that 7,000 faithful remain in Israel. Elijah then finds Elisha plowing, symbolically passes his mantle to him, and Elisha commits to follow Elijah after a farewell to his family and a sacrificial feast.

Elijah, strengthened by food, travels 40 days to Mount Horeb, where God asks why he's there. Elijah expresses his zeal and despair over Israel's unfaithfulness. God reveals Himself not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in a gentle whisper.

King Benhadad of Syria besieges Samaria and demands Ahab, king of Israel, surrender his wealth and family. Ahab initially agrees, but Benhadad plans to seize more, prompting Ahab to warn Israel's elders of Benhadad's deceit.

King Benhadad of Syria and his allies prepare to attack Samaria, while a prophet tells King Ahab of Israel that God will deliver the enemy into his hands. Ahab organizes his forces, including young princes, as Benhadad drunkenly waits in his pavilion.

The young princes of Israel lead an attack against Benhadad's Syrian forces near Samaria, defeating them and causing the Syrians to flee. After the battle, a prophet warns King Ahab of another Syrian attack, while Benhadad's advisors plan to fight on flat ground.

A prophet confronts King Ahab after he spares Benhadad, whom God had appointed for destruction. The prophet warns Ahab of consequences, revealing his identity before Ahab returns to Samaria troubled by the message.

A prophet warns King Ahab that God will deliver the Syrian army into Israel's hands because the Syrians doubt God's power in the valleys. After a seven-day standoff, Israel defeats Syria at Aphek, and Benhadad's servants seek mercy from Ahab.

King Ahab of Israel consults the elders about Benhadad's demands for wives, children, silver, and gold, which he partially agrees to but refuses the full terms. Benhadad then prepares to besiege Samaria with his allies.

The Syrian king Benhadad, advised by his servants, changes tactics to fight Israel on flat ground at Aphek, replacing kings with captains. Israel, though outnumbered, is assured by a prophet that God will deliver the Syrians into their hands.

King Ahab of Samaria asks Naboth of Jezreel to sell his vineyard near the palace, but Naboth refuses, valuing it as his ancestral inheritance. Ahab becomes upset, and his wife Jezebel notices his distress.

Benhadad's servants, dressed in sackcloth and ropes, beg King Ahab of Israel for Benhadad's life. Ahab agrees to a covenant restoring cities. Meanwhile, a prophet tests obedience; a man refuses to strike him and is killed by a lion as a result.

In Jezreel, Jezebel orchestrates a false accusation against Naboth, leading to his execution by stoning so Ahab can seize Naboth's vineyard. God commands Elijah to confront King Ahab in Samaria about this injustice.

God commands the prophet Elijah to confront King Ahab in Naboth's vineyard in Samaria, condemning Ahab for Naboth's murder and predicting doom for Ahab, his family, and Jezebel for their evil deeds and causing Israel to sin.
Elijah pronounces judgment on King Ahab of Israel for his wickedness and Jezebel's influence. Ahab humbles himself by fasting and mourning, leading God to delay punishment until Ahab's son's reign.

King Ahab is upset because Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard near Ahab's palace in Jezreel. Jezebel, Ahab's wife, plots to seize the vineyard by falsely accusing Naboth of blasphemy, leading the city elders to condemn him.

After three years of peace between Syria and Israel, King Jehoshaphat of Judah visits King Ahab of Israel to discuss reclaiming Ramoth in Gilead. Ahab consults 400 prophets who urge battle, but Jehoshaphat requests a prophet of the LORD for guidance.

King Jehoshaphat of Judah urges King Ahab of Israel to seek a true prophet's counsel before battle at Ramothgilead. Ahab reluctantly summons Micaiah, known for prophesying bad news, while other prophets falsely predict victory.

The prophet Micaiah describes a vision where God’s heavenly court decides to send a lying spirit to deceive King Ahab’s prophets, leading Ahab to his downfall at Ramoth-gilead; Zedekiah, one of the false prophets, strikes Micaiah.

Micaiah is summoned by the kings of Israel (Ahab) and Judah (Jehoshaphat) to prophesy about the battle at Ramoth-gilead. Despite pressure to give a favorable prophecy, Micaiah insists on speaking God's true message, foreseeing Israel's defeat.

This passage summarizes King Jehoshaphat of Judah's reign, his military actions, and failed trade expedition. It also introduces Ahaziah, son of Ahab, who begins ruling Israel and continues his parents' idolatrous ways.

After King Ahab's death, Moab rebels against Israel. King Ahaziah of Samaria injures himself and sends messengers to inquire of Baalzebub, but God commands Elijah to tell them Ahaziah will die for seeking a foreign god.

After Ahab's death in battle at Ramoth-gilead, his body is treated as prophesied, and his son Ahaziah becomes king of Israel. Meanwhile, Jehoshaphat begins his 25-year reign over Judah, following his father Asa's righteous ways and making peace with Israel.

Elijah’s messengers report the LORD’s judgment to King Ahaziah in Samaria, who then sends soldiers to summon Elijah. Elijah calls down fire from heaven to consume the first captain and his men, showing his divine authority.

Elijah confronts the second captain sent by King Ahaziah to summon him, calling down fire from heaven to consume him and his men. The third captain pleads for mercy, and Elijah is instructed by an angel to go with him to the king.

The angel of the LORD tells Elijah to go with the captain to King Ahaziah in Samaria. Elijah delivers God's judgment that Ahaziah will die for seeking Baalzebub, and Ahaziah dies, succeeded by Jehoram. Further acts are recorded elsewhere.

Elijah prepares to be taken to heaven and travels with Elisha from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho, and Jordan. Despite Elijah's requests to stay, Elisha insists on staying with him, aware Elijah will soon be taken away.

After Elijah's ascension, Elisha's servants urge him to send men to search for Elijah, but he initially refuses. At Jericho, Elisha heals the city's bad water by casting salt into the spring, restoring the land's fertility.

Elijah and Elisha travel to the Jordan River, witnessed by prophets. Elijah parts the waters with his mantle so they cross on dry land. Elijah offers Elisha a request before his departure, then ascends to heaven in a fiery chariot.

Elijah is taken to heaven by a fiery chariot while Elisha watches at the Jordan River. Elisha picks up Elijah’s mantle, parts the waters, and crosses. Prophets at Jericho recognize Elijah’s spirit now rests on Elisha and offer to search for Elijah.

Micaiah warns King Ahab of Israel about his fate, is imprisoned for his prophecy, and then Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah go to battle at Ramothgilead, where Syria's army targets the king, mistaking Jehoshaphat for Ahab.
Elisha heals the water in Jericho, then travels to Bethel where children mock him. He curses them, and two bears maul 42 children. Afterwards, Elisha journeys to Mount Carmel and returns to Samaria.

Elisha responds reluctantly to King Jehoram of Israel, who seeks help against Moab alongside Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom. Elisha prophesies God's provision of water and victory over Moab, instructing them to prepare for battle.

Kings Jehoram of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah, and the king of Edom plan a seven-day journey through Edom's wilderness to fight Moab, but face no water. Jehoshaphat suggests consulting Elisha, the prophet, who initially rebuffs Jehoram.

Elisha instructs the allied kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom to devastate Moab’s land. Overnight, water miraculously fills the valley, deceiving Moabites into thinking their enemies are dead, leading to Israel’s surprise attack and victory.

Jehoram, son of Ahab, begins ruling Israel in Samaria and faces rebellion from Mesha, king of Moab. Jehoram counts his troops and asks Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, to join him in battle, planning to march through Edom's wilderness.

During the battle at Ramothgilead, Syrian captains mistake Jehoshaphat for Israel's king and attack him, but stop when they realize their error. King Ahab is wounded by an arrow, dies that evening, and his death fulfills Elijah's prophecy.

A widow of a prophet's family asks Elisha for help because her dead husband's creditor threatens to enslave her sons. Elisha instructs her to borrow many empty vessels and miraculously fills them all with oil to sell and pay her debt.

After helping a widow with oil to pay her debts, Elisha visits Shunem, where a generous woman hosts him regularly. Recognizing his holiness, she and her husband prepare a special room for him, and Elisha offers to help her in return.

Elisha discusses with Gehazi how to reward the Shunammite woman who cared for him; she is promised a son despite her husband's old age. The son grows up but suddenly falls ill and dies, and the mother places him on Elisha's bed before leaving.

The Israelite-led coalition defeats the Moabites in battle, devastating their land and cities except Kir-haraseth. Facing defeat, the Moabite king sacrifices his son, causing outrage and ending the conflict as the coalition returns home.

Elisha revives the Shunammite's dead son by praying and laying on him; then at Gilgal, during a famine, Elisha purifies poisoned stew so the prophets can eat safely, showing his ongoing prophetic ministry.

The Shunammite woman, whose son has died, urgently seeks Elisha's help, traveling to Mount Carmel despite it not being a festival day. Elisha senses her distress but is unaware of her son's death until she confronts him.

Elisha miraculously purifies a poisonous stew during a famine in Gilgal, then feeds a hundred men with a small amount of barley loaves and corn, demonstrating God's provision through the prophet's actions.

Naaman, a respected Syrian army commander and leper, learns from an Israelite captive girl about Elisha, the prophet in Samaria who can heal him. The Syrian king sends Naaman with a letter and gifts to the king of Israel requesting healing.

Naaman refuses Elisha's offer of a gift after being healed of leprosy and requests permission to take soil to worship the LORD in Syria. Gehazi, Elisha's servant, decides to pursue Naaman to deceitfully accept gifts.

Naaman, a Syrian commander with leprosy, initially refuses Elisha's simple healing method of washing in the Jordan River, but after his servants persuade him, he obeys, is healed, and acknowledges the God of Israel, offering a gift which Elisha declines.

The king of Syria sends Naaman to Israel with a letter requesting healing for his leprosy. The Israelite king is distressed, but Elisha invites Naaman to come to him. Elisha instructs Naaman to wash in the Jordan River to be healed, but Naaman is initially angry and skeptical.

The Shunammite woman confronts Elisha after her son dies; Elisha sends Gehazi with his staff to revive the child, but it fails. Elisha then prays, lies on the child, and miraculously restores him to life.

Gehazi, Elisha's servant, deceitfully pursues Naaman to accept gifts meant for Elisha. After hiding the gifts, Gehazi lies to Elisha but is confronted and cursed with Naaman's former leprosy as punishment.

Elisha and the sons of the prophets move to the Jordan to build a new dwelling. Elisha miraculously retrieves a borrowed axe head from the water. Meanwhile, Elisha warns the king of Israel about Syrian military plans, helping him avoid ambushes.

The king of Israel avoids Syrian attacks by following Elisha's warnings. The Syrian king suspects a spy and learns Elisha reveals his plans, so he sends troops to capture Elisha in Dothan. Elisha's servant fears, but Elisha reassures him.

King of Israel consults Elisha about captured Syrian soldiers; Elisha advises kindness, leading to peace. Later, Syrian King Benhadad besieges Samaria, causing severe famine, prompting a desperate woman to cry out to the king for help.

Elisha comforts his servant during a Syrian army siege by revealing a heavenly army protecting them. He then blinds the enemy soldiers, leads them to Samaria, and restores their sight before the king debates attacking them.

Elisha prophesies food prices will drop in Samaria despite famine; a skeptical royal advisor doubts it. Meanwhile, four lepers outside the city decide to risk approaching the Syrian camp, only to find it mysteriously deserted.
