Four lepers at Samaria, desperate from famine, find the Syrian army camp abandoned after God causes the Syrians to flee in fear. They plunder the camp but decide to report the good news to the king instead of keeping silent.

In Samaria, the king's servant suggests sending horses to spy on the fleeing Syrians. They find abandoned goods, confirming the Syrians' retreat. The people plunder the camp, fulfilling Elisha's prophecy about food prices, but the king's trusted lord dies in the crowd.

King of Israel assigns his trusted officer to guard the city gate during a famine; the officer dies trampled by the crowd, fulfilling Elisha's prophecy that he would see the food prices drop but not eat the food himself.

The four lepers realize they must share the good news that the Syrian army has fled Samaria's camp. They inform the city gatekeeper, who alerts King Jehoram, prompting him to send men to investigate the abandoned Syrian camp.

During a severe famine caused by the siege of Samaria by Benhadad, a desperate woman tells King Israel about cannibalism among the people. The king mourns and blames Elisha, who prepares for the king's attack as a messenger arrives.

Elisha tells the woman whose son he revived to leave Samaria due to a coming seven-year famine. After living in Philistine territory, she returns and appeals to the king for her property, with Gehazi confirming her identity and Elisha's miracle.

Gehazi identifies the woman whose son Elisha revived as she appeals to the king for her property, which the king restores. Meanwhile, Elisha arrives in Damascus where King Benhadad of Syria is ill, and sends Hazael to ask Elisha if he will recover.

This passage summarizes King Joram of Judah's reign and death, introduces his son Ahaziah who ruled briefly, and describes their alliance with King Joram of Israel in a battle against Hazael of Syria, leading to Joram's injury and Ahaziah's visit to Jezreel.

Elisha anoints Jehu king of Israel, commanding him to destroy Ahab's family and avenge the prophets killed by Jezebel. Jehu reveals this to his servants, who then proclaim him king with trumpet blasts.

Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat and married to Ahab's daughter, begins his 8-year reign over Judah during Joram of Israel's rule. Edom and Libnah rebel; Jehoram fights Edom but the revolt persists. His deeds are recorded in Judah's chronicles.

Elisha sends a young prophet to Ramothgilead to anoint Jehu as king of Israel, commanding him to destroy Ahab's family and avenge the prophets killed by Jezebel. This marks the start of Jehu's rebellion against Ahab's dynasty.

Elisha tells Hazael, messenger of the sick Syrian king Benhadad, that the king will die despite seeming recovery. Hazael then kills Benhadad and becomes king. Meanwhile, Jehoram begins to reign in Judah during Joram of Israel's fifth year.

After Jehu kills King Joram and Ahaziah, he arrives at Jezreel where Queen Jezebel confronts him. Jehu orders her thrown from a window, fulfilling Elijah’s prophecy about her death and disgrace in Jezreel.

Jehu is proclaimed king by the army and secretly plans to overthrow King Joram of Israel, who is recovering from battle wounds in Jezreel. Jehu approaches Jezreel with his forces, refusing peace when Joram sends messengers to inquire.

Jehu approaches Jezreel aggressively, ignoring peace inquiries from King Joram's messengers. Joram and Ahaziah prepare to confront Jehu, but Joram senses betrayal and flees, fearing Jehu's violent intentions.
Jehu kills King Joram of Israel in Jezreel, fulfilling God's judgment for Naboth's murder. Ahaziah, king of Judah, tries to flee but is also killed. Ahaziah's reign begins as Jehu's revolt unfolds.

Jehu sends a second letter to Jezreel's leaders ordering them to kill Ahab's seventy sons, who are under their care. They obey, sending the heads to Jehu, who publicly declares God's prophecy against Ahab's house is fulfilled.

Jehu, having killed King Ahab, writes to Jezreel's leaders urging them to crown one of Ahab's 70 sons and defend the dynasty. The leaders fear Jehu's power and pledge loyalty, but he demands they kill all Ahab's sons and send their heads to him.

Jehu confirms God's prophecy by killing all remaining members of Ahab's family and officials in Jezreel, then kills 42 relatives of King Ahaziah of Judah at a shearing house. He meets Jehonadab, who joins him in his mission.

Jehu meets Jehonadab, allies with him, then kills Ahab’s remaining family in Samaria as prophesied. Jehu calls all Baal worshippers to a large assembly, planning to destroy them under the guise of a great sacrifice.

Jehu calls all Baal worshippers in Israel to a large assembly in the Baal temple. After ensuring only Baal followers are present, he orders his men to kill them all, beginning his purge of Baal worship in Israel.

After King Ahaziah's death, his mother Athaliah kills the royal family to seize power in Judah. Jehosheba secretly hides young Joash in the temple for six years while Athaliah rules, then priest Jehoiada organizes a protective guard to secure Joash's safety.

Jehoiada the priest organizes a strong guard around young Joash to protect him during his public crowning as king in the temple of the LORD, while Athaliah, the usurping queen, hears the commotion and approaches the temple.

Athaliah confronts the crowd in the temple as Jehoash is revealed as king, but Jehoiada orders her execution outside the temple. Jehoiada then renews the covenant with the people, who destroy Baal's temple and kill its priest in Jerusalem.

After Jehoiada the priest orchestrated Jehoash's coronation, the people destroyed Baal's temple and killed its priest Mattan in Jerusalem. Jehoash was brought to the throne, Athaliah was executed, and peace returned to the city.

This passage summarizes Jehu's reign as king of Israel in Samaria, noting his failure to fully follow God's law, the military losses Israel suffered under Hazael, and his death after 28 years, succeeded by his son Jehoahaz.

Jehoash begins his 40-year reign in Jerusalem, guided by priest Jehoiada, aiming to repair the temple using dedicated funds. After 23 years, he confronts the priests for not fixing the temple's damages as instructed.

King Jehoash confronts the priests about not repairing the temple, then Jehoiada sets up a chest to collect funds transparently for repairs, with officials counting the money to ensure accountability in Jerusalem.

Jehu orders the killing of Baal worshippers in Samaria, destroys Baal's temple and idols, fulfilling God's judgment on Ahab's house. Yet, Jehu continues idol worship from Jeroboam's time, though God promises his descendants will rule for four generations.

King Jehoash’s officials counted the funds collected for temple repairs and entrusted them to overseers, who paid workers to fix the temple. The money was used solely for repairs, and the overseers managed it honestly. Sin offerings remained with the priests.

After overseeing temple repairs, King Jehoash of Judah sends treasures to Hazael of Syria to stop his attack on Jerusalem, but later Jehoash is assassinated by his servants Jozachar and Jehozabad, and his son Amaziah becomes king.

Jehoahaz began his 17-year reign over Israel in Samaria during Joash of Judah's 23rd year. Despite his evil ways, he prayed to God amid Syrian oppression by kings Hazael and Benhadad, who devastated Israel's military forces.

Jehoahaz of Israel suffered heavy losses to the king of Syria, leaving him with a small army before his death and burial in Samaria. His son Jehoash then reigned, continuing evil practices and fighting Amaziah of Judah, before dying and being buried in Samaria.

After King Joash of Israel died and was buried in Samaria, he visited the sick prophet Elisha before his death. Elisha gave Joash a symbolic bow and arrows, prophesying Israel's victory over Syria but rebuked Joash for not striking enough times.

Elisha rebukes King Joash of Israel for not fully defeating Syria; Elisha then dies and is buried. Moabites invade, but a dead man revived after touching Elisha's bones. Hazael rules Syria, oppressing Israel until his death, after which Joash reclaims cities.

Amaziah king of Judah was killed in Lachish after a conspiracy; his son Azariah became king. Meanwhile, Jeroboam son of Joash began a 41-year reign over Israel, restoring its borders despite continuing sinful practices.

Amaziah becomes king of Judah at age 25 during Joash of Israel's reign. He follows his father Joash's ways, punishes his father's murderers but spares their children per Mosaic law, and defeats Edom, capturing Selah (Joktheel).

God noticed Israel's severe suffering and chose to preserve them through King Jeroboam's leadership, who regained lost territories like Damascus and Hamath; Jeroboam's reign ended with his son Zachariah succeeding him in Samaria.

After Amaziah of Judah refused to heed Jehoash of Israel's warning, Jehoash defeated him at Bethshemesh, captured him, and plundered Jerusalem. Amaziah later faced a conspiracy, fled to Lachish, and was killed there.

King Amaziah of Judah defeated Edom and renamed Selah, then challenged King Jehoash of Israel to battle. Jehoash warned Amaziah not to overreach, but Amaziah ignored him, leading to Israel's victory over Judah at Bethshemesh.

Azariah, son of Amaziah, begins his 52-year reign over Judah in Jerusalem at age 16, continuing his father's policies but not removing high places. He becomes a leper, and his son Jotham governs. Meanwhile, Zachariah briefly rules Israel in Samaria.

After Shallum's brief reign and conspiracy, Menahem violently seized power in Israel, attacking Tiphsah. He ruled ten years in Samaria, paid tribute to Assyria's King Pul to secure his throne, and taxed Israel's wealthy men heavily.

Zachariah, son of Jeroboam, ruled Israel in Samaria for six months before being assassinated by Shallum, son of Jabesh. Shallum then ruled briefly before Menahem from Tirzah killed him and took the throne, continuing the violent power struggles in Israel.

After Menahem's reign in Israel, his son Pekahiah ruled briefly in Samaria but was assassinated by Pekah, a military captain, who then ruled for twenty years, continuing the sinful practices established by Jeroboam.

Pekah ruled Israel but continued sinful practices; during his reign, Assyrian king Tiglathpileser captured northern territories. Hoshea killed Pekah and became king. Meanwhile, Jotham began his 16-year reign over Judah, following his father Uzziah's example.

King Ahaz returned from Damascus and ordered priest Urijah to build and use a new altar modeled after one in Damascus, changing the temple's furnishings and rituals in Jerusalem to match his commands.

King Jotham of Judah ruled righteously like his father Uzziah but allowed high place worship to continue. He built the temple's upper gate. During his reign, Syria's King Rezin and Israel's Pekah attacked Judah. After Jotham's death, his son Ahaz became king.

King Ahaz of Judah, threatened by Syria and Israel, seeks help from Tiglathpileser, king of Assyria, sending treasures from the temple as tribute. After Assyria conquers Damascus, Ahaz visits the city, copies a foreign altar, and has it built in Jerusalem.

King Ahaz altered temple furnishings and structures in Jerusalem, redirecting parts of the temple for Assyrian use. His other deeds are recorded elsewhere. After his death, his son Hezekiah became king of Judah.

This passage describes the Assyrian king capturing Samaria and exiling the Israelites to various locations. It explains that Israel's exile was due to their idolatry and disobedience to God, despite His deliverance from Egypt.

Hoshea becomes king of Israel in Samaria during Ahaz's reign in Judah, serves Assyria but rebels by seeking Egypt's help. Assyria imprisons Hoshea, besieges Samaria for three years, then conquers Israel and exiles its people to various places in Assyria.

Ahaz, son of Jotham, begins his 16-year reign over Judah at age 20, doing evil like Israel's kings. Syria's Rezin and Israel's Pekah besiege Jerusalem; Ahaz loses Elath and seeks help from Assyria's Tiglathpileser against them.

This passage describes how the people of Israel and Judah ignored God's warnings through prophets, continued idol worship, rejected His covenant, and followed pagan practices despite clear commands not to do so.

This passage describes the Israelites' idolatry and evil practices under King Jeroboam, leading to God's anger and their exile, while Judah also disobeys God by following Israel's sinful ways after the kingdom split from David's line.

This passage explains how Jeroboam led Israel away from following God, causing their exile to Assyria. The Assyrian king resettled foreign peoples in Samaria, who did not honor God, leading to problems like lion attacks.

After Assyria resettled foreign peoples in Samaria, these new inhabitants suffered lion attacks, prompting the Assyrian king to send a captured Israelite priest to teach them the local God. Yet each group also worshipped their own gods in the cities.

This passage describes foreign peoples settled in Samaria by the Assyrians who worship their own gods alongside the LORD, ignoring Israel's covenant laws given by God to their ancestors after the Exodus from Egypt.

This passage records God's commands to Israel to obey His laws and fear only Him, promising deliverance from enemies, but Israel disobeyed and continued idol worship, a pattern repeated by successive generations after exile to Assyria.

Hezekiah becomes king of Judah at 25, ruling in Jerusalem for 29 years. He reforms worship by removing idols, trusts God, opposes Assyria, and defeats the Philistines, marking a contrast to Israel's decline under Hoshea.

Assyrian envoy Rabshakeh confronts Hezekiah’s officials Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah, mocking Judah’s trust in Egypt and God, and demands tribute while challenging Hezekiah’s religious reforms and rebellion against Assyria.

Rabshakeh, an Assyrian envoy, mocks Judah's trust in Egypt and claims the LORD supports Assyria's attack. Judah's officials ask him to speak privately in Aramaic, but Rabshakeh loudly insults them in Hebrew to intimidate Jerusalem's people.

King Hezekiah of Judah defeated the Philistines near Gaza. Meanwhile, Assyrian King Shalmaneser besieged and captured Samaria, deporting Israel's people for disobedience. Later, Assyrian King Sennacherib attacked Judah's fortified cities.

In Hezekiah's 14th year, Assyrian king Sennacherib captured Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah paid heavy tribute from temple and royal treasures to Assyria. Assyrian officials then arrived at Jerusalem, where Hezekiah's officials met them.

Rabshakeh, an Assyrian commander, threatens Jerusalem, urging the people to distrust King Hezekiah and God’s protection, claiming no gods have saved lands from Assyria. The people remain silent as Hezekiah’s officials report the message to him.

Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, mocks Judah’s leaders and loudly warns Jerusalem’s people not to trust King Hezekiah or God for deliverance, urging them to surrender to Assyria for survival during the siege.

King Hezekiah reacts to Assyrian threats by mourning and seeking God's help, sending officials to prophet Isaiah to pray for Judah's survival. Isaiah reassures Hezekiah that God will protect Jerusalem and defeat the Assyrian king.

King Hezekiah reads a threatening letter from Assyrian king Sennacherib, prays to God for deliverance, and Isaiah the prophet responds with God's assurance that He has heard Hezekiah's prayer against Assyria's threat to Jerusalem.

The prophet Isaiah delivers God's response to King Hezekiah's prayer, condemning Assyrian King Sennacherib's blasphemy and boasting about his military conquests, reminding him that God has long controlled these events.

Isaiah delivers God's message to Hezekiah, assuring that despite Assyria's past conquests, Jerusalem will be spared. God promises to limit the siege's impact and restore Judah's survivors, emphasizing divine protection amid Assyrian threats.

God tells Isaiah to assure Hezekiah that Assyria's king will retreat and be defeated. Rabshakeh finds Assyria fighting elsewhere and sends threatening messages to Hezekiah, who then prays in the temple, seeking God's help for Jerusalem.

Isaiah delivers God's promise to King Hezekiah that the Assyrian king Sennacherib will not capture Jerusalem; that night, an angel kills many Assyrian soldiers, leading to Sennacherib's retreat and eventual assassination by his sons in Nineveh.

King Manasseh of Judah commits many sins, including child sacrifice and idolatry in the temple in Jerusalem, defying God's commands given to David and Solomon, and leading the people into greater evil than previous nations.

King Hezekiah of Judah is gravely ill, and the prophet Isaiah delivers God's message that he will die. Hezekiah prays, and God responds through Isaiah, promising healing and 15 more years of life, protecting Jerusalem from Assyria.

Manasseh begins his long reign as king of Judah at age twelve, reversing his father Hezekiah’s reforms by restoring pagan worship and altars in Jerusalem, including in the temple, and practicing occult rituals, provoking God's anger.

Isaiah warns King Hezekiah that his descendants will be taken to Babylon as eunuchs. Hezekiah accepts this, valuing peace in his lifetime. The chapter concludes with a summary of Hezekiah’s achievements and his death, succeeded by his son Manasseh.

The LORD, through prophets, condemns King Manasseh of Judah for leading the people into worse idolatry than previous nations, warning of severe judgment and destruction on Jerusalem and Judah for their persistent evil and rebellion.
King Amon of Judah abandoned the worship of the LORD, was assassinated by his own servants, but the people avenged him and made his son Josiah king, continuing the royal line in Jerusalem.

The passage summarizes King Manasseh's reign in Jerusalem, highlighting his great evil and shedding of innocent blood, then introduces his son Amon, who also ruled briefly and followed Manasseh's idolatrous ways, forsaking God.

King Hezekiah shows Babylonian envoys all his treasures, but the prophet Isaiah warns him that these riches and his descendants will one day be taken captive to Babylon, signaling future exile and loss for Judah.

King Josiah begins his reign at age eight in Jerusalem, following his father Amon. At 18, he orders Shaphan to oversee temple repairs, entrusting funds to workers without strict accounting due to their faithfulness.

Priest Hilkiah and officials consult prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem about the newly found book of the law. She delivers God's message warning of coming judgment on Judah for idolatry and disobedience.

King Josiah, who began to reign young and sought to repair the temple in Jerusalem, receives a book of the law found by High Priest Hilkiah; upon hearing it, Josiah reacts with distress, signaling the importance of the discovery.

King Josiah reacts with distress upon hearing the book of the law found by Hilkiah. He sends priests and officials to consult the prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem about God's message concerning Judah's disobedience.

The prophetess Huldah delivers God's message to King Josiah's envoys in Jerusalem, warning of coming judgment on the land for idolatry but promising Josiah peace because of his humble response to the discovered law book.

Isaiah heals King Hezekiah by applying figs to his boil and gives a sign of healing by reversing a shadow on a sundial. Meanwhile, Babylon's king sends gifts to Hezekiah, who proudly shows him all his treasures.

King Josiah gathers the elders and people of Judah and Jerusalem to the temple, reads the discovered Book of the Covenant, renews a covenant to follow God's laws, and orders the removal and burning of idolatrous items linked to Baal and other false gods.

King Josiah of Judah removes and destroys pagan worship objects near the temple in Jerusalem, including horses and chariots dedicated to the sun, altars built by previous kings, and high places for foreign gods, fulfilling his religious reforms.

King Josiah orders that the bones of a prophet remain undisturbed, then continues his reforms by destroying high places in Samaria, killing their priests, and commands a grand Passover in Jerusalem, the greatest since the time of Israel's judges.

King Josiah orders the high priest Hilkiah and temple officials to remove and destroy idols and altars dedicated to Baal and other deities from the temple and surrounding areas in Jerusalem, as part of his religious reforms.

King Josiah destroys pagan idols and altars at Bethel, including those made by Jeroboam, and burns human bones on the altar as a sign of judgment. He spares the tomb of a prophet who had warned against these actions.

King Josiah continues his religious reforms in Jerusalem and Judah by destroying places of idolatry near the temple, removing pagan priests, defiling sites of child sacrifice in the valley of Hinnom, and burning sun chariots linked to pagan worship.

King Josiah of Judah held a major Passover in Jerusalem and removed all idols and occult practices to follow God's law found by priest Hilkiah. Despite Josiah's faithfulness, God declared judgment on Judah for past sins, as recorded in the royal chronicles.

After Josiah's reforms and death at Megiddo fighting Pharaoh Nechoh of Egypt, Josiah's son Jehoahaz was made king in Jerusalem but reigned only three months before Nechoh captured him and imposed heavy tribute on Judah.

Pharaoh Nechoh arrested Jehoahaz at Riblah, imposed heavy tribute on Judah, and installed Eliakim (renamed Jehoiakim) as king. Jehoiakim ruled Jerusalem for 11 years, taxed the people to pay tribute, and continued his ancestors' evil ways.

During Jehoiakim's reign in Judah, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon conquered the region; Jehoiakim served Babylon for three years before rebelling. God sent various enemies against Judah as punishment for Manasseh's sins, leading to Jehoiakim's death and Jehoiachin's succession.

After Babylon conquered territory from Egypt to the Euphrates, Jehoiachin became king of Judah at 18 but reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, captured Jehoiachin, and took temple treasures to Babylon.

Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon plunders Jerusalem, taking treasures and captives including King Jehoiachin, then appoints Mattaniah (Zedekiah) as king. Zedekiah reigns in Jerusalem but continues evil ways and eventually rebels against Babylon.

After capturing King Zedekiah, Nebuchadnezzar's captain Nebuzaradan burns Jerusalem, destroys the temple and king's palace, breaks the city walls, exiles many, but leaves some poor people to work the land, and takes temple bronze items to Babylon.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem during King Zedekiah's reign, leading to famine and the city's fall. Zedekiah flees but is captured near Jericho; his sons are killed, and he is blinded and taken to Babylon.

After capturing Jerusalem, Nebuzaradan, the Babylonian captain, dismantles and seizes the bronze pillars, large basin, and various temple vessels made of brass, gold, and silver, all crafted by Solomon, as spoils to take back to Babylon.

Nebuzaradan, Babylon's captain, destroyed Jerusalem's temple pillars and captured key priests and officials, who were executed by King Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah; the remaining people in Judah were placed under Gedaliah's rule.

After Gedaliah's assassination, the remaining people fled to Egypt fearing Babylon. Years later, Evilmerodach, new Babylonian king, released former Judah king Jehoiachin from prison, honored him, and provided for him during his lifetime.

This passage lists the descendants of Adam through Noah's sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, detailing their families and tribes, setting the foundation for the nations and peoples known in biblical history.

After Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah governor over remaining Judahites at Mizpah. Gedaliah urged them to serve Babylon, but Ishmael assassinated him, causing the people to flee to Egypt out of fear.

This passage traces the genealogy from Arphaxad to Abraham and his descendants, including Ishmael, Keturah's children, Isaac, and Esau, linking key patriarchs and their families in the early history of Israel and surrounding peoples.

This passage lists the succession of Edomite kings after Husham, noting their cities and notable deeds, followed by the naming of Edom's regional leaders or dukes, continuing the genealogy and leadership history of Edom, neighbors to Israel.

This passage lists the descendants of Esau and the chiefs of Seir, then details the early kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings, showing the lineage and leadership in the region near Moab and Bozrah.

This passage lists the twelve sons of Israel (Jacob) and details the descendants of Judah, including notable figures like Pharez and Zerah, connecting Israel's tribes to their family origins and setting the stage for later genealogies.

This passage lists the descendants of Hezron, focusing on notable figures in Judah's lineage, including Nahshon, Boaz, Jesse, and David, and details Caleb's family and their territorial connections in Gilead.

This passage continues the genealogy of Hezron's descendants, focusing on Segub's son Jair who controlled many cities in Gilead, and Jerahmeel's sons and grandsons, detailing their families and territories in the region east of the Jordan River.

This passage lists the descendants of King Josiah through several generations, tracing the royal lineage and family branches during and after the Babylonian exile, connecting David's line to Zerubbabel and his descendants.

This passage lists the descendants of Caleb, including his children by concubine Maachah and his daughter Achsa, as well as the families and clans associated with Kirjathjearim, Bethlehem, and Jabez, highlighting their tribal and territorial connections.

This passage continues the genealogy of Jerahmeel's family, noting Sheshan's daughter marrying his Egyptian servant Jarha, and traces their descendants. It also lists the sons of Caleb, Jerahmeel's brother, and their families in Hebron.

This passage lists the descendants of Judah, focusing on families like the Zorathites and the sons of Hur, and highlights Jabez, who prayed for God's blessing and protection, connecting genealogies to notable individuals in Judah's lineage.

This passage lists King David's sons born in Hebron and Jerusalem, naming their mothers and noting David's reign length in each city. It then traces Solomon's descendants through several generations, connecting David's lineage to later kings of Judah.

This passage highlights Jabez's prayer for blessing and protection, followed by genealogies of various families descended from Judah, including notable figures like Kenaz and Caleb, connecting to the broader record of Israelite tribes and their settlements.

This passage lists descendants of Mered and his wives Jehudijah and Hodiah, including notable families from Judah and Simeon, highlighting their roles, crafts, and ancient settlements connected to the kingdom's history.

Leaders from Judah's families expanded greatly and sought pasture near Gedor. During King Hezekiah's reign, they displaced old inhabitants and settled there. Simeon's descendants also defeated Amalekites on Mount Seir and lived there permanently.

This passage details the settlement and leadership of the tribes of Reuben and Gad east of the Jordan River, including their war with the Hagarites during King Saul's time, and notes their genealogies recorded under Kings Jotham of Judah and Jeroboam of Israel.

This passage lists the descendants of Mishma, their cities, and villages in Judah during King David's reign, noting Shimei's large family and naming local leaders, showing the growth and settlement of Judah's clans.

This passage lists the descendants of Reuben, Israel's firstborn, noting his loss of birthright due to sin, and describes their settlements in Gilead near Aroer, Nebo, and Baalmeon, with some taken captive by Assyria under King Tilgathpilneser.

During the reigns of Jotham in Judah and Jeroboam in Israel, the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, skilled warriors, fought and defeated the Hagarites and allies, capturing livestock and settling in their lands until their later exile.

This passage lists the descendants of the Levite clans—Kohath, Merari, and Gershom—highlighting their roles in temple worship. King David appointed them as singers for the tabernacle before Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem.

The half-tribe of Manasseh lived from Bashan to Mount Hermon, led by notable chiefs. They sinned by worshiping local gods, so God allowed Assyrian kings Pul and Tiglath-Pileser to exile them to places like Halah and the river Gozan.

This passage lists the descendants of Levi, focusing on Aaron's priestly line through Solomon's temple, and notes Jehozadak's exile to Babylon. It also names Levi's three sons and Gershom and Kohath's descendants, connecting priestly heritage to Israel's history.

This passage lists Levite musicians from the Kohathite and Gershomite families who served by singing at the tabernacle before Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, highlighting their lineage and role in worship.

This passage lists the Levite families descended from Gershom and Merari, their roles in serving the tabernacle, and details Aaron's priestly lineage and their assigned cities, including Hebron in Judah, highlighting their religious duties and territorial settlements.

This passage lists the cities and surrounding lands given to the Levite families—Aaron's descendants, Kohathites, and Gershomites—across Judah, Benjamin, Manasseh, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and Bashan, detailing their allotted territories.

This passage lists the cities given by lot to the Levite families—Gershom, Merari, and Kohath—across various Israelite tribes, including cities of refuge like Shechem, detailing their assigned territories after the Israelites settled in the Promised Land.

This passage lists cities and their surrounding areas assigned to the Levite families of Kohath, Gershom, and others from the tribes of Manasseh, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali, continuing the distribution of Levitical towns across Israel.

This passage lists the descendants of Issachar and Benjamin, highlighting their leaders and military strength during King David's time, continuing the genealogical record of Israel's tribes and their notable warriors.

This passage lists cities with their surrounding areas given to the Levite family of Merari from the tribes of Naphtali, Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad, showing the distribution of Levitical towns east and west of the Jordan River.

This passage lists the sons and military leaders of the tribes of Benjamin, including Bela, Becher, and Jediael, highlighting their numbers and valor during King David's reign in Israel. It continues the genealogical record from the previous verses.

This passage lists the descendants of Naphtali, Manasseh, and Ephraim, highlighting family connections and noting a conflict where Ephraim's sons were killed by men of Gath, leading to mourning and consolation among their relatives.

This passage lists the descendants of Hushim and Elpaal, including leaders who built towns like Ono and Lod, and chiefs living in Jerusalem and Gibeon, showing the family heads and their settlements among the tribe of Benjamin.
This passage lists the descendants of Japhlet, Shamer, Helem, Zophah, Jether, and Ulla, all sons of Asher, highlighting their leadership and military strength during King David's time.

This passage continues the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, listing descendants from Ner to Saul, Israel's first king, and his sons, highlighting notable warriors like Ulam and their families living in Jerusalem.

This passage continues the genealogy of Ephraim's family, noting his mourning and the birth of his son Beriah, then lists his descendants and their towns. It also introduces the sons of Asher and their families, connecting to the broader tribal settlements in Israel.

This passage lists the descendants of Benjamin, including Bela and his sons, and mentions families living in Geba and Manahath, as well as Shaharaim's children born in Moab, continuing the genealogical record from the previous chapter.

The passage lists the genealogies of Israelites living in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, including priests, Levites, and families from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh, showing the resettlement of God's people in their ancestral cities.

This passage lists the leaders among the priests and Levites in Jerusalem, highlighting their genealogies and roles in serving the house of God, continuing the record of those responsible for temple duties after Israel's return from exile.

This passage lists Levite gatekeepers like Obadiah and Shallum, descendants of Korah, who served as porters at the tabernacle gates near Jerusalem, a role established by King David and the prophet Samuel to manage temple access and security.

This passage describes the Levite porters appointed by King David and Samuel to guard the gates and manage the treasuries and sacred vessels of the tabernacle in Jerusalem, organizing their duties by quarters and villages.
This passage continues the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, tracing the descendants of Micah down to Azel and his six sons, linking the family line to those living in Jerusalem after the exile.

This passage details the duties of Levites and priests in Jerusalem, including making ointments, preparing shewbread, and singing. It also traces the genealogy of Jehiel of Gibeon and the lineage leading to Saul and his descendants.

The Philistines defeat Israel at Mount Gilboa, killing King Saul and his sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua. Saul, wounded, commits suicide to avoid capture, and Israel's forces flee, allowing Philistines to occupy their cities.

This passage lists David’s elite warriors and commanders, highlighting Benaiah’s leadership over the royal guard, as David consolidates his kingdom with loyal fighters from various Israelite tribes and regions.

After Saul and his sons died in battle on Mount Gilboa, the Philistines desecrated their bodies and displayed Saul's head in Dagon's temple. The men of Jabesh-Gilead recovered and buried them, marking Saul's death as punishment for disobedience, leading to David's rise.

After Saul's death, all Israel gathers in Hebron to affirm David as their king, recalling his leadership under Saul. David is anointed king, then captures Jerusalem (Jebus) from the Jebusites, establishing it as his royal city with Joab as military leader.

David is hiding in a stronghold while Philistines occupy Bethlehem. Three warriors risk their lives to bring him water from Bethlehem's well, but David pours it out as an offering to God. The passage also highlights the bravery of Abishai and Benaiah, David's mighty men.

David's power grows as the LORD supports him; his mighty warriors, including Jashobeam and Eleazar, perform great feats against the Philistines. David is hiding in the cave of Adullam while the Philistines camp nearby at Bethlehem.

David’s warrior Benaiah, known for his bravery in battles against Moabites, a lion, and a giant Egyptian, is honored among David’s top fighters and appointed leader of his personal guard, showing David’s trust in his valor.
This passage lists some of David's warriors from various tribes and regions, highlighting their loyalty and military roles as part of the larger group supporting David's kingship in Israel.

David is gathering warriors from various tribes, including mighty men from Gad skilled in battle, who crossed the Jordan River during flood season and defeated enemies. Fighters from Benjamin and Judah also joined David at his stronghold.
David is at Ziklag, hiding from King Saul, when a group of skilled warriors, including some from Saul’s own tribe of Benjamin, come to support him, led by chiefs like Ahiezer and Ismaiah.

David meets men from Benjamin and Judah who come to support him at his stronghold; Amasai pledges their loyalty. Some from Manasseh join David during his conflict with Saul and the Philistines but are initially held back by Philistine leaders.

As David traveled to Ziklag, captains from Manasseh joined him, aiding against raiders. More warriors from Judah, Simeon, Levi, Aaronites, and Benjamin gathered at Hebron, preparing to support David's claim to Saul's kingdom as God had promised.

This passage lists the warriors from various Israelite tribes, including Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, Zebulun, Naphtali, Dan, Asher, Reuben, and Gad, who gathered at Hebron to support David as king.

David consults God twice about fighting the Philistines, receiving guidance that leads to victories at Baalperazim and near the mulberry trees, expanding his fame and causing fear among surrounding nations.

Tribes east of the Jordan—Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh—joined David at Hebron with 120,000 warriors ready for battle. All Israel united to make David king, celebrating together with abundant provisions and joy.

King David prepares a special place in Jerusalem for the ark of God and insists only Levites, whom God chose for this duty, carry it. He gathers the Levite families and priests to bring the ark to its new home.

David consults military leaders and the people of Israel about gathering all Israelites and priests to bring the ark of God from Kirjathjearim, starting a unified effort to restore the ark to Jerusalem after Saul's reign.

King David gathers the leading Levites and priests in Jerusalem, instructing them to sanctify themselves to properly carry the ark of God, correcting a previous failed attempt, and appoints musicians to joyfully accompany the procession.

King David, priests, Levites, and Israel's leaders joyfully bring the ark of the covenant from Obededom's house to Jerusalem with music and offerings, while Michal, Saul's daughter, watches David dancing and disapproves.

King Hiram of Tyre sends materials and workers to David in Jerusalem to build a house, confirming David's reign over Israel. David expands his family, then prepares to face the Philistines who gather in the valley of Rephaim, seeking God's guidance before battle.

David and Israel transport the ark of God from Abinadab's house with music and celebration, but Uzza dies after touching the ark to steady it at Chidon, causing David to fear and temporarily place the ark in Obededom's home, where blessings follow.

King David instructs the Levite leaders to organize musicians and singers with various instruments to joyfully accompany the procession of the ark. Key Levite musicians and doorkeepers are named, highlighting their roles in this sacred event in Jerusalem.

David leads a psalm of praise, urging Israel to remember God's covenant with their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and to celebrate God's protection and justice as they worship Him together in Jerusalem.

David places the ark of God in a tent he prepared, offers sacrifices, blesses the people, and distributes food and drink to all Israel. He appoints Levites to minister and lead worship, then gives Asaph and his group a psalm to praise the LORD.

David leads a psalm praising God's greatness and sovereignty over all nations, urging all creation to rejoice and worship the LORD, emphasizing His enduring mercy and power as the true God above idols.

David concludes the celebration by praising God’s enduring mercy, appointing Levites and priests like Asaph, Obededom, and Zadok to minister continually before the ark in Jerusalem, then the people return home as David blesses his household.

After defeating Hadarezer king of Zobah, David received tribute from his cities Tibhath and Chun, and King Tou of Hamath sent his son to congratulate David. David dedicated spoils to the LORD, secured Edom, and established his officials and family around him.

After Nahash, king of the Ammonites, died, David sent messengers to comfort his son Hanun, but Hanun's officials accused them of spying and humiliated them by shaving and partially stripping them, causing shame and delay before their return.

After God promised to build David a house, David led military campaigns against the Philistines, Moabites, Zobah, and Syrians, conquering territories and gaining tribute, while securing valuable spoils brought back to Jerusalem.

King David speaks to the prophet Nathan about his desire to build a permanent temple for the ark, but God reveals to Nathan that David will not build the temple, reminding him of his rise from shepherd to king and God's presence with him.

David learns of the insult to his servants by Hanun, king of Ammon, and advises them to stay in Jericho until their beards grow back. Ammon hires foreign troops, and David sends Joab with Israel's army to confront them near Ammon's cities.

After Nathan delivers God's message to David, David prays before the LORD, expressing humility and gratitude for God's promises to establish his house and recognizing God's unique relationship with Israel as His chosen people.

King David prays to God, affirming Israel as God's chosen people and asking God to fulfill His promise to establish David's house and bless his descendants forever. This follows God's covenant message delivered through Nathan.

God speaks to Nathan, instructing him to tell King David that He has been with him, defeated his enemies, and will establish David's descendants and kingdom forever, promising a lasting dynasty and divine relationship. Nathan relays this message to David.

After initial defeats, the Syrians gathered reinforcements led by Shophach to fight Israel. David assembled his army, defeated them decisively, killing many and Shophach, leading to peace and Syrian withdrawal from aiding Ammon.

Joab leads Israel's forces against the Syrians while his brother Abishai faces the Ammonites outside their city. After defeating both, Joab returns to Jerusalem, but the Syrians call for reinforcements led by Shophach.

After defeating the Syrians, David's army, led by Joab, attacks and destroys Rabbah, the Ammonite capital. David takes the king's crown and spoils the city. Later, Israel fights the Philistines at Gezer, where Sibbechai and Elhanan kill giant warriors.

This passage describes battles between Israel and the Philistines, highlighting warriors like Elhanan and Jonathan, relatives of David, who killed giant descendants in Gath, continuing Israel’s military struggles after the Ammonite conflict.

After David admits his sin in ordering a census, God offers him a choice of three punishments through the prophet Gad. David chooses to face God's mercy rather than human enemies, leading to a deadly pestilence in Israel.

After battles with giants, David is tempted by Satan to count Israel’s fighting men, despite Joab’s objections. Joab obeys, numbers the troops, but God is displeased, leading David to confess his sin and seek forgiveness.

David follows Gad’s instruction to build an altar at Ornan’s threshing floor in Jerusalem. Ornan offers the land and offerings for free, but David insists on paying full price to stop the plague on Israel.

David buys Ornan's threshing floor in Jerusalem to build an altar to stop the plague. God answers by fire, and the angel ceases destruction. The tabernacle is still at Gibeon, but David fears approaching it due to the angel's sword.

King David encourages his son Solomon to follow God's laws to succeed in building the temple. David has prepared abundant materials and skilled workers, urging Israel's leaders to support Solomon in constructing the sanctuary for the LORD.

King David declares the site for God's house and begins gathering materials and workers, including foreigners, to build the temple. He tells his son Solomon to build it, explaining God forbade David because of his many wars.

David tells Solomon that God has forbidden him from building the temple because of his violent past, but promises Solomon peace and success in building it. David encourages Solomon to seek God's wisdom and courage to lead Israel well.

God sends a deadly plague on Israel for David's census sin, stopping the angel's destruction at Ornan's threshing floor in Jerusalem. David, in sackcloth, confesses his sin and is instructed by Gad to build an altar there.

As David nears the end of his life in Jerusalem, he appoints Solomon king and organizes the Levites, numbering 38,000 men aged 30 and up, assigning them roles for temple service and dividing them into families of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

David organizes the Levites, descendants of Levi including Mushi's sons, assigning them duties in Jerusalem's temple service from age twenty, emphasizing their role in assisting Aaron's descendants and performing daily worship and offerings.

David lists the descendants of Levi's sons—Kohath and Merari—including Aaron and Moses, detailing their roles and leadership within the tribe, as part of organizing the Levites for temple service in Jerusalem.

David outlines the duties of the Levites in Jerusalem, emphasizing their daily worship, sacrifices on special occasions, and care for the tabernacle and support of Aaron's priestly family in the temple service.

King David organizes the priestly duties by dividing the descendants of Aaron—Eleazar and Ithamar—into groups by casting lots. Shemaiah records the divisions before David, priests Zadok and Ahimelech, and other leaders.

King David and his military leaders assign the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun—Levitical musicians and prophets—to lead worship with instruments in the temple, organizing their service by family under their fathers' guidance.

This passage lists the families of the Levites, descendants of Aaron's brothers, detailing their genealogies and roles. King David, priests Zadok and Ahimelech, and leaders oversee the casting of lots to assign their temple duties.

David and his commanders organize the Levite musicians into 24 groups, each led by a head and including their sons and relatives, all assigned to temple music duties with twelve members per group, continuing the detailed division of temple service.

Shemaiah the Levite recorded the priestly divisions before King David, priests Zadok and Ahimelech, and leaders. Lots were cast to assign 24 priestly families, descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar, their order for service in the temple as commanded by God.

This passage lists the Levite families—sons of Kore, Merari, Laadan, and others—who managed the treasures and dedicated items for the house of God, including spoils from battles dedicated by King David and Israel's leaders.

This passage lists the families of Meshelemiah and Hosah, Levite gatekeepers assigned to guard the temple. They cast lots to determine their duties at different gates around the house of the LORD, organizing temple security by divisions.

David organizes 288 skilled musicians and singers under Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman for temple worship in Jerusalem. They cast lots to assign groups, each led by a chief and including his family and relatives, ensuring orderly service in God's house.

This passage lists military leaders assigned to the eleventh and twelfth months and names tribal rulers under King David, noting he did not count men under twenty, trusting God's promise to multiply Israel.

This passage lists military leaders appointed by King David to command monthly rotations of 24,000 soldiers each, detailing captains from various tribes of Israel, continuing the organization of Israel's army and governance.

King David's military leaders are organized into monthly rotations, each commanding 24,000 men. Notable captains include Jashobeam, Dodai, Benaiah, and Asahel, who lead Israel's forces throughout the year.

This passage lists the families of Korhite porters, focusing on Meshelemiah and Obededom's descendants, who served as strong, valiant gatekeepers in the temple, continuing the organization of Levitical duties begun earlier.

King David avoided counting soldiers under twenty, trusting God's promise to multiply Israel; Joab began a census but stopped due to divine wrath. The passage then lists officials managing David’s treasures, fields, vineyards, and livestock across Israel.

King David encourages his son Solomon to be strong and build the sanctuary. David then shares detailed plans and provides gold and silver for the temple's furnishings and priestly services in Jerusalem.

King David addresses all Israel, urging them to obey God's commandments to secure their land's future, and he specifically charges his son Solomon to serve God wholeheartedly as he is chosen to build the sanctuary.
This passage lists officials managing King David's livestock and wealth, followed by key advisors and military leaders serving David during his reign in Israel.

King David tells the leaders of Israel that God forbade him from building the temple because of his warrior past, but chose his son Solomon to build it and rule, urging all Israel to obey God's commands to secure their land and legacy.

This passage describes how spoils from battles were dedicated to maintain the house of the LORD, overseen by Shelomith and his brethren. It also lists leaders from the Izharites and Hebronites, including Jerijah, appointed by King David to govern Israelite tribes west of the Jordan.

King David gathers Israel's leaders and warriors in Jerusalem to address them, explaining his desire to build a temple for God's ark but revealing that God forbade him because of his history as a warrior.

King David details the gold and silver weights for temple items to Solomon, explaining these plans were divinely revealed. He encourages Solomon to be strong and courageous, assuring God's presence in building the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.
King David encourages his son Solomon to be courageous in building the temple, assuring him of God's presence and support from priests, Levites, skilled workers, princes, and the people in Jerusalem.

King David addresses the assembly, acknowledging Solomon's youth and God's choice of him to build the temple. David details his extensive preparations and offerings of precious materials for the temple's construction, inviting others to dedicate themselves to the LORD.

King David calls on Israel's leaders and people to dedicate resources for the temple; they give generously, rejoicing in their offerings. David praises God publicly, celebrating the people's willing contributions for the house of the LORD.

This passage summarizes King David's 40-year reign over Israel, noting his death and Solomon's succession. It references records of David's life kept by prophets Samuel, Nathan, and Gad, linking to earlier historical accounts.

King David acknowledges that all the resources for building God's temple come from God, expresses his sincere offering, and prays for Solomon's wisdom to lead. He then invites the assembly in Jerusalem to bless and worship the LORD together.

Solomon, son of David, strengthens his kingdom and gathers Israel's leaders at Gibeon, where the tabernacle is located. He offers many sacrifices at the bronze altar, and God appears to him, inviting Solomon to ask for a gift.

Solomon prays to God at Gibeon, asking for wisdom to rule Israel, acknowledging God's promise to his father David. God grants wisdom plus wealth and honor, then Solomon returns to Jerusalem to begin his reign over Israel.

After receiving wisdom from God at Gibeon, Solomon returned to Jerusalem to rule Israel, building a powerful military with chariots and horsemen, amassing wealth, and trading horses and linen with Egypt and neighboring kingdoms.

King David addresses the assembly, leading them in blessing God and worship. They offer many sacrifices, joyfully celebrate, and officially anoint Solomon as king, who then rules successfully with full support from Israel’s leaders and people.

King David praises God before the assembly, acknowledging God's supreme power and expressing gratitude for the people's generous offerings for the temple, recognizing that all things come from God and humans are temporary sojourners on earth.

King Solomon decides to build a temple for the LORD and a palace for his kingdom in Jerusalem, organizing tens of thousands of workers. He requests cedar wood from Huram, king of Tyre, to honor God with ongoing worship and sacrifices.

Solomon acknowledges God's greatness and requests skilled craftsmen and abundant timber from Huram, king of Tyre, to build the temple. Huram responds with blessings, recognizing Solomon's wisdom and God's favor on Israel.

King Huram of Tyre promises to send abundant timber from Lebanon by sea to Joppa for Solomon's temple. Solomon counts foreign workers in Israel, assigning tens of thousands to carry burdens, cut stone, and supervise the construction.

King Huram of Tyre replies to Solomon, praising God and Solomon's wisdom, and sends a skilled craftsman from Tyre to help build the temple. He agrees to supply timber from Lebanon, shipped by sea to Joppa for transport to Jerusalem.

King Solomon is constructing the temple in Jerusalem, richly decorating the main hall and the most holy place with gold and carved cherubim, and making a colorful veil embroidered with cherubim to separate the sacred space.

Solomon is completing the temple in Jerusalem by making a richly decorated veil and erecting two large pillars named Jachin and Boaz at the entrance, continuing the detailed construction begun earlier on Mount Moriah.

King Solomon continues building the temple in Jerusalem, creating a large brass altar, a massive round basin called the molten sea supported by twelve oxen statues, and ten lavers for ceremonial washing by priests.

King Solomon begins constructing the temple of the LORD on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem, at the site David prepared. He follows detailed instructions, using gold, precious stones, and carved cherubim to adorn the structure.

King Solomon arranges ten lavers, candlesticks, and tables inside the temple, placing them evenly on both sides. He also builds the priests' court and the great court with brass-covered doors, positioning the large "sea" basin at the temple's southeast corner.

After completing the temple, Solomon gathered Israel's leaders in Jerusalem during the seventh-month feast to bring the ark of the covenant from Zion. Priests and Levites carried the ark, tabernacle, and holy vessels, and Solomon led a massive sacrifice.

King Solomon and the Israelites offer countless sacrifices as priests place the ark of the covenant in the temple's most holy place in Jerusalem, under cherubim wings; the ark contains only the stone tablets from Moses at Horeb.

King Solomon completes making numerous gold and brass vessels and furnishings for the temple in Jerusalem, including altars, tables, candlesticks, and doors, emphasizing the temple's grandeur and sacred function.

King Solomon places the large basin called the "sea" at the temple's east side, while Huram and his father craft various bronze temple vessels and pillars, casting them in the Jordan plain near Succoth and Zeredathah, completing abundant temple furnishings.

During the dedication of Solomon's temple in Jerusalem, the priests placed the Ark containing Moses' tablets in the most holy place. As Levite musicians praised God, a cloud filled the temple, signifying God's glory filling the house.

King Solomon speaks to all Israel, affirming God's promise that David would not build the temple, but Solomon would; he has built it, placed the ark inside, and now prays before the altar on a bronze platform he made in Jerusalem.

King Solomon stands on a bronze platform in Jerusalem, praying before all Israel. He praises God for keeping His promises to David and asks that David's descendants continue to rule Israel if they remain faithful to God's law.

King Solomon prays at the newly built temple in Jerusalem, asking God to confirm His promises to David and to hear the prayers of Israel, especially regarding justice and forgiveness when people make oaths or seek judgment before the altar.
King Solomon prays before all Israel in Jerusalem, asking God to hear both Israelites and foreigners who pray in the temple, and to support Israel in battle when they follow God's guidance.

King Solomon prays before all Israel, asking God to hear the prayers of exiled Israelites who repent and pray toward Jerusalem, and to bless the priests and remember David's covenant as God dwells in the temple Solomon built.

King Solomon addresses the assembly of Israel, reflecting on God's promise to David that Solomon would build the temple in Jerusalem, fulfilling God's plan to establish His name there and David's desire to build a house for the Lord.

After Solomon's prayer, priests and Levites led worship with music and trumpet, honoring God's mercy. Solomon dedicated the altar with offerings, held a seven-day feast, and dismissed the joyful people across Israel from Hamath to Egypt.

King Solomon prays at the temple in Jerusalem, asking God to hear and forgive the prayers of Israel during hardships like famine, disease, or enemy attacks, so the people may fear God and live rightly in the land given to their ancestors.

After Solomon's dedication of the temple, God appears to him at night, affirming the temple as His chosen place for sacrifice and promising to hear prayers and forgive Israel if they repent and seek Him. Solomon completes the temple and his palace successfully.

God speaks to Solomon at night, affirming the temple's sanctification and promising to establish Solomon's throne if he follows God's laws, but warns of exile and disgrace if Israel turns to other gods, explaining future consequences for disobedience.

King Solomon prays before all Israel at the newly built temple in Jerusalem, asking God to hear and judge His people justly, forgive their sins when they repent, and bless the land with rain as a sign of His favor.

After Solomon finishes praying at the newly built temple in Jerusalem, fire from heaven consumes the offerings, and God's glory fills the house. The people worship, and Solomon and Israel dedicate the temple with many sacrifices and music.

After 20 years of building the temple and his palace, King Solomon expanded his kingdom by rebuilding cities restored by Huram, conquering Hamathzobah, and fortifying key cities. He imposed tribute on remaining non-Israelite peoples in the land.

The queen of Sheba praises Solomon’s wisdom and blessings from God, gifts him gold and spices, and Solomon uses rare materials from Ophir to enhance the temple and palace before granting her requests and sending her home.

Solomon established regular offerings and priestly duties as David commanded, completing the temple. Then he expanded trade by sending ships from Edom to Ophir, bringing back large amounts of gold with Huram's help.

The queen of Sheba visits King Solomon in Jerusalem to test his wisdom with difficult questions. Impressed by his answers, his palace, and his court, she praises Solomon’s renowned wisdom and the prosperity of his kingdom.

King Solomon's wealth and wisdom surpass all other kings; his golden throne and vessels display his grandeur. His ships trade with Tarshish, bringing luxury goods, while rulers from distant lands visit Jerusalem, offering gifts and acknowledging his vast kingdom.

King Rehoboam rejects the advice of his father's elders and instead follows the harsher counsel of his young peers, responding to Israel's request for lighter burdens with threats of even greater oppression.

This passage summarizes King Solomon's extensive reign over Israel, highlighting his wealth, trade, and influence from the Euphrates River to Egypt. It notes his 40-year rule, death, burial in Jerusalem, and succession by his son Rehoboam.

After Solomon's death, Rehoboam travels to Shechem where all Israel gathers to crown him king. Jeroboam returns from Egypt, and the people ask Rehoboam to lighten Solomon's harsh rule. Rehoboam seeks advice from his elders and young peers.

King Solomon rules over Israel, making non-Israelite children pay tribute while Israelite men serve as warriors and officers. He brings Pharaoh’s daughter to live in a separate house and regularly offers sacrifices to the LORD following Mosaic law.

King Rehoboam rejects the elders' advice and harshly responds to Israel's request to lighten their burdens, fulfilling God's word through Ahijah. Israel rebels, rejecting David's line, while Rehoboam retains Judah; a tax collector is killed during the conflict.

After Israel's rebellion, King Rehoboam of Judah gathered 180,000 warriors from Judah and Benjamin to fight Israel, but the prophet Shemaiah, speaking God's word, told them not to fight their brethren, so they returned home. Rehoboam then fortified cities in Judah for defense.

After granting the queen of Sheba's requests, Solomon received vast amounts of gold annually, including gifts from Arabian kings. He crafted ornate gold shields, targets, and an elaborate ivory and gold throne adorned with lions, unmatched by any other kingdom.

King Rehoboam fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin, gaining support from priests and Levites rejected by Jeroboam. Devout Israelites came to Jerusalem, strengthening Rehoboam's rule for three years. He married Mahalath and Maachah, who bore him children.

King Rehoboam of Judah married Maachah, daughter of Absalom, and favored her above his many wives and concubines. He appointed their son Abijah as leader among his siblings and strategically placed his children across Judah and Benjamin.

After humbling himself, King Rehoboam avoided total destruction and ruled Judah from Jerusalem for 17 years, though he did evil by not seeking the LORD. His reign included ongoing wars with Jeroboam, and he was succeeded by his son Abijah.

King Rehoboam and the princes of Judah humbled themselves before God after Shishak of Egypt invaded Jerusalem. The prophet Shemaiah relayed God's mercy, sparing the city from destruction but allowing Shishak to plunder its treasures.

King Abijah of Judah rebukes Jeroboam and Israel for rejecting the true priests and worship of God, accusing them of idolatry with golden calves, contrasting Judah's faithful worship led by Aaron's descendants.

Abijah begins his three-year reign over Judah in Jerusalem during Jeroboam's eighteenth year as king of Israel. War breaks out between them, and Abijah addresses Jeroboam and Israel from Mount Zemaraim, recalling God's covenant with David and Jeroboam's rebellion.

King Abijah of Judah declares their faithfulness to God and proper worship, contrasting with Jeroboam's idolatry. During battle, Judah is ambushed but prays and triumphs, killing many Israelites and securing victory through God's help.

King Abijah of Judah defeats Jeroboam of Israel in a major battle, capturing key cities and weakening Jeroboam's power until his death. Abijah grows strong, has many children, and his reign is recorded by the prophet Iddo.

After King Abijah's death, his son Asa became king of Judah, ruling peacefully for ten years. Asa removed idols and pagan worship sites, encouraged faithfulness to God, fortified cities, and assembled a large, well-armed army from Judah and Benjamin.

After Asa's victory over the Ethiopians, the prophet Azariah, inspired by God's Spirit, encourages Asa and the people of Judah and Benjamin to remain faithful to God, prompting Asa to remove idols and renew the altar in Jerusalem.

King Asa of Judah leads a large army against Zerah the Ethiopian's vast forces near Mareshah. After praying to God for help, Asa's troops defeat the Ethiopians, pursue them to Gerar, and plunder the surrounding cities before returning to Jerusalem.

King Asa and the people of Judah loudly pledged to seek the LORD wholeheartedly, rejoicing in their renewed faith. Asa removed his mother Maachah as queen for idolatry, yet kept some high places; peace lasted until his 35th year.

King Asa, encouraged by the prophet Oded's message, removes idols from Judah and Benjamin, renews the altar in Jerusalem, gathers people from surrounding tribes, offers sacrifices, and leads them in a solemn covenant to wholeheartedly seek the LORD.

This passage summarizes King Asa of Judah's reign, noting his illness in the 39th year, his death in the 41st year, and his burial in the city of David with elaborate preparations, concluding the record of his deeds.

Asa, king of Judah, faces a siege by Baasha, king of Israel, who fortifies Ramah to block movement. Asa pays Benhadad, king of Syria, to attack Israel’s northern cities, forcing Baasha to stop building Ramah. Asa then repurposes Ramah’s materials for Geba and Mizpah.

After Asa's death, his son Jehoshaphat became king of Judah, fortified cities, and followed God's ways like David. He removed idols, gained wealth and respect, and sent leaders and Levites to teach the law throughout Judah's cities.

After Rehoboam strengthened his kingdom, he and Israel abandoned God's law. Shishak, king of Egypt, invaded Judah. The prophet Shemaiah told Rehoboam and leaders their defeat was due to forsaking God, so they humbled themselves.

King Jehoshaphat sent Levites and priests throughout Judah to teach the law of the LORD, leading to peace with neighboring kingdoms. He gained wealth, built fortifications, and maintained a strong army with thousands of valiant warriors in Jerusalem.

King Jehoshaphat of Judah, wealthy and honored, allies with King Ahab of Israel. Ahab invites Jehoshaphat to join him in battle at Ramothgilead. Jehoshaphat urges seeking God's guidance, but Ahab distrusts the prophet Micaiah.

King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah prepare for battle at Ramothgilead, summoning the prophet Micaiah despite Ahab's dislike, while other prophets falsely predict victory with iron horns symbolizing strength.

Micaiah, a prophet, speaks to King Ahab and Jehoshaphat about the battle at Ramothgilead, first giving a favorable prophecy, then revealing a vision where God allows a spirit to deceive Ahab’s prophets, leading to Ahab’s downfall.

This passage lists military leaders and their forces under King Jehoshaphat of Judah, showing the organized and strong army supporting his reign after he fortified cities and promoted religious reforms.

King Asa of Judah dismantles Baasha's fortifications at Ramah to build defenses at Geba and Mizpah. The prophet Hanani rebukes Asa for trusting Syria over God, warning of future wars, which angers Asa, leading to Hanani's imprisonment and oppression of some people.
King Ahab of Israel and King Jehoshaphat of Judah go to battle at Ramothgilead. Ahab disguises himself, but the Syrians mistake Jehoshaphat for Ahab. Ahab is wounded by an arrow and dies at sunset.

In Samaria, the prophet Micaiah reveals a vision where a spirit deceives King Ahab's prophets with lies, leading to conflict with Zedekiah. Ahab orders Micaiah imprisoned, then he and Jehoshaphat prepare to battle at Ramothgilead.

After the battle where Israel's king was killed, Jehoshaphat returns peacefully to Jerusalem. The prophet Jehu rebukes him for allying with ungodly people but praises his reforms; Jehoshaphat then appoints judges and religious leaders across Judah to enforce God's laws.

King Jehoshaphat and all Judah, including families, gather to seek God's help against a vast enemy. The Levite Jahaziel, filled with God's Spirit, assures them the battle belongs to God, urging faith and worship before the coming fight.

King Jehoshaphat prays in the temple, recalling God's past help in giving Israel the land and a sanctuary. He asks for God's judgment on their enemies—Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir—and expresses Judah's dependence on God amid the coming attack.

After Jehoshaphat appointed judges, enemies from Moab, Ammon, and others gathered near Engedi to attack Judah. Jehoshaphat feared, called a fast, and led all Judah to seek God's help in the temple, reminding God of His past deliverance.

King Jehoshaphat and the people of Judah worship and praise God in the temple, then march with singers leading the army. As they praise, God causes their enemies—Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir—to destroy each other.

As Judah, led by King Jehoshaphat, praised God, their enemies—Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir—turned on each other and were defeated. Judah found great spoils and gathered to bless God in the Valley of Berachah.

After God delivers Judah from their enemies, King Jehoshaphat leads the people back to Jerusalem with joy and praise. His reign is marked by peace and faithfulness, though some local high places remain.

King Jehoram of Judah built unauthorized worship sites, leading Jerusalem's people into idolatry. The prophet Elijah sent a letter condemning Jehoram's evil ways and foretold a severe plague and painful illness as punishment.

Jehoram, king of Judah, suffers a painful, incurable bowel disease as punishment from God. During his reign, enemies invade Judah, taking his family and possessions, and he dies after eight years, buried without royal honors in Jerusalem.

After King Jehoshaphat of Judah died and was buried in Jerusalem, his son Jehoram became king. Jehoram killed his brothers to secure power, married Ahab’s daughter, and ruled wickedly, though God preserved David’s line by covenant.

Despite Jehoshaphat's earlier faithfulness, the people still worshipped at high places. He allied with the wicked King Ahaziah of Israel to build ships at Eziongaber, but the prophet Eliezer declared God's judgment, and the ships were destroyed before sailing.

Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, reigns over Judah but faces revolts from Edom and Libnah due to his unfaithfulness to God. Despite this, God's covenant with David keeps the dynasty intact, though Jehoram leads military action against Edom.

King Jehoshaphat appoints Levites, priests, and leaders in Jerusalem to judge disputes and instruct the people in God's laws, emphasizing faithful and courageous service under chief priest Amariah and ruler Zebadiah.

After Ahaziah's death, his mother Athaliah killed all royal heirs to secure power, but Jehoshabeath, Ahaziah's aunt and wife of priest Jehoiada, secretly saved Joash, hiding him in the temple for six years while Athaliah ruled Judah.

Jehoiada the priest orders strict security around the temple in Jerusalem, allowing only priests and Levites inside, arming Levites and soldiers to protect the hidden king Joash, preparing for a coup against Athaliah.

Jehoshaphat's priest Jehoiada gathers military leaders, Levites, and Israel's elders in Jerusalem to pledge loyalty to young King Joash, organizing priests and Levites to guard the temple and support the king, preparing for a royal restoration.

After Athaliah's death, young King Joash begins his 40-year reign in Jerusalem, guided by priest Jehoiada. Joash plans to repair the temple, instructing priests and Levites to collect funds, but the Levites delay, prompting Joash to question Jehoiada.

Jehoshaphat assigned gatekeepers to keep the temple pure, then led the officials and people to bring young King Joash from the temple to the palace, crowning him after Athaliah's death, restoring peace in Jerusalem.

King Joash and priest Jehoiada oversee repairs to the temple in Jerusalem, using collected funds to restore it and make sacred vessels. Jehoiada dies at 130, honored for his faithfulness, after which the king begins listening to Judah's princes.

King Joash and priest Jehoiada respond to Athaliah's sons desecrating the temple by collecting funds from Judah and Jerusalem to repair it, managing the offerings carefully and hiring workers to restore the house of the LORD.

Jehoiada organizes armed guards around the temple and publicly crowns Joash as king. Athaliah hears the celebration, confronts the crowd, and is declared a traitor. Jehoiada orders her arrest but forbids killing her inside the temple.

Jehoiada orders the execution of Athaliah outside the temple to avoid defiling it, then renews a covenant with the people and king to serve the LORD. The people destroy Baal's temple, and Jehoiada restores proper worship in Jerusalem's temple.

King Joash kills Zechariah, son of Jehoiada, then faces a Syrian attack that devastates Judah due to his unfaithfulness. Later, his servants assassinate him, and his son Amaziah succeeds him as king in Jerusalem.

After Jehoiada's death, Judah's leaders influenced King Joash to abandon God and worship idols. Prophets, including Jehoiada's son Zechariah, warned them, but Zechariah was killed by stoning on the king's orders in the temple courtyard.

Ahaziah, wounded in battle against Syria, returns to Jezreel to heal. Jehu, anointed to destroy Ahab's house, kills Ahaziah and his supporters. After Ahaziah's death, his mother Athaliah kills Judah's royal heirs to seize power.

After defeating the Edomites, King Amaziah of Judah cruelly executed captives but faced attacks from the Israelite soldiers he had dismissed. He then worshipped Edomite gods, prompting a prophet's warning of God's judgment against him.

After King Jehoram of Judah died from disease, his youngest son Ahaziah became king in Jerusalem. Influenced by his mother Athaliah, Ahaziah allied with Israel's king Jehoram and fought Syria's king Hazael, where Jehoram was wounded.

King Uzziah fortified Jerusalem with towers, dug wells for his large herds, and supported farmers. He organized a powerful army of over 300,000 men, equipping them with weapons and armor to defend the kingdom.

After King Amaziah's death, the people of Judah made his 16-year-old son Uzziah king. Uzziah sought God, prospered in battles against Philistines and neighbors, gained fame, and fortified Jerusalem with new towers.

Amaziah, son of Joash, begins his 29-year reign over Judah at age 25 in Jerusalem. He executes his father's killers but spares their children per Mosaic law, then organizes a large army including 100,000 mercenaries from Israel.

King Amaziah of Judah dismisses a prophet's warning about his idolatry and then challenges Joash, king of Israel, who warns him against pride and conflict. Amaziah ignores this, leading to divine judgment through defeat by Israel.

King Amaziah of Judah hires 100,000 soldiers from Israel but a prophet warns him not to take them to battle. Amaziah sends them away, angering them, then leads his own troops to defeat Edomites at the Valley of Salt.

King Uzziah of Judah strengthens his army with weapons and siege engines, gaining fame for his success. However, his pride leads him to unlawfully enter the temple to burn incense, where priest Azariah and 80 priests confront him, forbidding this act reserved for priests.

Amaziah of Judah ignored God's warning and fought Joash of Israel at Bethshemesh, where Judah was defeated. Joash captured Jerusalem, plundered the temple, and Amaziah later fled to Lachish, where conspirators killed him.

King Uzziah tries to burn incense in the temple, but priests led by Azariah stop him, saying only priests may do this. Uzziah is struck with leprosy, lives separately, and his son Jotham governs. Isaiah records Uzziah's acts.

Jotham, son of Uzziah, begins his 16-year reign in Jerusalem at age 25, building fortifications and defeating Ammon. Though he follows his father's righteous ways, he avoids the temple, and the people remain corrupt.

Ahaz became king of Judah at 20 and ruled 16 years in Jerusalem, but he did evil by worshiping Baal and burning his children. As a result, Syria and Israel attacked Judah, killing many, including the king's son Maaseiah.

During King Ahaz's reign in Judah, the Israelite army, led by Zichri of Ephraim, killed royal officials and captured many Judahites, bringing them to Samaria. The prophet Oded urged the Israelites to release these captives, warning of God's anger.

Leaders from Ephraim confront Israelite soldiers returning with Judahite captives, urging them to release the prisoners to avoid further sin. They care for the freed captives and return them to Jericho, while King Ahaz of Judah seeks Assyrian aid.

King Ahaz of Judah, facing attacks from Edomites and Philistines, seeks help from Assyria by giving treasures from the temple, but Assyria weakens him instead. Ahaz worsens his disobedience by worshiping foreign gods from Damascus.

King Ahaz of Judah worshipped the gods of Damascus, hoping for their help, but this led to his ruin. He desecrated the temple, made altars in Jerusalem and Judah, angering God. After his death, his son Hezekiah became king.

King Hezekiah restores the sacred vessels discarded by his father Ahaz and leads the leaders of Jerusalem in offering multiple sin offerings to atone for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and all Israel, marking a religious renewal.

Hezekiah becomes king of Judah at 25, ruling in Jerusalem. He acts righteously, reopening and repairing the temple, calling priests and Levites to purify it after neglect and idolatry under previous kings.

King Hezekiah addresses the Levites, explaining how worship was neglected under previous kings, leading to God's anger and Judah's suffering. He urges them to serve God faithfully, and the Levite leaders respond by rising to sanctify themselves and the temple.

King Hezekiah leads priests and Levites in Jerusalem to offer sacrifices and music as atonement for Israel, restoring proper worship with instruments and song following David's traditions, uniting the people in praise before the altar.

King Hezekiah and the people worship after completing offerings, then he commands the Levites to sing praises. The congregation brings many sacrifices, but priests are few, so Levites assist in preparing the offerings during temple restoration in Jerusalem.

During King Hezekiah's temple restoration in Jerusalem, the priests were too few to handle all the burnt offerings, so the Levites helped until the priests were ready, leading to a well-ordered worship service that brought joy to Hezekiah and the people.

Hezekiah’s Levites, including leaders from Heman and Jeduthun’s families, sanctify themselves and cleanse the temple of impurities, restoring vessels discarded by King Ahaz, completing the purification in Jerusalem within sixteen days.

King Hezekiah of Judah sends letters across Israel and Judah, including Ephraim and Manasseh, inviting them to Jerusalem to celebrate Passover in the second month, since priests were not yet sanctified for the original time.

King Hezekiah sent messengers with letters throughout Israel and Judah, urging the people to return to God to receive mercy and avoid destruction like their ancestors. The messengers traveled through Ephraim, Manasseh, and Zebulun but were mocked by many.

During the Passover in Jerusalem, priests and Levites performed rituals despite many attendees not being fully purified; King Hezekiah prayed for them, and God responded by healing the people, leading to a joyful seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread with praise and music.

Messengers sent by King Hezekiah traveled through Israel inviting people to Jerusalem for the Passover, facing mockery in some regions, but many from Asher, Manasseh, Zebulun, and Judah humbled themselves and gathered to celebrate, removing pagan altars and following Mosaic law.

King Hezekiah and the people of Judah, including priests, Levites, and Israelites, joyfully celebrated the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread in Jerusalem, extending it by another week with abundant offerings and prayers, marking a rare time of great unity and worship.
