After the Passover celebration, King Hezekiah led the people of Israel to destroy pagan idols and altars across Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. He then organized the priests and Levites for temple service and ensured their support through offerings and royal provisions.

Azariah, chief priest, reports abundant offerings to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. Hezekiah orders storage chambers for these gifts, appointing Cononiah, Shimei, and other Levites to oversee the offerings and their distribution in the temple.

Kore, a Levite porter in Jerusalem, oversees the distribution of sacred offerings, assisted by other Levites in priestly cities, ensuring daily portions are given to all priests and Levites and their families according to their genealogies and duties.

King Hezekiah organized the priests and Levites, ensuring their families received proper portions and lived holy lives. He faithfully led Judah in serving God, following the law wholeheartedly and succeeding in his efforts.

King Hezekiah ordered Jerusalem's people to provide for priests and Levites, leading to abundant offerings of crops and animals. The collected tithes were stored from the third to seventh month, and Hezekiah praised God upon seeing the large supply.

King Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah, threatening Jerusalem. King Hezekiah prepares by consulting leaders, cutting off water sources outside the city, and repairing and strengthening Jerusalem’s walls and defenses.

King Hezekiah of Judah fortifies Jerusalem’s walls and arms his people, encouraging them to trust God against the Assyrian threat. Meanwhile, Sennacherib besieges Lachish and sends envoys to challenge Jerusalem’s confidence.

King Sennacherib of Assyria sends a message to Jerusalem, mocking King Hezekiah's trust in God and urging the people to surrender, claiming no god has ever saved nations from Assyria's power, while his servants insult God and Hezekiah.

Sennacherib’s servants insult God and Hezekiah, trying to scare Jerusalem’s people during the Assyrian siege. In response, King Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, and God sends an angel to defeat the Assyrian army, forcing Sennacherib to retreat.

King Hezekiah humbled himself and avoided God's wrath, then amassed great wealth and secured Jerusalem's water supply. When Babylonian envoys visited, God tested Hezekiah to reveal his true character.

God miraculously defeats the Assyrian army threatening Jerusalem, leading to Sennacherib's humiliating return and death by his own sons. Hezekiah recovers from illness but later becomes proud, though he humbles himself to avoid God's wrath on Judah.

Manasseh became king of Judah at age 12, ruling Jerusalem for 55 years. Unlike his father Hezekiah, he rebuilt pagan altars, worshipped idols, practiced witchcraft, and led the people into evil, provoking God's anger.

After returning to Jerusalem, King Manasseh restored the LORD's altar and urged Judah to worship God, though people still sacrificed at high places. He died and was succeeded by his son Amon, who began his reign at age 22.

Josiah became king of Jerusalem at age eight and ruled for 31 years. Early in his reign, he sought God and began removing idols and pagan altars from Judah, Jerusalem, and surrounding Israelite cities, cleansing the land from idolatry.

God warns King Manasseh and Judah, but they ignore Him; Assyrian captains capture Manasseh and take him to Babylon. In distress, Manasseh prays and is restored to Jerusalem, where he fortifies the city and removes idols, renewing worship of God.
King Manasseh of Judah practiced idolatry and witchcraft, even placing an idol in God's temple in Jerusalem, leading the people astray despite God's warnings through him and his people.

After Babylonian princes sent ambassadors to Hezekiah to inquire about his miraculous deeds, God tested Hezekiah's heart. His further acts are recorded by Isaiah and in royal records. Hezekiah died and was succeeded by his son Manasseh.

Amon, son of Manasseh, ruled Jerusalem for two years, continuing his father's idolatrous practices without repentance. His servants assassinated him, but the people avenged him and made his son Josiah king.

King Josiah destroyed idols across Israelite territories and then sent officials to high priest Hilkiah with funds collected for repairing the temple in Jerusalem, initiating restoration after purifying the land.

During King Josiah's reign in Jerusalem, Levites supervised faithful repairs of the LORD's house, restoring what previous kings had destroyed. Hilkiah the priest discovered the book of the law, which he gave to Shaphan to deliver to Josiah.

Shaphan reports to King Josiah about the temple repairs and presents a discovered book of the law. Upon hearing it, Josiah is deeply distressed and sends officials to seek God's guidance about the nation's disobedience and impending judgment.

The prophetess Huldah delivers God's message to King Josiah's envoys, warning of coming judgment on Jerusalem for idolatry but promising Josiah peace for his humility. Josiah then summons Judah and Jerusalem's elders to hear this news.

King Josiah sends priests to ask the prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem about the discovered book of the law, seeking God's guidance due to the people's disobedience and the resulting divine wrath predicted for Judah and Jerusalem.

King Josiah gathers the elders and people of Judah and Jerusalem to the temple, reads the newly found Book of the Covenant, and leads them in renewing their commitment to follow God's laws, resulting in widespread religious reform throughout Israel.

King Josiah organizes a Passover celebration in Jerusalem, assigning priests and Levites their duties and instructing them to follow the traditions established by David and Solomon, ensuring the people observe the Lord's commands as given through Moses.

King Josiah organized a grand Passover in Jerusalem with priests, Levites, and singers following David's commands, marking the best celebration since Samuel's time. Afterward, Josiah confronted Necho, king of Egypt, who was heading to battle near Charchemish.

King Josiah leads a Passover celebration in Jerusalem, organizing priests and Levites to perform sacrifices and rituals according to Moses' law, with singers and gatekeepers fulfilling their duties as part of the temple service.

King Josiah confronts Necho of Egypt, who warns him not to interfere as he marches to battle at Charchemish. Ignoring the warning, Josiah fights at Megiddo, is wounded, brought back to Jerusalem, and dies, leading to mourning in Judah.

King Josiah commands the people and priests in Jerusalem to prepare and kill the Passover lambs and offerings according to Moses' law, providing many animals from his own resources and those of his officials to ensure the proper observance.

King Josiah was wounded in battle against Necho of Egypt, brought back to Jerusalem where he died and was buried. Judah mourned him deeply, with Jeremiah and others composing lasting lamentations; Josiah’s deeds are recorded in Israel’s royal records.

This passage summarizes the reigns of Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah in Judah, highlighting their evil actions and rebellion against Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, despite Jeremiah's prophetic warnings.

After King Josiah's death, his son Jehoahaz briefly ruled Jerusalem before Egypt's king deposed him and installed his brother Jehoiakim, who reigned wickedly. Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar later captured Jehoiakim and took temple treasures to Babylon.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, took its treasures and people captive, fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecy of 70 years of desolation and exile before Persia's rise. This marks Judah's punishment for disobedience.

This passage describes the fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy during the Babylonian exile, noting the land's 70-year desolation. It introduces Cyrus, king of Persia, who is inspired by God to allow the Jewish people to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.

King Cyrus of Persia issues a decree allowing the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem in Judah to rebuild the temple, fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecy. Leaders from Judah and Benjamin, including priests and Levites, prepare to go and rebuild the house of the LORD.

Leaders and priests from Judah and Benjamin, inspired by God, prepare to return to Jerusalem to rebuild the temple, supported by gifts. King Cyrus orders the return of sacred temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar, handed to Sheshbazzar for the journey.

King Zedekiah of Judah rebelled against Babylon's Nebuchadnezzar despite his oath, while priests and people defiled the temple in Jerusalem. God sent prophets, but they were rejected, leading to Babylon's violent conquest and temple plundering.
This passage lists the numbers of people from various towns and families who returned from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem, continuing the detailed census of the exiles led by Zerubbabel.

After the return from Babylonian exile led by Zerubbabel, this passage lists the families and numbers of Israelites who resettled in Jerusalem and Judah, showing the organized restoration of the community under leaders like Jeshua and Nehemiah.

Ezra lists families of Solomon’s servants and Nethinims returning to Jerusalem, noting some from various towns who couldn’t prove Israelite descent. Certain priests who married outside were excluded from priesthood due to missing genealogical records.

The leaders in Jerusalem exclude some priests without genealogical records from sacred duties until a priest with Urim and Thummim arises. The returning exiles number over 42,000, bring animals, offer donations, and settle in their cities.

Ezra lists the numbers of various groups returning from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem, including the large families of Senaah, priests from Jeshua's house, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, showing the community's organized resettlement.

After returning to Jerusalem, Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the priests began offering sacrifices before laying the temple foundation. They funded craftsmen and imported cedar from Lebanon, organizing Levites and workers to rebuild God's house under Persian King Cyrus's authorization.

After returning from exile, the Israelites gathered in Jerusalem in the seventh month. Led by Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel, they rebuilt the altar and resumed sacrifices and festivals as prescribed, though the temple foundation was not yet laid.

Jeshua, Kadmiel, and the Levites lead the workers rebuilding God's temple in Jerusalem. As the foundation is laid, priests and Levites praise God with music, and the people shout with joy while some elders weep, remembering the first temple.

After the temple foundation is laid in Jerusalem, local adversaries offer to help rebuild but are rejected by Zerubbabel and Jeshua, who insist on building alone as commanded by King Cyrus; these opponents then hinder the work through opposition and legal complaints during Persian rule.

Local officials from Samaria and nearby regions send a letter to King Artaxerxes, accusing the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem of rebellion and warning that restoring the city will harm the king's revenue and control over the area.

Officials Rehum and Shimshai report to King Artaxerxes, warning that rebuilding Jerusalem threatens royal revenue. The king orders the work stopped, and the adversaries halt the temple construction until Darius's reign.

During the reigns of Persian kings Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, local officials including Rehum and Shimshai, representing various peoples settled in Samaria, wrote a formal complaint to King Artaxerxes against the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem.

Officials Tatnai and Shetharboznai report to King Darius about the ongoing rebuilding of God's temple in Judea, questioning the Jewish elders who explain the temple's history, destruction by Nebuchadnezzar, and Cyrus's decree to rebuild it.

King Darius orders a search in Babylon's archives and finds King Cyrus's decree authorizing the rebuilding of God's temple in Jerusalem, specifying its dimensions and funding, and ordering the return of sacred vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar.

After work on the temple stopped under Artaxerxes, prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem to resume building. Zerubbabel and Jeshua led the effort, but Tatnai, governor west of the Euphrates, questioned their authority and reported to King Darius.

King Darius orders the return of temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar to Jerusalem and commands local governors Tatnai and Shetharboznai to stop interfering, providing funds from the royal treasury to support the Jewish elders rebuilding the temple.

King Darius orders financial support and daily offerings for the Jewish elders rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, commanding strict enforcement against anyone who opposes this decree to ensure the temple's completion.

After completing the temple in Jerusalem, the returned Israelites dedicated it with sacrifices, organized priests and Levites for worship, observed Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, celebrating joyfully as God supported their efforts and influenced the king of Assyria.

King Darius orders protection for the temple in Jerusalem and commands officials Tatnai and Shetharboznai to allow the Jews to build it. The elders, encouraged by prophets Haggai and Zechariah, complete the temple, and the Israelites celebrate its dedication with sacrifices.

Officials Tatnai and Shetharboznai report to King Darius about the rebuilding of God's temple in Jerusalem, recounting King Cyrus's earlier decree and the return of temple vessels by Sheshbazzar, who began the reconstruction but did not finish it.

Ezra, a descendant of Aaron and skilled scribe, leads a group including priests and Levites from Babylon to Jerusalem during King Artaxerxes' reign, arriving after a four-month journey to restore worship and teach God's law.

Ezra leaves Babylon in the first month and arrives in Jerusalem by the fifth, ready to follow and teach God's law. King Artaxerxes sends a letter authorizing Ezra to lead willing Israelites, priests, and Levites back to Jerusalem.

Ezra lists the families of the porters and the Nethinims, temple servants who returned with Zerubbabel from Babylonian exile to Jerusalem, detailing their names and numbers as part of the census of exiles rebuilding the community.

King Artaxerxes of Persia authorizes Ezra to lead willing Israelites, priests, and Levites from Babylon to Jerusalem, carrying royal and voluntary offerings to fund sacrifices and temple needs, ensuring proper worship and service in Jerusalem's temple.

King Artaxerxes issues a decree exempting temple workers from taxes and authorizes Ezra to appoint judges to enforce God's and the king's laws among the exiles beyond the Euphrates. Ezra praises God for favor and prepares to lead leaders back to Jerusalem.

King Artaxerxes of Persia authorizes Ezra to receive temple vessels and funds from the royal treasury for God's house in Jerusalem, instructing officials to promptly fulfill Ezra's requests and exempt temple workers from taxes.
Ezra lists the leaders and genealogies of the Israelites who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem under King Artaxerxes, detailing the family heads and the number of males in each group.

Ezra lists groups of returning exiles by family and numbers, then gathers them at the Ahava River. Noticing no Levites, he sends leaders to Casiphia to request temple servants (Nethinims) to join their journey to Jerusalem.

Ezra, leading the return to Jerusalem, chooses to fast and pray for protection instead of requesting royal military aid, trusting God's help. He then entrusts priests with weighing and safeguarding the valuable offerings given for the temple.

Ezra entrusts priests and Levites with sacred offerings of silver, gold, and vessels to bring to Jerusalem. They depart from the river Ahava, safely arrive, and weigh and record the offerings in the temple under priestly supervision.

Ezra sends messengers to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levite ministers for the temple. They gather priests, Levites, and Nethinims, then fast by the Ahava River, seeking God's guidance and protection on their journey to Jerusalem without royal military aid.

After arriving in Jerusalem, Ezra and the returning exiles carefully recorded the offerings brought for the temple and made burnt offerings to God. They also distributed the king’s orders to local officials to support the people and the temple’s restoration.

After the return from exile, the leaders report to Ezra that the Israelites, including priests and Levites, have intermarried with local pagan peoples, violating God's commands; Ezra reacts with shock and mourning in Jerusalem.

Ezra gathers those who fear God to confess Israel's sins of intermarriage with foreign peoples. He mourns deeply, praying for mercy and acknowledging God's grace in preserving a remnant during their captivity in Persia.

After confessing and praying before the temple in Jerusalem, Ezra leads a large, weeping assembly of Israelites. Shechaniah urges them to repent by separating from foreign wives, and Ezra gets the leaders to swear to follow this covenant.

Ezra prays in Jerusalem, urging the Israelites not to intermarry with surrounding peoples, acknowledging God's mercy despite their sins, and fearing total destruction if they disobey again after their recent deliverance from exile.

Ezra leads priests, Levites, and Israelites in swearing to follow God's law, mourns the people's sins, and calls all exiles in Judah and Jerusalem to gather in three days. The people assemble, trembling, as Ezra confronts them about their forbidden marriages.

Ezra prays, acknowledging God's mercy in allowing a remnant of Israelites to return from Persian captivity and rebuild Jerusalem, but he warns against intermarriage with the local peoples whose land is defiled, urging separation to preserve their inheritance.

Ezra confronts the people of Judah and Benjamin in Jerusalem about marrying foreign wives, urging confession and separation to avoid God's wrath. The community agrees but notes the difficulty due to numbers and weather; leaders are appointed to manage the process.

Ezra and leaders identify many Levites, singers, porters, and Israelites from various clans who have married foreign wives, continuing the investigation into this issue as part of the community's covenant renewal in Jerusalem.
Ezra lists many men from various families in Judah who had married foreign wives, highlighting the widespread nature of this issue among the returned exiles and their descendants in Jerusalem.

Nehemiah prays earnestly to God, confessing the sins of Israel and his own family, recalling God's promises through Moses, and asking for mercy and success as he serves the Persian king as cupbearer in Shushan.

Nehemiah, serving as cupbearer in King Artaxerxes' palace at Shushan, learns from his brother Hanani about the suffering of Jews in Jerusalem and the city's ruined walls. Deeply distressed, Nehemiah prays and fasts, confessing Israel's sins.

Ezra appoints Jonathan, Jahaziah, Meshullam, and Shabbethai to investigate men who married foreign wives. They examine the issue starting in the tenth month, identifying priests, Levites, and others who pledge to separate from these wives.

Nehemiah, serving King Artaxerxes, requests and receives permission to travel to Judah with letters for local governors and timber supplies. He arrives in Jerusalem, while opponents Sanballat and Tobiah are upset by his mission to help Israel.

Nehemiah encourages the people of Jerusalem to rebuild the city's walls after seeing its destruction. They agree to work, but local enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock them, questioning their loyalty to the king. Nehemiah asserts God's support.

Nehemiah arrives in Jerusalem, secretly inspects the damaged city walls at night with a few men, then reveals the destruction to local leaders, urging them to rebuild the walls to restore the city's honor and security.

Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, appears before King Artaxerxes in Susa, visibly sad about Jerusalem's ruined state. After praying, he requests permission to go rebuild the city, and the king grants his request.

Nehemiah records the priests, led by Eliashib, and various groups from Jericho, Gibeon, and Mizpah, repairing key gates and walls of Jerusalem, while some nobles of the Tekoites refuse to help in the rebuilding effort.

Local leaders and craftsmen from Gibeon, Mizpah, and Jerusalem work together to repair sections of Jerusalem's wall, including the broad wall and valley gate, strengthening the city's defenses after Nehemiah's call to rebuild.

Local leaders and groups in Jerusalem, including Hanun and the people of Zanoah, Malchiah of Bethhaccerem, Shallun of Mizpah, Nehemiah of Bethzur, and Levites like Rehum, work together to repair various gates and sections of the city wall.

Local leaders and priests, including Bavai, Ezer, Baruch, and Meremoth, along with others from Keilah, Mizpah, and nearby areas, continue repairing sections of Jerusalem’s wall near the high priest Eliashib’s house and the king’s high house.

Nehemiah lists the individuals and groups, including Palal, Pedaiah, the Nethinims, priests, and merchants, who repaired specific sections of Jerusalem's wall near key gates and towers, continuing the city's restoration after opposition.

Nehemiah reports that when Sanballat and Tobiah, leaders of Samaria and Ammon, heard about the wall rebuilding in Jerusalem, they mocked the Jews. Despite opposition and insults, the people continued building with determination.

Nehemiah organizes the people of Jerusalem into armed groups along the wall for defense, encouraging them to trust God and protect their families. Half work on the wall while the other half stand guard, showing their readiness amid threats from enemies.

Nehemiah describes how the people united to rebuild Jerusalem's wall halfway, provoking anger and a conspiracy to attack from Sanballat, Tobiah, and neighboring groups. Nehemiah responds by praying and organizing armed guards to protect the workers.

Nehemiah confronts the Jewish nobles and rulers in Jerusalem about charging interest on loans to their fellow Jews, urging them to stop and restore lands and goods. They agree and swear an oath to keep this promise.

Nehemiah organizes the builders in Jerusalem to work with weapons ready, assigns trumpet signals for gathering, and sets up a day-and-night guard system to protect the city from enemies during the wall's reconstruction.

Nehemiah confronts Jewish nobles in Jerusalem who were exploiting their brethren with usury; they promise to restore what was taken. Nehemiah swears an oath with the priests, and he emphasizes his own integrity as governor during the twelve years of King Artaxerxes.

Nehemiah describes his dedication to rebuilding Jerusalem’s wall without personal gain, hosting many guests, and refusing the governor’s food allowance to avoid burdening the people, asking God to remember his faithful service.

Nehemiah hears the people of Jerusalem crying out about economic hardship and exploitation by fellow Jews who charge interest and take lands. He becomes angry and confronts the nobles and rulers, calling a large assembly to address the injustice.

Nehemiah reports that after completing the wall in Jerusalem, his enemies Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem invite him to meet in Ono, but he suspects a trap. They accuse him of plotting rebellion and claim he aims to be king.

Nehemiah responds to false accusations from Sanballat and Geshem, who claim he plans to rebel and become king. Despite threats and a warning from Shemaiah to hide in the temple, Nehemiah refuses to flee, realizing the prophecy is a trap set by his enemies.

After rebuilding Jerusalem's wall, Nehemiah appoints his brother Hanani and Hananiah to oversee the city, instructing strict gate security and watches, noting the city is large but sparsely populated with many houses still unbuilt.

Nehemiah observes Jerusalem is large but sparsely populated with unfinished houses. He feels led to gather leaders and people to record genealogies of those returning from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and others, listing their numbers by family groups.

Nehemiah realizes the prophet Shemaiah was bribed by enemies Tobiah and Sanballat to intimidate him into sinning. Despite opposition, Nehemiah finishes Jerusalem's wall in 52 days, while political alliances with Tobiah cause tension among Judah's nobles.

Nehemiah lists the families of the porters and the Nethinims, groups responsible for guarding the temple gates and serving in the temple, as part of the census of those who returned to Jerusalem after exile.

Nehemiah lists families of the Nethinims and Solomon’s servants who returned from exile, noting some lacked clear genealogy and were excluded from priesthood, reflecting efforts to organize and purify the community in Jerusalem after the wall's completion.

Nehemiah lists the numbers of people from various clans and towns, including priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, as part of a census to organize the repopulation and religious leadership of Jerusalem after the wall's completion.

Ezra the scribe stands on a wooden pulpit with leaders beside him, reading the law aloud to the gathered people at Jerusalem's Water Gate. Levites help explain the scripture clearly so everyone understands.

Nehemiah records that some priests lacked genealogical records and were barred from priesthood privileges until a legitimate priest appeared. He then lists the large community, their animals, and donations from leaders to support the temple work in Jerusalem.

Nehemiah lists the families and their numbers who returned from exile to Judah, detailing the population distribution among various clans and towns, continuing the census begun to organize the restored community in Jerusalem.

Nehemiah records generous contributions from leaders and the people for the temple work, then notes that priests, Levites, and all Israelites settled in their cities by the seventh month, marking a period of organization and restoration in Jerusalem.

After the people of Jerusalem settled in their cities, they gathered at the water gate where Ezra the priest read the law of Moses aloud to all who could understand, standing on a wooden platform with leaders beside him.

Ezra and the Levites read and explained God's law to the people, who wept upon hearing it. Nehemiah and Ezra encouraged them to rejoice instead, and the next day leaders gathered to further understand the law.

The Israelites gathered in Jerusalem on the 24th day, fasting and confessing their sins. Led by Levites Jeshua and others, they read God's law, worshiped, and praised God as the Creator and Sustainer of all.

The Levites, including Jeshua and others, lead a prayer praising God as the sole Creator who chose Abraham, fulfilled His covenant, delivered Israel from Egypt with mighty signs, and parted the Red Sea to save them from their enemies.

The Levites recount God's provision of manna and water during Israel's wilderness journey, despite the people's repeated disobedience and idolatry, highlighting God's mercy and guidance through the cloud and fire pillars.

In a communal confession, the Israelites recall God's provision during their 40 years in the wilderness, His granting them victory over nations like Sihon and Og, and their peaceful settlement in the promised land with abundant resources.

In a communal prayer, the Levites recount God's miraculous deliverance of Israel from Egypt, guiding them by pillars of cloud and fire, giving laws at Sinai, providing manna and water, and promising the land of Canaan as their inheritance.

The Levites recount Israel's repeated cycles of disobedience, punishment by enemies, repentance, and God's merciful deliverance, highlighting their persistent pride and refusal to obey God's laws despite prophetic warnings.

The leaders, priests, and Levites gathered with Ezra in Jerusalem to understand the law about dwelling in booths during the seventh month feast. The people then made booths and celebrated joyfully, reading the law daily for seven days plus a solemn assembly.

The Israelites confess their ancestors' disobedience and acknowledge their current servitude under foreign kings due to their sins. They commit to a renewed covenant, with leaders and priests sealing the agreement to restore faithfulness.

The Levites recount Israel's history, describing how the people prospered in the Promised Land but then rebelled, rejecting God's law and prophets, leading to their oppression by enemies until God mercifully sent saviors to rescue them.

The Levites confess Israel's repeated disobedience despite God's patience and mercy, acknowledging that their leaders and ancestors failed to keep God's laws, leading to suffering under foreign powers since Assyria's time.

Nehemiah and a long list of priests, Levites, and leaders from Jerusalem seal the covenant, showing their commitment to follow God's law after confessing Israel's sins and hardships under foreign rulers.

Nehemiah and the leaders, along with priests, Levites, and others who separated themselves to follow God's law, make a solemn covenant to obey God's commandments, avoid intermarriage with local peoples, honor the Sabbath, and observe the sabbatical year.

Nehemiah and the leaders of Jerusalem vow to honor the Sabbath by not buying goods from locals on that day, observe the sabbatical year, and annually contribute a third of a shekel for temple offerings and maintenance.

Nehemiah and the leaders of Jerusalem commit to regular offerings and sacrifices as prescribed in the law, including firstfruits and firstborns, to support the temple priests and maintain worship in the house of God.

Nehemiah and the leaders of Israel in Jerusalem commit to bringing their firstborn, firstfruits, and tithes to support the priests and Levites serving in the temple, ensuring ongoing offerings and care for God's house.
This passage lists the priests and Levites who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua during the post-exilic restoration, naming key leaders and tracing Jeshua's priestly lineage to Jaddua.

Nehemiah records the leaders living in Jerusalem while the rest of the people cast lots to settle one in ten in the city and nine elsewhere in Judah. The passage lists prominent families of Judah and Benjamin residing in Jerusalem after the city's restoration.

This passage lists the families of Perez and Benjamin living in Jerusalem, naming their leaders and warriors, along with priests and temple workers, highlighting the organized community and leadership in the city after the people's resettlement.

Nehemiah lists leaders and groups serving in Jerusalem’s temple, including Levites, porters, and singers, detailing their roles and numbers. The Nethinims live in Ophel, with overseers managing temple duties and worship activities.

During Nehemiah and Ezra's leadership, Levite leaders and gatekeepers organized praise and thanksgiving at Jerusalem's wall dedication, gathering singers from nearby villages; priests and Levites purified themselves, the people, gates, and wall to prepare for the celebration.

This passage lists the priestly genealogies from Joiada to Jaddua and names chief priests during Joiakim's time, noting Levite leaders who led worship in Jerusalem, with records extending to Persian King Darius's reign.

Nehemiah lists leaders overseeing Levites and singers in Jerusalem, appointed by the king, and details where the tribes of Judah and Benjamin live in various villages and cities across the region, showing the organized settlement after the return from exile.

Nehemiah leads Judah's leaders and priests in a purification and thanksgiving procession along Jerusalem's walls, starting at the dung gate and moving past the city of David to the water gate, with musicians and trumpeters accompanying them.

During the dedication of Jerusalem's wall, the people celebrated with sacrifices and appointed officials to manage offerings and tithes, continuing the traditions of David and Solomon. This joyful event involved priests, Levites, singers, and porters under Nehemiah and Zerubbabel.

Nehemiah leads two groups of people giving thanks as they walk along Jerusalem's newly rebuilt walls, from the fountain gate to the sheep gate. Priests and singers join in joyful praise, celebrating with sacrifices and widespread rejoicing.

King Ahasuerus, ruler of a vast empire from India to Ethiopia, holds a lavish feast in his palace at Shushan during the third year of his reign, showcasing his kingdom's wealth and power to his nobles and servants over many days.

During King Ahasuerus's lavish feast in Shushan, guests drank freely without compulsion. On the seventh day, the king ordered Queen Vashti to appear wearing her crown to display her beauty, but she refused, angering the king.

Memucan, one of King Ahasuerus's princes, advises the king to punish Queen Vashti for refusing his command, warning her defiance could inspire disrespect among women in Persia and Media, and suggests replacing her to uphold royal authority.

Nehemiah confronts Judah's leaders about neglecting the temple, restores proper management of tithes, and rebukes people and Tyrian merchants for working and selling goods in Jerusalem on the Sabbath, violating its sanctity.

Nehemiah confronts merchants who stayed near Jerusalem's walls on the Sabbath, enforcing rest by stationing Levites at the gates. He also opposes intermarriage with foreign women, recalling Solomon's downfall, to preserve Israel's religious purity.

Queen Vashti refuses King Ahasuerus's order to appear before him during a feast in Susa, angering him. The king consults his seven top advisors, including Memucan, who warns her disobedience could inspire widespread disrespect among women in the empire.

Nehemiah returns to Jerusalem after a period away and discovers that Eliashib the priest has given a room in the temple to Tobiah, an enemy. Nehemiah removes Tobiah's belongings, restores temple items, and confronts leaders about neglecting the Levites.

Nehemiah reads the law to the people in Jerusalem, revealing that Ammonites and Moabites are excluded from God's assembly. Meanwhile, Eliashib the priest has improperly given Tobiah a room meant for sacred offerings.

Nehemiah rebukes the people of Judah for marrying foreign wives, citing King Solomon's sin as a warning. He expels a priest's son allied with Sanballat, purifies the priesthood, and reinstates proper duties for priests and Levites in Jerusalem.

Nehemiah confronts Judah's leaders about Tyrian merchants selling goods in Jerusalem on the Sabbath, orders the city gates closed before the Sabbath, and prevents trade to enforce Sabbath observance and stop profaning the holy day.

King Ahasuerus agrees with Memucan's advice to issue a decree across his vast empire, commanding all wives to honor their husbands, and sends letters in every language to enforce this law throughout Persia and Media.

After King Ahasuerus calms down from his anger over Queen Vashti, his servants suggest finding new young women for the king to choose a new queen. Meanwhile, Mordecai, a Jewish exile in Shushan, is introduced.

Esther, a Jewish maiden raised by Mordecai, keeps her identity secret as she prepares for her turn to meet King Ahasuerus after a year of purification rituals; Mordecai watches over her daily from outside the women's quarters in Susa.

Mordecai, a Jew exiled from Jerusalem, raised his cousin Esther as his daughter. When the king gathered young women for a new queen, Esther was taken to the palace, gained favor with Hegai, and kept her Jewish identity secret as Mordecai instructed.

Esther, a Jewish maiden raised by Mordecai, enters King Ahasuerus's palace for a royal selection. She gains favor, becomes queen, replacing Vashti, and the king celebrates with a feast and gifts to his officials and provinces.

Mordecai informs Esther, through Hatach, about Haman's plot to kill the Jews and urges her to petition King Ahasuerus despite the law forbidding uninvited visits, warning her she won't be safe just because she is queen.

King Ahasuerus holds a feast celebrating Esther becoming queen and grants gifts across the provinces. Mordecai, Esther’s cousin, uncovers a plot by two chamberlains to harm the king, reports it through Esther, and the conspirators are executed.
King Ahasuerus promotes Haman above all princes, commanding everyone to bow to him. Mordecai refuses, angering Haman, who learns Mordecai is Jewish and decides to destroy all Jews in the kingdom.

Mordecai mourns publicly in sackcloth and ashes after Haman's decree to kill the Jews spreads, causing widespread Jewish grief. Esther learns of this and sends Hatach to Mordecai to find out what is wrong.

Haman, angry that Mordecai won't bow to him, plans to destroy all Jews in King Ahasuerus's kingdom. He casts lots to choose the date and convinces the king to authorize the destruction, receiving the king's ring to seal the decree.

King Ahasuerus authorizes Haman to destroy the Jews and gives him his ring to seal the decree. Official letters are sent throughout the empire ordering the extermination of all Jews on a set day, causing distress in the capital, Shushan.

Mordecai urges Esther to act to save the Jews, warning her of the consequences of silence and suggesting her royal position may be purposeful. Esther agrees to fast with the Jews in Susa before risking approaching King Ahasuerus uninvited.

Esther, after fasting and praying with the Jews in Susa, courageously approaches King Ahasuerus, who welcomes her and offers to grant her request. Esther invites the king and Haman to a banquet she has prepared, setting the stage for her plea.

At Esther's banquet in Susa, King Ahasuerus offers to grant her any request, and she invites him and Haman to another banquet. Haman leaves happy but becomes angry when he sees Mordecai refusing to honor him.

Haman boasts to his wife Zeresh and friends in Susa about his wealth, children, and royal favor, but resents Mordecai for not honoring him. They advise building a gallows to execute Mordecai before Haman’s banquet with King Ahasuerus and Queen Esther.

King Ahasuerus can't sleep and reviews royal records, discovering Mordecai's past loyalty in foiling a plot. As Haman arrives to ask for Mordecai's execution, the king unexpectedly asks Haman how to honor a man he wishes to praise.

At Esther's second banquet in Susa, King Ahasuerus offers to grant her any request. Esther reveals the plot to destroy her people, identifying Haman as the enemy, causing him to fear the king's wrath and plead for his life.

King Ahasuerus leaves the banquet in anger, and Haman pleads for his life to Queen Esther, but the king returns, finds Haman threatening Esther, and orders him hanged on the gallows Haman built for Mordecai, ending the king's anger.

King Ahasuerus asks Haman how to honor a favored man, and Haman suggests a royal parade. The king orders Haman to honor Mordecai, whom Haman despises, by dressing him in royal clothes and parading him through Susa's streets.

Esther pleads with King Ahasuerus to stop Haman’s plan to destroy the Jews. The king grants Esther and Mordecai authority to issue a new decree protecting the Jews across the vast Persian Empire, from India to Ethiopia.

Haman is forced to honor Mordecai publicly by dressing him in royal clothes and parading him on horseback through Susa. Haman returns home ashamed, warns from his wife and friends that he will fail against Mordecai, then is summoned to Esther’s banquet.

After Haman's execution, King Ahasuerus gives Haman's estate to Queen Esther and honors Mordecai by giving him Haman's ring and position. Esther pleads with the king to reverse Haman's harmful orders against the Jews.

King Ahasuerus’ decree allowing the Jews to defend themselves was sent throughout his vast empire from Shushan. Mordecai was honored publicly, and the Jews celebrated with joy and feasting, gaining respect and converts across the provinces.

King Ahasuerus’ scribes wrote and sealed a royal decree, commanded by Mordecai, allowing Jews across 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia to defend themselves and defeat their enemies on a set day in the twelfth month, Adar.

As the king's decree against the Jews was about to be enforced in the month of Adar, the Jews across King Ahasuerus's provinces defended themselves, gaining support from local officials due to Mordecai's rising influence, and defeated their enemies, including 500 in Shushan.

In Shushan palace, the Jews killed 500 men including Haman's ten sons. King Ahasuerus asks Esther what more she wants; she requests another day for the Jews to defend themselves and to hang Haman’s sons, which the king grants.

King Ahasuerus orders the execution of Haman's ten sons in Shushan. The Jews defend themselves across the empire on Adar 13-14, then rest and celebrate with feasts and gift-giving, establishing these days as annual festivals of joy.

This passage introduces Job, a wealthy and righteous man from Uz with a large family. Job regularly offers sacrifices for his children. Meanwhile, a heavenly scene unfolds where God and Satan meet to discuss Job's faithfulness.

Esther and Mordecai officially confirm the Purim festival by sending letters to all Jewish communities across King Ahasuerus's 127 provinces, establishing the annual observance of these days with fasting and celebration.

God permits Satan to test Job by taking away his possessions, but not harming him personally. While Job's children feast at their eldest brother's house, messengers arrive one after another with news of attacks and disasters that have destroyed Job's livestock and servants.

Esther appeals to King Ahasuerus to punish Haman and his sons, reversing their plot against the Jews. The Jews establish the annual festival of Purim to commemorate their deliverance, with Esther and Mordecai formalizing the observance.

God questions Satan about Job’s faithfulness, highlighting Job’s righteousness and protection. Satan challenges that Job is faithful only because of his blessings, and God allows Satan to test Job’s possessions but not harm him personally.

After the Jews' victory over their enemies, those in unwalled villages celebrated the 14th of Adar with feasting and gift-giving. Mordecai formalized this by sending letters to all Jews in King Ahasuerus's provinces to observe these days annually.

Mordecai instructs the Jews to celebrate their deliverance from Haman's plot by observing days of joy, feasting, and charity. This follows Esther's successful appeal to King Ahasuerus to reverse Haman's plan to destroy the Jews.

Messengers report to Job in Uz that Chaldeans raided his camels and killed servants, then a wind destroyed his children’s house, killing them. Despite these losses, Job mourns, worships God, and remains faithful without blaming Him.
King Ahasuerus imposes a tax across his empire, while the record highlights Mordecai's rise to power as second to the king, respected by the Jews and working for their welfare and peace.

Job, suffering great loss and pain in the land of Uz, breaks his silence to lament his birth, expressing deep anguish and wishing he had never been born, following the silent mourning of his friends in the previous chapter.

God and Satan meet again in heaven, discussing Job's faithfulness despite suffering; Satan challenges Job's loyalty if physically harmed, and God allows Satan to afflict Job with painful sores, while Job's wife urges him to curse God.

Job's wife urges him to curse God and give up, but Job refuses to sin. His three friends—Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar—travel to comfort him, mourning silently with him for seven days, recognizing his deep suffering.

Eliphaz continues speaking to Job, describing how God protects the poor and punishes the wicked, encouraging Job to accept God's discipline as it leads to peace, prosperity, and long life, urging him to trust in God's justice and care.

Eliphaz continues speaking to Job, warning that foolishness and envy lead to destruction and suffering, describing how God controls human fate by humbling the proud and thwarting the plans of the crafty, emphasizing human trouble is inevitable.

Job responds to his friends, lamenting their lack of true support and accusing them of deceit and abandoning him in his suffering. He challenges their accusations, asking for understanding and asserting his innocence.
Job continues his lament, questioning why he was born and expressing a desire for death as an escape from his suffering, contrasting the rest of the dead with his ongoing misery and fear.

Eliphaz the Temanite recounts a terrifying vision he had, emphasizing human frailty and the folly of claiming to be more righteous than God, contrasting mortal weakness with divine judgment and the fate of the wicked.
Job responds to Bildad’s speech by expressing the immense weight of his suffering, describing his pain as unbearable and questioning his own strength and wisdom amid his afflictions.

Eliphaz, a friend from Teman, responds to Job’s lament, reminding him of his past wisdom and strength but suggests Job’s current suffering is due to fear and trouble. Eliphaz shares a fearful vision he received in the night.

Job continues his lament, expressing his suffering and fleeting life on earth, comparing his days to a hired worker's. He feels watched and tormented by God, questioning why he is so closely observed in his misery.
Job continues his lament, expressing anguish over God's constant scrutiny and his own suffering, feeling overwhelmed and longing for relief from his pain and the burden of his sin.

Bildad the Shuhite responds to Job, warning that those who forget God have fragile hopes like spider webs and unstable homes, but God supports the righteous and will ultimately bring joy and shame to the wicked.

Bildad the Shuhite responds to Job's complaints, accusing him of speaking empty words and suggesting that Job's suffering is due to his or his children's sin, urging Job to seek God and learn from past generations about the consequences of forgetting God.

Job continues his response to Bildad, expressing his deep sorrow and fear before God's overwhelming power, lamenting the absence of a mediator to reconcile him with God and his inability to speak freely without fear.

Job continues his lament, speaking directly to God in his suffering, questioning why God oppresses him despite being His creation, and expressing his confusion over God's scrutiny of his actions and sin.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, responds to Job's complaints by accusing him of falsehood and arrogance. He urges Job to repent, warning that God's wisdom and justice are beyond human understanding and that God will punish the wicked.

Job responds to his friends' speeches by asserting his own understanding and pointing out that God's power is evident in all creation, from animals to humans, emphasizing God's control over life and wisdom beyond human reach.

Job continues his response to Bildad, expressing his despair that even if he were righteous, he could not argue with God or expect fair judgment, as God's power is overwhelming and the wicked often prosper while his own life passes swiftly without relief.

Job continues his lament, expressing confusion and despair over God's relentless judgment despite his innocence, questioning why he was born only to suffer and longing for relief before his inevitable death in the land of darkness.

Zophar, one of Job's friends, advises Job to abandon sin and wickedness to find peace and security, promising a hopeful future and safety, contrasting the fate of the wicked who will lose hope and fail.

Job responds to his friends by emphasizing God's supreme power over nature and rulers, describing how God controls life, death, and the fate of nations, showing that human wisdom and strength are ultimately subject to divine authority.

Job responds to his friends, asserting his equal understanding and accusing them of falsehoods and useless advice. He insists on speaking directly to God, expressing his trust despite suffering, and demands they listen carefully to his defense.

Job continues his defense before his friends, asserting his innocence and pleading with God to reveal his sins and not to punish him harshly, expressing his feeling of being closely watched and severely afflicted.

Job responds to Bildad's speech by acknowledging God's unmatched power and wisdom, describing His control over nature and human fate, and expressing his own inability to argue or justify himself before God.

Eliphaz the Temanite responds to Job, criticizing human sinfulness and warning that the wicked suffer constant pain and impending judgment from God, who is powerful and just. He describes the oppressor's futile struggle against the Almighty.

Eliphaz the Temanite continues his rebuke of Job, describing the fate of the wicked who live in luxury but face ruin and destruction, warning that deceitful and hypocritical people will ultimately be desolate and consumed by judgment.

Eliphaz the Temanite responds to Job, challenging his claims of innocence and wisdom, questioning Job's understanding of God, and accusing him of speaking arrogantly against God despite human imperfection. This continues the debate on Job's suffering and righteousness.

Job continues his lament, reflecting on human mortality and the finality of death, questioning if there is life after death, and expressing a desire for God’s mercy and remembrance despite human frailty and sin.

Job continues lamenting his suffering and isolation, feeling mocked and abandoned by friends and God. He reflects on his failing health, lost hopes, and the inevitability of death, expressing despair over his broken plans and the futility of life.

Bildad the Shuhite responds to Job's complaints, criticizing Job's words and describing the downfall and destruction that befalls the wicked, emphasizing consequences of sin and loss of strength and security.
Job responds to his friends' harsh words, calling them poor comforters, and describes his deep suffering and feeling abandoned by God, who has allowed him to be attacked and broken by enemies.
Bildad the Shuhite continues his rebuke of Job, describing the complete destruction and disgrace that befalls the wicked, emphasizing the loss of legacy and honor as a consequence of not knowing God.

Job continues his response to his friends, describing his intense suffering and innocence despite their accusations. He expresses his desire for a mediator between himself and God as he faces despair and anticipates death.

Job continues his speech, reflecting on human mortality and frailty, comparing life to a fleeting flower and shadow, and contrasting the hope of a tree's regrowth with the finality of human death under God's appointed limits.
Job laments his isolation as even his household and friends reject him in Uz. Despite his suffering, he expresses hope in a living redeemer and urges his friends to reconsider their harsh judgment.
Zophar warns Job that the wicked will face severe divine punishment, describing vivid imagery of destruction and loss that will come upon them as a just consequence from God for their sins.

Zophar, one of Job’s friends, responds quickly to Job’s defense, arguing that the success of the wicked is brief and their downfall inevitable, describing the internal torment that follows hidden sin. This continues the debate on suffering and justice.

Job responds to his friends' harsh accusations, expressing his deep suffering and isolation. He feels abandoned by God and estranged from family and servants, highlighting his complete social and spiritual alienation.

Zophar the Naamathite responds to Job, describing how the wicked, despite their wealth and efforts, will suffer God's wrath and lose all they have gained, emphasizing the consequences of oppressing the poor and unjustly taking what is not theirs.

Eliphaz the Temanite responds to Job, accusing him of great wickedness and social injustice, questioning Job's righteousness before God, and emphasizing God's supreme knowledge and presence above all earthly matters.

Eliphaz continues speaking to Job, promising that if Job prays and remains pure, God will hear him, grant his requests, and bring deliverance and hope to the humble and innocent, contrasting with Job's current suffering.

Job continues his response to his friends, reflecting on the fate of the wicked who seem prosperous but ultimately face God's judgment and destruction, challenging his friends' assumptions about justice and the afterlife.
Job responds to his friends, asking them to listen carefully as he questions why the wicked often prosper and live long lives, enjoying wealth and family, despite their disregard for God’s ways.

Job responds to his friends, challenging their claims about the fate of the wicked, pointing out that though the wicked prosper now, they are ultimately destined for destruction and death, questioning the comfort his friends offer.

Job responds to his friends, expressing his deep desire to find and present his case before God, acknowledging God's unchanging will and his own suffering, while affirming his faithfulness despite feeling abandoned and troubled by God's hidden presence.
Bildad the Shuhite responds to Job, emphasizing God's supreme power and purity, questioning how any human can be justified before Him, highlighting human insignificance compared to God's holiness.

Job describes the wicked in the land who harm the vulnerable—murderers, adulterers, and thieves—acting without fear of God. Despite their power and cruelty, their fate is destruction and forgetfulness, showing the consequences of sin.

Job continues his speech, lamenting injustice in the land where the poor, widows, and orphans suffer as the wicked exploit and oppress them without punishment, questioning why God allows this despite His awareness of all times and deeds.

Job responds to Bildad's speech by questioning his ability to help the powerless and then praises God's mighty creation and control over the earth, sky, and sea, highlighting human inability to fully grasp God's power.
Job reflects on how even the powerful are subject to God's control and mortality, emphasizing that their temporary success ends in downfall, challenging anyone to prove otherwise.

Job reflects on the hidden treasures mined from the earth—silver, gold, iron, and precious stones—describing nature’s mysteries and the difficulty of finding true wisdom, which is not accessible even in the depths or seas.

Eliphaz the Temanite continues speaking to Job, urging him to recognize God's sovereignty despite human wickedness, encouraging Job to return to God for restoration, peace, and blessings, contrasting the fate of the wicked with the security of the righteous.

Job reflects on the priceless nature of wisdom, stating it cannot be bought with gold or jewels and is hidden from all living creatures. He concludes that only God fully knows wisdom, who reveals it as fearing the Lord and turning from evil.

Job reflects on his past blessings in Uz, recalling when God protected him, his family was with him, and he was respected for helping the poor and needy, gaining honor and silence from city leaders at the gate.

Job reflects on his past when he was a respected leader in his community, known for helping the vulnerable and delivering justice, with people eagerly listening to his wise counsel and honoring him like a king among his people.
Job laments that younger men, once lowly and destitute, now mock him and oppose him, reflecting his fall from honor to suffering and isolation in the land of Uz after previously being respected.

Job continues his speech, warning that the wicked's wealth and offspring will not protect them from death and divine judgment, describing their downfall and disgrace as inevitable despite their earthly riches.

Job continues speaking, declaring his innocence and integrity despite his suffering, and warns that the wicked and their descendants will face God's judgment and destruction, contrasting their fate with his own steadfast righteousness.

Job laments his suffering and isolation, describing how enemies worsen his troubles and God seems unresponsive. He reflects on his past compassion for the needy, contrasting it with his current affliction and despair.

Job continues his defense, declaring his commitment to purity and justice, asserting that God observes all his actions. He challenges any wrongdoing in his behavior toward others, including servants, anticipating God's judgment.

Job laments his suffering and isolation, recalling his past compassion for the poor, but now faces darkness and affliction. He describes his physical and emotional pain, feeling like an outcast and mourning openly among his community.

Job continues his defense, insisting he has treated servants and the poor with fairness and compassion, fearing God's judgment and acknowledging their shared creation by God. He calls for severe punishment if he has wronged the vulnerable.

Job continues his self-defense, affirming his reverence for God and integrity in wealth, hospitality, and justice. He longs for God to hear him and respond, wishing his accuser would document his case for a fair hearing.

Job expresses a deep wish for God to respond and for his accuser to document his case, confidently asserting his innocence and willingness to defend himself like a noble. He concludes by affirming his integrity regarding his land and its produce.

After Job's three friends stop responding, Elihu, a younger man from Ram, becomes angry at both Job and his friends for their arguments. Though younger, Elihu decides to speak up, claiming that wisdom comes from God's spirit, not just age.

Elihu, a younger man from the Buzites, speaks after Job's three friends fail to answer him, expressing his eagerness to share his thoughts honestly and without favoritism, feeling compelled by the spirit within him.

Elihu begins speaking to Job, urging him to listen carefully. He claims to speak honestly and with divine inspiration, challenges Job's self-righteousness, and reminds him that God's ways are beyond human understanding.

Elihu continues speaking to Job, explaining how God communicates through dreams and suffering to guide and correct people, offering hope of restoration and forgiveness through a mediator who intercedes on their behalf.

Elihu continues addressing Job, explaining that God is merciful to those who repent and seek Him, offering restoration and life. He urges Job to listen carefully and respond if he wishes, promising to teach him wisdom.

Elihu begins his speech addressing the wise, challenging Job's claim of innocence and questioning his attitude toward God. He defends God's justice and sovereignty over the earth and humanity, emphasizing that all will perish if God withdraws life.

Elihu continues speaking to Job and others, emphasizing God's justice and power over all people, rich or poor. He warns that all will die and that God sees all actions, punishing the wicked and replacing rulers as He wills.

Elihu continues his speech to Job and the wise men, asserting that God judges the wicked and hears the cries of the afflicted. He challenges Job's words as rebellious and calls for wise men to respond, emphasizing God's justice and authority.
Elihu continues speaking to Job, describing God's greatness and mysterious power over nature, using rain, clouds, and light as examples of God's control and provision for people and animals.

God speaks to Job from a whirlwind, challenging him with questions about the creation of the earth and control over nature, highlighting Job's limited understanding compared to God's power and wisdom.

Elihu continues speaking to Job and his friends, challenging Job’s claims about righteousness and sin. He argues that human actions don’t affect God directly and urges trust in God’s judgment despite suffering.

Elihu continues addressing Job, urging him to recognize God's control over nature and weather as signs of His power and wisdom, emphasizing human limitations in understanding and the fear due to God's majesty and justice.

Elihu resumes speaking to Job, claiming he has more to say about God's justice. He describes God's power, fairness, and discipline, explaining that God cares for the righteous and punishes the wicked, urging obedience for prosperity and warning of consequences for rebellion.

God speaks to Job from the whirlwind, challenging Job's understanding by describing His control over natural forces like rain, frost, stars, and lightning, highlighting divine wisdom beyond human grasp.
God speaks to Job from a whirlwind, challenging Job's understanding by describing His control over the earth, death, light, darkness, and weather, emphasizing divine power beyond human knowledge.

Elihu continues speaking to Job, warning him about the consequences of wickedness and urging him to recognize God's power and justice, which are beyond human understanding, and to avoid choosing sin over correction.

Elihu continues speaking to Job, describing God's powerful control over nature—thunder, lightning, snow, rain, and winds—emphasizing God's authority over the earth and his purposeful use of weather for correction, mercy, or sustenance.

God continues speaking to Job, describing the unique behaviors and instincts of animals like the proud ostrich and the powerful war horse, highlighting their natural traits and God's control over them.

God speaks to Job from a whirlwind, questioning Job's understanding of creation and control over nature, highlighting God's wisdom in providing for animals like lions and ravens, contrasting Job's limited knowledge with divine power.

God continues speaking to Job, describing various wild animals like goats, deer, wild donkeys, unicorns, peacocks, and ostriches, highlighting their natural behaviors and independence in the wilderness.
God continues speaking to Job, describing the mighty leviathan, a powerful sea creature, emphasizing that no human can control or capture it, highlighting God's unmatched power over all creation.

God continues describing Leviathan's terrifying strength and impenetrable scales, emphasizing its fiery breath and invincibility to weapons, highlighting the creature's unmatched power and the fear it inspires among the mighty.

God continues speaking to Job, describing the horse's fearless charge into battle and then shifts to birds of prey like the hawk and eagle, highlighting their instinctive hunting skills and nesting habits in high, secure places.

God continues describing Leviathan's immense power and fearlessness, emphasizing its dominance over nature and other creatures, highlighting that no one on earth compares to this mighty, fearless beast.

God responds to Job from the whirlwind, challenging Job's right to question Him and describing His own power, then introduces the mighty behemoth as a symbol of God's creative strength, continuing the divine speeches that began earlier.

This psalm describes earthly kings and rulers plotting against God and His anointed king, who is established by God on Zion. God warns them to serve Him with reverence and trust in His appointed Son to avoid judgment.

This psalm contrasts the blessed person who follows God's law with the ungodly who do not, using imagery of a fruitful tree versus chaff blown by the wind, highlighting the outcomes for each before God's judgment.

God continues speaking to Job from the whirlwind, describing the mighty behemoth, a powerful creature of His creation that lives in the mountains and rivers, emphasizing God's unmatched power in making and controlling such a beast.

Job's family is restored with seven sons and three daughters, noted for their beauty and receiving inheritance. Job lives a long life, witnessing four generations before he dies peacefully, concluding his story of suffering and restoration.

Job responds to God's speeches, acknowledging God's power and his own limited understanding, expressing repentance. Then God rebukes Eliphaz and Job's other friends for misrepresenting Him and instructs them to offer sacrifices with Job praying for them.

God instructs Job's friends Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar to offer sacrifices and have Job pray for them, leading to God's acceptance of Job and restoration of his fortunes, including family reunion and increased wealth.

David prays to God for protection as enemies multiply and doubt his safety. He trusts God as his shield and praises Him for past deliverance, expressing confidence in God's salvation despite overwhelming opposition.

David prays to God for mercy and protection, addressing those who dishonor him. He encourages trust in God, urging reflection and righteousness, expressing confidence that God grants peace and safety despite adversity.
David prays to God, expressing deep distress and pleading for mercy and healing. He feels overwhelmed by enemies and sorrow but trusts God hears his prayers and will bring justice.

David prays to God early in the morning, asking for protection from wicked enemies who speak lies and rebel against God, while expressing trust that God will bless and defend the righteous in His temple.
David prays to God for protection from his enemies who persecute him unjustly, affirming his innocence and asking God to judge him fairly while condemning the wicked and defending the righteous.

The psalmist affirms God's daily judgment of the righteous and anger toward the wicked, describing divine justice against evildoers who plot harm, and concludes with a vow to praise God's righteousness and sovereignty.

The psalmist praises God's majestic name and creation, reflecting on humanity's honored place just below angels and given dominion over animals and nature, highlighting God's care and power over all the earth.
The psalmist praises God wholeheartedly for His justice and protection, celebrating God's judgment against enemies and wicked nations, and affirming God as a refuge for the oppressed in Zion.
David expresses his trust in the LORD despite advice to flee danger, describing the wicked's threats and affirming God's watchful judgment from heaven over both the righteous and the violent.

The psalmist prays to God in Zion, asking for mercy and justice against enemies who cause suffering, affirming God's righteous judgment on the wicked and protection of the poor, urging God to act so nations recognize their mortality.

The psalmist prays to God, asking Him to act against the wicked who believe God ignores their evil deeds, affirming God's eternal kingship and His role as protector of the humble, fatherless, and oppressed.

The psalmist questions why God seems distant during times of trouble, describing the wicked's pride and cruelty toward the poor, who are trapped by deceit and violence, while the wicked falsely believe God is unaware of their actions.

David cries out to God in deep distress, feeling forgotten and oppressed by enemies, yet he expresses trust in God's mercy and vows to praise Him for His salvation, continuing the theme of seeking God's help amid adversity.

The psalmist cries out to God for help as godly and faithful people disappear, describing widespread deceit and pride among people. God promises to protect the oppressed and preserve His pure words amid rising wickedness.

David prays to God for protection and expresses his trust in the LORD as his true inheritance and guide. He rejects false gods, praises God's counsel, and looks forward to eternal joy and hope in God's presence.

David asks who is worthy to live in God's presence, describing the qualities of a righteous person who acts justly, speaks truthfully, respects others, honors God-fearers, keeps promises, and avoids exploitation or corruption.

The psalmist condemns those who deny God and act wickedly, describing God's watchful judgment over humanity. He contrasts the corrupt with the righteous, expressing hope for Israel's salvation and restoration from captivity.

David prays to God, asking for justice and protection from his enemies who surround him like lions. He affirms his innocence and trust in God's guidance, seeking refuge and deliverance from those who oppose him.

David compares his enemies to a lurking lion and prays for God's intervention to protect him from these wicked men who live for worldly gain; he expresses confidence in seeing God's righteousness and being satisfied in His presence.

David praises God for rewarding his righteousness and faithfulness, describing how God strengthens and protects him like a shield, enabling him to overcome enemies and challenges. This follows David’s testimony of deliverance and trust in God’s power.

David praises the LORD as his protector and deliverer who defeats his enemies and exalts him above foes. He commits to thanking God publicly for saving him and showing mercy to his descendants forever.

David praises God as his protector and strength, recalling how he called on the LORD in distress and witnessed God's powerful, awe-inspiring presence descending with thunder, fire, and darkness, showing divine intervention against his enemies.

David praises God for powerful deliverance, describing God's mighty acts in nature and how He rescued David from overwhelming enemies because of David's faithfulness and righteousness. This follows David's plea for help and trust in God.

David praises God's creation and law, describing how the heavens reveal God's glory and how His perfect law guides and protects. He asks for cleansing from hidden faults and for his words and thoughts to be pleasing to God.

This psalm praises God for granting the king strength, blessings, and protection against enemies. It follows a prayer for the king's victory and expresses confidence in God's power to defeat foes and bring honor to the king.

This psalm is a prayer for the king's protection and victory, asking God of Jacob to help and strengthen him from Zion. It contrasts trust in military power with trust in God, affirming faith in God's saving power for the anointed king.

David cries out to God in deep distress, feeling abandoned despite his past trust and God's faithfulness to Israel's ancestors; he describes enemies surrounding him like fierce bulls and lions, highlighting his vulnerability and isolation.

David describes intense suffering and enemies surrounding him like fierce animals, feeling physically broken and abandoned. Despite this, he calls on God for help and promises to praise Him publicly, affirming God's faithfulness to those in distress.

David praises God for giving him strength and victory over his enemies, enabling him to conquer and lead nations. He acknowledges God's protection and exaltation as the source of his success and deliverance.

David expresses trust in God’s guidance and protection, portraying the LORD as a shepherd who provides, restores, and comforts even in danger, promising lifelong goodness and eternal fellowship with God.

Psalm 24 praises God's creation and sovereignty over the earth, asking who may approach Him with purity. It calls for gates to open for the victorious King of glory, affirming God's power and presence.

David prays to God, affirming his integrity and trust while rejecting evil company. He seeks God's judgment and mercy, expressing his devotion to God's house and commitment to righteousness among the faithful.

David expresses his trust in the LORD as his protector and source of strength amid enemies and danger. He desires to live in God's presence and asks for mercy and guidance, affirming his commitment to seek the LORD's face.

David prays to God, expressing trust and seeking mercy amid affliction and enemies' hatred, asking for guidance, forgiveness, protection, and deliverance for himself and for Israel from their troubles.

David prays to the LORD, expressing trust and seeking guidance, forgiveness, and teaching. He asks God to remember His mercy and promises blessings for those who fear and follow Him, emphasizing God's faithfulness and covenant.

The psalmist affirms God's attentive care for the suffering and vows to praise Him publicly. He envisions all nations honoring God, recognizing His sovereign rule and enduring righteousness across generations.

David prays to God, asking for protection and guidance amid enemies and false accusers, expressing trust that God will not abandon him even if his own parents do, and encouraging patience and courage while waiting on the Lord.

David prays to God, asking for help against wicked enemies who deceive others. He trusts God as his protector, praises Him for answered prayers, and asks for God's continued blessing and strength for His people.

The psalmist praises God for healing and rescuing him from death, reflecting on past troubles and expressing gratitude for restored joy and strength, encouraging the faithful to sing and give thanks for God's enduring mercy and help.

The psalmist calls on mighty beings to praise God, describing His powerful voice over nature—waters, cedars, wilderness—and affirming His eternal kingship and blessing of strength and peace for His people.

David prays to the LORD, expressing deep trust and asking for rescue from hidden traps set by enemies. He describes his suffering, isolation, and physical weakness, seeking God's guidance and protection amid adversity.

The psalmist laments being forgotten and slandered by enemies plotting his death, yet he expresses trust in God’s protection and mercy, praising God’s kindness and refuge amid persecution. This continues his plea for deliverance and faithfulness.

The psalmist praises God for protection and kindness during distress, affirming trust despite feeling abandoned. He encourages all faithful believers to love God, be courageous, and rely on His strength and justice.

The psalmist calls the righteous to praise God with music, celebrating His creation and justice. God’s word is powerful, sustaining the heavens and earth, and His eternal counsel prevails over all human plans.

The psalmist reflects on the relief and blessing of confessing sins to God, contrasting the pain of silence with the joy of forgiveness. He encourages the faithful to trust God’s guidance and mercy, urging rejoicing among the righteous.

The psalmist praises God continually, sharing personal deliverance and encouraging others to trust and seek the Lord, emphasizing God's protection and care for the righteous and the importance of living rightly.
David prays to the LORD for protection and justice against his enemies who falsely accuse and persecute him without cause, expressing trust in God's salvation and deliverance for the vulnerable.

The psalmist describes God's sovereign watchfulness over all people, emphasizing that human strength and armies cannot save, but those who fear and trust God receive His protection and mercy. This follows praise of God's creative power and justice.

David laments betrayal by false accusers who rejoice in his suffering despite his kindness, pleading with the LORD for rescue and justice while affirming his intent to praise God publicly. This follows his call for divine protection against enemies.

The psalmist assures that God watches over the righteous, listens to their cries, and delivers them from troubles, while opposing evildoers; God is near to the brokenhearted and protects those who trust in Him.

The psalmist contrasts the wicked, who act without fear of God and plot evil, with God's mercy, faithfulness, and protection. He praises God's righteousness and asks for continued favor and protection from the proud and wicked.

David prays to the LORD, asking Him to act against his enemies who falsely accuse and rejoice over his suffering, seeking God's righteous judgment and protection while promising to praise Him publicly for His justice and deliverance.

The psalmist advises not to worry about evildoers who seem successful, urging trust in God and patience. He contrasts the fate of the wicked, who will soon perish, with the meek who will inherit peace and the land.

The psalmist contrasts the wicked who plot harm against the righteous with God's protection and justice, assuring that the wicked will fail while the upright, whose lives are guided by God, will be upheld and inherit the land.

The psalmist encourages trust in God’s guidance and protection for the righteous, contrasting their lasting security with the fleeting power of the wicked, emphasizing God’s justice and faithfulness over a lifetime.

The psalmist reflects on the fate of the wicked who disappear despite their power, contrasts this with the peaceful end of the righteous, and affirms that God protects and saves those who trust in Him during difficult times.

The psalmist reflects on God's protection for those who care for the poor, describes betrayal by a trusted friend, and prays for mercy and healing amid enemies' plots, affirming God's ongoing favor and eternal praise.

The psalmist describes feeling overwhelmed by enemies and personal sin, choosing silence amid attacks, yet placing hope in God’s help and pleading for swift deliverance from those who wrongfully oppose him.
The psalmist reflects on God's rescue from despair, praising Him and expressing trust. He acknowledges God's works and his commitment to obey and proclaim God's will openly to the community.

David prays to the Lord, expressing deep distress and physical suffering caused by his sins and enemies. He feels abandoned by friends and overwhelmed by pain, yet remains silent amid their plots against him.

The psalmist declares openly proclaiming God's righteousness and faithfulness to the assembly, pleads for God's mercy amid overwhelming troubles and enemies, and expresses trust in God's timely help and deliverance.

The psalmist expresses deep longing and sorrow for God, recalling joyful worship with others at the temple. Despite feeling overwhelmed by enemies and despair, he encourages his soul to hope in God’s help and praise.

David reflects on controlling his speech amid wickedness, feeling deep sorrow and recognizing human frailty and life's brevity. He prays to God for understanding, forgiveness, and strength, acknowledging his transient existence as a sojourner like his ancestors.

The psalmist pleads with God for justice against hostile nations and deceitful enemies, expressing feelings of abandonment and sorrow. He asks for God's guidance to the sacred place to worship, reaffirming his hope and trust in God despite inner turmoil.

The psalmist laments Israel's suffering and disgrace among surrounding nations, despite their faithfulness to God's covenant, and pleads for God to awaken, remember their affliction, and deliver them from oppression.

The psalmist recalls God's past deliverance of Israel's ancestors, emphasizing that their victories came by God's power, not their own. They praise God as King but lament current defeat and scattering among nations, feeling abandoned despite their faithfulness.

The psalmist praises a king, describing his divine blessing, majesty, and righteous rule, highlighting his power in battle and honor among noble women, including a queen from Ophir, following a plea for God's help in the previous psalm.
