God promises that Judah and Israel will reunite and return to their ancestral land, despite their past unfaithfulness. The people acknowledge their sins and shame, pleading for God's mercy and healing after turning away from Him.

God speaks through Jeremiah, urging Israel, Judah, and Jerusalem to repent and remove their sins to avoid destruction. He warns of an approaching enemy from the north who will devastate the land and cities.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Jerusalem of an unstoppable invading army from the north causing destruction. He urges the city to repent, lamenting the coming devastation and the people's rebellion that brought this judgment upon them.

Jeremiah laments Israel's foolishness and rebellion, describing a vision of desolation as God's fierce anger leads to the land's ruin and cities abandoned, warning of coming destruction despite God's unchanging judgment.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Jerusalem of coming invasion causing mass flight and desolation; despite attempts to appear beautiful, the city will be rejected and mourns deeply over the violence and destruction about to unfold.
God, through Jeremiah, warns Judah and Jerusalem of an unstoppable invading force from the north that will destroy their cities and leaders, bringing devastation instead of peace as they had hoped.

God, through Jeremiah, searches Jerusalem for anyone who acts justly and seeks truth, but finds none. The people are stubborn and unrepentant, so God warns that fierce enemies will attack because of their many sins.

God, through Jeremiah, warns that Israel and Judah’s many sins and betrayals will bring violent destruction by foreign enemies, despite their false confidence that disaster will not come and their reliance on false prophets.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Judah that their punishment is due to forsaking Him and worshipping other gods; despite clear signs of His power in nature, the people remain rebellious and fail to fear Him, causing their blessings to be withheld.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns the people of Judah for their sins, deceit, and injustice, highlighting corrupt leaders and false prophets who mislead the nation, setting the stage for divine judgment and consequences.

Jeremiah warns Jerusalem that God will abandon the city if it doesn't repent, describing how the people ignore His warnings and live in false peace. He announces coming judgment affecting all, from young to old, due to widespread corruption.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Israel that false prophets will be powerless, and He will send a foreign, powerful nation to conquer them and consume their resources as punishment for idolatry, though He will not completely destroy them.

Jeremiah warns the people of Benjamin and Jerusalem about an approaching enemy from the north, urging them to prepare for war and flee. He describes Jerusalem as a vulnerable woman besieged by violence and corruption, with God's judgment imminent.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns false peace and unrepentant sin in Jerusalem, urging a return to the right path, but the people refuse to listen; God warns nations of coming judgment due to their rejection of His laws and empty rituals.

God, through Jeremiah, rejects the people's empty sacrifices and warns Jerusalem (daughter of Zion) of an impending ruthless invasion from the north, urging mourning and caution as destruction approaches suddenly.
God warns Jerusalem to mourn deeply for the coming sudden destruction, describing the people as rebellious and corrupt. Despite efforts to refine them, they remain wicked and rejected by the LORD.

God speaks to Jeremiah in Jerusalem, instructing him to warn the people of Judah at the temple gate to change their sinful ways and practice justice, or face judgment despite trusting in the temple's protection.

God, speaking through Jeremiah at the temple gate in Jerusalem, condemns the people's hypocrisy and warns of judgment like that on Shiloh, rejecting their prayers due to persistent wickedness in Judah and Jerusalem.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns the people of Jerusalem for their unrepentant wickedness and false claims of wisdom, comparing their ignorance to birds that know their seasons, and warns of judgment due to their deceit and false peace.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns Judah's false peace and shameless sins, warning of coming destruction and famine. The people are urged to seek refuge in fortified cities as invading forces from Dan bring devastation across the land.

God speaks through Jeremiah, reminding Israel of His commands and their repeated disobedience despite prophets sent since Egypt; He declares their stubbornness and rejection, instructing Jeremiah to warn Jerusalem of coming judgment and lamentation.

God, through Jeremiah, warns that the bones of Judah's leaders and people will be exposed and dishonored because they worship false gods. Despite this, the people of Jerusalem persist in sin without repentance, continuing their rebellious ways.

God, speaking through Jeremiah in Jerusalem, condemns Judah's idolatry and false worship practices, warning that their disobedience and offerings to other gods will bring unquenchable judgment and destruction upon the land and its people.

God, through Jeremiah, warns of invading forces from Dan devastating the land of Judah, causing deep sorrow and questioning why the people have turned to idols despite God's presence in Zion. The prophet laments the people's suffering and lack of healing.

Jeremiah delivers God's judgment on Jerusalem and Judah for their evil deeds, including child sacrifice in Tophet. He warns of desolation and mourning as God's rejection leads to destruction and silence in the land.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns the deceit and betrayal among His people in Judah, warning of coming destruction and desolation of Jerusalem and the land, which will become deserted and uninhabitable.

God, through Jeremiah, laments Judah's destruction due to their rejection of His law and idolatry with Baal. He declares judgment: exile, suffering, and calls for mourning as the land becomes desolate and people are scattered among foreign nations.

Jeremiah laments deeply over the betrayal and deceit among the people of Judah, describing their lies and treachery. God declares He will test and punish them for their unfaithfulness and refusal to know Him.

God, speaking through Jeremiah to Israel, contrasts the lifeless idols made by skilled craftsmen from precious metals with Himself as the living, powerful Creator who controls nature and will judge false gods and their makers.

God speaks to Israel, warning them not to follow pagan customs or fear their idols, which are lifeless man-made objects decorated with silver and gold. He emphasizes His unmatched power and greatness compared to these foolish idols.

Jeremiah warns Judah that idols are worthless and will perish, unlike the LORD who created all. He laments the destruction of his people and calls for God's correction and judgment on unfaithful leaders and foreign nations attacking Israel.

God speaks to Jeremiah, recalling how He warned Israel from Egypt onward to obey Him, but they disobeyed and worshiped other gods. Now, God declares judgment on Judah and Jerusalem for breaking the covenant, promising punishment they cannot escape.
God declares that true pride should come from knowing Him and His justice, not worldly status, and warns that He will judge both Israel and surrounding nations for their spiritual unfaithfulness.

Jeremiah urges mourning over Jerusalem's destruction and exile, calling women to teach lamentation as death and desolation come. God warns against pride in worldly power, emphasizing knowing Him who values mercy, justice, and righteousness.

God speaks to Jeremiah, instructing him to warn the people of Judah and Jerusalem to obey the covenant made with their ancestors when God delivered them from Egypt, promising blessings if they follow His commands. Jeremiah agrees to proclaim this message.

Jeremiah reveals God's judgment on Israel and Judah for idolatry, sharing his awareness of plots against him by men of Anathoth who want him silenced. God promises to punish these conspirators severely in their time of reckoning.
Jeremiah questions God about why the wicked prosper while he suffers, expressing his frustration over betrayal by his own kin in Judah and the ongoing destruction in the land caused by evil people.

God, speaking through Jeremiah, condemns Judah and Jerusalem for idolatry, warning their many gods won't save them in trouble. He laments their unfaithfulness, likening them to a once flourishing olive tree now broken by judgment for worshipping Baal.

God declares judgment on Israel's hostile neighbors who threaten His people, promising to remove them but also to restore them if they repent and follow His ways; otherwise, He warns of their complete destruction.

Jeremiah laments betrayal by his own family and the destruction of his people’s land, describing how enemies and false leaders have devastated Israel, leading to widespread desolation and the LORD’s judgment across the land.

God speaks to Jeremiah about a severe drought in Judah, describing the suffering of people and animals in Jerusalem and the fields. Despite their sins, the people plead with God to remember His name and help them.

Jeremiah protests to God that other prophets falsely promise peace to Judah, but God reveals these prophets lie in His name and will face judgment, while Jerusalem suffers greatly from sword and famine due to the people's sins.

Jeremiah prays to God, pleading for help as Judah faces disaster, but God declares the people's unfaithfulness and rejects their prayers, warning Jeremiah not to pray for their welfare despite false prophets promising peace.

Jeremiah warns Judah's leaders and people to humble themselves and honor God before disaster strikes, predicting captivity by northern enemies due to their pride and sins, continuing his message of judgment and urging repentance.

God speaks to Jeremiah, using the ruined linen girdle as a symbol of Judah's pride and disobedience; despite God's closeness to Israel and Judah, they reject Him, so He warns of judgment and destruction upon all, including leaders in Jerusalem.

God instructs Jeremiah to use a linen girdle as a symbol, hiding it by the Euphrates and later finding it ruined, illustrating how God will ruin Judah and Jerusalem for their pride and idolatry. Jeremiah obeys God's commands in this prophetic act.

God, speaking through Jeremiah, warns Jerusalem that their persistent sins and unfaithfulness have exposed them to judgment and scattering, emphasizing that just as natural traits cannot change, their evil ways will not suddenly become good.
God speaks to Jeremiah, promising restoration and protection if he remains faithful, assuring him that despite opposition from the people of Judah, God will save and redeem him from their enemies.

Jeremiah conveys God's sorrow over Judah's suffering from war and famine, pleading for mercy despite their sins. The people acknowledge their guilt and appeal to God, the true source of rain, to restore them in Jerusalem.

God declares judgment on Judah for their sins, promising exile and loss of wealth. Jeremiah pleads for God's remembrance amid suffering, affirming his faithfulness. God responds, offering restoration if Jeremiah remains faithful and separates the righteous from the wicked.

God speaks to Jeremiah, expressing frustration with Judah's unfaithfulness and announcing judgment through destruction and suffering, yet also promising eventual well-being for the faithful remnant despite ongoing conflict and hardship.

God speaks to Jeremiah, declaring that even great leaders like Moses and Samuel cannot save Judah; He announces judgment through death, exile, and destruction because of Jerusalem's sins, especially those of King Manasseh.

God commands Jeremiah not to marry or have children in Jerusalem, foretelling severe judgment where many will die violently without mourning or burial, signaling the loss of peace and mercy for the people due to their sins.

Jeremiah speaks God's message to the people of Judah, explaining their exile is due to their and their ancestors' idolatry and disobedience, but God promises future restoration by bringing them back from exile to their ancestral land.
God commands Jeremiah not to mourn or celebrate with the people in Jerusalem, signaling coming judgment. When Jeremiah shares this, the people will question why such disaster is declared upon them.

Jeremiah speaks about trusting in the LORD as a source of strength and blessing, contrasts deceitful hearts with God's judgment, and prays for healing amid doubts from people in Judah questioning God's word.

God commands the people of Jerusalem through Jeremiah to honor the Sabbath by not carrying burdens or working, warning that obedience will bring lasting peace and royal presence, but disobedience will bring destruction to the city.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns Judah's deep-rooted sin and warns of exile and destruction for their idolatry, contrasting those who trust in humans with those who trust in the LORD, promising blessing for the faithful.
God speaks to Jeremiah in Judah, showing him a potter reshaping clay to illustrate God's control over Israel and other nations, warning that their fate depends on their actions and obedience to Him.

Jeremiah responds to people demanding God's word, affirming his faithful role as prophet despite persecution. God commands him to warn Judah's kings and people in Jerusalem to honor the Sabbath by ceasing all work and burdens on that day.

God speaks to Jeremiah, warning Judah and Jerusalem that if they disobey, He will withdraw blessings and bring disaster. Despite this, the people reject hope and continue in sin, causing their land to become desolate and scorned.

Jeremiah warns that Israel's land will become desolate and its people scattered by enemies. Despite plots by priests and leaders to silence him, Jeremiah prays for God's justice against those who seek his harm in Jerusalem.

God commands Jeremiah to take leaders and priests to the valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem's east gate to warn the people of Judah about coming disaster due to their idolatry and child sacrifice, predicting the valley will be renamed "Valley of Slaughter."

Jeremiah struggles with his prophetic mission amid mockery and threats in Jerusalem, feeling burdened yet compelled to speak God's words. He prays for justice and laments his birth, expressing deep personal anguish over his calling.

God speaks through Jeremiah, promising to restore Israel from exile despite their sins, warning of judgment, and declaring that even Gentiles will recognize God's power and the futility of idols. This follows warnings of judgment on Judah.

Jeremiah laments his birth and the suffering he endures as a prophet in Jerusalem, expressing deep anguish over his calling and the hardships it brings after Pashur, a temple official, punished him for his prophecies.

God, speaking through Jeremiah in Jerusalem near the valley of Hinnom, warns that the city will face devastating destruction and famine, symbolized by breaking a potter’s vessel, because of their idolatry and violence.

God commands Jeremiah to declare that Jerusalem and its people will be destroyed like a broken pot, defiled for their idolatry. Jeremiah returns from the Valley of Hinnom and warns the people in the temple courtyard of coming judgment.

Pashur, chief governor at the temple in Jerusalem, punishes Jeremiah for his prophecies. Jeremiah warns Pashur that he and Judah will face terror and captivity by Babylon, who will plunder the city's treasures.

Jeremiah warns Pashur, a priest in Jerusalem, that the city's treasures and people will be taken captive by Babylon. Despite feeling mocked and conflicted, Jeremiah cannot stop proclaiming God's message.

King Zedekiah of Judah sends Pashur and Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to pray for relief from Babylon's siege. Jeremiah delivers God's message that He will turn their weapons inward, fighting them with anger and causing a deadly plague in Jerusalem.

God, through Jeremiah, warns King Zedekiah and Jerusalem's people that a deadly plague will strike the city, followed by Babylonian conquest and destruction, offering a choice between death inside the city or life by surrendering to Babylon.

God commands Jeremiah to deliver a message to the king of Judah and his people in Jerusalem, urging them to act justly and protect the vulnerable. If they obey, their kingdom will thrive; if not, destruction and desolation will come.

God, speaking through Jeremiah to King Zedekiah's house in Jerusalem, warns that the city will be handed to Babylon and destroyed by fire due to their evil deeds, urging justice to prevent unstoppable divine wrath.

God warns Judah through Jeremiah that foreign armies will destroy the city and its prized cedars because the people abandoned God's covenant. He announces that King Shallum (Jehoahaz) will die in exile and condemns those who build grand homes through injustice.

God condemns false prophets in Samaria and Jerusalem for leading Israel astray with lies and immoral behavior, warning that their deceit will bring judgment and urging the people not to trust their false promises of peace.

God promises a future righteous king from David's line who will bring safety to Judah and Israel, shifting their deliverance from Egypt to exile return. Jeremiah laments corrupt prophets and priests causing moral decay and impending judgment on them.

God condemns the leaders ("pastors") of Israel for neglecting and scattering His people, promising to punish them but also to restore and protect the faithful remnant. He foretells raising a righteous king from David's line to bring justice and safety to Judah and Israel.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns King Jehoiakim of Judah for selfishness and injustice, contrasting him with his righteous father Josiah, and predicts a dishonorable death and destruction of his allies due to his persistent disobedience.

God condemns King Coniah (Jeconiah), son of Jehoiakim of Judah, for disobedience and announces his exile to Babylon, declaring his descendants will not prosper on David's throne, linking to prior warnings of judgment on Judah's kings.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns false prophets in Judah who claim to speak in His name but spread lies and deceit, misleading the people with false dreams and stolen words, contrasting their falsehood with His powerful, true word.

God condemns false prophets in Judah who falsely promise peace to those who reject Him, warning of coming judgment. He declares He sees all and has not sent these prophets, who speak lies from their own hearts.

God shows Jeremiah a vision of two baskets of figs after King Nebuchadnezzar exiled Jeconiah and others to Babylon; the good figs represent the exiles whom God will watch over and restore to their land.

God condemns false prophets who mislead people with lies and dreams they did not receive from Him, warning Jeremiah to tell others that God's message will no longer be proclaimed due to widespread corruption among prophets, priests, and people.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns false prophets in Jerusalem who misuse His words, warning they will be forgotten, forsaken, and shamed, along with the city given to their ancestors, for falsely claiming to speak the LORD's burden.

God speaks to Jeremiah, promising restoration and blessing for the exiled people in Babylon, while condemning King Zedekiah, remaining Jerusalem residents, and Egyptians to exile and destruction as consequences of their disobedience.
Jeremiah, speaking for the LORD, declares that many nations—including Jerusalem, Judah, Egypt, and surrounding kingdoms—will suffer devastation and madness due to coming war and judgment sent by God.

God tells Jeremiah that after 70 years of Babylonian exile, He will punish Babylon for its sins, fulfilling Jeremiah's prophecies against nations. Jeremiah is commanded to symbolize God's wrath by making nations drink a cup of fury.

Jeremiah addresses the people of Judah and Jerusalem in Jehoiakim's fourth year, reminding them that God sent prophets for years urging them to repent and worship only Him, but they have ignored these warnings and continued in sin.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Judah that because they ignored His commands, He will use Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to destroy the land and its neighbors, causing desolation for seventy years before punishing Babylon for its sins.

Jeremiah delivers God's message to many kings and nations, warning them they will face judgment and destruction like a cup of wrath they must drink. God declares He will bring punishment starting with Jerusalem, His own city.

Jeremiah, speaking God's judgment, warns all nations of a worldwide disaster and divine punishment. He describes the coming destruction and the helplessness of leaders ("shepherds") as God's anger brings widespread death and desolation.

Jeremiah warns that Judah’s leaders ("shepherds") will be trapped and suffer as God punishes the land for their sins, leaving it desolate under the harsh rule of oppressors, continuing the prophecy of judgment against Jerusalem and its rulers.

At the start of King Jehoiakim's reign in Judah, God commands Jeremiah to deliver a warning to all worshippers in the temple, urging them to repent or face destruction like Shiloh; priests, prophets, and people hear his message.

Jeremiah delivers God's warning in the temple in Jerusalem during King Jehoiakim's reign. After speaking, priests, prophets, and people accuse him of prophesying doom and demand his death, confronting the city’s leaders at the temple gate.

Jeremiah defends his prophecy before Judah's leaders and people, urging them to repent so God may relent. Despite threats, the princes and people declare Jeremiah not guilty of deserving death for speaking God's words.

In Jerusalem, the princes and people defend Jeremiah, citing past prophets Micah and Urijah who warned of destruction but were not killed, urging caution to avoid bringing harm upon themselves by killing Jeremiah.

Urijah, a prophet from Kirjathjearim, spoke against Jerusalem and Judah like Jeremiah. King Jehoiakim sought to kill him, so Urijah fled to Egypt, but was captured and killed. Meanwhile, Ahikam protected Jeremiah from a similar fate.

At the start of King Jehoiakim's reign in Judah, God commands Jeremiah to make yokes and send them to neighboring kings, declaring that God has given their lands to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, who will rule over many nations for generations.

Jeremiah warns the priests and people of Jerusalem not to trust prophets claiming the temple vessels will soon return from Babylon, urging them instead to submit to Babylon’s king to avoid destruction, and challenges false prophets to pray for the remaining sacred items.

God, speaking through Jeremiah early in King Jehoiakim's reign in Judah, warns that all nations must submit to Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar, punishing those who resist and exposing false prophets who claim otherwise.

Jeremiah delivers God's message that the remaining sacred vessels in Jerusalem, not taken by Nebuchadnezzar during Jeconiah's exile, will also be taken to Babylon and kept there until God decides to restore them.

In Jerusalem's temple, early in King Zedekiah's reign, Hananiah of Gibeon prophesies peace, claiming God will free Judah from Babylon and restore the temple vessels and captives soon; Jeremiah initially agrees publicly.

In Jerusalem's temple, Hananiah proclaims God's promise to end Babylon's control and restore captives and temple vessels soon. Jeremiah initially agrees but warns that true prophets' words must come true to be trusted.

Jeremiah sends a letter from Jerusalem to the Jewish exiles in Babylon, delivered by Elasah and Gemariah, urging them to settle down, build homes, and start families despite their captivity under Nebuchadnezzar's rule.

Jeremiah sends a letter from Jerusalem to the Jewish exiles in Babylon, urging them to settle, marry, and seek the city's peace. He warns against false prophets and promises God will restore them after seventy years.

Hananiah boldly proclaims Babylon's yoke will be broken in two years, breaking Jeremiah's wooden yoke. God then tells Jeremiah to warn Hananiah he falsely promises freedom; instead, iron yokes await, and Hananiah dies that same year for his false prophecy.

God promises the exiled people in Babylon that if they sincerely seek Him, He will end their captivity and gather them back to Jerusalem. He warns that those remaining in Jerusalem will face severe judgment for their evil.

Jeremiah delivers God's message to King Zedekiah and the people of Judah, urging them to submit to Babylon's king to survive, warning against false prophets who claim they won't serve Babylon or that temple vessels will soon return from exile.

God warns the exiled people in Babylon that those left in Jerusalem will face sword, famine, and disease because they ignored His prophets' warnings, leading to their scattering among nations as a disgrace.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns false prophets Ahab and Zedekiah in Babylon who mislead the exiles with lies, warning they will be executed by King Nebuchadnezzar as punishment for their deceit and immoral actions in Israel.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns false prophets in Jerusalem like Shemaiah who oppose Jeremiah's true message to the exiles in Babylon, highlighting their deceit and failure to rebuke Jeremiah’s counsel about the long captivity.

Zephaniah the priest reads a letter to Jeremiah in Jerusalem, then God commands Jeremiah to warn the exiles in Babylon that Shemaiah the Nehelamite falsely prophesied and will be punished for leading people astray.

God speaks to Israel (Jacob), promising restoration and a future king like David, while acknowledging their suffering and punishment due to their sins, assuring they will not be destroyed but corrected and ultimately saved from exile.

God speaks to Israel, promising restoration and love for the survivors of war. He envisions rebuilding Israel, joyful celebrations, and a future gathering of the people from Samaria and Ephraim to Zion, praising the Lord.

God speaks to Jeremiah, instructing him to record His words about the future restoration of Israel and Judah from captivity. God describes a time of great distress called Jacob’s trouble, but promises deliverance and freedom from foreign oppression.

God promises to gather the scattered people of Israel, including the vulnerable, from distant lands and lead them safely back. He calls for joyful praise and declares His protection and redemption over Israel and Ephraim.

God speaks to Jeremiah, promising restoration for Israel and Judah after captivity, with their leaders arising from among themselves. God warns of judgment on the wicked and affirms His enduring commitment to His people.

God speaks to Israel, explaining that their suffering is due to their sins but promises to punish their enemies, restore their health, bring them back from captivity, rebuild their cities, and bless their future generations.

God promises to redeem Israel (Jacob) from captivity, bringing them joy and abundance in Zion. Despite past sorrow symbolized by Rachel's weeping at Ramah, God assures comfort and restoration as the exiles return home.

God speaks to Israel, expressing hope for their return and repentance after punishment. Ephraim (representing Israel) acknowledges God's discipline and seeks restoration. God promises mercy and urges Israel to return to their cities, highlighting a new, mysterious event.

God speaks through Jeremiah, promising restoration for Israel and Judah after exile, describing a new era of blessing and justice in their land, where past judgments will be replaced by care and growth.

God promises a new covenant with Israel where all will know Him personally, forgiving their sins. He assures Israel's enduring nationhood and foretells Jerusalem's future restoration and holiness, with specific landmarks named around the city.

During the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem, the prophet Jeremiah is imprisoned by King Zedekiah for prophesying the city's fall. God tells Jeremiah that his cousin Hanameel will offer to sell him a field in Anathoth, affirming Jeremiah's right to buy it.

While imprisoned in Jerusalem during Babylon's siege, Jeremiah follows God's command to buy a field from his cousin Hanameel in Anathoth, completing the legal purchase with witnesses and documentation despite the city's impending capture.

God promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, where each person is responsible for their own sins. Unlike the old covenant broken by their ancestors, God's law will be written on their hearts, and all will know Him personally.

Jeremiah, imprisoned in Jerusalem during Babylon's siege, hands Baruch the deed for a field he bought in Anathoth, then prays, praising God's power and recalling His past wonders in Egypt and deliverance of Israel.

God condemns Judah's idolatry and child sacrifice in the valley of Hinnom, then promises to restore the exiled people, bring them back to Jerusalem, make them His people, and establish an everlasting covenant with them.

Jeremiah, imprisoned in Jerusalem during Babylon's siege, gives the deed of a purchased field to his scribe Baruch, instructing him to preserve it as a sign that the land will be restored to the people in the future.

God declares through Jeremiah that Jerusalem will be captured and burned by Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans because of the persistent evil and idolatry of Israel and Judah’s leaders and people, provoking His anger from the city's founding.

Jeremiah recalls God's deliverance of Israel from Egypt and their disobedience, leading to Jerusalem's siege by the Chaldeans. God commands Jeremiah to buy a field as a sign, affirming His power over all things despite the city's fall.

Jeremiah condemns the people of Israel and Judah, including their leaders and priests, for turning away from God, defiling His temple, and practicing idolatry and child sacrifice in Jerusalem, despite God's repeated teachings.

God promises the people of Judah an everlasting covenant and restoration after exile, assuring them they will return to their land, buy fields, and live safely despite the current desolation caused by the Chaldeans' conquest.

While imprisoned in Jerusalem, Jeremiah receives a second message from God promising restoration and healing for the city and its people, despite the destruction caused by the Chaldeans and their captivity.

God speaks to Jeremiah in prison, promising restoration and joy in Jerusalem and Judah after captivity, with shepherds tending flocks again. He foretells a righteous descendant of David who will rule justly over Israel and Judah.

God speaks to Jeremiah in prison, promising a future righteous leader from David's line who will bring justice and safety to Judah and Jerusalem, assuring an unbroken covenant with David's descendants and the Levitical priests.
God speaks to Jeremiah from prison, promising to forgive Israel's sins and restore joy and worship in desolate Jerusalem and Judah, reversing their exile by bringing the captives back to their land.

God reassures Jeremiah in prison that He will greatly multiply David's descendants and Levite priests despite the people's doubt that God has rejected Israel and Judah, promising to restore their captivity and show mercy.

Jeremiah reports God's message to Judah's leaders who initially freed their Hebrew servants as promised but then re-enslaved them, breaking the covenant God made with their ancestors about freeing servants every seven years.

Jeremiah delivers God's message to King Zedekiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem and Judah's remaining cities. Zedekiah had made a covenant freeing Hebrew servants, and the people initially obeyed by releasing them.

God speaks to Jeremiah during Babylon's siege of Jerusalem, instructing him to warn King Zedekiah that the city will be handed to Nebuchadnezzar, who will capture him and take him to Babylon, though he will die peacefully, not by the sword.

God, through Jeremiah, reminds the people of Judah their ancestors disobeyed the law to free Hebrew servants every seven years. Though they initially obeyed Zedekiah's recent covenant to free servants, they reversed it, breaking God's command and facing exile and disaster.

God, through Jeremiah, warns King Zedekiah and Judah's leaders that because they broke their covenant by re-enslaving freed Hebrew servants, they will face destruction by sword, famine, and exile by Babylon's army.

During King Jehoiakim's reign, God instructs Jeremiah to bring the Rechabites into the temple and offer them wine, but they refuse, explaining their ancestor Jonadab's command to avoid wine and live nomadically in tents.

Jeremiah speaks to the Rechabites, who explain their ancestor Jonadab's command to live simply in tents and avoid wine or farming. They obeyed faithfully, but fled to Jerusalem when Babylon and Syria threatened Judah. God then challenges Judah to listen.

God, speaking through Jeremiah during King Jehoiakim's reign, contrasts the Rechabites' obedience to their ancestor Jonadab's commands with Judah and Jerusalem's refusal to listen to God's prophets and repent.

God, through Jeremiah in Jerusalem during King Jehoiakim's reign, contrasts the Rechabites' obedience to their ancestor Jonadab's commands with Judah's disobedience to God's prophets, warning of coming judgment but promising lasting honor to Jonadab's line.

Baruch reads Jeremiah's prophecies aloud to the people at the temple in Jerusalem. Michaiah hears the words, reports them to the king's princes, who then summon Baruch to read the scroll again before them.

Jeremiah instructs Baruch to publicly read God's warnings from a scroll during a fast in Jerusalem, hoping the people of Judah will repent. Baruch obeys, reading the words in the temple before the gathered crowd.

After King Jehoiakim of Judah burned Jeremiah's scroll with God's warnings, God commands Jeremiah to rewrite the message, including new words, reaffirming judgment on Jehoiakim and Judah for ignoring God's warnings.

King Jehoiakim of Judah burns the scroll containing Jeremiah's prophecies read by Jehudi, ignoring pleas to spare it. He orders Baruch and Jeremiah arrested, but God hides them. God then commands Jeremiah to rewrite the burned scroll.

In Judah under King Jehoiakim, God commands Jeremiah to have Baruch write down all His messages since King Josiah's reign, hoping Judah will repent. Jeremiah, unable to enter the temple, instructs Baruch to read the scroll publicly on a fasting day.

Baruch reads Jeremiah's written prophecy to the princes in Jerusalem, who fear the message and plan to inform King Jehoiakim. They hide Baruch and Jeremiah, then present the scroll to the king, who listens while seated by a fire in his winterhouse.

King Zedekiah rules Judah after Coniah, but he and the people ignore Jeremiah's warnings. Zedekiah sends officials to ask Jeremiah to pray. Pharaoh's army arrives from Egypt, causing the Chaldeans to temporarily lift their siege of Jerusalem.

God warns King Zedekiah through Jeremiah that the Chaldeans will return to besiege and burn Jerusalem despite their temporary retreat due to Pharaoh's army. Jeremiah is then accused of siding with the Chaldeans and arrested by Irijah, a captain in Benjamin.

Jeremiah warns Jerusalem's leaders that staying in the city means death by sword, famine, or plague, but surrendering to Babylon means life. The princes accuse him of weakening morale, so King Zedekiah allows them to imprison Jeremiah in a muddy dungeon.

Jeremiah denies defecting to the Chaldeans but is arrested by Irijah and imprisoned by the princes in Jerusalem. King Zedekiah secretly questions him, learns of his prophecy of Babylonian capture, and confines him with daily bread in prison.

Ebedmelech rescues Jeremiah from a muddy dungeon using rags for support, then Jeremiah is brought before King Zedekiah in the temple. The king promises not to harm Jeremiah if he speaks openly, showing a tense trust between them in Jerusalem.

King Zedekiah secretly instructs Jeremiah to keep their conversation private and gives him a cover story if questioned by the princes. Jeremiah follows the king's command and remains imprisoned until Jerusalem falls to Babylon.

Jeremiah urges King Zedekiah of Judah to obey God's command to surrender to Babylon to save his life and family, warning of capture and destruction if he refuses. Zedekiah secretly promises Jeremiah safety and secrecy.

Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy dungeon by officials opposing his prophecies in Jerusalem. Ebedmelech, a eunuch in King Zedekiah’s court, pleads for Jeremiah’s rescue, and the king orders Jeremiah to be lifted out before he dies.

King Zedekiah secretly promises Jeremiah he won't be killed, then Jeremiah relays God's warning that if Zedekiah surrenders to Babylon, he and Jerusalem will survive; Zedekiah fears betrayal, but Jeremiah urges obedience to God's word for safety.

Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem during King Zedekiah's reign, capturing the city after two years. Zedekiah flees but is caught at Jericho; his sons and nobles are executed before him at Riblah.

Nebuchadnezzar orders Jeremiah's protection; Babylonian officials release him from prison to live with the people. While imprisoned, Jeremiah receives God's message to assure Ebedmelech of safety despite the coming destruction of Jerusalem.

After capturing Zedekiah, Nebuchadnezzar executed his sons and nobles, blinded and imprisoned Zedekiah, and destroyed Jerusalem. Nebuzaradan took captives but spared the poor, and the king ordered Jeremiah to be protected and treated well.

After Jerusalem's fall, Nebuzaradan frees Jeremiah from chains at Ramah, explaining God's judgment on the city for their sins, and offers Jeremiah freedom to choose whether to go to Babylon or stay in the land.

Nebuzaradan, Babylon's captain, frees Jeremiah from chains and offers him a choice to go to Babylon or stay in Judah. Jeremiah chooses to live with Gedaliah, the Babylon-appointed governor, at Mizpah among the remaining people.

Gedaliah, appointed governor by Babylon, stays at Mizpah and urges others to live in their cities and gather food. Jews scattered abroad return to Judah, but military leaders warn Gedaliah of a plot by Ishmael sent by the Ammonite king Baalis, which Gedaliah doubts.

After Babylon's conquest, Jeremiah stays with Gedaliah, the Babylon-appointed governor at Mizpah. Local military leaders come to Gedaliah, who assures them safety if they serve Babylon and encourages them to live peacefully in their towns.
Johanan warns Gedaliah at Mizpah that Baalis, king of the Ammonites, sent Ishmael to kill him, and offers to kill Ishmael first. Gedaliah refuses, believing Johanan's claim about Ishmael is false.
Ishmael, a royal descendant, and ten men visit Gedaliah in Mizpah, then kill him and his supporters. The next day, Ishmael deceitfully lures 80 mourners from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria to Gedaliah.

Ishmael, sent by Baalis the Ammonite king, deceitfully lures a group to Mizpah, then kills them and imprisons the remaining people, including royal family, before fleeing toward the Ammonites, escalating conflict after Gedaliah's murder.

Jeremiah delivers God's warning to the remnant of Judah, urging them to stay in their land for mercy and restoration, but warns that fleeing to Egypt to escape war and famine will bring death by sword, famine, and disease.

Johanan, Jezaniah, and the remaining people of Judah approach Jeremiah, asking him to pray to God for guidance. They promise to obey whatever God instructs through Jeremiah, seeking direction after fleeing from Babylonian threats.

Johanan and the people promise to obey God's guidance through Jeremiah. After ten days, Jeremiah delivers God's message urging them to stay in their land, promising protection from Babylon and restoration if they remain faithful.

After Ishmael killed Gedaliah in Mizpah, he captured the remaining people, including the king’s daughters, and fled toward the Ammonites. Johanan and his commanders pursued Ishmael, recovered the captives, but Ishmael escaped with eight men to Ammon.

After Ishmael kills Gedaliah and flees to the Ammonites, Johanan rescues the remaining people from Mizpah and leads them to Chimham near Bethlehem, planning to go to Egypt due to fear of the Babylonian Chaldeans.

Jeremiah warns the remnant of Judah, led by Johanan, that if they go to Egypt to escape Babylonian threats, they will face death by sword, famine, and disease, because they have not obeyed God's command to stay in Judah.

After Jeremiah delivers God's message warning against fleeing to Egypt, Azariah, Johanan, and others reject him, accusing Baruch of misleading them. Despite God's command, Johanan leads the remnant of Judah, including royal family members and Jeremiah, to Egypt.

Johanan and the remnant of Judah, including Jeremiah and Baruch, disobey God's command and flee to Egypt, settling in Tahpanhes. There, God instructs Jeremiah to hide stones as a sign that Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt.

God, speaking through Jeremiah in Egypt at Tahpanhes, warns that King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon will conquer Egypt, punish its people, destroy their idols, and carry captives away, fulfilling judgment despite the people's disobedience.
God speaks to Jeremiah about the Jews living in Egyptian cities like Migdol and Tahpanhes, reminding them of the destruction in Jerusalem caused by their idolatry despite prophetic warnings.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns the people of Judah living in Egypt for continuing idolatry despite Jerusalem's destruction, warning that their unrepentant sins bring judgment and desolation upon them and their descendants.

God warns through Jeremiah that the Judahite exiles in Egypt will not survive or return home, but the people in Pathros refuse to listen and insist on continuing their worship of the "queen of heaven," linking it to past prosperity.

God, through Jeremiah, warns the unrepentant people of Judah living in Egypt that they will face destruction by sword and famine, just as Jerusalem was punished, and only a few survivors will return to Judah.

In Egypt, the Jewish people defend their worship of the "queen of heaven," blaming their hardships on stopping it, while Jeremiah rebukes them, reminding them that their idolatry caused God's judgment and the desolation of Judah's land.

God, through Jeremiah, warns the Jews living in Egypt that despite their vows to worship the "queen of heaven," He will bring disaster upon them, with most dying by sword and famine, though a few will return to Judah to see whose prophecy is true.

Jeremiah speaks to Baruch, his scribe, during King Jehoiakim's reign in Judah, responding to Baruch's distress by conveying God's message of coming destruction on the land but promising to preserve Baruch's life amid widespread disaster.

God, speaking through Jeremiah to the Jews living in Egypt, warns that only a few will survive and return to Judah, and predicts Pharaoh Hophra's downfall, paralleling King Zedekiah's fate under Babylonian attack.

Jeremiah speaks to the Jewish exiles in Egypt, condemning their idolatry and disobedience to God, explaining that their land is desolate because of their sins, and warning them they are determined to continue worshiping the "queen of heaven" despite God's judgment.

God speaks through Jeremiah, announcing judgment against Egypt and Pharaoh Necho's army defeated by Babylon's Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish near the Euphrates during King Jehoiakim's reign. Egypt prepares for battle but is fearful and will fall.

God speaks through Jeremiah, announcing that Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon will attack Egypt. Cities like Migdol, Noph, and Tahpanhes are warned to prepare for destruction and captivity as Egypt faces defeat from the north.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Egypt—led by Pharaoh Necho and allied with Ethiopians, Libyans, and Lydians—that despite their military might, Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon will defeat them near the Euphrates, bringing judgment and defeat.

God speaks through Jeremiah, warning the Philistines of an impending attack from the north before Pharaoh's assault on Gaza, predicting destruction of their cities and allies like Tyre and Sidon, and urging the divine "sword" to carry out judgment.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Moab of coming destruction and exile due to their pride and false trust in their gods. Moab's cities will be deserted, their warriors defeated, and their confidence shattered, signaling imminent calamity.

God, through Jeremiah, pronounces judgment on Moab's cities like Nebo and Kiriathaim, warning of destruction and captivity because of their pride and false trust, urging Moab to flee as all their lands will be devastated.

God, through Jeremiah, announces Moab's destruction and calls its people to mourn as their cities, including Dibon and Aroer, fall. Moab's pride and mockery of Israel lead to its downfall and shame among neighboring nations.

God declares that Egypt will be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, but reassures Israel (Jacob) that despite exile, they will be saved, restored, and protected, with nations punished but Israel corrected, not destroyed.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns Moab's pride and mocks their joy over Israel's misfortune, warning of coming destruction and urging Moabites to flee. The passage mourns the loss of Moab's prosperity and the devastation of its land and harvests.

God, through Jeremiah, pronounces Moab's complete destruction and shame for opposing Him, describing the fall of its cities like Kerioth and the capture of its people, but also promises future restoration after this judgment.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Egypt of coming destruction from the north by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, predicting defeat and captivity for Pharaoh and his allies, but promises the land will be inhabited again as before.

God, through Jeremiah, pronounces judgment on Moab, describing widespread mourning and destruction across its cities like Heshbon and Horonaim, with rituals ceasing and the people lamenting their downfall and shame.

God, speaking through Jeremiah, pronounces judgment on the Ammonites for their pride and occupation of Israelite lands, predicting war and captivity in Rabbah, their capital, but also promises eventual restoration for the Ammonite people.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Edom and its cities like Teman and Bozrah of coming destruction and exile, declaring their wisdom lost and promising judgment and desolation, while assuring preservation for the vulnerable among them.

God, through Jeremiah, declares judgment on Edom and its city Bozrah, predicting their destruction and desolation like Sodom, due to their pride and violence, with enemies gathering against them for battle.

God, through Jeremiah, pronounces judgment on Edom, comparing its destruction to Sodom's fall and describing a sudden attack from the Jordan region; nearby cities Hamath and Arpad are also troubled by bad news, causing fear and unrest.

God, speaking through Jeremiah, declares judgment on Elam, promising to scatter its people across nations and bring destruction to its leaders, but also foretells a future restoration of Elam's captivity in the latter days.

Jeremiah prophesies God's judgment on Babylon, describing its sudden capture and destruction due to its pride and opposition to God. He calls for nations to attack Babylon and punish it for its sins against Israel and the LORD.

God, through Jeremiah, condemns Israel's leaders for leading His people astray, warns the exiles in Babylon to flee, and prophesies a northern coalition will conquer Babylon, leaving it desolate and ashamed for its pride and oppression.

God, through Jeremiah, pronounces judgment on Babylon, declaring it will become a desolate wilderness due to its sins. He calls nations to attack Babylon, while recalling Israel's past exile under Assyria and Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar.

God, through Jeremiah, warns the people of Hazor to flee as King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon plans to attack and scatter them, making Hazor desolate; then shifts to prophesy against Elam, predicting its defeat and exile during King Zedekiah's reign.

Jeremiah prophesies God's judgment on Babylon and the Chaldeans, announcing their coming destruction by a northern nation. He foretells Israel and Judah's return to seek God, lamenting their past wandering and lost guidance.

God, through Jeremiah, commands nations to surround and attack proud Babylon for oppressing Israel and Judah, declaring judgment on its people and leaders, promising deliverance for Israel and punishment for Babylon’s rulers and wise men.

Jeremiah prophesies God's judgment on Babylon for oppressing Israel, promising Israel's restoration to their land. He commands destruction of Babylon's territories Merathaim and Pekod, describing the coming battle and Babylon's downfall.

God, through Jeremiah, warns Damascus and nearby cities Hamath and Arpad of coming destruction and fear, with young warriors falling and palaces burning. He also announces Nebuchadnezzar's planned attack on Kedar and Hazor, urging them to flee.

God, through Jeremiah, pronounces judgment on Babylon and the Chaldeans, declaring their destruction and desolation like Sodom; a powerful northern nation will rise against them, signaling Babylon's downfall and exile of its people.

God declares judgment against Babylon, promising to raise enemies to destroy it and urging Israel and Judah to flee for safety. Babylon, once powerful and corrupt, will suddenly fall and suffer great devastation.

The LORD, through Jeremiah, predicts a powerful northern nation with many kings will attack Babylon, causing fear in its king. God declares His sovereign control over the timing and outcome of Babylon's downfall, which will shake the earth and be known among nations.

God declares Israel as His chosen instrument to punish Babylon and its leaders for their wrongs against Zion, promising to destroy their power and make Babylon a desolate, burnt mountain. This follows earlier prophecies of Babylon’s downfall.

God declares Babylon's sudden fall and destruction, urging mourning and abandonment as its judgment reaches heaven. He calls Zion to proclaim His work and announces the Medes' kings rising to execute His vengeance against Babylon's wealth and pride.

God declares judgment against Babylon, promising to destroy its land and cities, making it desolate and uninhabited. This prophecy follows warnings of Babylon's fall and calls for God's vengeance on the city and its idols.

God declares Babylon's warriors have lost courage and their city is besieged; He compares Babylon to a threshing floor about to be harvested. Jeremiah expresses personal suffering under Nebuchadnezzar, and God promises to avenge Jerusalem by drying Babylon's resources.

God declares His power as Creator and Judge, promising to overwhelm Babylon with invading forces. He contrasts the living God with lifeless idols, affirming Israel's unique role as His chosen people and inheritance.

God declares judgment on Babylon and its idol Bel, warning His people to flee the city to escape His wrath. He foretells ongoing conflict and destruction, urging survivors to remember Jerusalem as Babylon faces ruin from northern invaders.

Jeremiah urges survivors of Babylon's attack to flee and remember Jerusalem, lamenting the desecration of God's sanctuary. He prophesies God's judgment on Babylon's idols and declares that despite its strength, Babylon will face destruction by God's hand.
God declares the fall of Babylon, its leaders defeated and walls destroyed. Jeremiah instructs Seraiah, a prince with King Zedekiah in Babylon, to record these prophecies of Babylon's doom in a book.

God declares judgment against Babylon, calling it a destructive mountain to be destroyed completely. He summons nations including Ararat, Minni, Ashchenaz, and the Medes to prepare for battle, predicting Babylon's desolation and defeat.

This passage introduces King Zedekiah's reign in Jerusalem, noting his evil actions and rebellion against Babylon. It describes Nebuchadnezzar's siege of Jerusalem, the resulting famine, and the escape of the city's warriors by night.

King Zedekiah and his soldiers flee Jerusalem at night during the Babylonian siege, but the Chaldean army captures him near Jericho. Nebuchadnezzar judges Zedekiah at Riblah, executes his sons and princes, blinds him, and imprisons him in Babylon.

Jeremiah records all the prophecies against Babylon in a book and instructs Seraiah, a prince, to read it aloud in Babylon, then throw it into the Euphrates as a symbol of Babylon's inevitable destruction and desolation.

After Jerusalem's fall, Nebuzaradan spared some poor people as farmers but destroyed and took the temple's large bronze pillars and vessels, crafted by Solomon, to Babylon as spoils of war, marking the temple's desecration.

The city of Jerusalem mourns its destruction and desolation after being conquered; its people, priests, and leaders suffer captivity and betrayal, reflecting the consequences of their sins and the Lord's judgment.

After 37 years in Babylonian captivity, King Evilmerodach of Babylon released Jehoiachin from prison, honored him with a throne above other captive kings, and provided for him generously until his death.

Nebuzaradan, Babylon's captain, brings captured Judah leaders to King Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, where they are executed. The passage lists Jewish captives taken over years and ends with Jehoiachin's release from Babylonian prison by King Evilmerodach.

After capturing King Zedekiah, Nebuchadnezzar blinded and imprisoned him. Then Nebuzaradan, Babylon's captain, entered Jerusalem, burned the temple, royal and noble houses, destroyed the city walls, and took many captives, sparing only some poor for farming.

The speaker, representing Jerusalem (Zion), laments her desolation and captivity as enemies surround her. She mourns the loss of comfort and the death of leaders, acknowledging God's judgment for her rebellion and pleading for justice against her foes.

The speaker laments Jerusalem's loss of beauty and strength after being conquered by enemies who mock her. The city, once honored, is now desolate, her people suffer hunger, and foreign nations have violated her sacred places.

The passage describes the detailed measurements of the two brass pillars from Solomon's temple, then shifts to Nebuzaradan, Babylon's captain, capturing key Jerusalem leaders and officials during the city's fall, taking them to King Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.

Jerusalem laments her suffering and desolation after the Babylonian conquest; her people are starving and broken, feeling abandoned by God and overwhelmed by enemies, with no comfort or relief in sight.

The speaker laments God's fierce anger against Jerusalem (the daughter of Zion) and Israel, describing how God has destroyed their homes, strongholds, and leaders, causing great mourning and loss in Judah after the city's fall.

The speaker mourns how God has turned against Israel and Judah, destroying their palaces, places of worship, and leadership, leading to deep mourning and loss of law and prophecy in Jerusalem (the daughter of Zion).

The prophet mourns Jerusalem's destruction: city gates and defenses ruined, leaders exiled, and religious guidance lost. Elders and virgins grieve openly, while children suffer and die in the streets, highlighting the city's deep devastation.

The speaker laments Jerusalem's destruction, acknowledging God's judgment fulfilled as enemies rejoice. They urge constant prayer and mourning for the city's suffering children and leaders, highlighting the total devastation and loss in Zion.

The speaker, likely the prophet Jeremiah, describes his deep suffering and despair under God's punishment, feeling trapped and attacked, continuing the lament over Jerusalem's destruction and personal affliction after the city's fall.

The speaker laments relentless suffering and persecution in Jerusalem, crying out to the LORD from a dungeon for deliverance and justice against enemies who oppress him without cause, trusting God to judge and avenge his plight.

The speaker reflects on God's justice, affirming He does not afflict people without cause, urging self-examination and repentance for Israel's sins amid suffering and enemies' attacks, expressing deep sorrow for Jerusalem's destruction.

The speaker laments Jerusalem's great destruction and failed prophets, noting how passersby mock the once-beautiful city. Enemies rejoice as God's judgment fulfills ancient warnings against Zion's sins.

The prophet describes the severe famine and suffering in Jerusalem, where people are starving and even resorting to desperate acts. The city's leaders are corrupt, and the LORD's anger has led to the city's destruction and exile.

The speaker laments Jerusalem's destruction, describing how once precious people and sacred stones are now ruined and starving, comparing the city's suffering to greater punishment than Sodom's fall, highlighting the severe famine and death among its inhabitants.

The speaker laments Jerusalem's destruction and exile, describing how priests and elders are rejected and the people are hunted and scattered. The passage also warns Edom of coming judgment, linking their fate to Jerusalem's.

The speaker reflects on deep suffering and despair but recalls God's unfailing mercy and faithfulness, expressing hope despite affliction. This personal lament follows the city's destruction and highlights trust in God's compassion amid hardship.

The people of Jerusalem lament their fallen status and desolation of Zion, expressing sorrow for their sins and pleading with the LORD to remember and restore them, while acknowledging God's enduring throne and their feeling of abandonment.

The people of Jerusalem lament their suffering after the city's destruction, describing loss, famine, oppression by foreign powers like Egypt and Assyria, and the breakdown of social order and joy due to their sins and exile.

Ezekiel, a priest among Jewish exiles by the Chebar River in Babylon during King Jehoiachin’s captivity, receives a divine vision featuring a fiery whirlwind and four extraordinary living creatures with multiple faces and wings.

Ezekiel, among exiles by the Chebar River, describes a vision of four living creatures with wheels beside them, symbolizing divine mobility and presence, continuing his detailed account of God's extraordinary appearance.

Ezekiel, among exiles by the Chebar River, describes a vision of four living creatures with multiple faces and wings moving straight without turning, accompanied by fiery appearances and a mysterious wheel beside them, symbolizing divine presence and movement.

God speaks to the prophet Ezekiel, empowering him to stand and deliver a message to the rebellious Israelites, warning him not to fear their resistance as he is sent to proclaim God's words despite their stubbornness.

God commands Ezekiel to eat a scroll symbolizing His message and to speak to the Israelites, who are stubborn and rebellious. Ezekiel is strengthened to face their resistance as he delivers God's words.

Ezekiel, among exiles by the Chebar River, describes a vision where living creatures and wheels move in unison, with a crystal-like firmament above them. Above this is a sapphire-like throne with a human-like figure, signaling a divine presence.

Ezekiel, among the exiles by the Chebar River, sees a vision of a sapphire-like throne above the creatures, with a fiery human figure symbolizing God's glory, causing him to fall and hear a voice, continuing his divine revelation.

God strengthens Ezekiel, telling him to boldly deliver His message to the rebellious Israelites in exile at Telabib by the river Chebar. The Spirit lifts Ezekiel, and he sits silently among the captives for seven days, overwhelmed and astonished.

Ezekiel, among the exiles at Telabib by the Chebar River, spends seven days in shock before God appoints him as a watchman for Israel, responsible for warning the wicked and righteous about their paths and consequences.

God speaks to Ezekiel, warning him about his role as a watchman for Israel, emphasizing the responsibility to warn both the wicked and the righteous. Ezekiel is then instructed to isolate himself, bound and silent, except when God commands him to speak to the rebellious people.

God commands Ezekiel to faithfully deliver His message to rebellious Israel despite their resistance, instructing him to accept and internalize God's words symbolized by eating a scroll containing lamentations and woes.

God tells Ezekiel that Israel will eat defiled food in exile among the Gentiles. Ezekiel protests his purity, but God commands him to bake bread using cow dung, symbolizing the coming scarcity and hardship in Jerusalem due to Israel's sins.

God commands Ezekiel to face Jerusalem and prophesy about its siege while being bound and restricted in movement. Ezekiel must eat measured, mixed grain bread baked over human dung, symbolizing Israel's defiled exile among foreign nations.

God speaks to Ezekiel about Jerusalem's great wickedness and disobedience compared to surrounding nations, announcing unprecedented judgment including internal strife and exile as punishment for their abominations.

God instructs Ezekiel to perform a symbolic act by cutting and dividing his hair to represent Jerusalem's fate during the siege, highlighting the city's rebellion and worsening sins compared to surrounding nations.

God speaks to Ezekiel, commanding him to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, declaring judgment and destruction of their altars and idols, but promising to preserve a remnant who will remember Him after exile.

God speaks to Ezekiel, warning Jerusalem of severe judgment for defiling His sanctuary, predicting famine, pestilence, sword, and exile that will scatter the people and make the city a disgrace among surrounding nations.

God speaks to Ezekiel, warning Jerusalem that He will bring severe judgment through famine, wild animals, disease, and sword, making the city a disgrace and warning to surrounding nations for their sins and defiance.
God speaks to Ezekiel, declaring that judgment and destruction have come upon all Israel for their sins, signaling an imminent day of trouble and divine wrath across the land.

God speaks through Ezekiel, warning Israel that although most will face destruction by sword, famine, and pestilence, a remnant will survive exile among nations and come to regret their idolatry and sins.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, declares that the people of Israel will face death by pestilence, sword, and famine, with their land made desolate and their idols surrounded by their slain, showing God's judgment on their idolatry and sin.

God speaks through Ezekiel, warning Israel that His fierce judgment and punishment for their sins and abominations will soon come, bringing destruction and no escape for the people despite their preparations.

Ezekiel, speaking God's judgment to Israel, describes a time of total disaster with war, famine, and disease. Despite warnings, the people fail to fight or repent, and their wealth and idols cannot save them from God's wrath.

God commands Ezekiel in Babylon to use a clay tablet to model Jerusalem's siege and to lie on his sides for 390 and 40 days, symbolizing Israel's and Judah's sins, preparing to prophesy against Jerusalem's coming siege.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, warns Israel that their sacred places and treasures will be defiled and taken by foreigners due to their violence and idolatry; destruction and chaos will come, leaders will mourn, and judgment will reveal God's authority.

Ezekiel sees six men with weapons and a man in linen near the altar as God's glory departs the temple. God commands the man in linen to mark the foreheads of those mourning Jerusalem's sins, signaling judgment on the city.

Ezekiel, guided by God's spirit, witnesses seventy Israelite elders, led by Jaazaniah, secretly worshipping idols and burning incense. He then sees women mourning Tammuz and men sun-worshipping at the temple in Jerusalem, revealing escalating abominations.

God shows Ezekiel a vision in Jerusalem where about twenty-five men in the temple courtyard are worshiping the sun, provoking God's anger due to Judah's violence and idolatry, leading to a declaration of coming judgment without mercy.

Ezekiel sees a sapphire-like throne above the cherubim. God commands the man in linen to take coals of fire from between the cherubim’s wheels to scatter over Jerusalem, as the LORD’s glory fills the temple and the cherubim’s wings sound like God’s voice.

God commands a man clothed in linen to mark the faithful in Jerusalem, while six others kill the rest, starting at the temple. Ezekiel laments the destruction, but God declares the city's great sin and insists on judgment without pity.

Ezekiel describes a vision where a man in linen is commanded to take fire from between the cherubim's wheels, which are complex, eye-covered, and move in unison, symbolizing divine presence and action in Jerusalem.

Ezekiel, with Judah's elders present, is seized by God's spirit and taken in a vision to Jerusalem's inner northern gate, where he sees the "image of jealousy" and the glory of God, continuing his prophetic revelations about Israel's idolatry.

Ezekiel describes the cherubim and their wheels, each with four faces and wings, moving in perfect unity. The glory of the LORD departs the temple, signaling divine judgment on Jerusalem, connecting to his earlier vision by the river Chebar.

Ezekiel, guided by God's spirit, is shown visions in Jerusalem revealing Israel's idolatry and abominations, including elders worshipping idols and burning incense secretly, highlighting their betrayal of God's sanctuary.

Ezekiel, speaking by God's Spirit at Jerusalem's east gate, warns leaders including Pelatiah of coming judgment and exile for their wickedness. Pelatiah dies as Ezekiel laments the fate of Israel's remnant.

God speaks to Ezekiel, explaining that though Israel is scattered among nations, He will gather them back to their land, cleanse them, and renew their hearts so they will follow His laws and be His people.

The Spirit takes Ezekiel to Jerusalem's east gate, where 25 men, including leaders Jaazaniah and Pelatiah, plot evil and falsely claim peace. God commands Ezekiel to prophesy judgment on them for their violence and fear of war.

God commands Ezekiel in Jerusalem to act out a symbolic removal by packing and carrying his belongings visibly, even digging through a wall, to warn rebellious Israel of their coming exile and captivity.

God promises to give the exiled Israelites a new heart to follow His laws, while punishing the unrepentant. Ezekiel sees God's glory depart Jerusalem, then is taken in a vision to the exiles in Chaldea to share God's message.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, warns that He will scatter the prince's allies and bring judgment on Jerusalem and Israel, leaving only a few survivors to witness the destruction caused by violence and desolation in the land.

God, speaking through Ezekiel in Babylonian exile, condemns false prophets in Israel who deceive the people with lies and false peace, warning their protective efforts like a poorly built wall will collapse under divine judgment.

God commands Ezekiel to condemn false prophets in Israel who speak from their own ideas, not His word. These prophets mislead people with lies and empty visions, failing to protect Israel in the coming judgment.

Ezekiel acts out a prophetic sign in Jerusalem, preparing to go into exile as a symbol for the people. God explains this represents the prince and Israel's coming captivity and scattering by Babylonian forces.

God, speaking through Ezekiel in Babylon, condemns false prophets who falsely assure Jerusalem's peace, warning their protective "wall" will collapse in judgment, and also rebukes women who deceive God's people for personal gain.

God, speaking through Ezekiel in Babylon, condemns deceptive women prophets who exploit and mislead Israel’s people for profit, promising false salvation; He declares He will stop their harmful influence and rescue His people from their control.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns false prophets and prophetesses in Israel who deceive the people with lies, promising peace and life falsely. He declares He will stop their influence and rescue His people from their harmful control.

Ezekiel receives elders of Israel who seek his counsel, but God tells him they have idols in their hearts and are sinful. God commands Ezekiel to warn them to repent and abandon their idols, highlighting Israel's estrangement from Him.

God commands Ezekiel to tell Israel to repent from idolatry, warning that those who seek prophets while secretly worshipping idols will face judgment. Both false prophets and idolaters will be punished to restore Israel’s faithfulness.

God tells Ezekiel that the cities will be destroyed and the land desolate, addressing Israel's disbelief in timely prophecy. He declares that future visions will come true soon, ending the people's excuse that prophecies are delayed.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, warns that even the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job cannot save others from judgment in Israel; severe punishments like sword, famine, beasts, and pestilence will devastate Jerusalem and its people.
God warns through Ezekiel that severe judgments will come upon Jerusalem, but a faithful remnant will survive and their actions will bring comfort, showing that God's punishments have a just purpose.

God speaks to Ezekiel, comparing Jerusalem's people to useless vine wood burned by fire, symbolizing their coming destruction by judgment and desolation due to their sins. This follows warnings of severe punishments on Jerusalem.

God speaks to Ezekiel, warning Israel that their sins will bring severe judgment like famine and wild beasts destroying the land, and even the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job would only save themselves, not others or the land.

God speaks to Ezekiel, instructing him to tell Jerusalem about her origins and neglect at birth, then how God saved and prospered her despite her vulnerable beginnings in Canaan, with Amorite and Hittite ancestry.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes how He nurtured and adorned Jerusalem, transforming her from a vulnerable state into a prosperous kingdom, symbolizing His covenant and care before her later unfaithfulness.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, accuses Jerusalem of betraying His care by offering Him gifts to idols and sacrificing their own children, committing abominations and idolatry, and engaging in immoral alliances with neighboring nations, provoking God's anger.

God warns Jerusalem through Ezekiel that He will punish her harshly for her unfaithfulness, destroying her sacred places and exposing her shame, ending her sinful ways, and causing others to speak of her downfall as a warning.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns Jerusalem for unfaithfulness by forming alliances with Egypt, Assyria, and others, leading to punishment by enemies like the Philistines; Jerusalem is accused of adultery against God, likened to a wife betraying her husband.
God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes Jerusalem's former glory and prosperity, adorned with fine clothes and wealth, but then condemns her for idolatry and unfaithfulness despite His blessings.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, compares Jerusalem to her ancestral lineage and neighboring cities Samaria and Sodom, highlighting Jerusalem's greater corruption and sins, including pride and neglect of the needy, which led to divine judgment.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns Jerusalem for corrupting relationships by paying lovers to come to her, unlike other women. He warns that He will expose her sins publicly and bring judgment like that on unfaithful women who shed blood.

God instructs Ezekiel to tell Israel a parable about two great eagles and a vine, symbolizing political powers and alliances, showing how Israel was taken from Lebanon and planted elsewhere, growing under influence but dependent on these powers.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, promises that Jerusalem will be restored along with its "sisters" Sodom and Samaria, despite Jerusalem's past sins and broken covenant, and affirms an everlasting covenant to bring shame and eventual peace.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, warns that the king of Judah broke his covenant with Babylon by seeking Egypt's help, and as a result, he will be captured and punished in Babylon for his rebellion and broken oath.

God declares judgment on the rebellious king who broke his covenant, promising to capture him and scatter his followers. Then God promises to raise a new leader from Israel, symbolized by a tender twig planted on a high mountain.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, compares Jerusalem unfavorably to Sodom and Samaria, condemning her greater sins and hypocrisy. He declares that when these cities' exiles return, Jerusalem's captivity will also end, highlighting her shame and restoration.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, uses the image of a vine planted in good soil that withers to warn Israel (the rebellious house) that Babylon has captured their king and nobles, making a covenant to keep the kingdom weak and dependent.
God speaks to Ezekiel, addressing a proverb used by Israelites about inherited guilt, declaring each person is responsible for their own sins and outlining the righteous behavior that leads to life.

God explains through Ezekiel that a righteous man who obeys His laws will live, but if his son becomes wicked and commits sins like robbery and idolatry, the son will be held accountable and face death for his own actions.

God, speaking through Ezekiel to Israel, explains that a wicked man who commits many sins will die for them, but if his son sees his father's sins and lives righteously, the son will live, while the father dies for his own wrongdoing.

God speaks to Israel, addressing their complaint that His judgments are unfair, explaining that both the righteous and wicked are judged equally based on their actions and repentance, emphasizing personal responsibility and the possibility of redemption.

God, speaking through Ezekiel to Israel, explains that each person is responsible for their own sins, not their ancestors'. He emphasizes that the wicked can live if they repent and follow God's laws, highlighting God's desire for their repentance and life.
God responds to Israel's complaint about His justice, declaring He judges each person fairly and urges them to repent and change their ways to avoid destruction and live.

Ezekiel laments the downfall of Israel’s leaders, symbolized as lions captured and silenced by Babylon. Israel, once prosperous like a fruitful vine, is uprooted and withered, now struggling in exile and losing its power to rule.

Ezekiel delivers a lament for Israel's princes, symbolized as lion cubs raised by a lioness, representing powerful leaders who preyed on others but were eventually captured and exiled to Egypt and Babylon, silencing their rule over Israel.

In Babylon, Ezekiel receives a message from God after Israel's elders seek guidance. God refuses their inquiry, instructing Ezekiel to remind them of their ancestors' rebellion and idolatry despite His deliverance from Egypt.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns Israel for repeating their ancestors' idolatry and child sacrifice at high places called Bamah, refusing to seek God sincerely despite His past deliverance and warnings.

God promises to accept and sanctify the scattered Israelites when He gathers them back to their promised land, where they will recognize His actions and regret their past sins, acknowledging His justice beyond their wrongdoing.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, recalls giving Israel the Sabbath as a sign of their covenant, but Israel rebelled in the wilderness by disobeying laws and worshiping idols, leading God to threaten punishment yet showing mercy for His name's sake.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns Israel's idolatry and child sacrifice, refusing their inquiries. He warns of judgment but promises to gather them from exile and confront them in the wilderness, recalling the covenant made with their ancestors in Egypt.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, recalls sparing the Israelites in the wilderness despite their rebellion, commands their children to follow His laws and keep the Sabbath, but they disobeyed; yet God restrained His anger to protect His reputation among surrounding nations.

God speaks through Ezekiel, explaining how He restrained judgment on Israel for His reputation but allowed their scattering due to their disobedience and idolatry, even giving them harmful laws as punishment to make them recognize His sovereignty.

God speaks through Ezekiel, promising to discipline Israel as He did their ancestors in Egypt, purging rebels and gathering His people from exile to serve Him in His holy mountain, restoring their relationship and sanctifying them before other nations.

God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the southern forest, declaring a fire that will consume all trees from south to north, symbolizing judgment. Ezekiel notes people accuse him of speaking in parables.

God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Jerusalem and Israel, warning of an unavoidable judgment that will affect everyone, righteous and wicked alike, causing widespread fear and despair throughout the land.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, recounts how He commanded Israel to abandon Egyptian idols, but they rebelled. Despite their disobedience, God preserved His reputation among other nations and led them from Egypt to the wilderness, giving them laws and the Sabbath as a covenant sign.

Ezekiel, speaking God's message, warns Israel of coming destruction symbolized by a sharpened sword causing fear and despair among the people and leaders, emphasizing the certainty and severity of God's judgment.

God instructs Ezekiel to prophesy about coming judgment symbolized by a sword targeting Israel's leaders and cities, including Jerusalem and Rabbath, signaling imminent destruction by the Babylonian king's forces.

God tells Ezekiel to prophesy the removal of the Ammonite king's crown and the overturning of power, declaring judgment and destruction on Ammon for their sins, with their downfall certain and irreversible.

God speaks to Ezekiel about Israel's corruption, comparing the people to worthless metals in a furnace, warning that He will gather and purify them in Jerusalem through His wrath, revealing their punishment and His sovereignty.

God instructs Ezekiel to prophesy about the Babylonian king's siege plans against Rabbath and Jerusalem, revealing the king's use of divination. God declares judgment on Israel's leader, signaling the end of his reign due to their sins.

God speaks to Ezekiel, commanding him to judge Jerusalem for its violence, idolatry, and social injustices, highlighting the city's guilt and the princes' bloodshed, oppression, and profaning of holy things.
