Ezekiel, speaking God's judgment to Jerusalem, condemns its corrupt prophets, priests, princes, and people for deceit, violence, and oppression, highlighting widespread spiritual and social decay before impending punishment.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns Jerusalem for widespread violence, sexual sins, bribery, and greed, warning that He will punish and scatter the people among nations to cleanse their corruption and reveal His sovereignty.

God, speaking through Ezekiel in Jerusalem, condemns the people for oppressing the vulnerable and notes that no one stood up to prevent their destruction, so He declares He will punish them for their sins.

God speaks to Ezekiel, using two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), as symbols of Israel and Judah's unfaithfulness through alliances with Assyria, continuing sins from Egypt, leading to their punishment by those nations.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes Jerusalem (Aholibah) as unfaithful, loving Babylonian rulers despite past sins in Egypt. God warns He will bring these enemies against her from all sides as judgment for her unfaithfulness.

God warns Jerusalem (Aholibah) that He will punish her for idolatry and unfaithfulness like her sister Samaria (Aholah), delivering her into the hands of enemies who will disgrace and destroy her, ending her sinful alliances and causing deep sorrow.

God, through Ezekiel, describes how Samaria (Aholah) was punished by Assyria for unfaithfulness, and how Jerusalem (Aholibah) became even more corrupt, lusting after Assyrian rulers and then Babylonian princes, sending messengers to them.

God warns Jerusalem (Aholibah) through Ezekiel that armies from Babylon, Chaldea, and Assyria will attack her with full force, punishing her for idolatry and unfaithfulness, ending her past alliances and defilements from Egypt.

God warns through Ezekiel that Jerusalem, called the "bloody city," will face severe judgment by fire for its sins and lies. God also tells Ezekiel he will lose his wife but must not mourn, symbolizing the coming devastation.

God speaks to Ezekiel, condemning Jerusalem (Aholibah) for forgetting Him and committing idolatry and child sacrifice, defiling His sanctuary and Sabbath, linking her fate to that of Samaria (Aholah) and calling Ezekiel to declare their sins.

God declares judgment through righteous men against Jerusalem (Aholibah) and Samaria (Aholah) for their idolatry and bloodshed, promising their destruction by enemies who will kill their families and burn their homes to end their unfaithfulness.

God speaks to Ezekiel on the day Babylon's king attacks Jerusalem, commanding him to deliver a parable comparing Jerusalem to a pot boiling with blood and sin, warning of coming judgment and destruction for the city's violence and rebellion.

God, through Ezekiel, condemns Jerusalem (Aholibah) and Samaria (Aholah) for idolatry, child sacrifice, and profaning His sanctuary, describing their alliances with foreign peoples and declaring they will be judged like adulterous, bloodguilty women.

God tells Ezekiel that his wife will die and he must not mourn openly, symbolizing the coming judgment on Jerusalem where families will suffer loss and sorrow without traditional mourning, reflecting the people's punishment for their sins.

God speaks to Ezekiel, instructing him to prophesy against the Ammonites for mocking Israel's suffering. God declares He will hand Ammon over to eastern peoples, destroying them so all will know He is the LORD.

God tells Ezekiel that the people of Jerusalem will mourn silently for their sins, and Ezekiel's actions serve as a sign. When survivors come to him, he will speak for God, confirming God's judgment on the city.

God speaks to Ezekiel, condemning the city of Tyre for rejoicing over Jerusalem's destruction. He declares that many nations, led by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, will attack and destroy Tyre, making it desolate.
God, speaking through Ezekiel, pronounces judgment on Moab, Seir, and Edom for their hostility and revenge against Judah, declaring their destruction and exile to show His power and justice.
God, speaking through Ezekiel, pronounces judgment on Edom and the Philistines for their hostility toward Judah, declaring their destruction by Israel as a demonstration of His vengeance and power.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, prophesies the destruction of Tyre by invading nations, describing the city's riches plundered, walls destroyed, and its fall causing shock among surrounding islands and sea rulers.

God tells Ezekiel that King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon will attack the coastal city of Tyre with a large army, destroy its defenses, kill many people, and loot its wealth, fulfilling God's judgment against Tyre's pride and hostility toward Jerusalem.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, prophesies the complete destruction and desolation of Tyre, a powerful sea city, warning that it will be forgotten and feared, with its fall causing distress among nearby islands and nations.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes Tyre's extensive trade network and military alliances, highlighting its wealth and influence through merchants and warriors from various nations surrounding the Mediterranean and beyond.

God commands Ezekiel to mourn over Tyre, a wealthy island city known for its maritime trade and craftsmanship, highlighting its pride and extensive international commerce before its impending downfall.

God, through Ezekiel, lists many nations including Syria, Judah, and Arabia as merchants trading diverse goods with Tyre, highlighting its extensive trade network and wealth before its prophesied downfall.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes the mourning of Tyrus' sailors and merchants as the city faces destruction, highlighting its former wealth and influence and the shock of surrounding nations at its downfall.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes Tyre's extensive trade and wealth, highlighting its glory and the many merchants involved, but warns that a violent storm and destruction will cause its downfall, shaking the city and devastating its people and commerce.

God speaks through Ezekiel to the prince of Tyre, condemning his pride and wealth gained through trade, warning that foreign enemies will kill him despite his claims of divinity. This follows the judgment on Tyre's commerce in chapter 27.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, declares judgment on Sidon for its hostility toward Israel, promising punishment and eventual restoration and safety for the scattered Israelites in their land, affirming God's sovereignty and protection.
God speaks to Ezekiel, commanding him to lament the king of Tyre, describing his pride, wisdom, beauty, and former perfection as an anointed cherub in Eden before sin was found in him.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, declares that Egypt will be desolate and its people scattered for forty years, but afterward they will be gathered back to their land as a diminished, lowly kingdom, no longer a threat or a reminder of Israel's past sins.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns the "covering cherub"—a figure symbolizing the prince of Tyre—who was once perfect but became corrupt through pride and sin, leading to his downfall and destruction witnessed by all.

God speaks through Ezekiel, pronouncing judgment on Egypt for oppressing Israel. He declares Egypt will become desolate and uninhabited for 40 years, with its people scattered among nations, showing God's power over the land and its rulers.

God speaks to Ezekiel, commanding him to prophesy against Pharaoh and Egypt, condemning Egypt's pride and predicting their downfall and desolation, showing God's judgment for Egypt's oppression of Israel.

Ezekiel receives God's command to prophesy about coming destruction on Egypt and its allies, including Ethiopia, Libya, and Lydia. The passage warns of widespread defeat and desolation, signaling God's judgment on these nations.

God speaks to Ezekiel, declaring that He will empower Babylon's king to conquer Egypt, weaken Pharaoh, and scatter the Egyptians among nations, showing God's sovereignty over these nations and fulfilling earlier prophecies of Egypt's downfall.

God tells Ezekiel that Egypt will no longer be a threat or a reminder of Israel's sins, and announces that Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar will be rewarded with Egypt for his military service, while Israel will be restored and recognized.

God speaks to Ezekiel, declaring coming destruction on Egyptian cities like Sin, No, and Tehaphnehes, symbolizing Egypt's weakening power. Pharaoh's strength will be broken, and Egyptians scattered among nations, continuing the prophecy against Egypt and its king.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, warns that Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt and its allies, causing destruction and fear across key Egyptian cities like Noph, Zoan, and Sin, fulfilling divine judgment on Egypt's power and idols.

God speaks to Ezekiel, instructing him to address Pharaoh and his people, comparing Assyria's former greatness to a tall cedar tree nourished by abundant waters, symbolizing its power and influence over many nations.

God declares the mourning and stillness of nature at the fall of the great Assyrian king, symbolizing Pharaoh's downfall. This judgment brings terror to nations and confirms Pharaoh and his people will join the slain in the grave.

God, speaking to Ezekiel, describes the fall of the Assyrian empire as a mighty tree cut down by foreign nations, symbolizing its destruction and the mourning it causes in Lebanon and surrounding lands.
God instructs Ezekiel to mourn for Pharaoh, king of Egypt, describing his power and downfall. This prophecy follows the judgment on Pharaoh and foretells his defeat and desolation by foreign nations.

God speaks to Ezekiel, declaring the coming destruction of Egypt by Babylon's sword, darkening the skies and terrifying nations; Egypt's people and animals will perish, and its lands will become desolate and still.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes the fallen mighty nations Asshur and Elam lying dead in the underworld, uncircumcised and slain by the sword, surrounded by their graves, symbolizing their defeat and shame after terrorizing the living.

God speaks to Ezekiel, declaring Egypt's destruction and desolation by foreign powers, leading to widespread mourning among nations. Ezekiel is commanded to lament Egypt's downfall and its people lying slain among the uncircumcised in the underworld.

God, speaking through Ezekiel to the Israelites, urges the wicked to repent and live, explaining that righteousness won't save someone who sins, nor will past wickedness condemn one who turns to right living.

God speaks to Ezekiel, appointing him as a watchman for Israel to warn the people of coming danger. If the watchman warns and they ignore it, their punishment is their own responsibility; if not warned, the watchman is accountable.

God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman for Israel, commanding him to warn the wicked of their sins to save them. Ezekiel is to tell Israel that God desires their repentance and life, not their death, despite their doubts about living amid sin.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes the fallen kings and princes of Edom, the northern nations, and the Zidonians lying dead and uncircumcised in the underworld, alongside Pharaoh and his army, emphasizing their shared defeat and shame.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes the burial of defeated nations like Meshech, Tubal, and Edom among the uncircumcised dead slain by the sword, emphasizing their downfall despite their former terror in the land of the living.
God speaks to Pharaoh, comparing Assyria to a mighty cedar tree admired for its beauty and strength, but warns that due to pride and wickedness, Assyria will be cut down and abandoned by all nations.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, explains that both wicked and righteous people will be judged fairly based on their actions, addressing Israel's complaints about divine justice; then a survivor from Jerusalem reports the city's fall during their exile.

God tells Ezekiel that Israel will become desolate due to their sins, and though the people listen to Ezekiel’s words, they do not obey. Their disobedience will prove that Ezekiel truly was a prophet sent by God.
God speaks to Israel, condemning selfish leaders who harm the flock, promising to judge them and appoint David as the one true shepherd to care for and protect His people.

God speaks to Ezekiel, promising to personally search for and restore the scattered people of Israel, caring for them like a shepherd tending his flock, and to judge between the strong and weak among them.

God commands Ezekiel to condemn Israel's leaders, likened to selfish shepherds who exploit the people instead of caring for them, causing the flock to scatter and become vulnerable without guidance or protection.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, condemns Israel's leaders (shepherds) for neglecting and exploiting the people (the flock), promising to hold them accountable and personally rescue and care for the scattered Israelites.
God, speaking through Ezekiel, declares judgment on Mount Seir and Idumea for their envy and hatred toward Israel, promising their destruction so all will recognize God's sovereignty and justice.

Ezekiel, now able to speak again, receives God's message condemning the sinful inhabitants of Israel's wastelands who claim the land by inheritance, warning of destruction by sword, beasts, and plague, leading to desolation of the land.

God promises to be Israel's God and appoints David as their prince, establishing peace and safety in their land. He vows to bless the land, protect the people from enemies, and restore their prosperity, affirming Israel as His flock.

God commands Ezekiel to prophesy to the mountains of Israel, addressing their desolation caused by surrounding nations, including Edom (Idumea), who have taken possession of the land with hostile intent.

God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Mount Seir (Edom) for its longstanding hatred and violence against Israel, declaring that it will be destroyed and desolate so all will recognize God's judgment and sovereignty.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, declares judgment on the nations, including Idumea, that seized Israel's land with hostile intent, promising restoration and fruitfulness for Israel's mountains as His people prepare to return.

God speaks through Ezekiel, promising restoration and flourishing of the mountains of Israel, reversing their desolation and shame caused by surrounding nations, and ensuring Israel's return and possession of their land.

God speaks to Ezekiel, promising Israel will no longer suffer shame from other nations. He recalls Israel's past defilement of their land and exile among heathen nations, where they profaned God's name, yet God shows pity for His own holy name.

God speaks to Ezekiel, explaining that He will restore Israel not for their sake but to honor His holy name, promising to cleanse and renew them spiritually and bring them back from exile to their land.

Ezekiel, guided by God's spirit, is shown a valley of dry bones and commanded to prophesy to them. As he speaks, the bones reassemble with flesh and skin but remain lifeless without breath, symbolizing Israel's restoration yet incomplete revival.

God promises the reunified Israel will have one leader, David, and live peacefully in their ancestral land with His sanctuary among them, establishing an everlasting covenant and showing the nations His sanctification of Israel.

God tells Ezekiel that He will restore Israel by putting His spirit in them and bringing them back to their land. Ezekiel is then instructed to join two sticks symbolizing Judah and Joseph, representing the reunification of the divided tribes of Israel.

Ezekiel, guided by God's spirit, witnesses dry bones gaining flesh but lacking breath, symbolizing Israel's lifeless state. God commands him to prophesy breath into them, representing Israel's future restoration and return to their land.
God speaks to Ezekiel, commanding him to prophesy against Gog, leader of Magog and allies from various nations, who will come against a restored and peaceful Israel in the distant future.

God promises through Ezekiel to restore Israel by giving them a new spirit to follow His laws, bringing them back to their land, providing abundance, and rebuilding desolate cities, while Israel will recognize their past sins and feel shame.

God instructs Ezekiel to show the two sticks representing Judah and Israel joined as one, promising to gather the scattered Israelites, unify them under one king, cleanse them from idolatry, and restore them as His people with David as their leader.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, promises to restore the desolate land of Israel, making ruined cities fertile and inhabited again, so surrounding nations will recognize God's power and Israel will flourish like a thriving flock.

God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, who will invade Israel in the future when the land is restored and people live safely without walls, aiming to plunder the peaceful inhabitants gathered from many nations.

God speaks to Ezekiel, warning that Gog will attack Israel in the future, but God's anger will cause a great earthquake and internal conflict among Gog's forces, demonstrating God's power and fulfilling ancient prophecies about this invasion.
God declares He will fight against Gog and his armies with widespread conflict, disease, and natural disasters, showing His power and holiness to many nations, following Gog's attack on Israel.

God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, a leader from the north, who will invade Israel in the future when the people live securely. Neighboring nations question Gog's intent, while God declares this will reveal His power to the world.

God speaks through Ezekiel, promising to restore Israel after their punishment and exile for sins, gathering them back from captivity among nations and renewing His presence with them to show His holiness to many peoples.

God instructs Ezekiel to prophesy about the aftermath of Gog's defeat, where all people will help bury the dead over seven months to cleanse the land, and animals will feast on the fallen warriors on the mountains of Israel.

God, speaking through Ezekiel, describes a great sacrificial feast on the mountains of Israel after defeating Gog and his armies, revealing His glory to the nations and explaining Israel's past captivity due to their sins.

God declares the defeat of Gog's invasion, instructing the people of Israel to burn weapons for seven years and bury the dead in a valley named Hamongog, cleansing the land after the battle on Israel's mountains.

Ezekiel, in a vision by the land of Israel, is guided by a man with a measuring reed who measures the eastern gate and its surrounding structures, detailing the dimensions and features of the gate, chambers, and court pavement.

God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog, leader of Meshech and Tubal, declaring Gog's defeat on Israel's mountains. God will display His power, punish Gog's forces, and reveal His holiness to Israel and the nations.

Ezekiel, in a vision by the river Chebar, is shown a detailed measurement of a future temple complex by a man with a measuring reed, focusing here on the outer wall and the east gate's dimensions and structure.

Ezekiel, in exile during the 25th year of captivity, is taken in a vision to a high mountain in Israel where a man with a measuring reed instructs him to observe and report detailed measurements of a city to the Israelites.

Ezekiel, in a vision given by God, is being shown detailed measurements of a future temple complex in Israel, focusing here on the gates and courts facing north and south, continuing from the earlier description of the eastern gate.

Ezekiel, in a vision in Israel, is guided by a man measuring the detailed design of the temple gates and inner court, focusing here on the eastern and northern gates with their chambers, arches, palm decorations, and steps, including areas for washing burnt offerings.

Ezekiel, in a vision given by God, is being shown detailed measurements of a future temple in Jerusalem, focusing here on the southern gate and its architectural features, continuing from the eastern and northern gates described earlier.

Ezekiel is guided through a detailed measurement of the temple's structure, including the most holy place, walls, and side chambers built into the temple walls, continuing from the previous chapter's temple vision in Jerusalem.

Ezekiel, in a vision in exile, is shown detailed measurements of a future temple in Israel. Here, he describes the north gate area with chambers for washing burnt offerings, multiple stone tables for sacrifices, and chambers for temple singers.

Ezekiel is guided through detailed measurements of the temple in Jerusalem, focusing here on the side chambers' doors, the adjacent open space, and the dimensions of the building and separate place surrounding the temple's west and east sides.

Ezekiel, in a vision in Israel, is shown detailed measurements of the temple area, including chambers for singers and priests from the Zadok family, the altar, and the porch with its pillars and steps, emphasizing the temple's layout and priestly roles.

Ezekiel is shown detailed measurements of the temple's side chambers, which are stacked three high and built into the walls. The chambers have winding stairways and doors facing a central space around the temple.

Ezekiel is guided through detailed measurements of the temple's eastern side, including galleries and porches, noting intricate woodwork and decorations of cherubim and palm trees adorning walls and doors, continuing the vision of the temple's design.

Ezekiel is shown detailed decorations of the temple, including cherubim and palm trees carved on walls, doors, and windows. He is told about the wooden altar table before the LORD, highlighting the temple's sacred design.

Ezekiel is shown the temple's outer court chambers, describing their size, location, and entrances on the east side. He is told these north and south chambers are holy rooms where priests eat and store sacred offerings before the LORD.

Ezekiel is being shown a detailed vision of the temple's outer court, focusing on the northern chambers and their measurements, including galleries and walls, continuing the architectural description from the previous chapter.

Ezekiel is brought to the east gate of the temple where he sees God's glory entering, filling the house. God speaks to Ezekiel, declaring His permanent dwelling with Israel and condemning their past defilement by kings and idolatry.

Ezekiel is shown the holy chambers on the north and south sides where priests eat and store sacred offerings, changing garments before entering. Then he measures the temple's outer court, a square 500 reeds on each side, separating holy from common areas.

God speaks to Ezekiel, declaring His throne and presence will dwell among Israel forever if they abandon their sins and idolatry. He instructs Ezekiel to show Israel the temple design to make them aware of their past wrongs.

God instructs Ezekiel on the detailed rituals for cleansing and consecrating the altar in the new temple, including sin offerings and burnt offerings over seven days, to prepare the priests for ongoing worship in Jerusalem.

Ezekiel receives detailed measurements and instructions from God about the altar in the new temple, including its size, features, and the ritual use of blood for purification, emphasizing the role of Zadokite priests in these sacred duties.

God instructs Ezekiel to warn Israel about their past sins of allowing unfaithful outsiders into the sanctuary, defiling it and breaking the covenant, and declares that only faithful Levites may serve in the holy place.

Ezekiel is shown a vision of the temple gates, where God declares the east gate permanently closed because He has entered through it. The prince will use this gate, and Ezekiel is instructed to carefully observe all temple laws and rituals.

God instructs Ezekiel to show the Israelites the design of the temple so they may feel shame for their sins and follow its laws. He then begins detailing the altar's measurements and holiness atop the mountain.

God instructs Ezekiel about the priests' conduct in the temple: changing garments when entering the outer court, grooming rules, restrictions on drinking wine and marriage, their role in teaching and judging, and rules on ritual purity regarding the dead.

God speaks to Ezekiel about the Levites who abandoned Him when Israel worshipped idols; they will bear guilt and serve only in minor roles at the temple, barred from priestly duties or the holy place, but will maintain the temple's service.

God tells Ezekiel that the faithful Levite priests, descendants of Zadok, will serve in the sanctuary wearing special linen garments while ministering inside, and change clothes before entering the outer court to meet the people, maintaining ritual purity.

God instructs Ezekiel about priestly purity laws, detailing when priests may become ceremonially unclean for close relatives, their sin offerings, and their inheritance rights, emphasizing their role and separation within Israel's worship system.

God instructs Ezekiel on how the land in Israel is to be divided by lot, designating a large holy portion for the sanctuary, priests, and Levites, including space for the sanctuary, their residences, and chambers for their service.

God commands the princes of Israel to stop oppressing the people and to practice fairness with honest weights and measures. He also outlines specific offerings all Israelites must give for the prince’s sacrifices and reconciliation.

God instructs the people of Israel to give offerings for the prince, who is responsible for preparing various sacrifices during festivals and holy days. The passage details rituals for cleansing the sanctuary and observing the Passover feast.

God instructs Ezekiel about temple worship in Jerusalem, detailing how the eastern gate of the inner court remains closed on workdays but opens on Sabbaths and new moons for the prince and people to offer sacrifices and worship.

God instructs the prince of Israel to offer specific sin and burnt offerings during seven-day feasts in the first and seventh months, ensuring ongoing ritual sacrifices for the people as part of the temple worship regulations.
God shows Ezekiel the outer court of the temple, highlighting four smaller courts at each corner with buildings and boiling places where the temple ministers prepare the people's sacrifices.

God instructs Ezekiel about the prince's offerings on the new moon and during feasts in the temple at Jerusalem, detailing the animals and grain offerings, and the specific gates used by the prince and the people during worship.

God instructs Ezekiel about the prince's inheritance rights and fair treatment of the people's land, then shows him the priests' chambers and the outer court's four corner courts in the temple area, continuing the temple vision.

God instructs Ezekiel about offerings during feasts and daily burnt offerings at the temple in Jerusalem. The prince performs voluntary offerings at the east gate, and inheritance laws for the prince's gifts to his sons are established.

Ezekiel is led by a man to the east gate of the temple in Jerusalem, where water flows from beneath the threshold. The man measures the increasing depth of the water as it flows outward, showing a river growing too deep to cross.

God instructs Ezekiel to assign land portions to the Levites, the city, and the prince in Israel, promising justice and an end to oppression by the princes, urging them to act fairly and stop exploiting the people.

God reveals to Ezekiel that some marshy lands will remain salty and barren, while fertile trees will grow along the river from the sanctuary's waters. Then God outlines the northern boundary of the land to be divided among Israel's twelve tribes, with Joseph receiving two portions.

God outlines the borders of the land for the twelve tribes of Israel, naming specific locations around Israel's perimeter. He commands dividing the land by lot, including giving inheritance rights to foreigners living among the tribes.

Ezekiel describes the land allotment for Israel's tribes, starting from the north with Dan and moving southward, detailing each tribe's portion. The sanctuary is placed centrally within Judah's territory, following the land division instructions given earlier.

God instructs Ezekiel to describe the land division for the tribe of Judah, highlighting a large sacred area in the center for the sanctuary and a holy portion for the faithful priests, the sons of Zadok, near the Levites' border.

God shows Ezekiel a river flowing east from the temple, bringing life and healing to the desert and sea, supporting abundant fish and trees along its banks, except for some salty marshlands that remain barren.

Ezekiel describes the layout of the future city, detailing its suburbs and surrounding land set aside for food and service. The land is divided among Israel’s tribes, with a special portion reserved for the prince near the sanctuary.

God instructs Ezekiel on the sacred land allocation near the Levites' border, detailing dimensions for holy and common areas, including the city's size and its surrounding suburbs, emphasizing the holiness and permanence of these divisions.

God instructs Ezekiel on dividing the land among Israel's tribes, detailing the prince's land near the sanctuary and city, and assigning portions to Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun, and Gad along the borders.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieges Jerusalem during Jehoiakim's reign, capturing the king and sacred vessels. He orders Ashpenaz to select young Israelite nobles to be trained in Babylonian language and culture for royal service.

Daniel asks Melzar, overseer of the young captives, for a 10-day test to eat only vegetables and water instead of the king’s food, fearing defilement. After 10 days, Daniel and friends appear healthier, and God grants them wisdom and understanding.

God grants Daniel and his three friends exceptional wisdom and understanding, especially Daniel's insight into visions and dreams. After their training, they impress King Nebuchadnezzar far beyond his other advisors and continue to serve through to King Cyrus's reign.

King Nebuchadnezzar assigns royal food and wine to young Israelite captives, including Daniel and his friends, renaming them. Daniel chooses not to defile himself with the king’s food, causing concern for the eunuch overseeing them.

God instructs Ezekiel to describe the land boundaries for the tribe of Gad and the city's layout with gates named after Israel's tribes, emphasizing the city's size and its new name, "The LORD is there," symbolizing God's presence among His people.

King Nebuchadnezzar demands his dream and its meaning from the Chaldean wise men, who admit no one can do this except gods. Angered, the king orders the execution of all Babylonian wise men, including Daniel and his friends.

Daniel, a captive from Judah, is brought before King Nebuchadnezzar to interpret the king's troubling dream, explaining that only God can reveal such secrets, and he received this knowledge to help the king understand his own thoughts.

Daniel explains to King Nebuchadnezzar that the dream of a great image with various metals represents successive kingdoms, starting with the king's own powerful rule, and promises to reveal its meaning.

Daniel explains to King Nebuchadnezzar that the iron mixed with clay represents divided kingdoms, but God will establish an eternal kingdom. The king worships Daniel and acknowledges Daniel's God as the true revealer of secrets.

King Nebuchadnezzar, troubled by a mysterious dream, summons Babylon's magicians and astrologers to reveal and interpret it, but they demand he first tell them the dream, which he refuses, suspecting they seek to delay.

King Nebuchadnezzar praises Daniel’s God for revealing the dream’s meaning, promotes Daniel to high office over Babylon’s province and wise men, and appoints Daniel’s friends Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to governorships.

After King Nebuchadnezzar orders all Babylonian wise men killed for failing to reveal his dream, Daniel asks the king for time to interpret it, prays with his friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, and receives the secret in a night vision.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon sets up a massive golden statue in the plain of Dura and summons all provincial leaders to its dedication, commanding everyone to worship it when music plays or face death by fiery furnace.

Daniel receives a revealing dream from God about King Nebuchadnezzar's troubling vision. He praises God, then asks Arioch, the king’s captain, to spare the wise men and brings Daniel before the king to interpret the dream.

Daniel explains to King Nebuchadnezzar that the head of gold in his dream represents his powerful kingdom, followed by three other kingdoms of lesser strength, with the last divided and partly strong, symbolized by iron mixed with clay.

Accused by Chaldeans for not worshipping Nebuchadnezzar's golden image, Jewish officials Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are brought before the king, who threatens them with a fiery furnace if they refuse to comply. They confidently declare their faith in God’s power to save them.

King Nebuchadnezzar watches in amazement as Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego survive unharmed in the fiery furnace, joined by a mysterious fourth figure; he then calls them out, and the gathered officials witness their miraculous deliverance.

Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse King Nebuchadnezzar's order to worship his golden image, declaring their faith in God’s power to save them but refusing to worship false gods. Enraged, Nebuchadnezzar orders them bound and thrown into a blazing furnace.

King Nebuchadnezzar commands all people to worship a golden image or face death by fire. At the dedication in Babylon, everyone complies except Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who are reported to the king for disobedience.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon addresses all nations, recounting a troubling dream he had while at peace in his palace. He summons Babylon's wise men, including magicians and astrologers, to interpret the dream, but they fail to do so.

After Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego survive the fiery furnace unharmed, King Nebuchadnezzar praises their God, decrees punishment for blasphemy against Him, and promotes the three men in Babylon’s government.

King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree providing for all creatures, then a heavenly watcher orders it cut down but its stump preserved. This symbolizes the king's forthcoming humbling, decreed by divine beings to show God's sovereign rule over earthly kingdoms.

King Nebuchadnezzar summons Babylonian magicians and wise men to interpret his troubling dream, but only Daniel (Belteshazzar) understands it. The king describes a great, fruitful tree symbolizing his kingdom.

King Nebuchadnezzar shares his troubling dream with Daniel (Belteshazzar) in Babylon, asking for its meaning since other wise men failed; Daniel is deeply disturbed by the dream's message about God's control over earthly kingdoms.

Daniel interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, warning the king that he will lose his kingdom and live like an animal until he acknowledges God's sovereignty. Despite the warning, Nebuchadnezzar boasts about Babylon before a divine voice declares his kingdom taken.

Daniel (Belteshazzar) is troubled by King Nebuchadnezzar's dream about a great tree, which Daniel explains symbolizes the king's vast power and dominion over the earth, connecting to the king's earlier request for interpretation.

King Nebuchadnezzar hears Daniel interpret his troubling dream about a great tree symbolizing his vast kingdom, which will be cut down but its roots spared, meaning he will lose power temporarily but his kingdom will be restored after he learns God's sovereignty.

King Nebuchadnezzar experiences the fulfillment of Daniel's prophecy as he is driven from people and lives like an animal until he acknowledges God's sovereignty. After this period, his sanity and kingdom are restored.
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon acknowledges God's supreme power after his sanity and kingdom are restored, praising God's truth and justice, and recognizing that pride leads to downfall.

King Belshazzar holds a lavish feast with his nobles in Babylon, using sacred vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple to drink and praise idols, when a mysterious hand appears and writes on the palace wall, frightening the king.

King Belshazzar summons Daniel, a Jewish exile known for wisdom, to interpret mysterious writing on the palace wall after his own wise men fail. Daniel agrees to reveal the meaning without accepting the king's promised rewards.

King Belshazzar sees mysterious writing on the palace wall during a feast and becomes terrified. He summons Babylon's wise men to interpret it, promising rewards, but none can explain the message, causing fear among the king and his nobles.

Daniel speaks to King Belshazzar of Babylon, refusing gifts but promising to interpret the mysterious writing. He recounts Nebuchadnezzar’s rise, pride, and humbling, showing God’s control over kingdoms and rulers.

Daniel recounts King Nebuchadnezzar’s humbling by God and confronts Belshazzar for his pride and disrespect toward God’s temple vessels. Daniel then reveals the mysterious writing predicting the end of Belshazzar’s kingdom to the Medes and Persians.

King Belshazzar is alarmed by the mysterious writing during his feast in Babylon. The queen reminds him of Daniel, a wise man from Judah who served Nebuchadnezzar, and Daniel is summoned to interpret the message.

Daniel interprets the mysterious writing for King Belshazzar, predicting the fall of his kingdom to the Medes and Persians. Belshazzar honors Daniel, but that very night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Mede takes over the kingdom.

King Darius appoints 120 princes and three presidents over his kingdom, with Daniel as the top president. Daniel excels, but jealous officials plot against him, hoping to find fault related to his faith in God.

Daniel is caught praying despite King Darius's new law forbidding petitions to anyone but the king for 30 days. The accusers report this to Darius, who wants to save Daniel but is reminded that the law cannot be changed.

Daniel describes a vision of divine judgment with countless heavenly beings present; a powerful beast is destroyed, and a figure like the Son of man receives eternal dominion. Troubled, Daniel seeks and receives interpretation from a heavenly attendant.

Under King Darius in Persia, officials plot to trap Daniel by having the king decree that no one may pray to any god or man except him for 30 days. Daniel continues praying to God openly, defying the new law.

Daniel, during King Belshazzar's first year in Babylon, recounts a troubling dream featuring four distinct beasts rising from the sea, symbolizing powerful kingdoms, following the events of his deliverance from the lions' den under Darius.

King Darius reluctantly orders Daniel thrown into the lions' den after officials remind him that royal decrees cannot be revoked. The king hopes Daniel's God will save him and anxiously checks on him early the next morning.

Daniel tells King Darius that God sent an angel to protect him from the lions. The king joyfully frees Daniel, punishes his accusers, and proclaims Daniel's God as supreme throughout the kingdom, where Daniel continues to prosper under Darius and Cyrus.

Daniel asks a heavenly figure to explain his vision of four beasts, representing four kings. He learns the saints will ultimately receive eternal dominion, despite the fierce power and persecution by the fourth beast and its horns.

Daniel explains his vision of four beasts as four earthly kingdoms, focusing on the fourth kingdom's destructive power and its ten kings, including a blasphemous ruler. He sees God's final judgment giving eternal dominion to His holy people.

Daniel describes a vision of four beasts symbolizing kingdoms; the third is a leopard with four wings and heads, the fourth is a terrifying beast with iron teeth and ten horns, including a little horn speaking arrogantly. Then Daniel sees the Ancient of Days judging.

Daniel receives a new vision during King Belshazzar's reign, seeing himself at Shushan by the Ulai river, where a powerful two-horned ram appears, followed by a swift goat with a prominent horn attacking the ram.

Daniel describes a vision at Shushan where a powerful goat defeats a two-horned ram by breaking its horns, then grows strong but loses its great horn, replaced by four others, with a little horn rising and opposing the sanctuary and daily sacrifices.

The angel Gabriel explains to Daniel the vision's meaning: the ram represents Media and Persia, the goat is Greece, and a fierce king will arise later. Daniel is overwhelmed by the prophecy but resumes his duties in Babylon.

Daniel sees a vision where a power opposes the daily sacrifice, causing desolation. He hears saints discussing how long this will last—2300 days—then the sanctuary will be cleansed. The angel Gabriel appears to explain the vision to Daniel at the river Ulai.

The angel Gabriel explains to Daniel a prophecy about seventy weeks concerning the people of Israel and Jerusalem, detailing the timeline for restoration, the coming of the Messiah, destruction of the city, and future desolation.
Daniel prays earnestly for Jerusalem's restoration when the angel Gabriel appears to give him understanding about a prophetic timeline of seventy weeks concerning his people and the holy city.

Daniel confesses Israel's disobedience to God's prophets and laws, acknowledging the resulting shame and curses on Judah, Jerusalem, and all Israel scattered abroad due to their sins and rebellion against God.

Daniel prays to God in Jerusalem during exile, confessing Israel's sins and pleading for mercy and restoration, acknowledging God's past deliverance from Egypt and asking Him to turn away His anger from the desolate city and people.

Daniel confesses Israel's sins and acknowledges that the curses and calamities on Jerusalem are consequences of their disobedience to God's law, recognizing God's justice and pleading for mercy during the Babylonian exile under Darius's reign.

Daniel, now under King Darius of the Medes, reflects on Jeremiah's prophecy of Jerusalem's 70 years of desolation and begins earnest prayer and confession, acknowledging Israel's sins and disobedience to God's commands and prophets.

Daniel alone sees a powerful vision by the river Hiddekel while his companions flee in fear. A heavenly messenger encourages Daniel, explaining he was delayed by spiritual opposition from Persia's prince until helped by Michael.

Daniel, also called Belteshazzar, receives a true but distant vision during Cyrus's reign; he mourns for three weeks by the river Hiddekel, then sees a radiant man in linen, while his companions flee in fear.

An angel explains to Daniel that spiritual forces delayed his message for 21 days until Michael helped; the angel encourages Daniel, who is weak and overwhelmed, to be strong as he prepares to reveal future events concerning Daniel’s people.

A heavenly figure encourages Daniel to be strong and reveals ongoing spiritual battles involving the princes of Persia and Grecia, with Michael supporting God's people; this vision prepares Daniel for future revelations about his nation.

An angel continues to reveal future conflicts between the king of the north and the king of the south, describing the north's military successes, political alliances, setbacks, and the rise and fall of a tax collector in his kingdom.

An unnamed tax collector rises briefly to power but is quickly destroyed. Then a deceitful man gains the kingdom peacefully, overcomes enemies, breaks a covenant, and wages war against the king of the south with a large army.

An angel explains to Daniel a future alliance through marriage between the king of the south and the king of the north, followed by conflict where a descendant from the south conquers the north's fortress and takes captives to Egypt.

An angel continues to reveal future conflicts between the kings of the north and south, describing a proud king who exalts himself above all gods and honors a foreign god, leading to intense battles near the end times involving many nations.

An angel, speaking to Daniel, recounts historical and future Persian and Greek kings, describing their rise and fall, and a political alliance through marriage between the king of the south's daughter and the king of the north, which ultimately fails.

An angel continues revealing future conflicts between the kings of the north and south, describing battles, shifting alliances, and military campaigns involving their forces and fortified cities. This follows earlier prophecies about Persian and Greek rulers.

An angel explains to Daniel about a future conflict where the king of the north attacks the king of the south with a large army, but despite deceit and alliances, the king of the north will face setbacks and return with hostility toward the holy covenant.

An angel reveals to Daniel a future conflict where the king of the north attacks the king of the south, conquering many lands including Egypt, but faces trouble from the east and north before ultimately meeting his downfall.

An angel continues to reveal to Daniel future conflicts involving the king opposed by ships from Chittim (Cyprus), his desecration of the Jerusalem sanctuary, and the persecution and endurance of God's faithful people until the appointed end time.

Daniel receives a vision of Michael, protector of Israel, during a future unprecedented time of distress when the faithful will be saved and resurrected. Daniel is instructed to seal the prophecy until the end, while observing two figures by a river questioning its duration.

Daniel sees two figures by the river; one asks a man clothed in linen about the timing of future events. The man swears by God that after a set period, the holy people's power will be scattered and the end will come, but the full meaning is sealed until the end times.

God speaks to the prophet Hosea during the reigns of kings in Judah and Israel, instructing him to marry Gomer, a woman of unfaithfulness, symbolizing Israel's unfaithfulness to God and announcing judgment and mercy for Israel and Judah.

God promises to faithfully renew His covenant with Israel, restoring their relationship so they will recognize Him as their God. This follows His judgment and leads to a future of mercy and reconciliation for those once rejected.

God promises to comfort Israel, leading her to a place of hope and restoration like her youth after Egypt. He will remove false gods, establish peace, and renew a faithful, loving covenant with her forever.

God speaks to Israel, accusing her of unfaithfulness by worshiping Baal despite His blessings, and declares He will punish her by removing blessings and exposing her sins, yet promises to later comfort and restore her in the wilderness.

God speaks to Israel, calling them "Ammi" and "Ruhamah," and warns that because of their unfaithfulness and idolatry, He will punish them by blocking their paths and causing them to long for Him again, unaware of His past blessings.

God instructs Hosea to love an unfaithful woman as a symbol of His enduring love for Israel, despite their idolatry. Hosea redeems her, paralleling Israel's future restoration after a period of hardship and exile.

God speaks to Israel, condemning their widespread sins and lack of truth, mercy, and knowledge of Him. He warns that their land and people will suffer because of their rebellion and the priests' failure to lead rightly.

God tells Hosea that He will show mercy to Judah and save them through divine power, not military might. Hosea's wife bears a son named Loammi, symbolizing Israel's rejection by God, but a future restoration and unity of Israel and Judah is promised.

God, through Hosea, condemns Israel's leaders and people for their sinful practices, idolatry, and unfaithfulness, warning that their corrupt priests and people will face punishment, and urging Judah to avoid following Israel's example in places like Gilgal and Bethaven.

God, through Hosea, warns the priests, Israel, and the king of coming judgment for their betrayal and idolatry in places like Mizpah and Tabor. Ephraim and Judah face punishment for their pride and unfaithfulness.

God, through Hosea, condemns Israel's unfaithfulness and idolatry, warning Judah not to follow their example, highlighting Israel's spiritual decline and the shame their leaders bring upon the nation through corrupt practices.
God warns the tribes of Ephraim and Judah of coming judgment and destruction due to their sins. Despite seeking help from Assyria, they will face punishment until they repent and seek God again.

God calls the people of Ephraim and Judah to return to Him, promising healing after punishment. He condemns their fleeting faith, corrupt priests, and widespread sin in Israel and Gilead, warning of consequences after exile.

God speaks about Israel's unfaithfulness and corruption in Ephraim and Samaria, describing their deceit and moral decay. Despite God's desire to heal them, their leaders and people persist in wrongdoing, unaware of the consequences.

God, through the prophet Hosea, warns Israel and Ephraim of coming judgment for their deep corruption and idolatry, comparing their downfall to past sins and pleading for their punishment to be severe.

God, through Hosea, condemns Israel (Ephraim) for ignoring their decline and pride, seeking help from Egypt and Assyria instead of Him, warning of punishment and the fall of their leaders due to their rebellion and deceit.

God, through Hosea, warns Israel (Ephraim) of coming judgment for breaking the covenant and idolatry, symbolized by Samaria's calf idol; despite seeking foreign alliances like Assyria, they will face consequences and sorrow under divine punishment.

God warns Israel through Hosea not to celebrate as other nations because their unfaithfulness will lead to famine, exile to Egypt and Assyria, failed sacrifices, and destruction; the coming judgment days will reveal the consequences of their sins.

God warns Israel (Ephraim) that despite seeking help from foreign nations, He will gather them to face consequences for their idolatry and disobedience, recalling their sins and threatening destruction of their cities and palaces.

God, through the prophet Hosea, pronounces judgment on Ephraim (northern Israel), condemning their sins rooted in Gilgal and declaring they will face barrenness, exile, and loss of favor for their rebellion and failure to listen to God.

God, through Hosea, warns Israel that their sinful actions and reliance on their own strength will lead to violent destruction and the downfall of their king, similar to past brutal defeats like that of Betharbel.

Hosea warns Israel, especially in Samaria and Ephraim, that their idolatry and divided hearts will lead to destruction of their altars and images, loss of kingship, and shame before Assyria's king Jareb, signaling coming judgment.

God, through Hosea, warns Israel that their sinful worship sites will be destroyed and recalls their longstanding rebellion since Gibeah. He urges repentance, comparing Ephraim to a trained heifer, but condemns their trust in their own strength and wicked deeds.

God reflects on His past love and care for Israel (Ephraim), despite their idolatry and rebellion, expressing sorrow and mercy instead of destruction, contrasting His divine patience with Israel's unfaithfulness and impending judgment.

God, speaking through Hosea, criticizes Ephraim (Israel) for deceit and alliances with Assyria and Egypt, warns Judah of punishment, recalls Jacob's struggles with God, and urges faithfulness and justice, reminding them of God's past guidance through prophets.

God speaks to Israel (Ephraim), expressing mercy despite their sins, promising protection and restoration, while warning of their deceit; Judah remains faithful and close to God, contrasting with Israel's unfaithfulness.

God reminds Israel through Hosea that He has communicated via prophets and visions, recalls Israel's history from Jacob's time to the Exodus, and condemns Ephraim for provoking God's anger, linking past events to current judgment.

God speaks to Israel (Ephraim), recalling their past fear and pride, condemning their idolatry and increasing sin, warning of coming judgment like wild beasts, yet reminding them that help comes only from Him, their God who led them from Egypt.

The prophet Joel delivers God's message to the people of Judah, describing a devastating locust plague and a powerful invading nation that has destroyed their crops and offerings, causing priests and inhabitants to mourn deeply.

God calls Israel to repent and return to Him, promising forgiveness and restoration after their sins and reliance on foreign powers like Asshur. He describes the blessings and growth Israel will experience when they follow His ways.

God speaks to Israel (Ephraim), warning of judgment for their rebellion and sin, recalling He gave them kings in anger, and predicting destruction and desolation in Samaria due to their unfaithfulness.

Joel laments the devastation in Judah: crops spoiled, barns ruined, livestock suffering from lack of pasture, and wildfires destroying the land. He calls on the LORD for help amid this severe agricultural and environmental disaster.

Joel warns the people of Judah about a devastating famine that has stopped offerings at the temple, caused widespread crop failure, and led priests and farmers to mourn. He calls for a fast and assembly to seek God's help as disaster approaches.

The prophet Joel calls for an alarm in Zion, warning of an approaching, unprecedented army causing destruction like fire, bringing darkness and fear to the land, signaling the imminent "day of the LORD" after the earlier locust devastation.

God urges the people of Israel to sincerely repent with heartfelt sorrow, not just outward signs, and calls for a communal fast and assembly in Zion. Priests plead for mercy to prevent foreign nations from dominating God's people.

The prophet Joel describes a terrifying invading army causing widespread fear and destruction in Judah. God calls the people to repent sincerely with fasting and mourning, emphasizing His mercy and readiness to forgive.

God promises to restore the land of Israel and provide abundant crops after the devastation caused by the northern army. The people of Zion and the animals are called to rejoice in the renewal and blessings from the LORD.

God declares that when He restores Judah and Jerusalem from exile, He will gather all nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat to judge them for scattering His people and profiting from their suffering, including Tyre, Zidon, and the coasts of Palestine.

God promises to restore the land of Israel after devastation by locusts, providing abundant crops and blessings. He foretells pouring out His Spirit on all people and signs in the heavens before the coming day of the LORD, offering deliverance to those who call on Him.

God declares a decisive judgment in the valley of decision near Jerusalem, shaking earth and sky, promising hope for Israel, restoration of Judah’s land, desolation for enemies Egypt and Edom, and eternal dwelling for Judah and Jerusalem.

God declares judgment on nations, including the Greeks who sold Judah's people into exile, promising to reverse their fortunes. He calls all nations to prepare for battle in the valley of Jehoshaphat, where He will judge them for their wickedness.

The prophet Amos delivers God's judgment against Damascus, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Tyre for their violence and betrayal, declaring their people will face destruction and captivity as punishment.

The prophet Amos delivers God's judgment against Tyre, Edom, and Ammon for their violent and cruel actions, predicting destruction by fire and captivity for their leaders, continuing his series of oracles against neighboring nations.

God accuses Israel of mistreating their holy Nazirites and prophets by forcing silence and corruption, warning that no one—whether fast, strong, or brave—will escape judgment or save themselves from coming disaster.

God declares judgment on Judah and Israel for their injustices and idolatry, recalling His past deliverance and raising prophets and Nazarites, whom Israel rejected and silenced, highlighting their unfaithfulness despite His care.

God pronounces judgment on Moab for desecrating the bones of Edom's king, promising destruction of Kirioth and its leaders, then condemns Judah for rejecting God's law, warning of fire consuming Jerusalem's palaces.

God speaks through Amos to Israel, reminding them He chose them from Egypt and will punish their sins. Using vivid questions and images, He warns of coming judgment and calls for attention in places like Ashdod, Egypt, and Samaria amid turmoil.

Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa, prophesies during the reigns of Uzziah (Judah) and Jeroboam II (Israel), warning that God will punish Damascus for its brutal attack on Gilead, leading to Syrian exile and destruction.

God, through the prophet Amos, warns Israel and surrounding nations like Ashdod and Egypt about the coming judgment on Samaria for injustice and violence, predicting invasion, destruction of palaces, and punishment of religious sites like Bethel.

God warns Israel through Amos that their celebrations and sacrifices are rejected due to their injustice and idolatry; judgment and exile beyond Damascus will bring widespread mourning and destruction.

The prophet Amos warns Israel about injustice and corruption, condemning their oppression of the poor and bribery. He urges them to seek good and justice to avoid coming judgment and widespread mourning in their cities.

The prophet Amos condemns wealthy women in Samaria for oppressing the poor and warns of coming punishment. Despite God's repeated judgments like famine and drought, the people of Israel have not repented.

God, speaking through Amos to Israel, recounts various disasters—drought, pests, disease, and military defeat—that He sent as warnings, yet Israel did not repent; He warns them to prepare to meet Him, the Creator and Lord of all.

God shows Amos a vision of a plumbline symbolizing judgment on Israel for their sins. Amaziah, priest at Bethel, accuses Amos of conspiracy and tells him to leave Israel and stop prophesying at the royal sanctuary.

Amos responds to Amaziah, priest of Bethel, who forbids him to prophesy there, explaining he was called by God from being a herdsman to warn Israel. Amos then delivers God's judgment against Amaziah and Israel's coming exile.

The prophet Amos describes visions given by God: swarms of grasshoppers and fire threatening Israel's land, then God standing with a plumbline symbolizing judgment. Amos pleads for mercy, concerned for Jacob (Israel).

God declares judgment on Israel for their pride and injustice, promising destruction and captivity. The passage warns of widespread death and suffering as punishment for their corruption and false confidence in their own strength.

The prophet Amos delivers a lament to Israel, warning of severe population loss and urging them to seek God rather than worship at Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba. He describes God's power over nature and justice, highlighting Israel's moral failings.

God shows Amos a vision of ripe fruit symbolizing Israel's imminent judgment for exploiting the poor through dishonest trade practices, warning that the land will suffer devastation like the flood of Egypt.

Amos warns the wealthy and complacent people of Zion and Samaria, criticizing their luxury and indifference to Israel's suffering, and declares that God will bring captivity and destroy their city as punishment.

God warns through Amos that Israel will face overwhelming disaster like a flood, with darkness at noon and mourning replacing joy. A spiritual famine will cause people to desperately seek God's word but find none, leading to widespread despair across the land.

God declares His power over earth and nations, reminding Israel of their deliverance from Egypt and other peoples. He warns that He will judge the sinful kingdom, sifting Israel among nations but preserving a faithful remnant.
Obadiah delivers God's message against Edom, warning that despite Edom's pride and strong defenses, it will be humbled and betrayed by its allies, who have turned against it and exposed its secrets.

The prophet Amos describes a vision of the LORD standing on the altar, declaring judgment on Israel's sinners who will be hunted down and destroyed wherever they flee, with the land itself mourning and flooding like during Egypt's flood.

God warns that sinners in Israel will be punished by death, but promises to restore David's fallen kingdom, reclaim lands including Edom, and bring prosperity and security to the people of Israel after their captivity.

God, through Obadiah, condemns Edom for betraying its allies and rejoicing over Judah's defeat when foreigners captured Jerusalem, warning that Edom's leaders and warriors will be destroyed for their violence against their brother nation, Israel.

God, through Obadiah, condemns Edom for rejoicing over Judah's suffering and exploiting them during their calamity, warning that Edom will face the same judgment, while deliverance and restoration await Mount Zion and the house of Jacob.

The sailors cast lots to find who caused the storm, and it fell on Jonah. They questioned him, learning he is a Hebrew who fears God. Jonah admits fleeing God's command and tells them to throw him into the sea to calm the storm.

God promises deliverance and victory for Jacob's descendants over Edom (Esau) and their enemies, with territories changing hands and divine judgment coming from Mount Zion, affirming the Lord's ultimate rule.

The sailors try to row to land but fail due to the storm. They pray to God, then throw Jonah into the sea, calming the storm. They fear God, offer sacrifices, and Jonah is swallowed by a great fish prepared by the LORD.

God commands Jonah to go warn Nineveh, but Jonah tries to escape by ship to Tarshish from Joppa. A violent storm threatens the ship, the sailors pray to their gods, and cast lots, which point to Jonah as the cause of the storm.

Jonah prays to God from inside the great fish, reflecting on his distress and God's deliverance. After Jonah's prayer, God commands the fish to release him onto dry land, continuing the story of Jonah's mission.

God commands Jonah a second time to go to Nineveh and warn them of impending destruction. Jonah obeys, and the people and king of Nineveh repent, fasting and wearing sackcloth, leading God to relent from punishing the city.

The prophet Micah warns that Samaria will be destroyed and its idols destroyed due to Israel's sins, and this judgment will also reach Judah and Jerusalem, causing widespread mourning in towns like Gath, Aphrah, Saphir, Zaanan, and Maroth.

Jonah is angry that God spared Nineveh after its people repented. He prays, expressing his frustration, then sits outside the city. God provides a gourd for shade, which later withers, causing Jonah distress under the hot sun.

The prophet Micah warns the people of Maroth, Lachish, Moreshethgath, Achzib, and Mareshah in Judah that despite hopes for peace, God's judgment and exile are coming due to Israel's sins, signaling impending captivity.

God sends a harsh east wind and sun to distress Jonah, who laments his suffering. God questions Jonah's anger over the short-lived gourd and contrasts it with His own compassion for the large city of Nineveh and its many inhabitants.

The prophet Micah condemns the leaders of Israel for corruption and injustice, warning that false prophets will be silenced and Jerusalem will face destruction because of their sins and reliance on God without true repentance.

The prophet Micah addresses the leaders of Israel, condemning their injustice and cruelty toward the people. He warns that false prophets misleading the nation will be silenced, and God will refuse to answer them.

The prophet Micah condemns the leaders of Israel for their greed and oppression, warning that God will bring disaster on their families. Despite their rejection of true prophets, God’s justice will prevail over the corrupt house of Jacob.

God questions the people of Israel (house of Jacob) about their rebellion and injustice, condemning their oppression and false prophets. He promises to gather the faithful remnant and lead them to safety with their king and the LORD at their head.
The prophet Micah envisions a future time when Jerusalem's temple mount will be exalted, attracting many nations who seek God's guidance, leading to peace and security as God's law spreads from Zion.

The prophet Micah delivers God's message during the reigns of Judah's kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, warning Samaria and Jerusalem of divine judgment for their sins, predicting Samaria's destruction as a consequence.

God promises to gather and strengthen the scattered and oppressed people of Zion, who face enemies and exile to Babylon, assuring them of future redemption and the establishment of His eternal reign over Jerusalem.

God warns that many nations oppose Zion, unaware of His plan to defeat them. He encourages Zion to rise and fight, promising strength and victory, connecting to the theme of future restoration and divine justice for Jerusalem.
God promises to protect the remnant of Jacob from the Assyrian invasion by defeating Assyria and its lands, portraying Israel's survivors as powerful and victorious among many nations.

The prophet Micah warns of an enemy siege against Israel and highlights Bethlehem as the birthplace of a future eternal ruler who will restore and protect Israel, defeating the Assyrian invaders with appointed leaders.

God speaks to Israel, calling the mountains to witness His dispute with His people, reminding them of His past deliverance and prophets, and teaching that true worship requires justice, mercy, and humility rather than sacrifices or offerings.

God declares judgment on Israel's enemies and promises to remove their military power, idolatry, and false practices, purifying the land and executing unprecedented vengeance on the nations opposing His people.

The prophet Micah laments the moral decay and betrayal among the people of Israel, describing widespread corruption and broken relationships. Despite this, he expresses faith in God's salvation and hope for restoration.

God speaks to Israel, condemning their injustice, deceit, and violence, warning of punishment for their sins while reminding them that He desires justice, mercy, and humility rather than empty rituals or wealth.

The prophet Micah speaks of God showing wonders like the Exodus, causing nations to be humbled and fearful. He praises God's mercy in forgiving Israel's sins and fulfilling ancient promises to Jacob and Abraham.
God declares that He will completely destroy Nineveh and its wicked leaders, freeing Judah from oppression and promising peace, urging Judah to remain faithful and celebrate their deliverance.

The prophet Nahum warns Nineveh of an imminent violent attack, describing the city's defenses failing and its people fleeing despite their calls to stand firm, signaling the downfall of this once-powerful Assyrian capital.

The prophet Micah expresses hope amid adversity, trusting God to bring justice and restoration to Israel despite enemies and desolation. He envisions God gathering His people from distant lands like Assyria and restoring them as in ancient times.

The prophet Nahum delivers God's message of judgment against Nineveh, describing God's power and wrath against the wicked, while assuring protection for those who trust Him. This sets the tone for Nineveh's coming destruction.

The prophet Nahum describes the impending fall of Nineveh, once powerful and secure like a calm pool, now vulnerable and deserted. God declares judgment, promising destruction of its warriors and the end of its influence.

The LORD pronounces judgment on Nineveh, describing its violence, deceit, and downfall. The city faces destruction and shame, becoming a desolate spectacle, as enemies will flee and no one will mourn its ruin.

The LORD warns Nineveh of its coming destruction, comparing it to the fallen city of No, despite its past strength and allies. The prophecy describes the city's vulnerability, siege preparations, and inevitable downfall.

The prophet Habakkuk questions God about human helplessness, comparing people to fish caught in nets, highlighting how oppressors rejoice in their power and violence, leading to ongoing destruction of nations.

The LORD warns Nineveh to prepare for siege defenses, but destruction by fire and sword is inevitable. Assyria's leaders and people will be scattered and powerless, with no healing for their grievous wounds caused by their ongoing wickedness.

The prophet Habakkuk laments to God about ongoing violence and injustice in Judah, questioning why God allows wickedness to prevail. God responds, revealing He will raise the fierce Chaldeans (Babylonians) to punish the land.
Habakkuk watches and waits for God's response after questioning injustice. God instructs him to record a vision about a proud oppressor who greedily gathers nations but will face sudden judgment.

The prophet Habakkuk describes the swift and fierce Chaldean army invading violently, mocking kings and capturing many. He questions God about allowing the wicked to oppress the righteous, acknowledging God's role in using them for judgment.

Habakkuk warns a proud oppressor who has violently conquered many nations that those he has wronged will rise against him. He condemns injustice, bloodshed, and exploitation, emphasizing that God's glory will ultimately fill the earth.

Habakkuk warns against those who exploit others through drunkenness and idolatry, condemning violence in Lebanon and false gods. He contrasts this with the LORD's presence in His holy temple, calling for reverent silence on earth.

Habakkuk recalls God's powerful past acts of judgment and salvation, describing His mighty march through nature and nations to save His people and defeat the wicked, causing the prophet to tremble at God's overwhelming presence and power.

The prophet Zephaniah, during King Josiah's reign in Judah, delivers God's message of coming judgment to punish the people of Jerusalem and Judah for idolatry and wickedness, warning that even leaders will face punishment.
Zephaniah warns Judah during King Josiah's reign about the coming "day of the LORD," a time of severe judgment marked by distress, destruction, and divine wrath that no wealth can prevent.

Zephaniah warns Judah's leaders, merchants, and complacent people in Jerusalem of coming judgment on the "day of the LORD," describing widespread destruction and distress as God's punishment for their sins during King Josiah's reign.

The prophet Zephaniah condemns Jerusalem for its corruption and disobedience, describing its leaders and priests as violent and unfaithful, while God declares His justice and past judgments on surrounding nations.

The prophet Zephaniah declares God's judgment against Assyria and its capital Nineveh, predicting its complete destruction and desolation due to its arrogance, following earlier warnings to surrounding nations like Moab and Ammon.

God speaks through Zephaniah, lamenting Israel's continued rebellion despite warnings, announcing a future judgment gathering nations in anger, but promising restoration with a pure language and a faithful remnant trusting in the LORD.

Zephaniah prophesies that the remnant of Judah will reclaim the coastal cities like Ashkelon, while Moab, Ammon, Ethiopia, and Assyria face destruction for their pride and hostility against God's people, with Nineveh becoming desolate.

Zephaniah urges the people of Judah to repent and seek God before His judgment arrives. He prophesies the destruction of Philistine cities Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron, but promises restoration for Judah’s remnant on the coast.

Habakkuk prays to the LORD, recalling God's powerful past acts from Teman and Mount Paran, describing His judgment and salvation as He measures the earth and controls nations, calling for mercy amid His wrath.

Habakkuk describes his fearful reaction to God's powerful intervention against enemies, acknowledging coming hardships like famine and loss, yet affirms his trust and joy in God's strength and salvation despite these trials.

God promises to preserve a humble remnant in Jerusalem who will trust Him and live righteously. He will remove their enemies, restore their honor, and joyfully gather those who were scattered and oppressed.

In Jerusalem under Persian King Darius, the prophet Haggai delivers God's message to Governor Zerubbabel and High Priest Joshua, urging them to prioritize rebuilding the Lord’s temple, warning that neglect brings hardship despite their efforts.

The prophet Haggai delivers God's message to Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people of Judah, encouraging them to be strong and continue rebuilding the temple despite its current humble state, promising God's presence and future glory.

Zechariah sees a man measuring Jerusalem, symbolizing its future expansion and protection by God. An angel commands a message of hope for Zion, promising deliverance from enemies and God's presence as a protective wall.

Prophet Haggai tells Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people in Jerusalem that their efforts and offerings are unclean due to their disobedience, but from the day the temple's foundation was laid, God will begin to bless their work and crops.

Haggai urges Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people of Judah to rebuild the Lord’s temple, explaining their hardships stem from neglecting it. In response, they obey, fear God, and receive assurance of His presence with them.

The LORD, through Haggai, assures Zerubbabel and the people of Judah that though their crops have yet to yield, blessings will come from this day forward. God promises to shake nations and establish Zerubbabel as a chosen leader.

God declares judgment on the nations that harmed Judah and promises to dwell among His people in Jerusalem. He foretells many nations joining Him and calls for reverent silence before His holy presence.

Haggai encourages the people of Judah, assuring God's presence. Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the remnant are inspired to begin rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem on the 24th day of the sixth month, during King Darius's second year.

The prophet Zechariah receives God's message during King Darius's reign, urging the people of Judah to repent like their ancestors were called to but did not listen, reminding them of God's past judgments and the need for change.

Zechariah recalls how past prophets warned Israel’s ancestors, who acknowledged God’s judgment. Then, God reveals a night vision to Zechariah of horses sent to patrol the earth, symbolizing divine oversight during Persian King Darius’s reign.

Zechariah sees horses representing God's messengers surveying the earth, which is at peace. The angel prays for mercy on Jerusalem and Judah after 70 years of punishment, and God promises to return with mercy, rebuild His house, and bless the cities.

God, through the prophet Haggai, speaks to Zerubbabel, Joshua, and the people in Jerusalem, assuring them His ownership of wealth and promising greater glory for the new temple, while highlighting the people's offerings as unclean due to their spiritual state.

Zechariah receives a message from God promising future prosperity and comfort for Jerusalem and Zion. He then sees a vision of four horns symbolizing nations that scattered Israel, and four carpenters representing forces sent to overthrow those oppressors.

The LORD speaks to Joshua the high priest, promising him authority if he remains faithful, and foretells the coming of the "Branch," a servant who will remove the land's sin, leading to peace and security in Jerusalem.

Zechariah sees four chariots with different colored horses emerging between brass mountains; an angel explains they are heavenly spirits sent by God to patrol the earth, with some calming God's spirit in the north country.

The prophet Zechariah sees a flying scroll symbolizing a curse against thieves and false swearers, then an ephah (a measuring basket) with a woman inside representing wickedness, as an angel explains these visions about judgment over the earth.

Zechariah sees a vision of Joshua the high priest accused by Satan before God's angel. God defends Joshua, removes his filthy clothes, and promises him authority if he remains faithful in leading Jerusalem's temple worship.

God promises to restore the people of Judah and Israel to live in Jerusalem, assuring them of peace and prosperity after past hardships and conflicts, encouraging them to be strong as the temple's foundation is laid.

Zechariah sees a vision where a woman symbolizing wickedness is trapped in a lead-weighted basket (ephah). Two winged women carry it to Shinar, where it will be set up, continuing the angel's explanation of judgment on sin.

The angel tells Zechariah that Zerubbabel, governor of Judah, will complete the temple he began building, and explains that the two olive trees symbolize two anointed leaders who serve God’s purposes on earth.

God speaks to Zechariah, declaring His passionate commitment to Zion (Jerusalem), promising to return, dwell there, restore peace, and gather His scattered people from east and west to live righteously in Jerusalem.

In the fourth year of King Darius, Zechariah receives God's message after Sherezer and Regemmelech ask priests and prophets if they should continue mourning rituals. God questions the people's true intentions behind their fasting and calls them to heed past prophetic warnings.

God, through Zechariah, recalls how former prophets warned Jerusalem and surrounding cities to act justly and show mercy, but the people ignored these commands, leading to God's judgment and their exile, leaving the land desolate.

The angel speaks to Zechariah about the calming of God's spirit in the north, then God commands Zechariah to crown Joshua the high priest with silver and gold, symbolizing the coming leader called The Branch who will build and rule the Lord's temple.

God delivers a prophecy against cities near Israel—Hadrach, Damascus, Hamath, Tyre, Sidon, and Philistine cities like Ashkelon, Gaza, Ashdod, and Ekron—predicting their downfall and the rise of a faithful remnant aligned with Judah.

God promises to free Jerusalem’s captives and strengthen Judah and Ephraim against their enemies, symbolized by Greece. He will protect and empower His people, bringing joy and abundance to Zion as a sign of His favor and salvation.

God promises that traditional fasts for Judah will turn into joyful celebrations, and people from many cities and nations will come to Jerusalem to seek and worship the LORD, showing unity and recognition of God's presence with the Jewish people.
