God speaks through Zechariah, urging the people to seek Him for rain and guidance, condemning false idols and leaders, and promising to strengthen and restore the houses of Judah and Joseph with His mercy and protection.

The prophet Zechariah speaks of destruction in Lebanon, Bashan, and Jordan, symbolizing the downfall of leaders and nations. God declares judgment on unfaithful shepherds who harm their people, and Zechariah takes two staffs named Beauty and Bands as he tends the flock.

God declares judgment on Philistine cities like Ekron but promises protection for Jerusalem, urging Zion to rejoice as a just king arrives bringing peace and liberation for exiles, signaling God's defense and restoration of His people.

God promises to restore and strengthen the tribes of Judah, Joseph, and Ephraim, gathering them from Egypt and Assyria to settle in Gilead and Lebanon, defeating their enemies and renewing their joy and unity under His protection.

God declares a prophecy about Jerusalem and Judah facing siege by surrounding nations; despite this, God will protect Jerusalem, confuse their enemies, empower Judah's leaders, and restore Jerusalem as a secure and inhabited city.

God reassures the people of Judah and Israel that though they were once cursed among nations, He will save and bless them. He instructs them to live truthfully and peacefully, turning traditional fasts into joyful celebrations in Jerusalem.

Zechariah, acting as a prophetic shepherd, rejects three leaders, breaks his covenant symbolized by staffs named Beauty and Bands, receives thirty pieces of silver, and signals the breaking of unity between Judah and Israel, following God's instructions.

God instructs Zechariah to take tools symbolizing a foolish shepherd, predicting a leader who neglects and harms the people of Israel, bringing judgment on false leaders who abandon their responsibilities.

The angel reawakens Zechariah to show him a vision of a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees, symbolizing God's spirit empowering Zerubbabel to complete the temple rebuilding in Jerusalem despite obstacles.

God speaks about a future time when Judah's leaders will fiercely defend Jerusalem, restoring its people and protecting them from enemies. He promises to empower David's house and pour out grace, leading to mourning over one they have pierced.

God promises to pour out grace on Jerusalem's people, who will mourn deeply for one they have pierced, with widespread, family-by-family mourning across Jerusalem, reflecting a profound communal grief after conflict.
God speaks of a wounded shepherd whose harm causes the scattering of his followers; despite widespread loss, a faithful remnant will be purified and recognized as God's people in Jerusalem.

God promises to cleanse Jerusalem and the house of David from sin and idolatry, removing false prophets. People will reject lying prophets, who will deny their role and bear wounds from betrayal by close friends.

God declares Jerusalem will be safely inhabited after a devastating plague strikes those who fought against it, causing chaos among them. Survivors from the nations attacking Jerusalem will annually worship the LORD and celebrate the feast of tabernacles.

God warns of a future day when all nations will attack Jerusalem, leading to the city's capture and partial exile. Then, the Lord will intervene, standing on the Mount of Olives, which will split, providing refuge as He comes with His holy ones.

God, through the prophet Malachi, rebukes the priests of Israel for disrespecting His altar by offering defective sacrifices and treating worship as a burden, warning that deceitful offerings dishonor His great name among the nations.

God, speaking through the prophet Malachi to Israel, reminds them of His love for Jacob over Esau and condemns Edom's attempts to rebuild. He rebukes the priests for dishonoring Him by offering defiled sacrifices and treating His altar with contempt.

God, through the prophet Malachi, rebukes the priests of Israel for offering defective sacrifices and treating His altar with contempt, warning that He will not accept their offerings while His name will be honored among the Gentiles.

God promises that during a time of upheaval near Jerusalem, people will flee to a valley extending to Azal, recalling a past earthquake in King Uzziah's reign. God will come with the saints, bringing a unique day, flowing waters, and Jerusalem's restoration and safety.

God declares that after a great battle for Jerusalem, surviving nations will annually worship Him there during the feast of tabernacles, with blessings for obedience and punishments like drought for disobedience, marking a time of holiness in Jerusalem.

God addresses the priests of Israel, warning them that their failure to honor Him and uphold the covenant with Levi will bring curses and disgrace. He reminds them of Levi's faithful example and their role as His messengers.

God rebukes the priests of Judah for leading people astray, breaking the covenant of Levi, and being unjust. He condemns Judah for unfaithfulness, warning that those who profane His altar in Jerusalem will be cut off and their offerings rejected.

The LORD, through the prophet Malachi, rebukes the people of Israel for insincere worship and unfaithfulness in marriage, warning them against treachery toward their spouses and questioning their false claims that God accepts evil and ignores justice.

This passage lists the genealogy of Jesus, tracing his lineage from Abraham through King David and continuing through the generations leading up to the Babylonian exile, establishing Jesus' royal and Jewish heritage.

God warns of a coming day of judgment that will destroy the wicked but bring healing to those who fear Him. He reminds Israel to keep Moses' law and promises to send Elijah to restore family unity before this day arrives.

This passage traces Jesus' genealogy through Joseph, highlights the symbolic 14-generation periods from Abraham to Christ, and describes Joseph's initial doubts and the angel's reassurance about Mary's divine pregnancy.

God speaks to the people of Israel (sons of Jacob), urging them to return to His ways by bringing tithes and offerings. He promises blessings and protection if they obey, while addressing their complaints and accusations against Him.

God responds to the people of Israel, who complain that serving Him is pointless because the wicked prosper. He assures that He hears the faithful, records their devotion, and will distinguish between the righteous and the wicked in the future.

God speaks through the prophet Malachi, announcing a coming messenger who will prepare the way for the Lord's arrival to purify the priests of Levi and judge Israel for their sins, promising justice and restoration for Judah and Jerusalem.

An angel tells Joseph in a dream to name Mary's child Jesus, who will save people from sins, fulfilling prophecy about a virgin birth. Joseph obeys, marries Mary, and names the child Jesus after his birth.

Wise men follow a star to find Jesus in Bethlehem, worship him, and give gifts. Warned in a dream, they avoid Herod. Then an angel tells Joseph to flee to Egypt with Mary and Jesus to escape Herod's threat.

After fleeing to Egypt to escape King Herod's plot to kill Jesus, Joseph and his family stay there until Herod dies. Herod then orders the massacre of Bethlehem's young boys, fulfilling prophecy, before Joseph is told in a dream to return to Israel.
Joseph, warned by an angel, returns from Egypt with Mary and Jesus but avoids Judea due to Archelaus' rule, settling in Nazareth in Galilee, fulfilling prophetic words about the Messiah's upbringing.

John the Baptist warns of judgment and announces one greater than himself who will baptize with the Holy Spirit. Jesus comes from Galilee to be baptized by John in the Jordan, after which the Spirit descends and God's voice affirms Jesus as His Son.

After his baptism, Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness where he fasts for 40 days. The devil tempts him three times, but Jesus resists each by quoting Scripture, affirming his obedience to God alone.

John the Baptist begins preaching repentance in the Judaean wilderness, attracting crowds from Jerusalem and nearby regions. He warns religious leaders to produce genuine repentance, emphasizing the coming judgment and the nearness of God's kingdom.

After Jesus' birth in Bethlehem during King Herod's reign, wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem seeking the "King of the Jews" guided by a star. Herod, disturbed, consults Jewish leaders and sends the wise men to find Jesus.

Jesus rejects Satan’s final temptation in the wilderness; angels attend him. After learning John is imprisoned, Jesus moves to Capernaum in Galilee, begins preaching repentance, and calls fishermen Simon Peter and Andrew to follow him.

Jesus calls James and John, sons of Zebedee, to follow him, and they immediately leave their work and family. He then travels through Galilee, teaching, preaching, and healing many, gaining fame and attracting large crowds from surrounding regions.

Jesus, seeing the large crowds following him in Galilee, goes up a mountain and begins teaching his disciples, delivering the Beatitudes and calling them the salt of the earth, emphasizing their role and blessings in God's kingdom.

Jesus teaches his disciples on a mountain near Galilee, urging them to be like salt and light in the world, emphasizing the enduring importance of the law, and calling for a righteousness surpassing that of the scribes and Pharisees.

Jesus teaches his disciples on a mountain near Galilee, emphasizing that true righteousness must surpass that of the scribes and Pharisees, and urging reconciliation with others before worship to avoid judgment and punishment.

Jesus teaches his followers in Galilee how to pray sincerely, giving the Lord's Prayer as a model, emphasizing forgiveness, and instructing them to fast discreetly, contrasting genuine devotion with hypocritical public displays.

Jesus continues teaching his disciples on a mountain near Galilee, expanding on Old Testament laws about divorce, oaths, retaliation, and generosity, urging higher moral standards and nonresistance to evil.
Jesus continues teaching his disciples on moral conduct, expanding on commandments about anger, adultery, and divorce, emphasizing inner purity and the seriousness of sin in the kingdom of heaven.

Jesus continues teaching his disciples near the Sea of Galilee, warning against hypocritical judgment and encouraging persistent prayer, illustrating God's readiness to give good gifts to those who ask.

Jesus teaches his followers in Galilee to give and pray sincerely, not for public praise like the hypocrites, but privately to God who rewards what is done in secret. He warns against empty, repetitive prayers like those of the Gentiles.

Jesus continues teaching his disciples in Galilee, urging them to practice fasting and generosity privately to receive God's reward, to prioritize heavenly treasures over earthly wealth, and to trust God rather than worry about daily needs.

Jesus teaches his followers not to worry about daily needs like food, drink, or clothing, using birds and lilies as examples of God's care. He urges them to prioritize God's kingdom, trusting God to provide, emphasizing faith over anxiety.

Jesus concludes his teaching by warning that true discipleship is shown by actions, not just words, using the metaphor of wise and foolish builders. The crowd is amazed by his authoritative teaching, contrasting with the scribes' style.

Jesus teaches his followers in Galilee about God's generosity, urging them to treat others as they wish to be treated. He warns about false prophets, explaining that their true nature is revealed by their actions, like trees judged by their fruit.

After teaching on the mountain, Jesus is followed by crowds. A leper asks for healing and is cleansed by Jesus' touch. In Capernaum, a Roman centurion shows great faith, asking Jesus to heal his paralyzed servant by word alone.

Jesus praises the centurion's exceptional faith, heals his servant instantly, then heals Peter’s mother-in-law’s fever. He casts out many demons and heals the sick, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy, before instructing his followers to cross to the other side of the lake.

Jesus returns to his hometown, heals a paralyzed man, and forgives his sins, causing controversy with scribes. He then calls Matthew, a tax collector, to follow him and dines with many sinners, drawing criticism from religious leaders.

Jesus calls his twelve disciples, gives them authority to heal and cast out demons, and sends them to preach to Israel's "lost sheep," instructing them to rely on hospitality and freely share their gifts without money or extra supplies.

Jesus, seeing large crowds, decides to cross to the other side of the sea. A scribe and a disciple express their desire to follow him, but Jesus emphasizes the cost of discipleship. During the sea crossing, a storm arises, and Jesus calms it, amazing his disciples.

After calming a storm on the Sea of Galilee, Jesus arrives in the region of the Gergesenes, where two demon-possessed men confront him. He casts the demons into a herd of pigs, which then drown, causing the local people to ask Jesus to leave.

After healing a girl, Jesus is followed by two blind men who he heals in a house; then he casts out a demon from a mute man. Despite Pharisees' accusations, Jesus continues teaching, healing, and urges his disciples to pray for more workers to help the needy crowds.

Jesus instructs his twelve disciples as he sends them out to preach in towns of Israel, advising them to find worthy hosts, offer peace, and be prepared for rejection and persecution, assuring them that the Spirit will guide their words in trials.

Jesus dines with tax collectors and sinners, prompting Pharisees' criticism. Jesus explains his mission to call sinners, not the righteous, and responds to questions about fasting with parables about new and old cloth and wine, highlighting a new way of life.

Jesus is instructing his twelve disciples, warning them of upcoming persecution and betrayal, assuring them that the Holy Spirit will guide their words, and encouraging them to remain faithful despite opposition in Israel.

Jesus teaches his followers on a mountain near Galilee, urging them to love and pray for their enemies, showing God's impartial kindness, and calling them to live with perfect love like their heavenly Father.

Jesus teaches about new teachings needing a fresh approach, then responds to a synagogue ruler whose daughter has died. Along the way, a woman with a long illness is healed by faith, and Jesus raises the ruler’s daughter from death, spreading his fame.

Jesus teaches his twelve disciples about fearing God over humans, the value God places on them, the cost of discipleship, and the divisions his message may cause even within families, emphasizing commitment and the consequences of confessing or denying him.

Jesus concludes his instructions to the twelve disciples, emphasizing the cost of discipleship and the rewards for those who welcome his messengers, linking acceptance of his followers to acceptance of himself and God the Father.

After instructing his twelve disciples, Jesus travels to teach in nearby towns. John the Baptist, imprisoned, sends disciples to ask if Jesus is the expected Messiah. Jesus points to his miracles as proof and praises John as a great prophet preparing the way.

Jesus speaks to the crowds about John the Baptist, affirming his role as the prophesied messenger preparing the way for Jesus. He contrasts John’s ascetic lifestyle with his own and criticizes the generation’s rejection of both.

Jesus prays to the Father, acknowledging divine wisdom and authority given to him alone, then invites those burdened to come to him for rest, offering a gentle and humble guidance that brings relief and peace.

Jesus defends his lifestyle against criticism and rebukes the unrepentant cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, warning of harsher judgment than ancient cities like Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom, then thanks God for revealing truth to the humble.

Jesus teaches by the Sea of Galilee to a large crowd using the Parable of the Sower, explaining different responses to God's word. His disciples ask why he uses parables, and Jesus explains it's to reveal truths only to those given understanding.

Jesus responds to Pharisees accusing him of casting out demons by Beelzebub, explaining his power comes from God's Spirit, affirming the arrival of God's kingdom, and teaching that true character is shown by one's words and actions.

Jesus explains to his disciples why he teaches the crowds in parables: only they are given insight into the kingdom of heaven, while others remain spiritually blind, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy about hardened hearts. He then introduces the parable of the sower.

Jesus warns the crowd that those who reject him are like a man possessed by evil spirits who worsen without true faith. His family arrives, but he redefines kinship as those who follow God's will, emphasizing spiritual bonds over blood relations.

Jesus quotes Isaiah about the Messiah's gentle nature, then heals a demon-possessed blind and mute man, amazing the crowd. The Pharisees accuse Jesus of using demonic power, but he refutes them, explaining that his miracles show God's kingdom has arrived.

Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, challenging Pharisees who question the lawfulness of healing that day. After the healing, Pharisees plot against Jesus, who then withdraws while crowds follow and he continues healing, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy.

Jesus teaches that people's words reveal their true character and warns of judgment for careless speech. When scribes and Pharisees demand a sign, he refers to Jonah's story as a foreshadowing of his own death and resurrection, highlighting their unbelief.

Jesus explains the parable of the sower to his disciples by describing different responses to the message of the kingdom, then introduces another parable about good seed and tares sown in a field, highlighting the presence of both good and evil in the world.

Jesus continues teaching the gathered crowd by the sea, explaining the kingdom of heaven through parables about a field with wheat and tares growing together, a mustard seed growing into a tree, and leaven spreading through dough.

Jesus explains to his disciples that at the end of the world, angels will separate the wicked from the righteous, likening the kingdom of heaven to hidden treasure, a valuable pearl, and a net sorting fish, illustrating the value and judgment in God's kingdom.

Jesus concludes teaching parables by the sea, explaining the final judgment where angels separate the wicked from the righteous. He then returns to his hometown, Nazareth, where locals doubt him and his works due to familiarity and unbelief.
Jesus rescues Peter from sinking while walking on the sea, calming the storm. They reach Gennesaret, where locals bring the sick to Jesus, believing even touching his garment can heal them.

Jesus teaches his disciples near Galilee that moral corruption comes from the heart, not from eating without washing hands, addressing Pharisees' criticism. Afterward, he travels to the region of Tyre and Sidon.

Scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem confront Jesus about his disciples not following traditional handwashing. Jesus criticizes their traditions for overriding God's commandments and teaches the crowd that moral defilement comes from words, not food.

After John the Baptist's execution, his disciples bury him and inform Jesus, who retreats by boat to a remote place. Despite this, a large crowd follows, and Jesus heals them and miraculously feeds about five thousand men with five loaves and two fish.

After feeding 5,000 men plus women and children, Jesus sends his disciples ahead by boat while he prays alone on a mountain. Later, during a storm, Jesus walks on the sea to reach them, and Peter briefly walks on water before fearing and sinking.

Jesus travels to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman asks him to heal her demon-possessed daughter. After testing her faith, he grants her request and then moves near the Sea of Galilee to teach.

Jesus teaches the crowd by parables about the kingdom of heaven, fulfilling prophecy. After dismissing the crowd, he explains to his disciples the parable of the tares, describing the final judgment and separation of good and evil.

Jesus' disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, angering Pharisees. Jesus defends them with scripture, claiming authority over the Sabbath. He then enters a synagogue where a man with a withered hand awaits, and Pharisees plan to accuse him.

Jesus healed many sick people near the Sea of Galilee, then fed 4,000 men plus women and children with seven loaves and a few fish after his disciples worried about food. Afterward, he sent the crowd away and traveled to Magdala.

Pharisees and Sadducees ask Jesus for a heavenly sign to test him; Jesus rebukes their unbelief and warns his disciples to beware of their teachings, reminding them of the previous miracles of feeding thousands with loaves.

Jesus explains to his disciples that his warning about "leaven" refers to the teachings of the Pharisees and Sadducees, not literal bread. At Caesarea Philippi, Peter declares Jesus as the Messiah, prompting Jesus to affirm Peter's foundational role in his church.

Jesus teaches his disciples about the cost of true discipleship, emphasizing self-denial and the eternal value of the soul, and foretells his future return in glory to judge humanity, promising some present will witness his kingdom's arrival.

After discussing temple taxes, Jesus' disciples ask who is greatest in heaven's kingdom; Jesus uses a child to teach humility and warns against causing believers to sin, emphasizing the seriousness of leading others astray.

Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain where He is transfigured, appearing radiant with Moses and Elijah. God affirms Jesus as His Son, and Jesus instructs them to keep this vision secret until after His resurrection.

Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and thinks he’s John risen. John, imprisoned for opposing Herod’s marriage to Herodias, is beheaded at Herod’s birthday by Herodias’ daughter. John’s disciples bury him and tell Jesus.

After Jesus healed a boy possessed by a demon, his disciples asked why they failed to cast it out; Jesus explained that faith and prayer are needed. He then foretold his betrayal and resurrection, and later instructed Peter on paying temple tax in Capernaum.

Jesus declares Peter as the foundation for his church and gives him authority, then warns the disciples to keep his identity secret. He predicts his suffering and resurrection, rebukes Peter's objection, and teaches about self-denial and discipleship.

Jesus teaches his disciples about the seriousness of sin and the value of every believer, especially the vulnerable, using vivid imagery and a parable about a shepherd seeking a lost sheep to emphasize God's care for the lost.

Jesus responds to Peter's question about forgiveness by telling a parable of a king forgiving a huge debt of a servant who then refuses to forgive a small debt owed to him, highlighting the importance of mercy among believers.

After teaching in Galilee, Jesus travels to Judea beyond the Jordan, where large crowds follow him. The Pharisees question him about divorce laws, prompting Jesus to explain God's original design for marriage and the exception for marital unfaithfulness.

Jesus concludes a parable about forgiveness, describing a king punishing a servant who, after being forgiven a huge debt, refuses to forgive a smaller debt owed to him, warning that God will similarly judge unforgiving hearts.

Jesus tells a parable about a landowner hiring workers at different times of the day to work in his vineyard, illustrating God's kingdom and the equal rewards given regardless of when one begins serving.

Jesus' disciples are shocked by his teaching on the difficulty for the rich to enter God's kingdom. Jesus assures them that salvation is possible with God, promising rewards for those who have left everything to follow him, highlighting reversal of worldly status.

Jesus tells his disciples Elijah (John the Baptist) has come but was unrecognized. A man brings his demon-possessed son after the disciples fail to heal him. Jesus cures the boy, and the disciples ask why they couldn't cast out the demon.

Jesus teaches his disciples near Jericho that true greatness comes from serving others, not ruling over them. As they leave Jericho, two blind men call out to Jesus for mercy, and He heals them, restoring their sight.

Jesus explains to laborers in a vineyard why those hired last receive the same pay as those hired first, teaching about fairness and God's grace. Then, on the way to Jerusalem, Jesus predicts his betrayal and death, and the mother of James and John asks Jesus for a favor for her sons.

Jesus is approached by the mother of James and John, asking for her sons to have high positions in his kingdom. Jesus warns about the hardships ahead and teaches the disciples about true leadership, contrasting worldly power with servant leadership.
Jesus teaches about marriage and divorce to his disciples near Judea beyond Jordan, then welcomes children despite the disciples' objections. Afterwards, a man asks Jesus how to gain eternal life.

A rich young man asks Jesus how to gain eternal life; Jesus lists commandments and tells him to give his wealth to the poor and follow Him. The man leaves sad, prompting Jesus to teach about the difficulty for the rich to enter God's kingdom.

Jesus teaches his disciples about forgiveness and resolving conflicts within the community, emphasizing reconciliation and the authority given to them. Peter asks about forgiveness limits, and Jesus replies that forgiveness should be unlimited.
Jesus, returning to Jerusalem, curses a barren fig tree, demonstrating faith's power, then faces questioning by chief priests and elders about his authority as he teaches in the temple.

Jesus approaches Jerusalem near Bethphage on the Mount of Olives and sends two disciples to fetch a donkey and colt, fulfilling prophecy. He rides into Jerusalem amid crowds praising him as the coming King.

Jesus enters Jerusalem, recognized as a prophet from Nazareth, cleanses the temple by driving out merchants, heals the disabled, and responds to the chief priests' displeasure before staying overnight in Bethany and returning hungry to the city.

Jesus responds to the chief priests and elders questioning his authority by asking about John's baptism, exposing their dilemma. He then tells a parable about two sons to illustrate true obedience, contrasting religious leaders with sinners.

Jesus continues teaching in parables, describing a king who invites guests to his son's wedding. The original invitees refuse and mistreat the servants, so the king invites others from the streets, filling the wedding with guests.

Jesus tells religious leaders two parables about obedience and rejection, contrasting those who repent like tax collectors and sinners with those who refuse to believe, and describing wicked tenants who kill the landowner’s servants and son.

Jesus continues his parable about a king's wedding feast, highlighting a guest without proper attire who is cast out. Then Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to Caesar.
Jesus questions the Pharisees in Jerusalem about the Messiah's lineage, challenging their understanding by citing Psalm 110, leaving them unable to respond or question him further.

Jesus responds to the Sadducees' question about resurrection, explaining life after death and God's power, astonishing the crowd. Then, a lawyer asks Jesus about the greatest commandment, leading Jesus to summarize the law as love for God and neighbor.

Jesus tells a parable about wicked tenants killing the landowner's son to seize his inheritance, warning the chief priests and Pharisees that God's kingdom will be taken from them and given to others who produce its fruits.

Jesus responds to Pharisees about paying taxes to Caesar, then addresses Sadducees' question on resurrection and marriage, correcting their misunderstanding about life after death and the power of God.

Jesus criticizes the scribes and Pharisees in Jerusalem for focusing on minor religious details while neglecting justice, mercy, and faith, comparing their outward appearances to clean cups and whitewashed tombs that hide inner corruption and hypocrisy.

Jesus addresses the crowd and disciples in Jerusalem, condemning the scribes and Pharisees for hypocrisy, unjust actions, and misleading teachings, highlighting their pride and false piety while emphasizing humility and true righteousness.

Jesus addresses the crowd and his disciples in Jerusalem, warning against following the hypocritical actions of the scribes and Pharisees, who demand strict obedience but fail to practice what they preach. He teaches humility and servanthood as true greatness.

Jesus condemns the scribes and Pharisees in Jerusalem for their hypocrisy and warns they will continue persecuting prophets, bringing judgment upon their generation for the blood of all righteous people shed from Abel to Zacharias.

Jesus warns the people of Jerusalem that judgment will come upon their generation for rejecting and killing prophets, expressing sorrow over their refusal to accept his protection and foretelling their city's desolation and his future absence until they acknowledge him.

Jesus warns his disciples on the Mount of Olives about a time of great tribulation, false messiahs, and cosmic signs preceding his powerful return, emphasizing the need for discernment and faithfulness amid deception and suffering.

After leaving the temple in Jerusalem, Jesus warns his disciples on the Mount of Olives that the temple will be destroyed and describes signs of future turmoil, including deception, wars, and persecution before the end times.

Jesus warns his disciples about coming times of betrayal, false prophets, and widespread evil before the end. He instructs those in Judea to flee when they see the prophesied "abomination of desolation," urging readiness for severe tribulation.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, describing his future return with power and glory, urging them to recognize the signs and be ready, comparing his coming to the unexpected flood in Noah's time.
Jesus warns his disciples on the Mount of Olives about the unexpected timing of his return, urging them to stay vigilant and faithful like a wise servant managing his household responsibly.

Jesus concludes his teaching on readiness by contrasting a faithful servant rewarded with authority and an unfaithful servant punished unexpectedly, emphasizing the importance of vigilance before the Lord's return.

Jesus teaches about being ready for his unexpected return, then tells a parable of a master entrusting servants with money (talents) before traveling; two invest wisely and are praised upon his return for their faithfulness.

Jesus continues teaching about judgment, describing the punishment of an unfaithful servant and the final separation of people like a shepherd divides sheep and goats, highlighting acts of kindness as criteria for inheriting God's kingdom.

Jesus describes the final judgment where the Son of Man separates people like a shepherd divides sheep and goats, rewarding those who helped the needy and punishing those who did not, highlighting care for "the least" as service to Him.

Jesus explains a woman's anointing as preparation for his burial, then Judas agrees to betray Jesus for silver. The disciples prepare for the Passover meal, where Jesus reveals one will betray him, causing sorrow among them.
Jesus prays in the Garden of Gethsemane, struggling with his impending suffering while his disciples fall asleep. Judas arrives with armed men sent by the chief priests to betray and arrest Jesus.

Jesus tells his disciples about his upcoming betrayal and crucifixion during Passover. Meanwhile, the Jewish leaders plot to kill him but avoid doing so during the feast. In Bethany, a woman anoints Jesus with costly ointment, preparing him for burial.

Jesus predicts his disciples will abandon him that night but promises to meet them again after his resurrection in Galilee; Peter insists he won't deny Jesus, who then prays in deep sorrow at Gethsemane, asking God if the coming suffering can be avoided.

Jesus tells a parable about a master who rewards two servants for wisely investing talents, but rebukes the third for hiding his talent out of fear, instructing that his talent be given to the one with ten talents.

During the Last Supper in Jerusalem, Jesus tells his disciples one will betray him, identifying Judas indirectly. He institutes the Lord’s Supper, symbolizing his body and blood, then predicts the disciples will abandon him that night on the Mount of Olives.

Jesus tells a parable about ten virgins waiting for a bridegroom; five are prepared with oil, five are not. When the bridegroom arrives unexpectedly, only the prepared enter the wedding, illustrating the need for readiness for the Son of Man’s coming.

Jesus confronts the crowd arresting him in Jerusalem, noting his peaceful teaching in the temple. His disciples flee, and Jesus is taken to Caiaphas, the high priest, where religious leaders seek false testimony to condemn him. Jesus remains mostly silent.

Judas arrives with armed officials sent by chief priests to arrest Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane. Jesus is betrayed with a kiss, one disciple wounds a servant, but Jesus stops violence, emphasizing scripture must be fulfilled.

Jesus remains silent before the high priest Caiaphas, who demands if He is the Christ. Jesus affirms, leading to accusations of blasphemy and His mistreatment. Meanwhile, Peter denies knowing Jesus twice as bystanders accuse him.

Peter denies knowing Jesus three times after Jesus' arrest, fulfilling Jesus' earlier prediction; this happens outside the high priest's palace as the cock crows, leading Peter to remember Jesus' words and weep bitterly.

Early morning in Jerusalem, the Jewish leaders arrest Jesus and hand him to Roman governor Pilate. Judas, remorseful for betraying Jesus for thirty silver coins, returns the money, then dies. The priests use the coins to buy a burial field, fulfilling prophecy.

Pilate offers the crowd a choice to release Jesus or Barabbas, but the chief priests persuade them to choose Barabbas and demand Jesus' crucifixion. Pilate washes his hands, symbolizing his claimed innocence, then hands Jesus over to be scourged and mocked by Roman soldiers.

Roman soldiers mock Jesus by dressing him in a scarlet robe and crown of thorns, then lead him to Golgotha for crucifixion. Simon of Cyrene is forced to carry Jesus' cross, and Jesus is crucified alongside two thieves with a sign declaring him King of the Jews.

Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two thieves; passersby, chief priests, and elders mock him, challenging his claim as Son of God. Darkness covers the land from noon to 3 PM, and Jesus cries out in anguish before being offered vinegar to drink.

Jesus stands silently before Pilate, the Roman governor, who questions him about being King of the Jews. Despite accusations from Jewish leaders, Jesus remains silent. Pilate offers to release a prisoner, Barabbas or Jesus, but the crowd, urged by priests, demands Barabbas.

Joseph of Arimathaea, a disciple of Jesus, asks Pilate for Jesus' body and buries it in his own new tomb. Mary Magdalene and another Mary watch. The chief priests and Pharisees secure the tomb to prevent Jesus' disciples from claiming he rose.

Jesus instructs the women to tell his disciples to meet him in Galilee. Meanwhile, the guards report the events to the chief priests, who bribe them to spread a false story. The disciples meet Jesus in Galilee, worship him, and receive the Great Commission.

This passage introduces the gospel of Jesus Christ, highlighting John the Baptist preaching repentance and baptizing in the wilderness of Judea. Jesus from Nazareth is then baptized by John in the Jordan River, marking the start of his ministry.

At Jesus' crucifixion near Golgotha, soldiers offer him vinegar; Jesus dies, the temple veil tears, an earthquake occurs, and saints rise. A centurion declares Jesus the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathaea asks Pilate for Jesus' body.

Jesus calls James and John, sons of Zebedee, to follow him, and they leave their father. In Capernaum's synagogue, Jesus teaches with authority and casts out an unclean spirit, astonishing the people and spreading his fame across Galilee.

Mary Magdalene and the other Mary visit Jesus' tomb early Sunday morning, witnessing an angel roll away the stone. The angel announces Jesus' resurrection and instructs them to tell the disciples, then Jesus appears to them in Galilee.

Jesus heals a paralyzed man in Capernaum, demonstrating his authority to forgive sins, which amazes the crowd. He then calls Levi, a tax collector, to follow him, and dines with sinners, prompting criticism from religious leaders.

After Jesus taught in the synagogue in Capernaum, his fame spread across Galilee. He healed Simon's mother-in-law and many others, then prayed alone. His followers found him and he decided to preach in nearby towns, continuing his ministry.

Jesus responds to criticism from scribes and Pharisees in Capernaum for eating with tax collectors and sinners, explaining his mission to call sinners. He also addresses questions about fasting, using metaphors of new cloth and wine to illustrate change.

Jesus returns to Capernaum, where a large crowd gathers in a house to hear him. Friends bring a paralyzed man by lowering him through the roof, and Jesus forgives the man's sins, prompting skeptical thoughts from some scribes nearby.

Jesus from Nazareth is baptized by John in the Jordan River, affirmed by God's voice and the Spirit. Led into the wilderness for 40 days, he later begins preaching in Galilee and calls fishermen Simon, Andrew, James, and John to follow him.

Jesus continues preaching and healing across Galilee, casting out demons. A leper begs Jesus for healing, which Jesus grants by touching him. Jesus instructs secrecy, but the healed man spreads the news, causing Jesus to avoid towns and stay in remote areas.

Jesus, after healing many and being sought by crowds from Galilee and beyond, arranges a boat for space, commands demons to silence, then chooses twelve disciples, including Peter and Judas, to preach and heal; the large crowd presses in again.

Jesus teaches about new teachings needing new forms, then defends his disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath in Capernaum, citing David's example and asserting his authority over the Sabbath against Pharisees' objections.

Jesus is surrounded by a large crowd and accused by his friends and scribes from Jerusalem of being insane and possessed by Beelzebub. He responds with parables about division and warns against blaspheming the Holy Spirit. His family arrives to see him.

Jesus heals a man with a withered hand in a synagogue on the Sabbath, challenging the Pharisees who watch to accuse him. After healing, the Pharisees plot against him, and Jesus retreats to the sea, followed by large crowds from various regions.
Jesus' family arrives outside while he teaches a crowd, seeking to speak with him. He redefines family as those who follow God's will, emphasizing spiritual bonds over biological ties.

After teaching a parable by the sea, Jesus explains its meaning privately to his disciples near Galilee, describing different responses to God's message and why he uses parables to reveal truths to followers but not outsiders.

Jesus teaches a large crowd by the Sea of Galilee using the Parable of the Sower, describing different responses to God's word. Later, alone with his disciples, they ask him to explain the parable's meaning.

Jesus explains to his disciples the meaning of the parable of the sower, describing different responses to God's word and emphasizing the importance of hearing and acting on it. He also teaches about revealing truth and the principle of receiving in measure.
Jesus explains parables privately to his disciples, then sets out across the sea with them. A violent storm arises, but Jesus calms it, prompting his followers to marvel at his authority over nature.

Jesus continues teaching by the sea near Galilee, using parables to explain the kingdom of God. He compares it to growing seeds and a mustard seed's growth, speaking publicly in parables but privately explaining them to his disciples.

Jesus and his disciples arrive in the Gadarenes region across the sea. A man possessed by many demons, living among tombs and uncontrollable, meets Jesus and begs not to be tormented, revealing the demons' name as Legion and requesting to enter nearby pigs.

Jesus allows the many demons to enter a herd of swine, which then drown. The herdsmen report this, and the local people see the healed man, now sane and clothed, but ask Jesus to leave their region. The man spreads news of Jesus' mercy in Decapolis.

Jesus instructs the twelve disciples on how to travel lightly and handle rejection during their mission to preach repentance and heal the sick. Meanwhile, King Herod hears rumors about Jesus, mistakenly thinking he is John the Baptist resurrected.

Jesus returns to his hometown with his disciples, teaching in the synagogue where locals doubt him due to his ordinary background. He heals a few sick people, marvels at their unbelief, then sends out the twelve apostles in pairs with authority over evil spirits, instructing them to travel light.

Jesus senses healing power leaving him and asks who touched him; a healed woman confesses. Then news arrives that Jairus' daughter has died, but Jesus encourages Jairus to keep faith and goes with only Peter, James, and John to her home.

King Herod reluctantly orders John the Baptist's beheading due to a promise made at a banquet. John's disciples bury him, then report to Jesus, who retreats with them to rest, but crowds follow, and Jesus teaches them with compassion.

After healing the demon-possessed man, Jesus travels to the other side of the sea near Decapolis, where Jairus, a synagogue leader, pleads for Jesus to heal his dying daughter. Meanwhile, a woman with a long-term illness secretly touches Jesus' garment and is instantly healed.

Jesus arrives at Jairus's house where his daughter has died; he tells the mourners she is only sleeping, is mocked, then privately raises her to life, astonishing all present, and instructs them to keep it secret and care for her.

Jesus sees a large crowd in a remote place and teaches them. As evening comes, his disciples worry about feeding everyone, but Jesus miraculously multiplies five loaves and two fish to feed about five thousand people.

John the Baptist rebukes Herod for marrying his brother's wife, Herodias, who resents him. At Herod's birthday feast, Herodias's daughter dances, pleases Herod, and, prompted by her mother, requests John's head, which Herod reluctantly agrees to.

After feeding 5,000 men with five loaves and two fish, Jesus sends his disciples by boat to Bethsaida, prays alone on a mountain, then walks on the sea to his struggling disciples, calming the storm before they reach Gennesaret.

Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem confront Jesus about his disciples eating without ritual handwashing, criticizing their disregard for Jewish traditions. Jesus responds by accusing them of hypocrisy for prioritizing human traditions over God's commandments.

Jesus confronts Pharisees and scribes criticizing his disciples for not following traditional handwashing. He explains how their traditions override God's commandments and teaches the crowd that moral defilement comes from within, not external rituals.

Jesus explains to his disciples in a house that inner thoughts, not external things, defile a person. Then he travels near Tyre and Sidon, where a Syrophenician woman asks him to heal her demon-possessed daughter.

Jesus encounters a Syrophenician woman from Gentile territory who asks him to heal her demon-possessed daughter; after their exchange, he heals her. Then near the Sea of Galilee, Jesus heals a deaf man with a speech impediment, astonishing the crowd.

Jesus tells some disciples they will witness God's kingdom soon, then takes Peter, James, and John up a mountain where He is transfigured, appearing radiant with Moses and Elijah; God’s voice affirms Jesus as His Son before they descend.

Jesus responds to the Pharisees' demand for a sign by refusing and crossing the lake. He warns his disciples to beware of the corrupting influence ("leaven") of the Pharisees and Herod, then challenges their lack of understanding despite witnessing his miracles.

Jesus confronts the scribes questioning his disciples, then a man brings his son possessed by a harmful spirit that the disciples couldn't cast out. Jesus challenges their faith, and the boy's father expresses belief mixed with doubt, asking for help.

Jesus questions his disciples' understanding, then heals a blind man in Bethsaida with a two-step miracle. Traveling to Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks who people say he is; Peter declares Jesus is the Christ, but Jesus tells them to keep it secret.

After the Transfiguration on the mountain, Jesus tells Peter, James, and John to keep it secret until after his resurrection. They discuss the meaning of rising from the dead and ask about Elijah's coming. Jesus explains and then encounters a crowd with scribes questioning his disciples.

Jesus feeds a large crowd of about four thousand with seven loaves and a few fish in a wilderness near Dalmanutha, showing compassion after three days without food. Afterwards, Pharisees confront him, demanding a sign from heaven.

Jesus privately tells his disciples he must suffer, die, and rise again; Peter objects, but Jesus rebukes him and teaches about self-denial and the cost of following him, warning about shame and the value of the soul.

Jesus heals a boy possessed by a spirit after the father expresses faith mixed with doubt. He explains to his disciples that some demons require prayer and fasting to cast out. Jesus then predicts his death and resurrection, but the disciples don't understand and fear to ask.

In Capernaum, Jesus addresses the disciples' silent dispute about who is greatest, teaching humility by welcoming a child and affirming that those who do good in his name, even outsiders, are allies and will be rewarded.
After crossing the sea, Jesus and his disciples arrive in Gennesaret, where people immediately recognize him and bring sick individuals from nearby towns, hoping to be healed by touching his garment.

Jesus travels to Judea beyond the Jordan River, teaching crowds as usual. Pharisees question him about divorce to test him, and Jesus explains God's original design for marriage and condemns divorce and remarriage as adultery.

Jesus teaches his disciples about kindness to believers, warns against causing them to stumble, and uses vivid imagery to stress the seriousness of avoiding sin. He concludes by urging them to maintain purity and peace among themselves.

Jesus predicts his suffering and resurrection while traveling to Jerusalem. James and John ask to sit at his sides in glory, but Jesus teaches about true leadership, contrasting worldly power with servant leadership to his disciples.

A rich man tells Jesus he has kept the commandments, but Jesus challenges him to give up his wealth and follow Him. The man leaves sad, and Jesus teaches His disciples about the difficulty for the rich to enter God's kingdom, prompting Peter to speak.

Jesus teaches his disciples in Jericho about true greatness as serving others, contrasting worldly rulers. Then, blind Bartimaeus calls out for mercy, and Jesus heals him, showing faith's power and prompting Bartimaeus to follow Jesus.

Jesus and his disciples approach Jerusalem near Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives. Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a colt for him to ride, fulfilling a prophecy as crowds welcome him with garments and branches, shouting praises.

Peter reminds Jesus that they have left everything to follow him, and Jesus promises blessings despite persecutions. As they travel to Jerusalem, Jesus predicts his suffering, death, and resurrection to the twelve disciples.

Jesus teaches about forgiveness during prayer, then religious leaders confront him in the Jerusalem temple, questioning his authority. Jesus counters by asking about John's baptism, exposing their dilemma and avoiding their question.
Jesus tells a parable to the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem about a landowner whose tenants mistreat and kill his servants and son, symbolizing God's judgment on those who reject His messengers and Son.

Jesus cleanses the temple in Jerusalem, condemning its misuse, which alarms religious leaders plotting against him. The next day, his disciples notice a withered fig tree, prompting Jesus to teach about faith, prayer, and forgiveness.

Jesus concludes a parable condemning the religious leaders, predicting their punishment and the vineyard's transfer. The Pharisees and Herodians then try to trap Jesus with a question about paying taxes to Caesar, but he cleverly avoids their trap.

Jesus teaches about marriage and children near Judea beyond the Jordan; he welcomes children despite his disciples' objections, then a man asks Jesus how to inherit eternal life, affirming he has kept the commandments since youth.

Jesus responds to Pharisees and Herodians about paying taxes, then Sadducees question him on resurrection using a levirate marriage scenario; Jesus explains that in resurrection, people do not marry but are like angels.

Jesus enters Jerusalem amid praise, then visits the temple, clears out merchants, and condemns their misuse of the sacred space, linking to his earlier arrival with the disciples near Bethany and Bethphage.

Jesus teaches in the temple, responding to a scribe who affirms the greatest commandments about loving God and neighbor. Jesus then questions the common view of the Messiah as David’s son, citing scripture that calls the Messiah "Lord."

Jesus responds to the Sadducees' question about resurrection, explaining life after death and God's nature. Then a scribe, impressed by Jesus' answers, asks about the greatest commandment, leading Jesus to summarize the law with love for God and neighbor.

Jesus teaches in the temple, explaining David's reference to the Messiah and warning against hypocritical scribes who exploit others. He observes a poor widow's generous offering, highlighting her faith compared to the wealthy donors.

After leaving the temple in Jerusalem, Jesus warns his disciples about the temple's destruction. On the Mount of Olives, Peter, James, John, and Andrew privately ask about future signs, and Jesus begins describing coming deceptions, wars, and persecutions.

Jesus warns his disciples about upcoming persecution for their faith, including betrayal by family and trials before authorities, and instructs them to flee Judea when they see the prophesied "abomination of desolation" as a sign of coming tribulation.

Jesus warns his disciples about a coming time of great distress and urges immediate flight without delay, especially for vulnerable groups. He predicts false messiahs, cosmic disturbances, and his own future glorious return after this tribulation.

Jesus continues speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, describing his future return with power, the gathering of his followers, and urging them to stay vigilant and prepared, as no one knows the exact time of these events.

Jesus praises a woman's costly anointing as a lasting memorial, while Judas agrees to betray Jesus for money. Jesus instructs two disciples to prepare the Passover meal in a furnished upper room in Jerusalem, where he later arrives with the twelve.

Jesus warns his disciples they will abandon him that night, predicting Peter's denial; they arrive at Gethsemane where Jesus, deeply distressed, prays to God, asking if the coming suffering can be avoided but submits to God's will.

In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays to God, expressing his anguish but submitting to God's will. He finds his disciples sleeping instead of watching, then Judas arrives with soldiers to betray and arrest Jesus by identifying him with a kiss.

Jesus shares the Passover meal with his twelve disciples in Jerusalem, predicting one will betray him. He institutes the Lord’s Supper and warns they will all desert him, fulfilling scripture about the shepherd being struck and the sheep scattering.

At Jesus' trial before the high priest and council in Jerusalem, false witnesses fail to agree on accusations. Jesus affirms he is the Messiah, leading to charges of blasphemy and harsh mistreatment by the religious leaders.

Judas betrays Jesus with a kiss in Gethsemane; Jesus is arrested despite peaceful teaching. His disciples flee, except Peter who follows to the high priest's palace, where leaders seek false witnesses to condemn Jesus.

Early morning, Jewish leaders bring Jesus to Pilate in Jerusalem for trial. Pilate questions Jesus, who remains mostly silent, surprising Pilate. Pilate offers to release a prisoner, Barabbas, but the crowd, influenced by priests, demands Barabbas be freed instead.

Jesus is mocked and beaten by servants after his arrest, while Peter denies knowing Jesus three times in the high priest's courtyard, fulfilling Jesus' earlier prediction before the rooster crows twice.

Pilate, pressured by chief priests and the crowd in Jerusalem, releases Barabbas and hands Jesus over to be crucified. Roman soldiers mock Jesus with a purple robe and crown of thorns, then force Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross.

Roman soldiers force Simon of Cyrene to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha, where Jesus is crucified alongside two thieves. Passersby and religious leaders mock him, fulfilling scripture about being counted among criminals.

As Jesus is crucified at Golgotha, bystanders mock him, darkness covers the land, and he cries out before dying; a Roman centurion acknowledges his identity, while several women, including Mary Magdalene, watch from a distance.

Women who had followed Jesus in Galilee and Jerusalem watched as Joseph of Arimathaea, a respected council member, asked Pilate for Jesus' body. After confirming Jesus was dead, Joseph wrapped the body and laid it in a rock-cut tomb, with Mary Magdalene and another Mary present.

After Jesus' resurrection, he first appears to Mary Magdalene, then to two disciples, and finally to the eleven apostles, who receive his commission to spread the gospel worldwide; he ascends to heaven, and the apostles begin their mission with divine signs.

Just before Passover in Bethany, Jesus is anointed by a woman with expensive ointment while the chief priests plot to kill him, fearing unrest if they act during the feast. Jesus defends the woman's act as preparation for his burial.

Luke begins by addressing Theophilus, explaining his intent to provide an orderly account based on eyewitnesses. The scene shifts to Judea under King Herod, introducing Zacharias, a priest, and his wife Elisabeth, both righteous but childless, during Zacharias's temple service.

After Jesus' burial in a rock-hewn tomb in Jerusalem, Mary Magdalene, Mary mother of James, and Salome visit early Sunday to anoint his body but find the stone rolled away and a young man announcing Jesus' resurrection, who then appears to Mary Magdalene.

Zacharias questions the angel Gabriel's message about his wife Elisabeth conceiving despite their old age. Gabriel declares Zacharias will be mute until the prophecy is fulfilled. People wait outside the temple, then notice his silence. Elisabeth conceives and hides for five months.

While Zacharias was burning incense in the temple, an angel appeared to him, announcing that his wife Elisabeth would bear a son named John who would prepare Israel for the Lord. Zacharias, skeptical due to their old age, questioned the angel.

Mary visits her cousin Elisabeth in Judea; Elisabeth's unborn baby leaps with joy at Mary's greeting. Mary praises God for His mercy and greatness. After three months, Mary returns home, and Elisabeth gives birth to her son, John.

Elisabeth gives birth to a son, John, in Judea. At his circumcision, she insists on the name John, confirmed by his father Zacharias writing it down. Zacharias then speaks, praising God, causing awe among their neighbors.

Elisabeth reflects on God's blessing of her pregnancy, ending her shame. Meanwhile, the angel Gabriel visits Mary in Nazareth to announce she will miraculously conceive Jesus, heir to David's throne, prompting her question about how this will happen.

People who heard about John the Baptist's birth wondered about his future. His father Zacharias, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied about God's salvation through the house of David, fulfilling promises made to Abraham and Israel.

Mary questions the angel Gabriel about conceiving a child as a virgin; he explains the Holy Spirit will cause it. Mary visits her cousin Elisabeth, who is pregnant despite old age, and Elisabeth's unborn baby reacts joyfully at Mary's greeting.

During a Roman census ordered by Caesar Augustus, Joseph and Mary travel from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Mary gives birth to Jesus. Nearby shepherds receive an angelic announcement of the Savior's birth, marking a pivotal moment in the narrative.

Angels announce Jesus' birth to shepherds near Bethlehem, describing him as the Savior and a sign. The shepherds visit Mary, Joseph, and Jesus, then spread the news, while Mary reflects quietly on these events.

Simeon, a devout man in Jerusalem, is guided by the Holy Spirit to meet Jesus during His presentation at the temple. He blesses Jesus and Mary, prophesying Jesus' impact on Israel and the suffering Mary will endure.

After the shepherds praise God for Jesus' birth, Mary and Joseph follow Jewish law by circumcising Jesus and presenting him in Jerusalem, where Simeon, a devout man guided by the Holy Spirit, awaits the promised Messiah before his death.

Zacharias, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesies about his son John, who will prepare the way for the Lord by bringing knowledge of salvation and guiding people to peace. John grows strong and lives in the wilderness until his public mission begins.

Simeon warns Mary of future sorrow, then Anna, a devout prophetess, praises God and speaks of Jesus. After fulfilling Jewish law, Mary and Joseph return to Nazareth, where Jesus grows strong and wise. At age 12, they travel to Jerusalem for Passover.
In the time of Roman rulers Tiberius, Pilate, and Herod, John the Baptist begins preaching repentance near the Jordan River, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy and warning people about the coming judgment.

Jesus stays behind in the Jerusalem temple after Passover while his parents begin traveling home, unaware. After searching, they find him discussing scripture with teachers, amazing all with his insight before returning to Nazareth.

John the Baptist warns the crowd coming to be baptized to show true repentance through good deeds, not relying on heritage. When asked, he advises sharing possessions, honest tax collecting, and fair treatment by soldiers.

John the Baptist advises soldiers to act justly and warns the crowd about the coming Messiah who will bring judgment. He rebukes Herod for wrongdoing, leading to John's imprisonment by Herod in Galilee during Tiberius's reign.

John the Baptist is imprisoned by Herod for rebuking his marriage. Jesus is baptized, the Holy Spirit descends on him, and God affirms him as His Son. The passage then traces Jesus' genealogy, linking him to David and Adam.

This passage concludes Jesus' genealogy, tracing his lineage back through notable ancestors like Noah and Adam, ultimately to God, establishing his divine and human heritage as introduced earlier in Luke 3.

Jesus returns to his hometown Nazareth and reads from Isaiah in the synagogue, declaring the prophecy about the Messiah fulfilled in him. The people marvel but question his identity, doubting because he is known as Joseph’s son.

Jesus resists the devil’s temptations in the wilderness, quoting Scripture to reject offers of power and testing God’s protection. Afterward, filled with the Spirit, he returns to Galilee, gaining fame and teaching in synagogues, including his hometown Nazareth.

After his baptism in the Jordan, Jesus, filled with the Holy Spirit, is led into the wilderness where he fasts for forty days and faces temptation from the devil, who offers worldly power if Jesus worships him, but Jesus resists using scripture.

This passage continues the genealogy of Jesus, tracing his ancestry through many generations from Melchi back to Sala, connecting him to key figures in Israel's history and emphasizing his human lineage.

Jesus continues healing and casting out demons in Capernaum; the demons recognize him as the Messiah, but he silences them. He then withdraws to a solitary place, yet crowds follow, and he declares his mission to preach God's kingdom beyond Galilee.

In Capernaum's synagogue, Jesus commands an unclean spirit to leave a man, astonishing the crowd with his authority. He then heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, while demons recognize him as the Christ but he silences them.

Jesus teaches a crowd by the lake of Gennesaret, then instructs Simon Peter to fish despite a fruitless night. They catch so many fish their nets break, leading Peter to recognize Jesus' divine power.

Jesus heals a paralyzed man to prove his authority to forgive sins, astonishing the crowd. Then he calls Levi, a tax collector, to follow him, leading to criticism from Pharisees about associating with sinners.

After a miraculous catch of fish at Lake Gennesaret, Jesus calls Simon Peter, James, and John to follow him as "fishers of men." He then heals a man with leprosy in a city, increasing his fame, before withdrawing to pray in the wilderness.

Jesus, speaking in his hometown synagogue of Nazareth, warns that prophets are often rejected at home, citing Elijah and Elisha's aid to Gentiles. His words anger the crowd, who try to kill him, but he escapes and teaches in Capernaum, where he confronts an unclean spirit.

Jesus, aware of the Pharisees' intent to accuse him, heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, challenging their views on doing good. Afterward, Jesus prays all night on a mountain and selects twelve apostles from his disciples.

Jesus teaches his disciples and a large crowd near a plain, warning the rich and comfortable of future woes and urging love and generosity toward enemies, emphasizing mercy beyond common social expectations.

Jesus prays alone in the wilderness, then teaches a crowd including Pharisees and doctors of the law. Friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof to reach Jesus, who forgives the man's sins, prompting religious leaders to question his authority.

Jesus teaches his disciples about selfless love, mercy, and forgiveness, urging them not to judge others while warning against hypocrisy, using parables to illustrate spiritual blindness and the importance of self-examination.

Jesus names his twelve apostles, including Judas Iscariot, then teaches a large crowd from Judea, Jerusalem, and coastal regions. He heals many and pronounces blessings on the poor and warnings to the rich, highlighting reversal of fortunes.

Jesus responds to questions from Pharisees about his disciples not fasting like others, explaining his mission to call sinners, using parables about new and old garments and wineskins to illustrate the need for new ways with his coming kingdom.

Jesus teaches his disciples about hypocrisy, urging them to address their own faults before criticizing others, and emphasizes that a person's true nature is revealed by their actions and words, connecting to his earlier moral teachings.

Jesus teaches his followers about the importance of not just hearing his words but acting on them, comparing a wise builder with a strong foundation to one who builds without support and faces destruction. This concludes his Sermon on the Plain.

After finishing his teachings, Jesus enters Capernaum where a Roman centurion asks Jewish elders to request Jesus heal his dying servant. The centurion shows humility and faith in Jesus' authority, impressing Jesus and the crowd.

John the Baptist's disciples ask Jesus if he is the expected Messiah. Jesus points to his miracles and preaching as proof, then praises John as a true prophet, addressing the crowd in the region near Capernaum.

Jesus praises the centurion's faith after healing his servant remotely. The next day, Jesus raises a widow's only son in Nain, leading the crowd to recognize him as a great prophet and spreading news of his miracles throughout Judea.

Jesus travels through towns with the twelve disciples and several healed women supporters, including Mary Magdalene. He teaches a large crowd using the parable of the sower, describing different responses to God's word.

Jesus speaks to the crowd about John the Baptist's role as a great prophet preparing the way for the Messiah, contrasting people's rejection of both John’s asceticism and Jesus’ fellowship with sinners in Galilee.

Jesus explains to Simon the Pharisee how the woman's actions show her great love because she has been forgiven much, then publicly forgives her sins, prompting surprise from the guests at Jesus' authority to forgive sins.

Jesus explains the parable of the sower to his disciples, describing how different people receive God's word with varying results, emphasizing the importance of truly hearing and acting on it. This follows his teaching to large crowds in Galilean towns.

Jesus teaches about openly sharing God's word and warns to listen carefully. His family tries to see him but he redefines kinship by obedience to God's word. Then Jesus and his disciples set sail across the lake, where a sudden storm threatens them.

Jesus and his disciples face a violent storm on the lake; Jesus calms it, revealing his authority over nature. They reach Gadarenes, where a demon-possessed man living among tombs confronts Jesus, recognizing him as the Son of God.

Jesus accepts an invitation to dine at Simon the Pharisee's house in an unnamed city. A sinful woman anoints Jesus' feet, prompting Jesus to teach Simon about forgiveness through a parable of a creditor forgiving two debtors.

Jesus' disciples pick grain on the Sabbath; Pharisees object. Jesus cites David and claims Lordship over the Sabbath. Later, in a synagogue, Jesus heals a man with a withered hand while Pharisees watch, seeking to accuse him.

Jesus confronts a man possessed by many demons called Legion near Gadarenes. The demons beg to enter a herd of pigs, which then drown. The healed man is found calm and clothed, causing fear and amazement among the locals.

Jesus reassures Jairus, a synagogue leader, after hearing his daughter has died. He enters the house with Peter, James, and John, raises the girl from death, and instructs her parents to keep the miracle private.

After healing the demon-possessed man in Gadara, Jesus faces fear from the locals and leaves. The healed man spreads the news, and Jesus is welcomed back, where Jairus, a synagogue leader, urgently asks for help for his dying daughter.

Jesus is on his way to heal Jairus's dying daughter when a woman with a long-term bleeding condition touches his garment and is instantly healed. Jesus acknowledges her faith, then reassures Jairus to trust despite news of his daughter's death.

After the apostles report their work to Jesus, he retreats with them near Bethsaida, but a large crowd follows. Jesus teaches, heals, and miraculously feeds about five thousand men with five loaves and two fish.

Jesus warns his disciples about the consequences of denying him, then takes Peter, John, and James up a mountain where he is transfigured and speaks with Moses and Elijah about his upcoming death in Jerusalem.

Jesus empowers his twelve disciples to cast out demons and heal, sending them out with minimal provisions to preach God's kingdom. Meanwhile, Herod hears rumors about Jesus, is puzzled, and wants to meet him. The apostles report back, and Jesus retreats with them to a quiet place near Bethsaida.

Jesus is transfigured on a mountain with Peter, John, and James witnessing a divine voice affirming him as God's Son. The next day, Jesus heals a boy possessed by a spirit after his disciples fail to cast it out.

Jesus heals a boy possessed by a spirit after his disciples fail, then warns them about his coming suffering. When they argue about greatness, Jesus teaches humility using a child and advises acceptance of others who act in his name.

After feeding 5,000, Jesus prays with his disciples and asks their opinion on his identity. Peter declares him the Christ, but Jesus warns them to keep it secret and foretells his suffering, urging them to follow him selflessly.
Jesus calls two men to follow him; one wants to bury his father first, and the other wants to say goodbye to family. Jesus emphasizes the urgency of commitment to God's kingdom over personal affairs.

Jesus tells his disciples not to oppose those who do good in his name, then sets out for Jerusalem. In Samaria, locals reject him; James and John want to call down fire, but Jesus rebukes them and moves on. A man offers to follow Jesus, who warns of hardships.

Jesus speaks to the seventy disciples after their successful mission, affirming their spiritual authority and the revelation given to them. A lawyer then challenges Jesus, asking how to inherit eternal life, beginning a teaching moment.

Jesus sends seventy disciples ahead to towns he plans to visit, instructing them to heal the sick and proclaim God's kingdom. He warns of judgment on unrepentant cities and affirms their authority over evil spirits, who return rejoicing.

Jesus appoints seventy disciples and sends them in pairs ahead of him to towns he plans to visit, instructing them on how to travel lightly, offer peace, stay with receptive hosts, heal the sick, and proclaim God's kingdom near.

Jesus, while praying, is asked by a disciple to teach them how to pray. He gives the Lord's Prayer and follows with a parable about persistence in asking, encouraging them to ask, seek, and knock for what they need.

A lawyer questions Jesus about inheriting eternal life, prompting Jesus to tell the parable of the Good Samaritan, illustrating who truly acts as a neighbor by showing mercy to a wounded man ignored by a priest and Levite on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.

Jesus teaches his disciples about persistent prayer and God's generosity, then casts out a demon from a mute man, prompting some to accuse him of using demonic power, which Jesus refutes by explaining that a divided kingdom cannot stand.

Jesus warns about the danger of returning evil spirits and responds to a woman's praise by emphasizing the blessing of hearing and obeying God's word. He then criticizes the current generation for demanding signs, comparing himself to Jonah and Solomon.

Jesus responds to accusations that he casts out demons by Beelzebub, arguing that a divided kingdom cannot stand and explaining how a stronger power overcomes evil. He warns about the danger of unclean spirits returning worse than before.

Jesus finishes the parable of the Good Samaritan teaching mercy, then visits Martha and Mary in a village; Martha is busy serving while Mary listens to Jesus, who tells Martha to focus on what truly matters.

Jesus teaches a crowd near Galilee, comparing their unbelief unfavorably to Nineveh's repentance under Jonah, then uses light and eye metaphors to stress spiritual clarity. A Pharisee invites Jesus to dinner, surprised Jesus hasn't washed first, prompting Jesus to criticize Pharisees' hypocrisy.

Jesus rebukes the Jewish religious leaders in Judea for continuing their ancestors' pattern of killing prophets and obstructing others from learning God's truth, provoking the scribes and Pharisees to plot against him.

Jesus rebukes the Pharisees and lawyers for their hypocrisy, criticizing their focus on outward rituals while neglecting justice and love. A lawyer responds, prompting Jesus to condemn their oppressive actions and their ancestors' killing of prophets.

Jesus teaches his disciples near a large crowd, urging them to trust God's provision like the lilies and sparrows, seek God's kingdom first, and live ready and generous lives, prepared for the coming of the Son of man.

Jesus teaches his disciples about faithful stewardship and warns of judgment for unprepared servants. He explains his mission will bring division, not peace, even among close family, highlighting the cost of following him.

Jesus tells a parable about a rich man planning to store his abundant crops for comfort, but God calls him foolish for not being spiritually rich. He then teaches his disciples not to worry about material needs, using ravens and lilies as examples of God's care.
Jesus warns the crowd in Galilee that his message will cause division even within families, urging them to recognize the signs of the times and to settle disputes quickly to avoid harsh judgment.

Jesus addresses a large crowd and warns his disciples to beware of the Pharisees' hypocrisy. He encourages them not to fear human threats but to revere God, who values and knows even the smallest details of their lives.

Jesus warns his disciples about denying him and blasphemy, assures them the Holy Spirit will guide their words, then addresses a dispute about inheritance, teaching against greed through a parable about a rich man storing abundant crops.

Jesus teaches his disciples about being watchful and ready for his unexpected return, using the example of servants awaiting their master’s arrival from a wedding. Peter asks if this applies to them, and Jesus emphasizes the blessing of faithful stewardship.

Jesus teaches about the kingdom of God using parables of a mustard seed and leaven, then warns listeners about the difficulty of salvation, emphasizing the need for earnest effort to enter, as many will be rejected despite familiarity with his teachings.

Jesus responds to reports about Galileans killed by Pilate and victims of a tower collapse, denying they were worse sinners and urging repentance. He then tells a parable about a fruitless fig tree given one more year to bear fruit before being cut down.

Jesus heals a woman crippled for 18 years in a synagogue on the Sabbath, provoking the synagogue ruler's anger. Jesus defends his healing, shaming his critics, and then begins teaching about the kingdom of God.

Jesus warns that many who presume to belong to God's kingdom will be rejected, while others from all directions will be accepted. Pharisees warn Jesus to flee Herod, but He insists on fulfilling His mission in Jerusalem despite the danger.

Jesus visits a leading Pharisee's home on the Sabbath, heals a man with dropsy, and challenges the Pharisees about Sabbath laws. He then observes guests choosing places and teaches humility through a parable about seating at a wedding feast.

Jesus is teaching guests at a Pharisee's house about humility and generosity, advising to take lowly seats and invite the poor to feasts. A guest responds, and Jesus begins a parable about a man hosting a great supper inviting many.
Jesus warns a crowd following him that true discipleship requires total commitment, using examples of building and war to illustrate the need to count the cost before following him fully.

Jesus is speaking to a crowd including tax collectors and sinners near him, while Pharisees complain. He tells parables about a lost sheep and lost coin to illustrate God's joy over repentant sinners.

Jesus tells a parable to the Pharisees and sinners gathered around him, about a younger son who wastes his inheritance in a distant land, faces famine, and decides to return home repentant, highlighting God's joy over a sinner's repentance.

Jesus tells the parable of the prodigal son, where the younger son returns home repentant and is warmly welcomed by his father, while the elder son reacts with anger upon hearing the celebration for his brother's return.

The elder son expresses anger to his father over the celebration for his repentant younger brother, who had wasted his inheritance. The father reassures him of his constant presence and explains the joy in the younger son's return.

Jesus tells a parable about a dishonest steward who acts shrewdly to secure his future, teaching his disciples about faithfulness and the impossibility of serving both God and wealth. The Pharisees mock him, but Jesus challenges their self-righteousness.

Jesus tells a parable at a Pharisee's house about a man whose invited guests refuse to come to his banquet, so he orders his servant to invite the poor and disabled from the streets to fill the house, emphasizing the rejection of the original invitees.

Jesus tells his disciples a parable about a rich man and his steward, who is accused of wasting his master's goods and then cleverly reduces debts to secure future favor before losing his position. The master praises the steward's shrewdness.

Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for self-righteousness and affirms the enduring law, then begins the parable of a rich man and the beggar Lazarus, contrasting their fates after death to teach about justice and mercy.

Jesus tells a parable about a rich man in torment after death who sees Lazarus comforted with Abraham. The rich man asks Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his brothers, but Abraham insists they must heed Moses and the prophets instead.

Jesus teaches his disciples about the inevitability of offenses and the importance of forgiveness, urging them to forgive repeatedly. The apostles ask for increased faith, and Jesus explains faith's power and the duty of servants to obey without expectation of thanks.
Jesus teaches his disciples about humility in service, then heals ten lepers in a village between Samaria and Galilee. Only one, a Samaritan, returns to thank him, highlighting gratitude and faith.

Jesus contrasts a proud Pharisee and a humble tax collector praying in the temple, then welcomes children, teaching their importance for God's kingdom. A ruler asks Jesus about inheriting eternal life, affirming his knowledge of the commandments.

Jesus tells two parables: one about a persistent widow seeking justice from an unjust judge, teaching the need for continual prayer; the other contrasts a self-righteous Pharisee and a humble tax collector praying in the temple, highlighting true humility.

Jesus teaches his disciples using examples from Noah's flood and Lot's destruction to warn about sudden judgment at the coming of the Son of Man, urging readiness and detachment from worldly possessions, as some will be taken and others left behind.

A rich ruler tells Jesus he has kept the commandments, but Jesus challenges him to give up his wealth and follow Him. Jesus then speaks to His disciples about the difficulty for the rich to enter God's kingdom and foretells His journey to Jerusalem.
