Paul advises the Corinthian church on marriage, urging those who struggle with self-control to marry, commands faithfulness in marriage, and addresses mixed-faith marriages, emphasizing peace and individual calling in the Christian community.

Paul advises the Corinthian believers to remain in their current social and religious status, emphasizing faithfulness to God's commandments over external rituals like circumcision. He offers personal counsel on marriage and singleness amid present difficulties.

Paul advises the Corinthian believers about marriage, urging contentment with their current state due to the urgent times, contrasting the focus of unmarried and married people on serving the Lord versus worldly concerns.

Paul warns the Corinthian believers to be careful that their freedom to eat food offered to idols does not cause weaker believers to stumble or sin, emphasizing love over knowledge to protect the faith of others.

Paul addresses the Corinthian believers about eating food sacrificed to idols, emphasizing that true knowledge is humble and love builds up. He warns that some have weak consciences and cautions against causing them to stumble by exercising freedom without care.

Paul advises the Corinthian church on marriage and singleness, highlighting the different focuses of married and unmarried women, and encourages believers to remain devoted to the Lord, whether married or single, emphasizing personal choice and spiritual priorities.

Paul defends his apostleship to the Corinthian believers, asserting his right to material support for his ministry, using examples from everyday life and Mosaic law to argue that those who preach the gospel deserve to benefit from their work.

Paul explains to the Corinthian church that though he and other apostles have the right to receive material support for their ministry, he chooses to preach without charge to avoid hindering the gospel and to serve willingly.

Paul advises the Corinthian believers to avoid causing others to stumble by respecting their consciences, especially regarding food offered to idols, emphasizing living for God's glory and seeking others' good over personal freedom.

Paul reminds the Corinthian believers of Israel's ancestors who experienced God's guidance and provision during the Exodus but faced judgment for disobedience, using their failures as warnings to avoid idolatry, immorality, and complaining.

Paul warns the Corinthian believers to stay humble and resist temptation, assuring God's faithfulness. He urges them to avoid idolatry, explaining that participating in pagan sacrifices conflicts with communion in Christ, highlighting the spiritual danger of such associations.

Paul explains his approach to preaching the gospel without charge, adapting to different groups—Jews, law-keepers, and the weak—to save some. He compares his disciplined efforts to an athlete striving for an incorruptible prize.

Paul continues addressing the Corinthian church, discussing proper conduct in worship, including head coverings and unity. He criticizes divisions and selfish behavior during the Lord’s Supper, urging respect and consideration among believers.

Paul urges the Corinthian believers to imitate him as he follows Christ, commending their faithfulness to his teachings. He explains the order of authority in relationships and gives instructions on head coverings during prayer and prophecy, emphasizing mutual dependence in the Lord.

Paul rebukes the Corinthian believers for selfish behavior during the Lord’s Supper, reminding them of Jesus’ institution of the meal and warning against partaking unworthily, which leads to weakness and judgment among them.

Paul explains to the Corinthian believers how the Holy Spirit distributes different spiritual gifts to each person, comparing the church to a body with many parts that all work together, emphasizing unity despite diverse roles.

Paul teaches the Corinthian believers in Greece that all members of the church, like parts of a body, are important and interdependent. He lists spiritual roles and gifts, urging them to desire the best gifts while preparing to explain a superior way.

Paul addresses the Corinthian believers, reminding them of their past as Gentiles worshipping idols, and explains that the Holy Spirit grants different spiritual gifts to each person for the common good, all from the same God.

Paul advises the Corinthian believers to self-examine to avoid God's judgment and encourages them to wait for each other during communal meals to prevent division and condemnation, promising to address remaining issues when he visits.

Paul advises the Corinthian church to pursue love and desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy, emphasizing clear communication that builds up the church rather than speaking in unknown tongues that only benefit the speaker.

Paul continues his letter to the Corinthian church, emphasizing that without love (charity), spiritual gifts like speaking in tongues, prophecy, and faith are meaningless, and he describes the enduring, selfless nature of true love.

Paul concludes his teaching on spiritual gifts by contrasting partial understanding with complete knowledge, using the analogy of growing from childhood to adulthood, and emphasizes that faith, hope, and especially love (charity) remain essential.

Paul continues teaching the Corinthian church, emphasizing that speaking in tongues without understanding does not build up others, but prophecy does. He warns that tongues confuse unbelievers, while prophecy convinces and leads them to worship God.

Paul teaches the Corinthian church that speaking in tongues must be understandable to benefit others; otherwise, it is like speaking into the air. He urges praying and singing with both spirit and understanding to truly edify the church community.

Paul instructs the Corinthian church on orderly worship, emphasizing prophecy and interpretation of tongues for edification, allowing multiple prophets to speak in turn, and commands women to remain silent in church, reflecting cultural norms and law.

Paul instructs the Corinthian church on orderly worship, emphasizing women's silence in church and urging respect for his teachings as the Lord's commands, while encouraging prophecy and speaking in tongues done properly.

Paul reminds the Corinthian believers of the gospel he preached: Christ's death, burial, and resurrection, witnessed by many including Peter, James, and himself, emphasizing the foundation of their faith and his role as an apostle despite his past persecution of the church.

Paul explains to the Corinthian believers that mortal bodies must transform to inherit God's kingdom, describing a future resurrection and victory over death through Jesus Christ, encouraging them to remain faithful and diligent in their service to God.

Paul continues his teaching to the Corinthian believers, affirming the resurrection of Christ as the foundation of their faith and addressing doubts about the resurrection of the dead, explaining Christ's resurrection as the first of many to come.

Paul warns the Corinthian believers against bad influences and urges them to live righteously. He then answers questions about resurrection, explaining that just as seeds grow into different bodies, God gives each a unique form, comparing earthly and heavenly bodies.

Paul explains the order of resurrection: Christ rises first, then believers at His coming. He emphasizes Christ's reign until all enemies, including death, are defeated. Paul challenges doubts about resurrection, citing baptism for the dead and his own sufferings in Ephesus.

Paul encourages the Corinthian church to respect Timothy and await Apollos's visit, urges steadfast faith and love, commends Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus for their service, sends greetings from Asian churches, and closes with a personal blessing.

Paul encourages the Corinthian believers by sharing his hardships in Asia, emphasizing reliance on God for deliverance, and expressing mutual joy and sincere fellowship between him and the church as they share in suffering and comfort.

Paul explains to the Corinthian believers that just as the sun, moon, and stars differ in glory, so too will resurrected bodies differ from earthly ones, transforming from natural and corruptible to spiritual and incorruptible, reflecting the difference between Adam and Christ.

Paul and Timothy greet the church in Corinth and all believers in Achaia, praising God for comforting them in troubles so they can comfort others. Paul explains that their sufferings and consolation are connected to the believers' salvation and hope.

Paul explains his decision not to visit the Corinthian church again with sadness, expressing his deep love and concern for them, urging forgiveness and comfort for a repentant individual to maintain unity and obedience in the community.

Paul writes to the Corinthian church, expressing mutual joy and explaining his travel plans through Macedonia to Judea. He affirms the sincerity of his intentions, God's faithfulness, and that their faith stands by God's Spirit, not human authority.

Paul explains his purpose in writing—to test the Corinthians' obedience and urges forgiveness to prevent Satan's advantage. He recounts his journey from Troas to Macedonia seeking Titus and praises God for triumph in Christ, emphasizing sincere ministry.

Paul continues his letter to the Corinthians, emphasizing that their transformed lives are his true recommendation, contrasting the old covenant of the law given through Moses with the new, life-giving covenant of the Spirit from God.

Paul explains to the Corinthians how he and his companions endure suffering for Jesus, showing Christ's life through their hardships, trusting in resurrection and eternal glory beyond present troubles.

Paul contrasts the old covenant's glory, symbolized by Moses' veiled face, with the surpassing glory of the new covenant through Christ's Spirit, which brings freedom and transforms believers into God's image.

Paul continues his letter to the Corinthians, explaining that despite hardships and opposition, he and his companions faithfully serve God by preaching Christ, relying on God's power rather than their own, and living out Jesus' life even amid suffering.

Paul explains to the Corinthian church that anyone united with Christ becomes a new person, reconciled to God through Jesus, and entrusted with sharing this message of reconciliation as Christ’s representatives.

Paul continues his letter to the Corinthians, urging them to live for Christ who died and rose again, reminding them all will face Christ's judgment and encouraging them to embrace their new identity in Him.

Paul instructs the Corinthian church on collecting offerings for Jerusalem, plans his travel through Macedonia to visit them, intends to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, and encourages them to welcome Timothy, who is coming to join him.

Paul urges the Corinthians to accept God's grace seriously, describing his and his companions' hardships and faithfulness as ministers of God, emphasizing their sincerity and deep care for the Corinthian believers.

Paul continues his letter to the Corinthians, explaining that though our earthly bodies will perish, believers have an eternal heavenly dwelling from God. He expresses hope for life beyond death and emphasizes accountability before Christ's judgment.

Paul encourages the Corinthians to open their hearts and avoid close partnerships with unbelievers, emphasizing their identity as God's temple and urging them to live separately from impurity to receive God's fatherly care.

Paul encourages the Corinthian believers to purify themselves and affirms his integrity, expressing joy despite hardships in Macedonia. He finds comfort in Titus’s report of their repentance after receiving his previous letter.

Paul explains to the Corinthian church that his previous harsh letter caused temporary sorrow leading to godly repentance, clearing misunderstandings and restoring relationships, which brought comfort to Paul, Titus, and the believers in Macedonia.

Paul expresses joy and comfort because Titus was refreshed by the Corinthians' positive response, confirming Paul's truthful praise of them; he rejoices in their obedience and his full confidence in them.

Paul encourages the Corinthian church to complete their earlier commitment to give generously, using Jesus' example of self-sacrifice. He praises Titus for eagerly supporting this effort and visiting them to help coordinate the collection.

Paul encourages the Corinthian believers to follow the example of the Macedonian churches, who gave generously despite their poverty, urging them to excel in grace and generosity as a demonstration of sincere love and faith.

Paul writes to the Corinthians about their readiness to support fellow believers, praising their eagerness and urging them to prepare generously and willingly, to avoid embarrassment when others visit from Macedonia and to show sincere generosity.

Paul expresses deep concern for the Corinthian believers, warning against false teachers preaching a different gospel, and defends his apostleship and sacrifices, including supporting himself by receiving wages from other churches to serve them freely.

Paul encourages the Corinthians to give generously and cheerfully, assuring them that God will provide for their needs and multiply their righteousness. Their generosity supports fellow believers and brings thanksgiving to God.

Paul defends his ministry to the Corinthian church, explaining he supported himself by taking wages from other churches to avoid burdening them. He warns against false apostles disguised as righteous workers and insists on his sincere love and boldness in preaching.

Paul continues his defense against false apostles by boldly boasting about his Jewish heritage and severe sufferings for Christ, contrasting his hardships with the deceitful teachers troubling the Corinthian church.

Paul appeals to the Corinthians with Christ's humility, addressing criticisms of his boldness in letters versus his meekness in person, explaining that his spiritual battle uses God's power, not human strength, and he seeks to build up, not intimidate them.

Paul addresses the Corinthian believers, responding to criticisms about his letters being strong but his presence weak, emphasizing his sincere authority from God, his focus on preaching the gospel to them and beyond, and that true commendation comes from the Lord, not self-praise.

Paul recounts his numerous hardships and dangers faced while spreading the gospel, including beatings, shipwrecks, and persecution in places like Damascus, emphasizing his endurance and care for the churches despite these trials.

Paul explains that Titus willingly went to the Corinthians, accompanied by trusted brothers chosen by the churches to oversee the collection for the saints, ensuring transparency and encouraging the Corinthians to demonstrate their love and support openly.

Paul continues his defense of his apostleship to the Corinthians, explaining how he prayed for relief from a "thorn in the flesh" but accepted God's grace instead. He expresses his commitment to them, emphasizing his selfless love and readiness to visit again.

Paul continues his letter to the Corinthians, describing a profound spiritual experience of being caught up to the third heaven, but he chooses to boast only in his weaknesses to avoid pride, explaining he prayed three times for relief from a persistent hardship.

Paul expresses his deep love and willingness to sacrifice for the Corinthian church, denies exploiting them, and shares his concern about potential conflicts and unrepentant sins when he visits them again.
Paul concludes his third letter to the Corinthians, expressing his desire for their spiritual growth and unity, urging peace and mutual love, and offering blessings before his farewell.

Paul warns the Corinthian church that this is his third visit and urges them to examine their faith seriously, affirming Christ's power in him and encouraging their spiritual growth and honesty despite past sins.

Paul explains to the Galatian churches that his gospel comes directly from a revelation of Jesus Christ, not from human teaching. He recounts his past as a zealous persecutor of Christians, his calling by God, and his early ministry in Arabia, Damascus, Jerusalem, Syria, and Cilicia.

Paul recounts a Jerusalem meeting with church leaders James, Peter (Cephas), and John, who affirm his mission to Gentiles while he opposes Peter for withdrawing from Gentile fellowship in Antioch due to pressure from Jewish Christians.

Paul, writing to the churches in Galatia with fellow believers, warns them against turning to a distorted gospel and emphasizes that his message comes directly from Jesus Christ, not from human teaching or approval.

Paul recounts his second visit to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, explaining how he privately shared his gospel for Gentiles with church leaders, resisted pressure to circumcise Titus, and opposed false believers seeking to impose legalistic bondage.

Paul explains that he has died to the law so he can live for God, with Christ living in him. He emphasizes faith in Jesus over the law for righteousness, connecting to his earlier argument against relying on the law for justification.

Paul rebukes the Galatians for turning from faith in Christ to relying on the law, reminding them that the Spirit and blessings come through faith like Abraham's, not by law-keeping, which brings a curse if not fully obeyed.

Paul explains to the Galatians that before knowing Christ, they were like heirs under guardianship, bound by worldly rules, but now through Jesus they are adopted as God's children and should not return to old religious observances.

Paul explains to the Galatians that God's promise to Abraham predates the law given 430 years later, which served as a temporary guide until Christ came. Through faith in Jesus, all believers—regardless of background—are united as God's children and heirs.

Paul explains to the Galatians that relying on the law brings a curse because no one can fully keep it, but Christ redeemed believers from this curse to extend Abraham’s blessing to Gentiles through faith, affirming God’s promise made to Abraham and fulfilled in Christ.

Paul appeals to the Galatians to imitate his example and recalls how they once accepted him despite his weaknesses. He expresses concern over their turning back to the law and introduces the allegory of Abraham's two sons to explain the difference between bondage and promise.

Paul confronts Peter in Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile believers out of fear of Jewish Christians from James, arguing that faith in Christ, not the law, justifies both Jews and Gentiles, emphasizing living by faith, not law.

Paul uses the story of Abraham's two sons, Ishmael (bondwoman) and Isaac (freewoman), as an allegory for two covenants: the old law from Mount Sinai causing bondage, and the new promise of freedom through faith, urging believers to identify as children of the free covenant.

Paul urges the Galatians to stand firm in the freedom Christ gave them, warning against returning to the Jewish law's bondage, especially circumcision, which nullifies Christ's grace and leads to judgment for those causing trouble.

Paul warns the Galatians against sinful behaviors that exclude from God's kingdom and contrasts these with the Spirit's virtues like love and peace, urging believers to live by the Spirit and avoid pride and jealousy.

Paul urges the Galatians to reject those causing division and to live by the Spirit’s guidance, contrasting the sinful acts of the flesh with the freedom and love that fulfill God's law, emphasizing unity and moral conduct.

Paul encourages the Galatian believers to gently restore those who sin, support one another, and live by the Spirit, warning that actions have consequences and urging perseverance in doing good, especially within the Christian community.

Paul writes personally to the Galatians, warning against those insisting on circumcision for acceptance, emphasizing faith in Christ and new life over the law, and closing with a blessing and a reminder of his sufferings for Jesus.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, greeting them with grace and peace from God and Jesus. He praises God for choosing and blessing them before the world began, adopting them as His children through Jesus according to His will.

Paul praises God for the Holy Spirit given to believers as a guarantee of their inheritance, thanks the Ephesian Christians for their faith and love, and prays for their spiritual wisdom to understand Christ's supreme power and authority over all, including the church.

Paul explains to the Ephesian believers how God has made them alive in Christ despite their past sinful lives, emphasizing salvation by grace through faith, not by works, and that they are created for good deeds prepared by God.

Paul explains to Gentile believers in Ephesus that they are God's creation, made for good works, and that through Christ's sacrifice, the division between Jews and Gentiles is removed, uniting both groups into one body with access to God through the Spirit.

Paul explains to Gentile believers in Ephesus that through Jesus and the Holy Spirit, both Jews and Gentiles have equal access to God, becoming part of God's household and spiritual temple built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets.

Paul explains to the believers in Ephesus that through Jesus, they receive redemption, forgiveness, and an inheritance, all part of God's wise plan to unite all things in Christ, and they are sealed with the Holy Spirit as a guarantee of this promise.

Paul explains his divine calling to preach the gospel to Gentiles, revealing God's hidden plan through Christ. He encourages believers in Ephesus not to lose heart over his sufferings, which serve their spiritual benefit.

Paul urges the Ephesians to live honestly and lovingly, avoiding sin and harmful speech, encouraging forgiveness and kindness as they embody their new life in Christ and maintain unity in the church community.

Paul, writing from prison, explains to the Ephesian Gentiles that God revealed to him the mystery that Gentiles are now included as heirs in Christ, a truth previously unknown, and that he was appointed as a minister to preach this gospel by God's grace.

Paul urges the Ephesians to live united and grow in love as one body in Christ, rejecting their former sinful ways and adopting a renewed mindset of truth and holiness, reflecting their new life in God.

Paul, writing from prison, urges the Ephesians to live humbly and united in faith, emphasizing one God and Spirit. He explains Christ’s descent and ascent, highlighting the gifts given to believers for building the church.

Paul explains that Christ, who descended to earth and ascended above all heavens, gave church leaders various roles to equip believers for unity, maturity, and growth in faith, building up the church as one body in love.

Paul, writing from prison, encourages the Ephesian believers not to be discouraged by his suffering, prays for their spiritual strength and deep understanding of Christ’s love, and praises God’s power working through them in the church.

Paul instructs the Ephesian believers to imitate God by living in love and holiness, avoiding immoral behaviors and false teachings. He contrasts their past darkness with their new life as children of light, urging them to expose evil and live righteously.

Paul instructs Christian husbands and wives in Ephesus on mutual love and respect, comparing the husband's love for his wife to Christ's love for the church, emphasizing unity and the spiritual bond between Christ and believers.

Paul continues his letter to the Ephesians, urging them to live wisely in the light of Christ, avoid sinful behaviors, be filled with the Spirit, and practice mutual submission. He instructs wives to submit to their husbands as the church submits to Christ.

Paul instructs the Ephesians on family and social roles: children obey parents, fathers nurture without anger, servants obey masters sincerely, and masters treat servants fairly. He then urges believers to be strong in God and spiritually prepared against evil.

Paul expresses his hope to boldly honor Christ through life or death while torn between living and dying. He encourages the Philippians to live united in faith, unafraid of opposition, sharing in his struggles for the gospel’s sake.

Paul, writing from prison, explains his role as a bold ambassador for Christ and sends Tychicus to update the Ephesians on his situation and encourage them, concluding with blessings of peace, love, and grace.

Paul encourages the Philippians to live obediently and without complaint, shining as examples in a corrupt world. He expresses hope to send Timothy, a trusted companion who genuinely cares for their well-being, to comfort him about their condition.

Paul urges the Ephesians to spiritually prepare by putting on God's armor to stand firm against evil forces. He emphasizes prayer and asks for boldness to proclaim the gospel while imprisoned in Rome.

Paul writes from prison, explaining that his imprisonment has actually helped spread the gospel in Caesar's palace and beyond. Despite some preaching Christ with wrong motives, Paul rejoices because Christ is preached, and he hopes to glorify Christ boldly, whether in life or death.

Paul and Timothy greet the believers in Philippi, expressing gratitude and joy for their partnership in spreading the gospel. Paul prays for their love, wisdom, and righteousness to grow as they remain faithful until Christ's return.

Paul speaks to the Philippians about Timothy, his trusted co-worker in the gospel, and explains sending Epaphroditus, who was seriously ill but recovered, as their messenger to bring comfort and encourage them to welcome him warmly.

Paul encourages the Philippians to live in unity and humility, following the example of Jesus Christ, who humbled himself by becoming human and dying on the cross, and was then exalted by God above all names.

Paul speaks to the Philippian believers, explaining how he values knowing Christ above all else, including his former status, and encourages them to keep striving toward their spiritual goal with faith and perseverance.

Paul encourages the Philippians to maintain unity and maturity in faith, urging them to follow his example and beware of those opposing Christ. He reminds them their true citizenship is in heaven, awaiting Jesus' return and transformation.

Paul encourages the Philippians to rejoice and warns them against false teachers ("dogs" and "concision"). He contrasts their spiritual worship with confidence in human heritage, then shares his own Jewish credentials before declaring he values Christ above all.

Paul encourages the Philippians to follow his example and expresses gratitude for their renewed support during his hardships, emphasizing his contentment in all circumstances and acknowledging their unique generosity since his departure from Macedonia.

Paul concludes his letter to the Philippians, expressing gratitude for their support sent through Epaphroditus, assuring God's provision for their needs, and sending greetings from fellow believers, including those in Caesar's household.

Paul, writing to the Colossian believers, shares how Epaphras reported their love in the Spirit. Paul prays for their growth in wisdom and strength through Christ, who created all things and brings redemption and forgiveness.

Paul encourages the believers in Philippi to remain steadfast in faith, urging unity between Euodias and Syntyche, and calls for joy, prayer, and focusing on virtuous things, promising God's peace to those who follow his example.
Paul and Timothy greet the believers in Colosse, thanking God for their faith, love, and hope in Jesus. They mention Epaphras, who taught the Colossians and reported their spiritual growth and love.

Paul explains Christ's supreme role in creation and the church, emphasizing reconciliation through Jesus' death. He encourages the Colossians to remain steadfast in faith, highlighting his ministry and sufferings for the church's sake.

Paul expresses deep concern for the believers in Colossae and Laodicea, encouraging them to remain united in love and faith in Christ, warning against deceptive human philosophies, and affirming that all divine fullness dwells in Christ.

Paul explains his role as God's appointed minister to the Colossian believers, revealing the long-hidden mystery of Christ living in Gentiles, and describes his dedicated efforts to teach and guide them toward spiritual maturity.

Paul warns the Colossian believers against false teachings like angel worship and legalistic rules, urging them to remain rooted in Christ, who is the true source of spiritual growth and freedom from worldly regulations.

Paul explains to the Colossians that Christ embodies God's fullness and believers are made complete in Him, symbolized by spiritual circumcision and baptism, which unites them with Christ's death and resurrection, freeing them from old religious laws and powers.

Paul urges the Colossian believers to focus on spiritual, heavenly things since they have risen with Christ, calling them to reject sinful behaviors and embrace a renewed life in Christ that transcends cultural and social divisions.
Paul instructs Christian families and servants in Colossae to act with sincere respect and diligence, emphasizing that their ultimate accountability is to the Lord Christ, who judges all impartially.

Paul instructs the Colossian believers to live united in Christ beyond cultural or social divisions, embracing virtues like mercy and forgiveness, and fulfilling family roles with love and respect, continuing his guidance on Christian conduct.

Paul instructs masters to treat their servants fairly and urges the Colossians to pray with gratitude, asking for boldness to share Christ's message. He sends Tychicus and Onesimus to update and encourage the church in Colossae.

Paul explains that he stayed in Athens and sent Timothy to Thessalonica to encourage the believers amid suffering, confirming their faith and love, which brought Paul and his companions comfort despite their hardships.

Paul reminds the Thessalonian believers of his bold and sincere preaching of the gospel despite suffering in Philippi, emphasizing his genuine care and hard work to avoid being a burden while sharing both the message and himself with them.

Paul reminds the Thessalonian believers of his hard work preaching the gospel without burdening them, his godly conduct, and their faithful reception of God's word. He also notes their suffering like the Judean churches and opposition from some Jews who reject salvation for Gentiles.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timotheus greet the Thessalonian church, praising their faith and transformation from idol worship to serving God. They highlight the Thessalonians' example spreading through Macedonia and Achaia after receiving the gospel with joy amid suffering.

Paul explains that some Jews opposed their mission to the Gentiles, causing suffering, but despite physical separation from the Thessalonian believers, Paul deeply desires to visit them again, finding joy and hope in their faith.

Paul sends greetings from his fellow workers and fellow prisoners, including Onesimus, Aristarchus, and Epaphras, who pray for the Colossians and nearby churches. He instructs them to share this letter with Laodicea and encourages Archippus in his ministry.

Paul urges the Thessalonian believers to continue living as they were taught, emphasizing holiness, avoiding sexual immorality, and loving one another, reminding them that God calls them to purity and has given them the Holy Spirit.

Paul encourages the Thessalonian believers in Macedonia to grow in love, live quietly and responsibly, and reassures them about the fate of deceased Christians, describing Christ’s return and the resurrection, urging them to find comfort in this hope.

Paul encourages the Thessalonian believers, praying that God strengthens their faith and glorifies Jesus in them, contrasting the eternal punishment of those who reject the gospel with the honor given to faithful followers at Christ's return.

Paul urges the Thessalonian believers to pray for him and his companions' safety and the spread of God's word, instructs them to avoid disorderly believers who refuse to work, and reminds them of his own hardworking example.

Paul expresses deep joy and gratitude for the Thessalonians' faith, prays earnestly to see them, and asks God to strengthen their love and holiness as they await Jesus' return. This follows Timothy’s encouraging report from Thessalonica.

Paul urges the Thessalonian believers not to be alarmed by false claims about Christ's return, reminding them of his previous teachings about a future rebellion and the revealing of a lawless figure opposing God, whose appearance is delayed by a restraining force.

Paul continues his letter to the Thessalonian believers, urging them to stay alert and live as children of light, prepared for the unexpected coming of the Lord, encouraging mutual comfort and spiritual growth.

Paul encourages the Thessalonian believers to support and respect their leaders, promote peace, and care for one another. He urges constant joy, prayer, gratitude, and discernment, concluding with blessings and instructions to share this letter with all the believers.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy write to the Thessalonian church, praising their growing faith and love amid persecution, assuring them that God will judge their oppressors and grant rest when Jesus returns with His angels.

Paul writes to Timothy, urging him to stay in Ephesus to correct false teachers promoting myths and pointless debates, emphasizing that true teaching leads to love from a sincere heart and genuine faith.

Paul concludes his letter to the Thessalonian believers, urging them to work quietly and responsibly, avoid idleness, and discipline those who disobey, while encouraging peace, brotherly correction, and grace among the community.

Paul continues his letter to the Thessalonian believers, warning them about the coming revelation of the "Wicked" one, empowered by Satan, and urges them to stand firm in the faith and traditions taught, offering comfort through Jesus and God the Father.

Paul warns Timothy about false teachers who misunderstand the law, explains the law's purpose against sinners, and shares his own transformation from persecutor to believer, emphasizing Christ's mercy and mission to save sinners like himself.

Paul affirms that Jesus came to save sinners, using his own mercy as an example, then charges Timothy to remain faithful and confront false teachers like Hymenaeus and Alexander, continuing the pastoral guidance given earlier in Ephesus.

Paul instructs Timothy to encourage prayers for all people, including leaders, to promote peace and godliness. He emphasizes Christ as the sole mediator, advises modesty and quiet learning for women, and references Adam and Eve to support his teaching.

Paul instructs Timothy on the qualifications for church leaders in Ephesus, detailing the moral and spiritual standards required for bishops and deacons to ensure proper governance of the church and their households.

Paul instructs Timothy on proper respect within the church community, emphasizing honoring true widows who are devoted to prayer and good works, and urging family members to care for their own relatives first.

Paul instructs Timothy on the qualities and responsibilities of deacons, emphasizing family leadership and faithfulness. He expresses hope to visit soon but provides guidance for managing the church, highlighting the core truth of Christ’s incarnation and resurrection.

Paul instructs Timothy on church discipline and leadership, emphasizing fair treatment of elders, careful appointment of leaders, personal purity, and practical advice for health, highlighting that both sins and good deeds are eventually revealed.

Paul instructs Timothy on the behavior and support of widows in the Ephesian church, emphasizing the good works of older widows, advising younger widows to marry, and urging respect and proper compensation for elders who lead and teach.

Paul encourages Timothy in Ephesus to remain faithful and teach others, urging him to be a strong example despite his youth, to use his spiritual gifts, and to stay devoted to sound doctrine for the benefit of himself and his listeners.

Paul instructs Timothy to teach servants to respect their masters, especially believing ones, to uphold God's name. He warns against false teachers promoting greed as godliness and urges contentment with basic needs to avoid destructive desires for wealth.

Paul warns Timothy in Ephesus about false teachers who promote heresies like forbidding marriage and certain foods, urging him to remind believers to hold to true faith and godliness, which benefits both present and future life.

Paul writes to Timothy, encouraging him to rekindle his God-given gift and reminding him of his sincere faith passed down from his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois, urging him to be bold and strong in faith despite challenges.

Paul warns Timothy about the dangers of desiring wealth, urging him to pursue virtues like righteousness and faith. He charges Timothy to remain faithful and blameless until Christ's return, emphasizing God's eternal power and authority.

Paul concludes his letter to Timothy by emphasizing God's unique immortality and urging the wealthy to trust God, do good, and be generous. He charges Timothy to guard the faith against false teachings and ends with a blessing.

Paul encourages Timothy to be bold and faithful despite suffering, reminding him that God gives power, love, and self-control, not fear. Paul affirms his calling as a preacher and urges Timothy to hold firmly to the gospel teachings.

Paul urges Timothy to protect the gospel entrusted to him by the Holy Spirit, notes that many in Asia have abandoned Paul, but praises Onesiphorus for faithfully supporting him during his imprisonment in Rome and ministry in Ephesus.

Paul encourages Timothy to endure hardships for the sake of believers' salvation, warns against false teachers Hymenaeus and Philetus who distort the resurrection, and urges Timothy to faithfully teach the truth and avoid useless arguments.

Paul encourages Timothy to remain faithful and pure in his service to God, avoiding pointless disputes and youthful desires, while gently teaching and guiding those who oppose the truth, so they may repent and be freed from the devil's control.

Paul encourages Timothy to be strong in Christ's grace, to pass on his teachings to trustworthy people, and to endure hardships like a dedicated soldier, farmer, or athlete, reminding him of Paul's own sufferings and commitment to spreading the gospel.

Paul warns Timothy about difficult times ahead, describing people with selfish and corrupt behaviors who resist the truth. He recalls his own sufferings in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, emphasizing God's deliverance.

Paul recounts his persecutions in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, urging Timothy to remain steadfast in the teachings and scriptures he has known since childhood, emphasizing scripture’s divine inspiration and its role in guiding believers toward righteousness and good works.

Paul, nearing the end of his life, charges Timothy to faithfully preach God's word despite challenges, warns of people rejecting truth for false teachings, and updates him on companions like Demas who has left for Thessalonica.

Paul updates Timothy on his companions and requests help, mentioning Demas's desertion and others' locations like Thessalonica, Galatia, and Dalmatia. He warns about Alexander, recalls past hardships, and sends greetings from various believers.

Paul writes to Titus in Crete, instructing him to organize the church by appointing qualified elders who live blamelessly and uphold sound teaching, emphasizing leadership qualities and faithfulness to God's word.

Paul instructs Titus in Crete to firmly uphold true teaching and correct false teachers, especially those promoting harmful Jewish customs for profit, warning that many Cretans are corrupt and urging Titus to rebuke them to restore sound faith.

Paul instructs Titus in Crete to teach sound Christian behavior for different groups—older men and women, young women, young men, and servants—emphasizing good conduct and faith to uphold God's teachings and avoid criticism.

Paul instructs Titus in Crete to encourage servants to be faithful and obedient, highlighting God's grace that brings salvation and calls for holy living while awaiting Christ's return, urging Titus to teach these truths confidently.

Paul instructs Titus to avoid pointless disputes and to reject persistent heretics, while also giving personal travel plans and urging support for fellow workers like Zenas and Apollos, emphasizing the importance of good deeds in Crete.

Paul instructs Titus to remind believers in Crete to obey authorities, live peacefully, and do good works, emphasizing salvation by God's mercy through Jesus, and warns against pointless disputes about the law and genealogies.

Paul, writing from prison, appeals to Philemon to welcome Onesimus, a former servant now seen as a beloved brother in Christ, and offers to repay any debt Onesimus owes, emphasizing love and partnership in their faith community.

Paul, writing from prison, expresses hope that Philemon will joyfully obey his request regarding Onesimus and asks him to prepare a place for Paul to stay, while sending greetings from fellow workers and praying for God's grace upon Philemon.

Paul, writing from prison with Timothy, addresses Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in Philemon's house, praising Philemon's faith and love, and choosing to appeal to him lovingly rather than command him.

The author of Hebrews explains that God spoke through prophets in the past but now speaks through His Son, Jesus, who is superior to angels, created the world, purified sins, and reigns eternally with a righteous kingdom.

The author addresses believers as holy brethren, urging them to focus on Jesus, the faithful Apostle and High Priest, who is greater than Moses. He warns them not to harden their hearts like the Israelites who tested God in the wilderness.

The author explains that Jesus became human, descended from Abraham, to free people from the fear of death and serve as a compassionate high priest who understands human suffering and helps those facing temptation.

The author explains that although all things are meant to be under human authority, this is not yet fully realized. Jesus, made lower than angels to suffer death, is honored and brings salvation by sharing human nature to defeat death and free those enslaved by its fear.

The author urges believers to pay close attention to the message of salvation delivered by Jesus and confirmed by witnesses, emphasizing that humans are made just below angels and given authority over creation, though full dominion is not yet realized.

The author urges believers to be cautious and faithful to enter God's promised rest, contrasting those Israelites who disbelieved and failed to enter the land. He references God's rest on the seventh day and a future rest still available to God's people.

The author of Hebrews addresses the readers, criticizing their spiritual immaturity for needing basic teachings again instead of advancing in understanding, contrasting beginners with mature believers able to grasp deeper truths about Christ as high priest.

The author explains that human high priests serve to offer sacrifices and empathize with people's weaknesses, but Jesus was appointed by God as a perfect high priest forever, learning obedience through suffering and becoming the source of eternal salvation.

The author warns believers to avoid unbelief like the Israelites who disobeyed God in the wilderness and were barred from entering His rest, urging mutual encouragement to remain faithful and confident in Christ until the end.

The author urges believers to strive to enter God's rest, warning against unbelief like the Israelites'. He highlights God's penetrating word and presents Jesus as a compassionate high priest who understands human struggles and offers mercy and grace.

The author encourages the Hebrew believers, praising their faithful service and urging them to remain diligent in hope, using God's promise to Abraham as an example of patient endurance leading to fulfillment.

The author urges believers to move beyond basic teachings about Christ and faith, warning about the dangers of falling away after receiving God's gifts, using agricultural imagery to contrast fruitful and unfruitful lives, while expressing confidence in the readers' salvation.

The author explains that God confirmed His unchanging promise to believers with an oath, providing them strong hope like an anchor for the soul. Jesus is described as the eternal high priest who has entered the heavenly sanctuary on their behalf.

The author explains Melchisedec's unique priesthood by recounting his meeting with Abraham after a battle, highlighting Melchisedec's eternal nature and superiority over the Levitical priests who descend from Abraham's lineage.

The author explains that Levi, the ancestor of the Levitical priests, symbolically paid tithes through Abraham, highlighting the superiority of Melchisedec’s priesthood. Jesus, from Judah, is a priest like Melchisedec, replacing the old law’s priesthood.

The author explains that the old priestly law was weak and ineffective, so God established Jesus as a permanent high priest by oath, who continually intercedes for people and offers a perfect sacrifice once for all.

The author summarizes that Jesus is the high priest in heaven, serving in the true heavenly sanctuary, unlike earthly priests who follow the law and serve a temporary tabernacle patterned after God's design given to Moses. Jesus mediates a superior covenant.

The author explains that the first covenant with Israel and Judah was flawed, prompting God to promise a new covenant with internalized laws and universal knowledge of Him, replacing the old covenant that is fading away.

The author explains that Christ entered the heavenly sanctuary once by his own blood, securing eternal redemption, unlike the repeated animal sacrifices under the old covenant, which required blood for purification but could not perfect the conscience.

The author explains the Old Testament priests' duties in the earthly tabernacle, highlighting the high priest's annual entry into the Most Holy Place with blood for atonement, then contrasts this with Christ's superior, once-for-all heavenly priesthood and sacrifice.

The author explains the first covenant's religious system, describing the earthly tabernacle in two parts: the sanctuary with its furniture and the Holiest of all containing the ark, where priests regularly performed God's service.

The author explains how Moses consecrated the first covenant with animal blood, symbolizing purification, and contrasts this with Christ's single, perfect sacrifice in heaven, which secures eternal redemption and promises a future return for salvation.

The author contrasts the Son's eternal throne and divine authority with angels, emphasizing the Son's role in creation and unchanging nature, highlighting his superiority and purpose to aid believers, unlike angels who serve as ministering spirits.

The author explains that the old Jewish law and its repeated animal sacrifices were only a shadow of the true salvation to come. Jesus Christ came to fulfill God's will by offering himself once to truly cleanse sins.

The author continues listing Old Testament figures who lived by faith, highlighting Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac, Isaac and Jacob's blessings, Joseph's instructions about his bones, and Moses' hidden infancy to avoid Pharaoh's decree.

The author highlights Abraham's faith as he obeys God's call to leave his home for an unknown land, living as a foreigner with Isaac and Jacob. Sarah conceives beyond childbearing age, and all look forward to a heavenly city, acknowledging their earthly pilgrimage.

The author explains that Jesus' single sacrifice perfects believers forever, unlike repeated animal sacrifices by priests. The Holy Spirit confirms God's new covenant, promising to forgive sins and write His laws in believers' hearts.

The author explains faith as trust in unseen hopes, highlighting elders like Abel, Enoch, Noah, and Abraham who acted on God's word. These examples show faith's power to please God and guide obedience despite uncertainty.

The author continues listing faithful figures from Israel's history, including Rahab and others like David and Samuel, highlighting their trials and victories. These heroes lived by faith but did not receive the ultimate promise, which God reserved for later believers.

The author warns Jewish Christians that rejecting Christ after knowing the truth brings severe judgment, referencing Moses' law and God's vengeance. He encourages them to remember past sufferings and to keep faith for the promised reward.

The author highlights Moses' early life and faith-driven choices, including his parents hiding him, his rejection of Egyptian royalty, leading the Israelites through the Red Sea, and Rahab's protection of spies, illustrating faith's power in Israel's history.

The author encourages believers to persevere in faith, inspired by Jesus who endured suffering, and reminds them that God's discipline is a sign of His love and their status as His children, contrasting with those who receive no correction.

The author encourages believers to confidently approach God through Jesus' sacrifice, urging faithfulness, mutual support, and regular gathering, while warning that deliberate sin after knowing the truth brings judgment with no further sacrifice available.

The author encourages believers to accept God's discipline as loving correction, comparing it to earthly fathers' guidance, urging perseverance, holiness, and caution against bitterness and sin, using Esau's story as a warning.

The author encourages believers to remain confident and patient in doing God's will, reminding them that Christ will return soon. He contrasts those who shrink back with those who live by faith and trust in salvation.

The author warns against falling like Esau, who lost his birthright, then contrasts the terrifying Sinai experience with believers' access to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, where Jesus mediates the new covenant among angels and the redeemed.

The author contrasts the old covenant's animal sacrifices with Jesus' sacrifice outside Jerusalem, urging believers to embrace his reproach and seek the eternal city. He encourages continual praise, good deeds, respect for leaders, and prayers for his safe return.

The author urges believers to continue loving one another, show hospitality, honor marriage, avoid greed, and respect their leaders who teach God's word. He warns against strange teachings and contrasts the eternal altar of Christ with the old temple sacrifices.

The author urges the recipients to pray for his quick return, praises God who raised Jesus, encourages perseverance in good works through Christ, mentions Timothy's release, sends greetings from Italy, and closes with a blessing.

The author urges believers to honor Jesus, mediator of the new covenant, warning against rejecting his heavenly message. He contrasts the shaking of earth at Sinai with a future shaking of earth and heaven, urging faithful reverence to God.

James encourages believers scattered among the twelve tribes to live out their faith actively, emphasizing that true religion involves controlling one's speech, caring for vulnerable people, and living a pure life, not just hearing God's word.

James encourages believers to endure trials and warns that temptation comes from personal desires, not God. He urges them to listen carefully, control their speech and anger, and recognize that every good gift comes from God, who is unchanging.

James continues addressing early Christian believers, emphasizing that genuine faith is demonstrated through actions, using Abraham and Rahab as examples to show that faith alone is insufficient without corresponding works.

James, a servant of God, writes to Jewish believers scattered abroad, encouraging them to find joy in trials as these develop patience and wisdom through faith, warning against doubt, instability, and the fleeting nature of wealth and status.

James addresses believers, emphasizing that breaking any part of God's law makes one guilty of all, urging them to act mercifully and warning that faith without accompanying good deeds is ineffective and lifeless.

James warns believers about the power and danger of the tongue, comparing it to small but controlling things like bits for horses and ship helms. He highlights how speech can bless God yet also curse people made in God's image.

James warns believers in the early Christian community about the power of the tongue to bless or curse, urging them to live wisely with humility and peace, contrasting earthly envy with godly wisdom that produces righteousness and harmony.

James warns wealthy oppressors about coming judgment for exploiting workers and living selfishly, urging believers to be patient and steadfast as the Lord's return approaches, connecting themes of humility and endurance from the previous chapter.
James addresses early Christian believers, explaining that their conflicts arise from selfish desires and urging them to seek humility, resist evil, and draw closer to God for grace and peace.

Peter writes to Christian believers scattered across regions of Asia Minor, reminding them they are chosen by God and kept safe through faith, with a living hope and an eternal inheritance secured by Jesus Christ's resurrection.

Peter explains that Old Testament prophets served future believers by revealing God's plan, now preached by the Spirit; he urges his readers scattered in Asia Minor to live holy, obedient lives in anticipation of Jesus Christ's return.

James urges believers to humble themselves before God, avoid judging others, and recognize God's authority as the sole lawgiver. He warns against boasting about future plans without acknowledging God's will, emphasizing the fleeting nature of life and the sin of neglecting to do good.

James encourages believers to confess sins and pray for each other for healing, citing Elijah's powerful prayers as an example. He urges the community to help restore those who stray from the faith, emphasizing the value of saving souls.

James addresses early Christian believers, warning them against showing favoritism between rich and poor in their gatherings, emphasizing that partiality violates God's law to love others equally and that breaking one part of the law makes one guilty of all.

Peter urges believers scattered in Asia Minor to live holy lives like God, reminding them they were redeemed not by silver or gold but by Christ’s sacrificial blood, and encourages sincere love and faith grounded in God’s eternal word.

Peter urges believers to reject harmful behaviors and crave God's word like newborns. He describes Jesus as the chosen "living stone," rejected by people but precious to God, forming a spiritual house with believers as living stones.

James encourages believers to avoid grudges, be patient like the prophets and Job, speak truthfully without oaths, and support each other through prayer, especially in sickness, emphasizing the power of faithful prayer and mutual confession in the early Christian community.

Peter encourages believers scattered across Asia Minor, assuring them that God protects their faith through trials, which refine and prove their devotion. He explains that Old Testament prophets foresaw Christ’s suffering and glory, now revealed through the gospel preached by the Spirit.

The apostle Peter urges believers, called from darkness into God's people, to live holy lives, avoid sinful desires, act honorably among Gentiles, and submit to authorities, demonstrating their freedom as servants of God in the Roman Empire.

Peter urges believers to live responsibly as God's servants, honoring all people and submitting to authorities, even in suffering, following Christ's example of patient endurance and sacrifice, who redeemed them as their spiritual Shepherd.

Peter instructs Christian wives to respect their husbands, even if husbands are unbelievers, so their behavior may win them over. He urges modesty and inner beauty, citing Sarah's example, and advises husbands to honor their wives to maintain harmony and effective prayer.

Peter refers to the spirits disobedient in Noah's time, saved through the ark's water, likening this to baptism's spiritual salvation through Jesus' resurrection, who now reigns in heaven with authority over all powers.

Peter instructs Christian husbands to treat their wives with respect and honor, urging all believers to live in unity, kindness, and peace, trusting that God watches over the righteous and protects those who do good.

Peter, addressing church elders in Asia Minor, urges them to lead willingly and humbly, setting an example for the younger members, while encouraging all to remain vigilant against spiritual dangers and to support one another in faith.

Peter encourages believers to remain steadfast and hopeful when facing suffering for doing good, urging them to honor God and be ready to explain their faith. He reminds them of Christ’s suffering and His proclamation to disobedient spirits from Noah’s time.

Peter encourages believers in Asia Minor to use their God-given gifts to serve others, glorify God through Jesus, and endure suffering for Christ without shame, reminding them that judgment begins with God's people and urging trust in God amid trials.

The apostle Peter urges believers to confirm their faith and live diligently to secure their salvation, reminding them of his impending death and affirming his eyewitness testimony of Jesus' divine glory and the Father's voice at the Transfiguration.

The apostle Peter urges Christians to adopt Christ’s mindset of suffering, turning from sinful Gentile behaviors to live by God’s will, emphasizing love, prayer, hospitality, and using spiritual gifts responsibly as the end times approach.

The apostle Peter encourages believers to firmly resist the devil, reminding them that fellow Christians worldwide face similar trials. He concludes his letter, sending greetings from Silvanus, the church in Babylon, and Marcus, urging love and peace among the community.

Peter recalls witnessing God's voice affirming Jesus as His Son on the holy mount, emphasizing the reliability of prophecy inspired by the Holy Spirit, urging believers to value it as a guiding light amid spiritual darkness.

The apostle Peter writes to fellow believers, encouraging them to grow in faith and moral qualities through God's power, promising they will share in God's nature and avoid spiritual corruption if they cultivate these virtues.

Peter warns early Christians about false teachers spreading harmful lies and greed, causing many to stray and discredit the truth. He recalls God's past judgments on sinful angels, the flood in Noah's time, and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, highlighting God's justice.

Peter warns about false teachers who harm others with their sinful actions and arrogance, contrasting them with Lot, a righteous man troubled by wickedness in Sodom. He describes their corrupt behavior and the certainty of God's judgment.

Peter writes a second letter reminding believers to recall the teachings of prophets and apostles about scoffers denying Christ's return. He explains God's timing differs from human time and warns of judgment by fire reserved for the ungodly.

Peter warns against false teachers who deceive unstable people with greed and sin, comparing them to Balaam's corrupt ways. He explains that though they promise freedom, they lead others back into bondage and worse ruin after knowing Christ.

The author of 2 Peter urges believers to understand God's timing differs from human time and emphasizes His patience for repentance. He warns of the coming judgment day when earth and heavens will be destroyed, encouraging holy living while awaiting a new, righteous creation.

The author, likely the Apostle John, testifies to the reality of Jesus Christ, the Word of life, urging believers to live in truth and fellowship with God and each other, emphasizing confession and forgiveness of sins to maintain fellowship.

The author, John, addresses believers as "little children," urging them to avoid sin and assuring them that Jesus Christ advocates for sinners before God. He emphasizes knowing Christ by obeying His commandments and loving others as evidence of living in the light.

Peter encourages believers to live holy lives while awaiting God's promised new creation, warns against misinterpreting scripture like some do, and urges growth in grace and knowledge of Jesus, referencing teachings from Paul to support his message.

The author encourages believers to love one another as a sign of living in the light, contrasts this with hatred as darkness, and addresses different groups—children, fathers, young men—urging them to reject worldly desires and remain faithful to God's will for eternal life.

John concludes his letter by assuring believers of the promise of eternal life, warning against deceivers, and encouraging them to remain faithful to Christ, guided by the Holy Spirit's teaching, so they may stand confidently at Jesus' return.

The author warns that those who have come to know Jesus and escape worldly sins but then return to them face worse consequences than before, emphasizing the seriousness of turning away from the teachings of righteousness.

The author addresses believers as God's children, explaining that God's love makes them His sons, unlike the world that rejects them. He contrasts righteousness and sin, emphasizing Jesus' role in defeating sin and the devil.

The author urges believers to live righteously and love one another, contrasting God's children with those of the devil, using Cain's story as a warning, and emphasizing that true love is shown through actions, not just words.
John urges believers to show love through actions, not just words, assuring them that keeping God's commandments and trusting in Jesus brings confidence and the presence of God's Spirit within them.

The author warns believers in the early Christian community to test spiritual teachings, distinguishing true faith in Jesus' incarnation from false prophets. He emphasizes God's love shown by sending Jesus, urging mutual love among believers.

John warns believers in Asia Minor that the world and its desires will fade, but those who follow God's will live forever. He speaks of many antichrists who left the community, urging believers to hold to the original teaching about Jesus to receive eternal life.

The author explains God's love shown by sending Jesus as a sacrifice for sins, urging believers to love one another. They affirm that God's Spirit dwells in those who confess Jesus, linking love with knowing and living in God.

The author of 1 John explains that believing Jesus is the Christ shows one is born of God, emphasizing love for God and others, faith overcoming the world, and the testimony of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit confirming Jesus' identity.

The author concludes by distinguishing sins that lead to death, affirming believers' protection from evil, and emphasizing Jesus as the true God who grants eternal life, urging the community to avoid idols and remain faithful.

The author emphasizes God's greater testimony about Jesus compared to human testimony, assuring believers of eternal life through faith in Jesus. He encourages prayer with confidence and discusses sin, distinguishing between sins that lead to death and those that do not.

The elder (likely John) writes to a chosen woman and her children, praising their faithfulness to God's commandments and warning against deceivers denying Jesus' incarnation, urging them to remain true to Christ's teachings to receive full reward.

The elder John writes to Gaius, praising his faithfulness and hospitality to traveling Christian brothers, while criticizing Diotrephes for rejecting John's authority and opposing those who welcome these missionaries in the local church.

The elder warns the elect lady and her children to reject anyone who denies Christ’s teachings, emphasizing the importance of true doctrine. He expresses hope to visit them soon and sends greetings from a mutual sister’s children.

Jude warns believers about rebellious angels punished for abandoning their place, compares them to sinful cities like Sodom, and condemns false teachers who disrespect authority and corrupt themselves, citing examples from Cain, Balaam, and Korah.

The elder John warns Gaius about Diotrephes, who opposes them and excludes believers from the church, urging Gaius to do good. He praises Demetrius and expresses hope to visit Gaius soon for a personal meeting.

John, exiled on Patmos, receives a vision of Jesus Christ, who declares his eternal nature and commands John to write to seven churches in Asia. John then sees a symbolic vision of Jesus among seven golden lampstands representing these churches.

Jude warns believers about ungodly men who follow sinful paths like Cain, Balaam, and Korah, causing harm in their community. He recalls Enoch’s prophecy of the Lord’s judgment on such people for their rebellious deeds and arrogant words.

John introduces the vision given by Jesus through an angel, addressing seven churches in Asia. He blesses those who hear and obey the prophecy, emphasizing Jesus' authority, sacrifice, and imminent return visible to all.

Jude warns believers about ungodly people who complain and follow selfish desires, reminding them of apostles' teachings about mockers in the last days. He urges faithful prayer, love, compassion, and trust in God's power to keep them safe.

Jesus, speaking to the churches in Smyrna and Pergamos, acknowledges their struggles and faithfulness amid persecution, promising rewards for those who overcome, and referencing Antipas, a martyr in Pergamos where evil is strong.

Jesus, holding the seven stars and walking among seven golden candlesticks, addresses the angel of the church in Ephesus, praising their hard work and patience but rebuking them for losing their initial love, urging repentance to avoid losing their place.

Jesus addresses the church in Pergamos, praising their faith despite living where "Satan's seat" is, but warns against false teachings like those of Balaam and the Nicolaitanes, urging repentance and promising rewards to those who overcome.
Jesus addresses the church in Thyatira, warning of judgment on those following false teachings but encouraging faithful believers to hold fast and promising them authority and reward when He returns.

Jesus, speaking to the church in Thyatira, praises their faith and works but condemns a false prophetess named Jezebel for leading believers into sin, warning of judgment unless they repent, emphasizing His authority to judge hearts and reward deeds.

Jesus addresses the church in Philadelphia, praising their faithfulness despite limited strength, promising protection from trials, victory over adversaries, and eternal honor in God's temple and the new Jerusalem.

Jesus addresses the church in Laodicea, warning them for being spiritually lukewarm and self-satisfied. He urges repentance and promises blessings to those who overcome, contrasting their current state with the riches and purity they need.

Jesus addresses the church in Sardis, warning them that though they seem alive, their deeds are incomplete before God. He urges them to be vigilant, repent, and hold fast, promising reward to those who remain faithful.

Jude, brother of James, urges believers to defend their faith against ungodly men who deny Jesus. He reminds them of God's judgment on unbelievers from Israel’s past and fallen angels kept for final judgment.
Jesus addresses the church in Laodicea, urging repentance and zeal, promising fellowship and shared authority to those who overcome, continuing his messages to the seven churches in Asia Minor.

John, on Patmos, sees a vision of Jesus among seven golden lampstands representing seven churches in Asia; Jesus reveals his divine authority, eternal life, and instructs John to record what he has seen and will see.

After the Lamb takes the sealed book from God’s right hand, the four living creatures and twenty-four elders worship Him with harps and prayers, joined by countless angels and all creation praising the Lamb’s worthiness and eternal reign.

John witnesses the Lamb opening the first four seals on a scroll, each unleashing a horseman symbolizing conquest, war, famine, and death, as the four living creatures invite him to observe these unfolding judgments.

John is taken in a vision to heaven where he sees a majestic throne surrounded by 24 elders, seven fiery lamps symbolizing God's Spirit, and four living creatures with distinct animal faces, all signifying divine authority and presence.
John describes cosmic disturbances and widespread fear among all people on earth as the Lamb opens the sixth seal, signaling the arrival of God's judgment and the Lamb's wrath.

John witnesses the Lamb opening the fourth, fifth, and sixth seals, revealing a pale horse symbolizing Death, the souls of martyrs under the altar, and cosmic disturbances signaling coming judgment on earth.

John sees four angels holding back the winds to prevent harm, while another angel seals 144,000 servants of God from the twelve tribes of Israel, protecting them before the earth is allowed to be harmed.

John describes four living creatures around God's heavenly throne, each with distinct faces and many eyes, continuously praising God. The 24 elders join in worship, honoring God's eternal power as Creator.

John sees a great multitude in white robes before God's throne; an elder explains they are those who endured great suffering and are now protected and comforted by God and the Lamb, living in His presence without pain or hunger.

John continues his vision in heaven, seeing 12,000 sealed from each Israelite tribe, then a vast, uncountable crowd from all nations worshipping God and the Lamb, prompting an elder to ask about the identity and origin of those clothed in white robes.

John describes the first four trumpet judgments as seven angels sound their trumpets, bringing disasters on earth, sea, rivers, and sky, causing destruction and warning of more woes to come for the inhabitants of the earth.

John describes the opening of the seventh seal, leading to silence in heaven and the appearance of seven angels with trumpets. Another angel offers incense with prayers, then casts fire to earth, triggering natural disasters as the first trumpet sounds.

John sees a sealed book in God's right hand; a mighty angel asks who can open it, but no one is found worthy. John weeps until an elder reveals the Lion of Judah, the Lamb, who takes the book, prompting worship from the creatures and elders.

John sees a vision of 200 million horsemen with fiery armor and lion-like heads, who kill a third of mankind with fire, smoke, and brimstone. Despite these plagues, the survivors refuse to repent from idol worship and sins.

John sees the fifth angel sound a trumpet, releasing a star fallen from heaven who opens the bottomless pit, sending out locust-like creatures that torment unsealed people on earth for five months with scorpion-like stings.

John describes terrifying locust-like creatures with human and animal features, led by the angel Abaddon, emerging from the bottomless pit. Then, the sixth angel releases four bound angels by the Euphrates River to kill a third of mankind with a vast army of horsemen.

John sees a powerful angel descending from heaven, symbolizing authority over earth and sea, holding an open little book. The angel proclaims God's eternal power and announces that time will end when the seventh angel sounds, fulfilling God's mystery.

John describes a vision in heaven of a woman giving birth and a red dragon trying to devour her child. The child is taken to God, the woman flees to the wilderness, and a war breaks out where Michael and angels defeat the dragon.

John describes a great earthquake in a city, causing deaths and fear, followed by the seventh angel's trumpet announcing God's eternal reign. The elders worship God as judgment begins, the temple in heaven opens, revealing the ark amid dramatic signs.

John is given a measuring rod by an angel to measure God's temple and worshippers, excluding the outer court given to Gentiles. Two empowered witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days, performing miracles, but are eventually killed by a beast from the abyss.

John sees a mighty angel declaring that God's mystery will be completed when the seventh angel sounds. John is told to take and eat a little open book, sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach, symbolizing his role to prophesy again widely.

John describes the beast from the abyss killing the two witnesses in the city where Jesus was crucified; after three and a half days, God resurrects them, they ascend to heaven, and a great earthquake strikes, causing fear and worship among the survivors.

The woman, representing God's people, is given eagle's wings to escape into the wilderness for protection from the serpent (Satan), who then attacks her with a flood, but the earth helps her. The dragon then wages war against her faithful followers.

The archangel Michael and his angels fight the dragon (Satan) and his angels in heaven, who are defeated and cast down to earth. A heavenly voice announces God's kingdom and warns of the devil's wrath on earth, while the woman who bore the child is protected in the wilderness.

John sees a beast with seven heads and ten horns rising from the sea, empowered by the dragon (Satan). The beast has a deadly wound healed, gaining worldwide worship and authority to blaspheme God and wage war against the saints for 42 months.
John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with 144,000 followers marked by God's name. They sing a unique song before God's throne, described as pure and faithful servants redeemed from the earth.

John describes a second beast from the earth performing miracles to deceive people into worshiping an image of the first beast, enforcing a mark for economic participation, and revealing the symbolic number 666 linked to the beast's identity.

John describes a beast empowered to wage war against God's followers worldwide, causing many to worship it. Then another beast appears, performing miracles to deceive people into worshiping the first beast and making its image.

John describes the 144,000 faithful followers of the Lamb as blameless before God. Then, angels proclaim God's judgment, call for worship of the Creator, and announce the fall of Babylon, symbolizing a corrupt world power influencing all nations.

In a vision, angels announce the fall of Babylon and warn of God's wrath on those who worship the beast and receive its mark. A heavenly voice blesses faithful believers who die in the Lord, promising them rest and reward.

John hears a heavenly voice blessing those who die in faith, then sees a figure like the Son of Man with a sickle harvesting the earth, symbolizing God's judgment, followed by angels gathering the earth's harvest and pouring out God's wrath outside the city.

John hears a voice from the heavenly temple commanding seven angels to pour God's wrath on earth. The angels unleash plagues on those marked by the beast, the sea, rivers, and sun, causing suffering and death, yet people do not repent.

John is spoken to by an angel who explains the symbolism of the woman and the beast with seven heads and ten horns, representing seven mountains, seven kings, and ten future kings united in power but destined for destruction.

John sees a vision in heaven of seven angels with the final plagues, symbolizing God's complete wrath. Victorious believers stand on a fiery sea, singing praise, as the heavenly temple opens and the angels receive God's wrath to pour out.

John describes the sixth and seventh angels pouring out God's wrath, causing darkness, pain, and drying the Euphrates to prepare for battle. Unclean spirits gather earthly kings for the final battle at Armageddon.

John describes the final angel gathering the kings for battle at Armageddon, followed by the seventh angel pouring out God's wrath, causing a massive earthquake, the fall of cities including Babylon, and a devastating hailstorm.

John sees a powerful angel announcing the fall of Babylon, symbolizing a corrupt city influencing nations and kings. A voice warns God's people to leave Babylon to avoid sharing in its sins and coming judgment.

The angel explains to John that ten kings will unite to empower the beast and wage war against Jesus (the Lamb), who will ultimately triumph. The "waters" represent many peoples, and the ten kings will turn against the great city (Babylon), destroying it as part of God's plan.

The angel announces Babylon's proud self-exaltation and impending sudden destruction by God's judgment. Earthly kings who allied with her mourn from a distance as they witness her burning and downfall.

A mighty angel throws a huge stone into the sea, symbolizing the violent destruction of Babylon, ending its music, crafts, light, and celebrations, because its merchants deceived nations and it caused the death of prophets and saints.

John sees merchants mourning Babylon’s sudden destruction, lamenting the loss of their luxury goods and wealth as the great city falls under judgment, highlighting its former splendor and the swift ruin that has come upon it.

John hears a vast heavenly crowd praising God for judging the corrupt "great whore" (Babylon) and avenging His servants. Elders and creatures worship God, celebrating the Lamb's marriage and the readiness of His bride, symbolizing the righteous saints.

John is visited by one of the seven angels with the seven vials, who invites him to witness the judgment of a symbolic woman called "Babylon the Great," representing a corrupt power influencing earthly kings and peoples, seated on a blasphemous beast.

John sees an angel from heaven who binds Satan, called the dragon, in the bottomless pit for 1,000 years to stop his deception. Thrones appear where martyrs who stayed faithful to Jesus reign with Christ during this first resurrection period.

John describes the blessed state of those in the first resurrection who will reign with Christ for a thousand years, followed by Satan's release and final defeat. Then, John sees the great white throne judgment where all the dead are judged by their deeds.

John describes the bride of the Lamb dressed in righteous linen, announces the blessedness of those invited to the marriage supper, and sees Jesus, called Faithful and True, leading heavenly armies on a white horse to judge and wage war.

John records a voice promising blessings to those who overcome and punishment to sinners, then an angel shows him the holy Jerusalem, a radiant city from heaven with twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for Jesus' apostles.

John describes a final judgment scene where all the dead stand before God, books recording their deeds are opened, and those not found in the book of life are cast into the lake of fire, symbolizing eternal punishment.

John sees a vision of a new heaven and earth replacing the old, with the holy city, New Jerusalem, descending from God. A voice declares God's presence with humanity, promising no more suffering, and God affirms making all things new and granting eternal life to the victorious.

Merchants, sailors, and shipmasters mourn the sudden destruction of Babylon, the wealthy city adorned with luxury. A mighty angel casts a huge stone into the sea, symbolizing Babylon's violent downfall and permanent end, fulfilling God's judgment.

John sees the rider on the white horse, called King of Kings, wielding a sharp sword from his mouth to strike nations. An angel summons birds to feast on the defeated kings and armies gathered against him, including the beast and false prophet, who are thrown into a fiery lake.

John is shown by an angel the detailed measurements and precious materials of the new Jerusalem, symbolizing the holy city’s perfection and divine foundation, following the vision of God's new creation after final judgment.

John describes the holy city, New Jerusalem, with twelve pearl gates and golden streets, illuminated by God's glory. The city has no temple because God and the Lamb are its temple, and only those written in the Lamb’s book of life may enter.

John is shown a vision of the New Jerusalem with a life-giving river and the tree of life, symbolizing healing and God's presence. An angel affirms the truth of these revelations and announces Jesus' imminent return. John responds by worshiping the angel.

John, the author, tries to worship the angel revealing the visions, but the angel redirects worship to God and instructs John not to seal the prophecy, emphasizing the imminent fulfillment and contrasting the fate of the righteous and the wicked.

Jesus speaks to John, affirming His identity and authority, warning against altering the prophecy, and inviting all to receive the water of life freely. The Spirit and the church join in calling for Jesus' return, concluding the vision with a blessing.
